body:
Split out of #409 (`[cloudflare][mcp][P2] Deploy & host a base MCP server on Cloudflare Workers from FerroGate`), whose scope was deliberately narrowed to **deployer + credential source + Worker template (OAuth variant)**. This is one of the three items that did not land there.

## What is missing

#409's `## Codebase seam` asks for an "Admin surface to create/update/delete a hosted MCP server (name, tools, auth mode) and report its URL/status". There is none — the only way to reach `McpWorkerDeployer` today is Rust code, and there is no such caller.

`McpWorkerSpec` is also not parameterized over two of the three fields the admin surface is supposed to expose:

| field | state |
|---|---|
| **name** | parameterized (`script_name`) |
| **tools** | NOT parameterized — the tool set is hardcoded in `workers/mcp-server/src/index.ts` (`echo` / `add` / `whoami`) |
| **auth mode** | NOT parameterized — OAuth-plus-automation-bearer is the only shape (see the authless-variant follow-up) |

So this is not only a missing REST surface; it is a missing parameterization underneath it.

## Scope

- Admin REST endpoints to create / update / delete / list a tenant's hosted MCP servers, reporting URL and deploy status (`McpWorkerDeployer::status_for` already returns exactly this pair, and returns no URL for a script Cloudflare is not hosting).
- Persist the hosted-server record in the control plane so status survives a restart and teardown knows what it owns.
- Parameterize the tool set. This is the real work: the repo currently bundles nothing (`crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/mcp_worker_deploy.rs` uploads a module source string it is handed, and nothing in-tree bundles `src/index.ts`), so "choose your tools" needs a decision about where the module bytes come from before it needs an endpoint.
- Tenant scoping and entitlement checks on every verb, consistent with the other Admin API surfaces.

## Depends on

- #638 (authless template variant), for `auth mode` to have more than one value to select.
- #639 (register back as upstream) gives `McpWorkerDeployer` its first production caller; this surface is the second.

## References

- `crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/mcp_worker_deploy.rs` — the deployer, and the `## Not in #409 — split out` section that points here.
- Split from #409.
title: [cloudflare][mcp][P3] Admin surface for hosted MCP servers: create/update/delete + parameterized tools and auth mode (split from #409)

body:
Split out of #409 (`[cloudflare][mcp][P2] Deploy & host a base MCP server on Cloudflare Workers from FerroGate`), whose scope was deliberately narrowed to **deployer + credential source + Worker template (OAuth variant)**. This is one of the three items that did not land there.

## What is missing

#409's `## Codebase seam` asks that a deployed MCP Worker be "register[ed] back as an upstream via the [mcp] upstream sub-issue". Nothing does this.

The consequence is concrete and is the reason this is the highest-value of the three splits: **`McpWorkerDeployer` has no caller outside its own tests.** Everything it builds — the multipart script `PUT`, the Secrets Store binding, `status_for`, `teardown` — is exercised only by unit tests against a scripted transport. The deploy path is modeled but dead.

The pieces it needs already exist:

- `McpWorkerSpec::mcp_endpoint_url()` returns `https://<script>.<subdomain>.workers.dev/mcp` — documented as "exactly the shape the #408 upstream detector accepts".
- `McpWorkerDeployer::status_for` fills that URL in **only** when the script is actually deployed, precisely so the value is safe to register as an upstream.

So the missing piece is the wiring, not the model.

## Scope

- A production path that deploys the Worker and then registers the resulting `mcp_endpoint_url` as an `McpServerConfig` upstream for the tenant.
- The automation bearer the Worker resolves (`MCP_BEARER_TOKEN_STORE` / `MCP_BEARER_TOKEN`) must be what the registered upstream authenticates with, sourced through the `cf://<store>/<name>` seam rather than copied.
- Teardown must deregister, not orphan: a torn-down Worker that stays registered is an upstream that 404s on every dispatch.
- Failure semantics stated and tested: a deploy that succeeds and a registration that fails must not leave a running Worker that nothing points at, nor a registration pointing at nothing.

## Acceptance

- `McpWorkerDeployer` has at least one non-test caller.
- A deployed server answers `tools/list` / `tools/call` **through the FerroGate MCP gateway path**, not just directly — which is the half of #409's "passes the same list/execute E2E as an external upstream" that the local workerd suite structurally cannot reach.

## References

- `crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/mcp_worker_deploy.rs` — `mcp_endpoint_url`, `status_for`, and the `## Not in #409 — split out` section that points here.
- Siblings split from #409: #638 (authless template variant), #640 (admin surface).
title: [cloudflare][mcp][P2] Register a deployed MCP Worker back as an upstream — give McpWorkerDeployer a production caller (split from #409)

body:
Split out of #409 (`[cloudflare][mcp][P2] Deploy & host a base MCP server on Cloudflare Workers from FerroGate`), whose scope was deliberately narrowed to **deployer + credential source + Worker template (OAuth variant)**. This is one of the three items that did not land there.

## What is missing

#409's `## Codebase seam` asks for "A template MCP Worker (**authless** + OAuth variants)". Only the OAuth variant exists.

`workers/mcp-server/src/index.ts` is built on the Agents SDK `McpAgent` Durable Object behind `@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider`, which requires an `OAUTH_KV` namespace to persist grants and an interactive `/authorize` round trip. Every deployment therefore pays for KV plus a DO per session, and every client must either complete OAuth or hold the automation bearer.

Cloudflare's stateless `createMcpHandler()` path needs neither. For a tool surface that is public, or that FerroGate itself fronts with its own auth, that is the cheaper and simpler shape.

## Scope

- An authless template variant alongside the current one, built on `createMcpHandler()` (stateless — no DO, no `OAUTH_KV` binding, no `new_sqlite_classes` migration).
- `McpWorkerSpec` grows an auth-mode parameter that selects which template's metadata is constructed: the authless variant must NOT declare the DO binding, the KV binding, or the migration, because a metadata part that declares bindings the module does not use is what a Workers Script `PUT` rejects.
- Worker-side coverage in the existing workerd harness (`workers/mcp-server/vitest.config.ts`) proving the authless variant serves `tools/list` / `tools/call` with no credential at all.
- Rust-side coverage that the authless spec's `metadata_json()` carries neither DO nor KV bindings.

## Not in scope

Deciding whether an authless MCP server should be exposed on a tenant's behalf at all. That is a product/policy call, and it belongs with the admin surface (see #640, the admin-surface follow-up).

## References

- https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/model-context-protocol/mcp-handler-api/
- `crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/mcp_worker_deploy.rs` — the deployer, and the `## Not in #409 — split out` section that points here.
- Siblings split from #409: #639 (register back as upstream), #640 (admin surface).

body:
## What happened

On a fresh `origin/main` checkout (`9ea3cc18`), the first `cargo check -p ferrogate-gateway` failed with:

```
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `&ferrogate_storage::StorageError::WalletHoldReleased { .. }` not covered
    --> crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/state_mcp_identity.rs:2118:11
```

I confirmed it reproduced on a clean tree (`git stash -u`, re-check, same error), which normally is conclusive evidence that main is red.

**It is not.** `WalletHoldReleased` does not exist anywhere in this repository:

```
$ grep -rn "WalletHoldReleased" . --include=*.rs --include=*.toml
(no output)
```

The variant belongs to another agent's in-flight branch. Re-running the identical command a minute later succeeded with no changes to the tree.

## Cause

`~/.cargo/config.toml` on this box pins every checkout to one shared artifact directory:

```toml
[build]
jobs = 20
target-dir = "/home/james/ferrogate/target"
```

Multiple agents build different checkouts into that single directory concurrently. The `Blocking waiting for file lock on build directory` line appears on essentially every invocation, and under that contention a dependency rlib built from a *different* source tree can be consumed by a build of *this* tree.

## Why it matters more than a flaky build

The failure is indistinguishable, from inside an agent run, from "main is broken". The delivery standard for the dev lane is a clean `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`, so an agent that hits this has three bad options, and all three are damaging:

1. Believe main is red and **edit an unrelated file** to add the phantom match arm — which then does not compile for anyone else, because the variant does not exist.
2. Abandon the issue as blocked and release the lock, burning the round. (Several issues already carry repeated `🤖 dev produced no committed changes vs main` comments.)
3. Report main as red in a handoff, sending the review/test/audit lanes after a defect that is not there.

It also silently corrupts the evidence value of `cargo check` output pasted into handoff comments.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Per-checkout target dirs**, or a target dir keyed by checkout path. This contradicts the recorded "exactly ONE cargo artifact dir on this box" directive, so it is a policy call — but that directive was about reclaiming disk, and correctness should win.
2. If the single directory must stay, **`sccache`** (or a shared *read-only* dependency cache plus per-tree output dirs) gives most of the reuse without cross-tree artifact bleed.
3. Cheapest partial mitigation: agents re-run a failing `cargo check` once before concluding main is broken, and treat "the symbol in the error does not exist in the repo" as the tell. Worth adding to the dev-agent prompt regardless of 1/2.

## Reproducing

Not deterministic — it needs two agents compiling different trees at the same time. The tell is an `E0004`/`E0433`/unresolved-symbol error naming an identifier that `grep -rn` cannot find anywhere in the working tree.

Found while delivering #522 (PR #629); noted in that issue's handoff comment as well.
title: [ci][infra][P2] Shared cargo target-dir lets one agent's artifacts fail another agent's build — agents conclude main is red when it is not

body:
Split out of the #428 code-review bounce (2026-07-25, finding 3), which asked the dev role to "say plainly whether D1 is in scope for this issue, or file the follow-up". Filing it: **D1 is out of scope for #428**, and PR #630 states the gap in `docs/cloudflare-integration.md` §4.1 rather than leaving it implicit.

## The gap

`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/control_plane_store_d1/mod.rs:566-591` returns `unimplemented_surface` for all three burn-ledger surfaces:

- `add_agent_burn`
- `get_agent_burn`
- `list_agent_cost_burn`

## Consequence on a D1 control plane

The typed error is the right call — it can never be mistaken for a zero burn — but it means that on the **Cloudflare-native store this epic targets**:

- configuring `agent_cost_budget_usd` anywhere in a tenant chain makes **every** agent run fail closed with `503 agent_budget_unavailable`, on all three run-start paths (`POST /v1/agent-runs`, `POST /v1/agent-jobs`, agent schedules);
- `GET /admin/v1/agent-cost-burn` errors instead of reporting;
- the #428 burn writer landed in PR #630 (fold settled `cost_usd` into the ledger from the metering path) is a no-op that logs a warn on every metered agent request.

So #428's "usage + model spend attributed and visible" and "budget that halts dispatch on breach" boxes are **undeliverable on D1** until this lands.

## Scope

Implement the three surfaces on the database-per-tenant D1 topology, following the sibling atomic families:

- Route through the per-tenant proxy binding (`tenant_database_binding`), not the control database — `agent_cost_burn` rows belong to the owning tenant, like wallets/usage/assets (#455/#456).
- `add_agent_burn` is the hard part: it must be **atomic and lossless under concurrency**, and SQLite/D1 has no `FOR UPDATE`. `control_plane_store_d1/workflow_budget.rs` already solves the same shape with a bounded optimistic-CAS retry over a guarded `UPDATE ... RETURNING`; reuse that pattern rather than inventing a second one. A read-modify-write **will** lose increments and silently under-count burn, which is exactly the way this feature fails open.
- Mind the #455 numeric-affinity lesson: the proxy binds every param as TEXT, so the accumulate sum needs an explicit `CAST(? AS REAL)`.
- Schema/migration for the `agent_cost_burn` table on the tenant databases.
- `list_agent_cost_burn` fans out over provisioned tenant bindings when no tenant scope is given; an unprovisioned tenant is EMPTY on the read path, not an error.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Concurrent `add_agent_burn` calls for one `(tenant_id, agent_key, period)` never lose an increment, proven by a test that races N adds and asserts the final total is exactly N × delta.
- [ ] `get_agent_burn` returns `Ok(None)` for an unseen key and the post-add total after an add.
- [ ] With a budget configured on a D1 control plane, an over-budget agent gets `402 agent_budget_exceeded` (not `503 agent_budget_unavailable`) on all three run-start paths.
- [ ] `GET /admin/v1/agent-cost-burn` reports rows on D1.
- [ ] The D1 caveat is removed from `docs/cloudflare-integration.md` §4.1 in the same change.

Refs #428, #456, #450.

labels.description: Validated follow-up; do not pull ahead of P0/P1

body:
Split out of #356 at code review's instruction: that slice must either land the runtime wiring or state plainly that it has not, and it states that it has not.

## Problem

`InboundX402Gate` and `load_inbound_x402_toml` ship in #356 as **libraries with no caller**:

- no code in `ferrogate-gateway` constructs an `InboundX402Gate`;
- nothing calls `ferrogate_config::load_inbound_x402_toml`;
- the root `Config` (`crates/ferrogate-config/src/config/types.rs`) has no `x402_inbound` field and no `deny_unknown_fields`, so `ferrogate run --config ferrogate-x402-inbound.toml` **silently ignores** the whole `[x402_inbound]` section and starts normally.

Consequence on a real deployment of `deploy/x402-sidecar/`: the priced route is served unmonetized. An unpaid call is not answered with 402, the sidecar credential is not checked on the upstream hop, and forward-once is not enforced. The network isolation in the compose file is real and is the only thing that holds today. This is documented in `docs/x402-inbound-sidecar.md` ("Runtime wiring is NOT landed") and in `deploy/x402-sidecar/README.md`.

## The part that needs design, not plumbing

`SidecarAdmissionPolicy::admit` refuses on `SidecarTransport` **before it reads any header**, which is what makes bypass refusal non-caller-assertable. Nothing in the Pingora request path derives that classification today, and it is not a value a request may assert. Wiring needs a real answer to:

- which listener the connection arrived on, and whether that listener is the private sidecar hop or the public data plane;
- whether mTLS terminated at FerroGate, and the verified peer subject (for `SidecarTransport::MutualTls { subject }`);
- what to classify a connection as when FerroGate sits behind an L7 proxy that terminates the sidecar hop — row 1 of the #356 threat model already names this as the residual that collapses the two-layer defence to one.

Getting this wrong fails **open**: classifying everything as `PrivateNetwork` makes the admission gate a no-op.

## Scope

- [ ] Add `#[serde(default)] pub x402_inbound: InboundX402Config` to the root `Config`, resolved through `validate_structure()` at load, so an enabled-but-unusable section is a startup error rather than silence.
- [ ] Decide and implement the `SidecarTransport` derivation from the Pingora listener/session, with the fail-closed default being `Untrusted`.
- [ ] Call `InboundX402Gate::evaluate` in `handle_request_filter` for requests matching the priced endpoint; short-circuit `Refused`/`PaymentRequired`/`AlreadyForwarded` with `http_status()`, and strip `headers_to_strip()` before the handler.
- [ ] Call `release_claim` on a connect failure / upstream 5xx produced before any handler bytes.
- [ ] E2E for the three acceptance behaviours #356 could not run: unpaid request gets 402; a direct (non-sidecar) call is refused 403; a settled request forwards exactly once.
- [ ] Remove the "Runtime wiring: NOT landed" section from `docs/x402-inbound-sidecar.md` and the warning banner from `deploy/x402-sidecar/README.md` once this lands, and un-caveat the two README curls.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `ferrogate run --config deploy/x402-sidecar/ferrogate-x402-inbound.toml` enforces the gate on the priced route.
- [ ] An `[x402_inbound]` section that is enabled but malformed fails startup rather than being ignored.
- [ ] A request arriving on a listener that is not the private sidecar hop is classified `Untrusted` and refused, proven by a test that flips the classification and observes the refusal disappear.

Related: #356 (the gate and its config surface), #601 (durable claim + revenue persistence + Admin query surface).

labels.name: priority:p1

body:
## Problem

When a tenant is suspended, FerroGate denies its traffic — but it does not say the same thing to every credential that belongs to that tenant.

An API key scoped with **both** `organization_id` and `project_id` answers `401 invalid_api_key` ("invalid API key"), while a config-seeded key and an admin-issued virtual key on the same suspended tenant both answer `403 tenancy_suspended`.

All three credentials return `200` on `GET /v1/models` immediately before the suspension, so all three are valid, resolvable keys. Only the denial contract diverges.

Reproduced against `origin/main` @ `9ea3cc18` with a provenance-verified `ferrogate-test` binary:

```
Error: suspended-tenancy denial for the project-scoped key

Caused by:
    GET /v1/models expected status 403, got 401
    {"error":{"message":"invalid API key","type":"ferrogate_error",
              "code":"invalid_api_key","request_id":"fg-8464c0b659cff0bf"}}
```

The key under test is created through the Admin API and declares a full chain:

```json
{"id":"lifecycle-project-only","name":"Lifecycle project-only key",
 "key":"lifecycle-project-only-secret","organization_id":"org_demo",
 "project_id":"project_gateway","scopes":["models.read"]}
```

This shape is the one #540 requires (a key naming neither `organization_id` nor
`platform_operator` is now refused at creation with `tenant_identity_required`),
so it is not a malformed fixture — it is the supported scoped-key shape.

Why it matters: fail-closed still holds — the request is denied either way — but
the caller cannot distinguish *"your organization is suspended, talk to
billing"* from *"your key is wrong, rotate it."* `401 invalid_api_key` sends an
operator down the wrong path, and it leaks a different fact than the `403` the
rest of the surface returns. `crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/tenant_suspension_e2e.rs`
already asserts `tenancy_suspended` as the intended contract for a scoped key
(and passes, 4/4, at a different provisioning layer), so the two layers disagree.

This was invisible until now because `ferrogate-test ci` never reached the
assertion: the `admin-api` scenario aborts earlier on the #182 self-hosted-worker
entitlement gate, so main's always-run CI is red and has been hiding every
downstream verdict in that scenario.

## Scope

- The request-time authentication path that resolves an `organization_id` +
  `project_id` scoped key and applies the lifecycle gate — the resolution appears
  to fail outright (key treated as unknown) rather than resolving and then
  reporting the suspended tenancy.
- Whatever difference lets the config-seeded and admin-issued virtual keys reach
  the lifecycle gate while this shape does not.
- Not the fail-closed behaviour itself, which is correct today.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A suspended tenant's `organization_id` + `project_id` scoped API key is
      refused with `403` / `tenancy_suspended`, matching the config-seeded and
      admin-issued keys.
- [ ] The `admin-api` harness scenario's labelled three-credential loop passes
      for all three labels without relaxing the expectation.
- [ ] A regression test pins all three credential kinds to the same denial code,
      so a future divergence fails rather than being reported as a bad key.
- [ ] `invalid_api_key` is no longer returned for a credential that resolved
      successfully moments earlier.

## Non-goals

- Changing the status code the *rest* of the suspension surface returns.
- Revisiting #540's `tenant_identity_required` creation-time refusal.
- Fixing the separate #182 harness/entitlement gap that masks this failure
  (already repaired on the test-gate branch `gate/harness-baseline`).
title: [gateway-core][P2] Suspended tenant answers 401 invalid_api_key to an org+project scoped key while other credentials get 403 tenancy_suspended

body:
## Problem

`POST /admin/v1/config/reload` with an **inline** payload (`config_toml` / `config_yaml` / `config_caddyfile`) silently and **permanently destroys every control-plane document that was provisioned at runtime through the Admin API**. The endpoint answers `200 {"valid":true,"committed":true}` while doing it.

An operator who reloads a config to flip one unrelated setting — e.g. appending `[scheduler] enabled = true` — revokes credentials they never mentioned.

### Mechanism

`reload_from_admin_payload`'s inline branch deliberately skips the durable reconcile that the `source=file` branch performs:

- `crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/server/local.rs:11885-11904` — inline payload calls `state.reload_process_local(config_from_admin_payload(...))`, and `parse_config_from_admin_payload` (`local.rs:11612`) is just `Config::from_toml_str(raw)`. Nothing durable is merged in.
- Contrast `reload_from_source_path` (`crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/state.rs:826-872`), which calls `apply_control_plane_snapshot_to_config` first — added precisely to avoid this class of loss (#80).
- `reload_process_local` → `AppState::with_reloaded_config` (`state.rs:4906`) ends with `let _ = self.sync_control_plane_storage_from_config(&next.config);` (`state.rs:4936`).
- That calls `repositories.replace_control_plane(control_plane_documents_from_config(config))` (`state.rs:4954`, projection at `state.rs:1874-1904`) → `replace_config_documents` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:13206`), which **replaces** each document class wholesale.

Because the candidate came only from the inline TOML, every runtime-provisioned document in those ten classes is deleted from durable storage: `api_keys`, `tenants`, `policies`, `gateway_configs`, `agent_workflows`, `skill_packages`, `prompt_templates`, `plugin_registrations`, `mcp_servers`, `agent_upstreams`.

Authentication then falls through `authenticate_durable` (`crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/auth.rs:1334`) and the static-key loop (`auth.rs:1254`) to the terminal `invalid_api_key` arm (`auth.rs:1318-1322`).

Two aggravating details:

- **The loss is permanent.** A follow-up `source=file` reload does not restore it — the durable rows were destroyed, not masked. The secret was one-time-issued, so there is no undo short of re-minting.
- **A failed destructive write is swallowed.** `let _ = ...` at `state.rs:4936` discards the error and the reload still reports `committed: true`.

### Reproduction

Observed on clean `main` (`9ea3cc18`) with a standalone gateway, suspending a tenant and then reloading an inline config:

```
=== AFTER suspend, BEFORE reload ===
  client-secret             -> 403   (static [[api_keys]] entry)
  virtual key (fg_...)      -> 403   (api-key *record* store)
  probe-project-only-secret -> 403   (control-plane api_keys document)
reload: 200 {"valid":true,"committed":true,"mode":"process-local"}
=== AFTER inline config reload ===
  client-secret             -> 403
  virtual key (fg_...)      -> 403
  probe-project-only-secret -> 401 "code":"invalid_api_key"     <-- revoked
GET /admin/v1/api-keys    after reload -> ['admin','client']    # probe-project-only GONE
GET /admin/v1/virtual-keys after reload -> ['probe-live']       # survived
```

A second class was confirmed empirically: an `agent_upstream` created via `POST /admin/v1/agent-upstreams` was present before the reload and gone after. The remaining classes go through the identical projection; that is inferred from code, not measured.

Which credentials survive:
- Static `[[api_keys]]` entries in the payload — re-declared by the payload, so they survive.
- `fg_` virtual keys — stored as api-key *records* (`crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/server/virtual_keys.rs:2079`), a store `ControlPlaneDocuments` does not cover, so they survive.
- Keys minted via `POST /admin/v1/api-keys` — control-plane documents, **destroyed**.

### Why this surfaced now

`ferrogate-test lifecycle-tenancy` and `admin-api` reach this through `enable_scheduler`, which posts an inline reload. The scenario's own `reload_config` helper carried a broken assertion (`assert_eq!(body["listener_reload_required"], false)` against a field that the reload contract never declares — it is validate-only), so it always panicked before this block ran. With that assertion corrected to the real reload contract, the defect is now reachable in CI.

## Scope

- `crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/server/local.rs` — `reload_from_admin_payload` inline branch.
- `crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/state.rs` — `with_reloaded_config`, `sync_control_plane_storage_from_config`, `control_plane_documents_from_config`.
- `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs` — `replace_control_plane` / `replace_config_documents` call contract.

Intended behavior: an inline reload should be **additive/merge**, not replace. The operator's payload keeps its explicit power to *introduce* documents and to *update by id*, but absence from the payload must never be inferred as deletion — deletion stays the job of `DELETE /admin/v1/api-keys/{id}` and its siblings. `sync_control_plane_storage_from_config` must not be reached with a candidate that was never reconciled against the durable snapshot, and its result must stop being discarded.

## Acceptance

- [ ] An inline `POST /admin/v1/config/reload` that does not mention a runtime-provisioned control-plane document leaves that document intact and usable; a key minted via `POST /admin/v1/api-keys` still authenticates after the reload.
- [ ] The same holds for every class in `ControlPlaneDocuments`: `api_keys`, `tenants`, `policies`, `gateway_configs`, `agent_workflows`, `skill_packages`, `prompt_templates`, `plugin_registrations`, `mcp_servers`, `agent_upstreams`.
- [ ] An inline payload can still *introduce* a new document and *update an existing one by id*; explicit `DELETE` remains the only way to remove one.
- [ ] A failure inside `sync_control_plane_storage_from_config` is surfaced, not swallowed: the reload must not report `committed: true` when the durable write failed.
- [ ] `ferrogate-test lifecycle-tenancy` and `ferrogate-test admin-api` pass without the scenario re-provisioning credentials after `enable_scheduler`.
- [ ] A harness scenario pins the invariant directly: provision a control-plane api-key, inline-reload an unrelated setting, and prove the key still authenticates.

## Non-goals

- Changing the 401-before-403 precedence in `authenticate_with_admission`. Resolving the credential before the tenancy gate is correct — the gate needs a resolved `organization_id`, and answering `403 tenancy_suspended` to an unrecognized bearer would be a tenant-existence oracle.
- Changing where `fg_` virtual keys are stored.
- Reworking the `source=file` reload path, which already reconciles correctly.

body:
Split out of #356 at the code-review gate's instruction ("Either land durable claim/revenue persistence + the Admin query surface for boxes 4–5, or split them into a tracked follow-up issue and explicitly de-scope those boxes on #356").

## Why this is a separate slice

#356 ships the inbound x402 decision path: sidecar admission, fixed-price settlement verification, and a forward-once claim. All of it is process-local:

- `InMemoryForwardClaimGuard` — claims are lost on restart, and a multi-replica deployment has one guard per replica.
- `InMemoryRevenueSink` — the durable backstop the gate consults before claiming is only as durable as this sink, which is not durable at all.

Concretely, on `main` after #356 lands:

- a proof replayed **after a process restart** would be forwarded again;
- the same proof sent to **two replicas** would be forwarded twice;
- there is **no query surface** for settled inbound revenue — no Postgres/Supabase table, no Admin API route, no OpenAPI entry.

That is why #356's acceptance boxes 4 ("attributed **durably**") and 5 ("revenue evidence **queryable**") are explicitly de-scoped there and owned here. `docs/x402-inbound-sidecar.md` states the residual in its Durability section rather than implying it is closed.

## Scope

1. **Durable forward-claim store.** A `ForwardClaimGuard` impl backed by the control-plane store, with the same three outcomes (`Admitted` / `DuplicateRetry` / `ProofReplay`) and the same fail-closed-on-error contract. Exactly-once must hold across restart and across replicas, which means the claim insert has to be atomic at the storage layer, not read-then-write.
2. **Durable `RevenueSink`.** Persist `InboundX402RevenueRecord` (idempotent on `id`, which is `x402-inbound:<challenge_hash_hex>:<transaction_signature>`). Lives in `ferrogate-storage`, which already depends on `ferrogate-billing`, so the crate direction is unchanged.
3. **Admin query surface.** List/get settled inbound revenue with tenant scoping, plus the OpenAPI entry so `scripts/check-openapi.py` has something to check. Revenue evidence must stay separate from the token-usage ledger and the prepaid-credit wallet — the `RevenueSink` / `LedgerSink` split already models that and must not be collapsed.
4. **Close the upstream-5xx hole.** `InboundX402Gate::release_claim` currently gives back the claim but deliberately does not delete the revenue record (deleting settled-payment evidence would make a refund unprovable), so once the sink is durable a released claim is re-refused by the backstop. Decide the semantics — a refund/void record, or a claim state distinct from "forwarded" — and implement it. See row 8 of the threat model in `docs/x402-inbound-sidecar.md`.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A replay of the same `PAYMENT-RESPONSE` after a process restart is refused, proven by a durability-layer test (restart, not just a dropped in-memory map).
- [ ] Two replicas sharing the store forward one settled payment exactly once under concurrent load.
- [ ] Settled inbound revenue is queryable through an Admin route with tenant scoping, and the route is in the OpenAPI spec.
- [ ] Querying revenue never reads or mutates the prepaid-credit wallet.
- [ ] The upstream-5xx path has defined, tested semantics — no state where the payer paid, was not served, and cannot retry.
- [ ] The Durability section of `docs/x402-inbound-sidecar.md` is updated to describe what is now closed, and row 8 of its threat model no longer says "incompletely closed".

## Not in scope

Streaming settlement, token-metered inference billing, subscriptions, multi-party payments, catalog publishing, mainnet defaults. Those stay out until the fixed-price loop is proven end to end.

body:
Split out of the third code-review pass on #353, which correctly refused to let an impossibility claim stand where the truth is a factoring choice.

## The claim that was wrong

#353's dev round asserted:

> the two 402 implementations still have no shared conformance fixture: a test that drives both needs a crate that can see both, and none exists

The second half is false. `crates/agent-worker/Cargo.toml:25` and `crates/ferrogate-gateway/Cargo.toml:50` **both** depend on `ferrogate-payments`. A crate that can see both sides exists today; nothing needs to be created for one to exist.

(The review named `ferrogate-cli/Cargo.toml:54`. That was accurate when written; the #553 extraction has since moved the gateway-side x402 state modules — `state_x402_negotiation.rs`, `state_x402_settlement.rs`, `state_x402_reconciler.rs`, `state_x402_sweeper.rs` — into `ferrogate-gateway`, which is where the dependency now sits. The conclusion is unchanged.)

## What is actually duplicated

Two independent implementations of the same 402 decision:

- **worker side** — `crates/agent-worker/src/x402_client.rs`: read the `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` header out of a raw HTTP response, parse the challenge, and select the requirement the caller is willing to satisfy (`parse_payment_required` + `select_requirement` + `RequirementFilter`).
- **gateway side** — `crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/state_x402_negotiation.rs`: the same header extraction and requirement selection on the gateway's own egress path.

Both call into `ferrogate-payments`, but each owns its own header-extraction and filter-construction step above that call. Nothing drives both from one fixture set, so the two can drift on exactly the questions that decide whether money moves: which header wins when the merchant sends more than one, how a header is matched case-insensitively, where the header block ends, and which requirement `RequirementFilter::default()` selects out of a multi-`accepts` challenge.

This is the #188 shape — one domain, two implementations, no conformance proof — and #352's third round bounced on the same axis in the SQL/Rust direction.

## Proposed shape

Hoist the shared decision (header extraction + `RequirementFilter` selection) into `ferrogate-payments`, the crate both sides already depend on, and drive it from one fixture set exercised from both sides. This is the move already made once in this family: `RequestWireStage`/`HoldDisposition` were hoisted into `ferrogate-runtime` for exactly this reason, and that hoist *is* what let `ferrogate-cli` name the type at all.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Header extraction and requirement selection exist once, in `ferrogate-payments`, and both call sites use it rather than re-deriving it.
- [ ] One fixture corpus is driven from both the `agent-worker` and `ferrogate-gateway` sides, covering at minimum: absent header, duplicate headers, case-insensitive match, header-block boundary, multi-`accepts` selection, and unparseable challenge.
- [ ] The corpus is a shared constant, not two copies — a divergence must red, not merely be noticed by a reader.
- [ ] Existing behaviour is preserved: the worker's duplicate-header refusal (#353) and the gateway's negotiation selection both keep their current verdicts, with the fixture proving they agree.

## Non-goals

Not a behaviour change. If the hoist reveals the two sides already disagree, that divergence is its own bug report, filed against whichever side is wrong — this issue only makes it visible.

Refs #353, #381, #188.

body:
Found while verifying #540 rework.

`cargo +1.88.0 test -p ferrogate-config` is red on `origin/main` (`8c32185d8797a562447ebcce9c854cdf4e1b2896`), independent of the #540 patch.

Confirmed in a clean detached worktree at `/home/dev/fg540-main-red-check`:

```bash
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/target-issue-540-main-red CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 \
  cargo +1.88.0 test -p ferrogate-config \
  unknown_physical_route_capabilities_fail_deserialization_at_every_route_level \
  --lib -- --nocapture
```

Result:

```text
thread 'config::tests::unknown_physical_route_capabilities_fail_deserialization_at_every_route_level' panicked at crates/ferrogate-config/src/config/tests.rs:339:9:
unexpected parse error: failed to parse TOML config: TOML parse error at line 6, column 17
  |
6 | capabilities = ["unknown_feature"]
  |                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
unknown variant `unknown_feature`, expected one of `chat`, `streaming`, `vision`, `images`, `embeddings`, `tools`, `structured_output`
```

Root cause from reading: the test asserts `error.to_string().contains("unknown variant `unknown_feature`")`, but the top-level anyhow message is only `failed to parse TOML config`; the serde TOML detail appears in the error chain / alternate debug output used by the panic message. The test is checking the wrong rendering.

Smallest likely fix: assert against the rendered error chain (`format!("{error:#}")`) or expose/inspect the parse-source message explicitly.

This blocked using full `cargo test -p ferrogate-config` as #540 proof; the #540 patch only changes two Caddyfile parser fixture strings in `crates/ferrogate-config/src/caddyfile/parser_tests.rs`.

## Decision

Move the Admin Console web application out of this FerroGate repository.

After this migration, this repository no longer owns or maintains the `admin-console` web application module. The Admin Console must be managed as an independent repository with its own source tree, dependency policy, CI, tests, release flow, and issue queue.

## Why

The Admin Console has become a product surface with its own frontend lifecycle, CI requirements, localization work, UI/API coverage backlog, and test failures. Keeping it inside the Rust gateway repository couples unrelated release gates and makes ownership unclear.

FerroGate should keep the gateway/runtime/control-plane contract clean. The Admin Console should consume that contract from a separate repository instead of living as an in-repo web app module.

## Scope for this repo

- Choose and document the destination repository for the Admin Console.
- Move the existing `admin-console` web application source, package metadata, frontend tests, frontend CI, and frontend docs to the standalone repository.
- Remove this repository's responsibility for maintaining the Admin Console web app module.
- Keep only the integration surface that belongs in FerroGate: Admin API contract, generated contract artifacts if required, and documentation that points operators/developers to the external Admin Console repository.
- Update old Admin Console related issues in this repository with a migration note explaining that Admin Console work is now owned by the standalone repository.

## Non-goals

- Do not implement new Admin Console product features in this repository.
- Do not change the Admin API runtime semantics as part of the repo split unless a separate gateway issue requires it.
- Do not delete useful history; preserve traceability from old FerroGate issues to the external Admin Console ownership path.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Admin Console web app no longer exists as a maintained module in this repository.
- The standalone Admin Console repository owns frontend source, package manager config, tests, CI, release instructions, and frontend issue tracking.
- FerroGate docs clearly state that Admin Console development moved out of this repository.
- Existing open Admin Console related issues in this repository carry a comment linking to this migration issue and explaining that follow-up frontend work should move to the standalone repository.

The #528 gateway contract is now explicit: a stored-but-withheld upload answers exact `202 Accepted` and returns `asset.visibility = pending_scan|quarantined`. The Admin Console still discards that result and reports an ordinary success.

## Reachability

Both upload paths are affected on current `main`:

- `admin-console/src/pages/assets.tsx:1484-1493`: the presigned commit mutation uses `onSuccess: () => toast.success(...)`.
- `admin-console/src/pages/assets.tsx:1803-1811`: the inline push mutation also uses `onSuccess: () => toast.success(...)`.

A configured async scanner threshold or unavailable scanner can therefore store and withhold an asset while the console says the upload/push succeeded, clears the form, and closes the presigned dialog. The subsequent normal registry refresh omits the row by design, leaving the operator with a success message and no visible asset.

This is the frontend sibling explicitly called out during #528 review; it is not part of the #528 API/harness Ask.

## Acceptance

- Branch both inline and presigned upload success handling on the returned `asset.visibility` (and/or the exact 202 response if the client exposes it).
- Show a non-success terminal for `pending_scan` and `quarantined`, with distinct operator copy; do not say the asset is published.
- Preserve the ordinary success message only for `visible`.
- Add focused component/browser coverage for both upload paths, including a positive `visible` control. Mutating the branch back to unconditional success must make the test red.
- Keep generated OpenAPI client types as the source of the response shape.

Refs #528.

Parent: #571

## Problem

`AppState::candidate_model_routes` currently applies strategy ordering and region filtering only. The logical `Model` has one free-form `capabilities` list, but `ModelFallback` and canary routes cannot declare their own capabilities or context window. The runtime therefore cannot prove that a cheaper/healthier fallback still supports the request's tools, structured output, streaming, modality, or context requirement before dispatch.

Trying the peer and adapting after failure is the wrong boundary: an incompatible provider must never receive the request.

## Scope

- Define a closed, typed model-route capability vocabulary for the request features FerroGate actually dispatches now.
- Let every physical route (primary, fallback, canary) declare its capabilities and relevant context limit without duplicating provider-family quirks in gateway core.
- Derive required capabilities from the parsed request/endpoint before candidate ordering.
- Return an explicit routing decision containing eligible routes and bounded exclusion evidence with stable reason codes.
- Keep strategy/region ordering over the eligible set and expose exclusion/selection evidence through existing request/investigation records.
- Do not add semantic/LLM routing or a parallel evidence store.

## Acceptance

- A fallback lacking a required tool, structured-output, streaming, modality, or context capability is excluded before dispatch.
- A deterministic handler/harness fixture includes an incompatible route that would otherwise win on price/health and observes that its peer receives zero requests.
- The compatible route receives the unchanged governed request.
- Admin investigation shows required capabilities, candidate identity, excluded capability, and a non-empty typed exclusion reason without raw prompt/tool arguments.
- Missing/unknown capability declarations fail closed for requests that require them; legacy configs remain usable for capability-neutral requests.
- Unit/invariant coverage mutates each filter/reason and reds; config/OpenAPI/docs state the exact vocabulary.
- Metrics remain low-cardinality.

Refs #571.

body:
Parent: #286
Related: #202, #215, #216, #570, #571
Research: `docs/design/ai-gateway-trend-research-2026-07-28.md` sections 3.2, 5.3, and 6

## Problem

FerroGate can authenticate a caller and maintain an isolated per-user MCP OAuth grant, but it cannot yet preserve and deliberately narrow identity across the enterprise delegation chain:

`employee -> agent/client -> FerroGate -> target MCP server/API`

There is no standards-based token-exchange boundary for RFC 8693, no typed representation of the actor/subject chain, and no proof that the token used at the target has the intended audience and no broader scope than policy permits. Operators can see that a user authenticated, but cannot prove which delegated subject and actor reached a downstream tool.

The market is moving from API-key storage to Enterprise-Managed Authorization, OBO, and cross-app identity. This is a P1 enterprise control point because it extends FerroGate's existing per-user OAuth, encrypted token storage, refresh leases, tenant isolation, and audit machinery instead of creating a second identity system.

## Required trust contract

For every delegated target call, FerroGate must be able to explain:

- authenticated subject, acting client/agent, tenant/workspace, and target resource;
- subject-token source and exchange mechanism without persisting or logging the token;
- requested versus granted audience and scopes;
- policy/config revision that authorized the exchange;
- exchanged-token expiry/cache identity and refresh outcome;
- final target call, tool/action identity, and allow/deny reason.

A downstream shared administrator credential is never an implicit fallback for a failed user exchange.

## Scope

- Add a narrow, provider-neutral delegated credential/token-exchange interface; keep Entra or other IdP quirks in adapters.
- Support the RFC 8693 token-exchange grant against a local standards-shaped authorization-server fixture. Add RFC 7523 JWT bearer only if it is required by the first real adapter and does not leak vendor semantics into the core contract.
- Reuse the existing MCP identity cipher, repository contracts, bounded async execution, refresh/lease semantics, and audit paths.
- Add typed MCP server configuration for trusted issuer/token endpoint, allowed audiences, maximum scopes, client credential reference, timeouts, and explicit exchange mode.
- Key cached grants by at least tenant, workspace, user/subject, acting client, target server, audience, and normalized scope set. No cross-user, cross-tenant, cross-target, or wider-scope reuse.
- Enforce scope non-escalation and target/audience allowlists before dispatch. Reject missing, inconsistent, expired, or outcome-unknown identity state with a typed fail-closed error.
- Propagate a bounded actor/subject fingerprint into the existing tool/action and investigation evidence chain without recording bearer tokens or raw identity assertions.
- Make one real enterprise IdP/OBO adapter a separately gated slice after the generic local contract passes; do not hardwire that vendor into `ferrogate-mcp`.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A tenant user authenticates to FerroGate, a local authorization-server fixture exchanges the user/actor credential for a target-scoped token, and the MCP peer receives that token on the governed tool call.
- [ ] The exchanged token is limited to the configured audience and scope intersection; a requested broader scope or untrusted audience fails before the token endpoint or target peer is called.
- [ ] A failed or timed-out exchange never falls back to shared headers, an application token, another user's cached token, or the original inbound bearer.
- [ ] Concurrent identical exchanges reuse one bounded owner/lease operation; different tenant, user, target, audience, or scope keys cannot coalesce.
- [ ] Token-exchange mutation tests cover definitive pre-commit cancellation versus outcome-unknown behavior where durable state is involved.
- [ ] Admin/investigation evidence joins caller, actor fingerprint, target, granted audience/scopes, policy revision, tool/action, and outcome without exposing any credential.
- [ ] RBAC tests prove one tenant cannot list, use, refresh, or investigate another tenant's delegated grants.
- [ ] Config, secret references, runtime dispatch, failure behavior, metrics/audit evidence, OpenAPI/Admin visibility, and focused regression coverage form one E2E path.
- [ ] `ferrogate-test` gains a named delegated-identity contract scenario; replacing the exchanged token with the original bearer or widening one granted scope makes it red.
- [ ] At least one real IdP adapter has an opt-in live contract test or is explicitly tracked as a follow-up; the generic fixture alone must not be marketed as provider certification.

## Non-goals

- Building a general-purpose identity provider or user directory.
- Persisting raw access tokens, refresh tokens, JWTs, authorization codes, or client secrets in audit/log records.
- Automatic fallback to shared administrator credentials.
- Supporting every enterprise IdP in the first slice.
- Implementing speculative ID-JAG fields before a stable artifact and a design-partner requirement exist.

## Verification

Focused identity/config/repository tests, async concurrency/invariant tests, MCP dispatch integration tests, Admin/RBAC coverage, the named `ferrogate-test` contract scenario, static gates, clippy, and full workspace tests. A real IdP test is opt-in and must record the exact provider/configuration tested.

body:
Parent: #286
Depends on: #570, #571
Research: `docs/design/ai-gateway-trend-research-2026-07-28.md` sections 3.9 and 6

## Problem

MCP Tasks is a plausible compatibility surface for long-running agent work, but current community demand is weaker than MCP protocol correctness, delegated identity, and unified decision evidence. Implementing a second task engine just to check a feature box would create state, cancellation, tenancy, and durability bugs without proving buyer value.

FerroGate already has the relevant runtime machinery: durable agent jobs, worker poll/ack leases, event cursors, cancellation of leased and unleased work, restart recovery, schedules, required capabilities, and tenant isolation. The opportunity is a thin MCP protocol adapter over that state machine, gated by one real design-partner workflow.

This is deliberately P2 and stays behind #570 and #571.

## Entry gate

Implementation starts only when all are true:

- the final/stable MCP Tasks artifact and conformance fixtures are identified;
- one design partner supplies a concrete long-running tool/job workflow;
- the required protocol subset and success metric are written down;
- the mapping proves no second scheduler, lease queue, or task repository is needed.

Until then, this issue tracks validation and remains Backlog.

## Proposed mapping to validate

| MCP Tasks concept | FerroGate owner |
| --- | --- |
| create/start | existing agent-job submission and durable run creation |
| task id | stable externally exposed mapping to existing run id |
| status/progress | existing run state and resumable event feed |
| result | existing terminal output/artifact contract |
| cancel | existing unleased withdrawal or leased `cancel_run` dispatch |
| capability requirement | existing `required_capabilities` matching |
| retry/idempotency | existing durable dispatch/lease generation and explicit request key |

The final mapping must be derived from the released protocol, not inferred from this table.

## Scope after entry gate

- Implement the smallest interoperable Tasks method subset required by the pilot as an adapter in the MCP boundary.
- Keep agent-job/run state authoritative; do not duplicate status, cancellation, scheduling, or result storage.
- Define typed translation for every task/run state, including cancelled, failed, expired, partial, and outcome-unknown.
- Preserve tenant/user/delegated identity, request/trace/run correlation, policy decision, capability envelope, and cost evidence.
- Make create/retry idempotent and ensure cancellation reaches the actual lease holder or durably withdraws unleased work.
- Add Admin visibility that shows the MCP task id and underlying run/dispatch identity without creating a separate investigation surface.
- Use an official SDK/conformance fixture plus a real pilot client; self-written mocks alone are insufficient.

## Acceptance

- [ ] The issue records the design partner, workflow, stable protocol artifact, selected method subset, and explicit go/no-go result before implementation begins.
- [ ] An unmodified supported MCP client creates a task, observes progress through a resumable mechanism, retrieves the terminal result, and correlates it to one existing FerroGate agent run.
- [ ] Repeating the create request with the same idempotency identity does not enqueue or bill duplicate work.
- [ ] Cancelling both an unleased and a leased task stops/withdraws the real runtime work and terminalizes the same underlying run.
- [ ] Gateway restart preserves task status, progress cursor, cancellation truth, and result because the adapter reloads existing durable state.
- [ ] Cross-tenant get/result/cancel attempts return the repository's non-disclosing not-found behavior and never touch the target run.
- [ ] Required capabilities are enforced by the existing worker-dispatch contract; an incompatible worker cannot lease the task.
- [ ] Investigation evidence joins MCP request, task id, run, worker lease, tool/action, outcome, and settlement.
- [ ] `ferrogate-test` gains a named MCP Tasks E2E scenario; bypassing the existing job state machine or duplicating a dispatch makes it red.
- [ ] Pilot success is measured and recorded before declaring general availability; failure produces a no-go conclusion rather than silent scope expansion.

## Non-goals

- A second task scheduler, task repository, lease protocol, or cancellation engine.
- MCP Apps/UI rendering.
- Broad Tasks coverage without a design partner.
- Pulling this work ahead of #570, #571, or delegated-identity P1 work.
- Treating transport statelessness as proof that task business state is stateless.

## Verification

Protocol fixture/SDK interoperability, existing agent-job E2E reuse, new adapter-focused unit/contract tests, restart and cancellation scenarios, Admin/RBAC coverage, static gates, clippy, and full workspace tests.

body:
Parent: #285
Related: #286, #570, #571
Research: `docs/design/ai-gateway-trend-research-2026-07-28.md` sections 3.7, 5.3, and 6

## Problem

Recent gateway advisories show that policy code can look correct while runtime framing invalidates it: a stateful MCP session can cross routes and inherit the wrong authorization policy, and authorization evaluated against a truncated body can miss attacker-controlled content outside the inspected buffer.

This issue does not claim FerroGate has either vulnerability. It requires executable evidence that FerroGate's actual Pingora/MCP paths preserve three invariants under hostile HTTP framing and legacy session behavior:

1. policy evaluates the same bounded semantic request that can reach the upstream;
2. a legacy MCP session cannot change target route, tenant, identity, or policy context;
3. oversized, ambiguous, compressed, malformed, or partially read input fails explicitly rather than bypassing governance.

The current security advantage is only commercially credible when these attack shapes are reproducibly rejected.

## Scope

- Define one adversarial matrix covering fixed and chunked bodies, declared and undeclared lengths, body-at/over-limit boundaries, supported content encodings, malformed/trailing JSON, duplicate/conflicting routing metadata, disconnect/partial-read behavior, and legacy MCP session reuse.
- Prove the request body inspected by auth/policy/guardrail code is the same complete bounded body parsed and dispatched upstream. If full inspection is impossible, reject before any side effect.
- Bind every supported legacy MCP session to its immutable tenant, authenticated subject, route/server, negotiated legacy version, and governing policy/config revision. Reject any conflicting reuse before dispatch.
- Prove modern MCP `2026-07-28` requests remain stateless and cannot acquire authorization context from a preceding request or gateway instance.
- Add cross-tenant and cross-route concurrency cases using barriers/channels where ordering matters; do not use timing sleeps as race proof.
- Assert the upstream peer receives no request on every rejected case, and that the operator-visible audit evidence carries a low-cardinality typed reason.
- Add the matrix to the contract/compliance layer in `ferrogate-test`, with focused async tests at the lowest reproducible layer.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A policy-relevant field placed after the normal body limit cannot reach an upstream unseen: the complete request is either governed or rejected.
- [ ] Chunked transfer, misleading/missing `Content-Length`, supported content encoding, malformed/trailing JSON, and partial reads have explicit tested outcomes with no silent truncation.
- [ ] A legacy MCP session created for route/server A cannot be replayed against route/server B, another tenant/workspace/user, another protocol version, or a conflicting policy context.
- [ ] Two concurrent requests cannot race session binding so that both incompatible contexts dispatch; the losing request fails before the peer is called.
- [ ] Modern stateless requests can land on different gateway instances and never consume cached identity/capability state from an earlier request.
- [ ] Every rejection emits a typed audit/trace reason without body, credential, session, user, or request IDs becoming metric labels.
- [ ] The named `ferrogate-test` security-conformance scenario checks peer non-receipt; deleting the body-completeness gate or one session binding field makes it red.
- [ ] Existing normal streaming/non-streaming AI requests and modern/legacy MCP compatibility paths remain green.
- [ ] The report and product security claims identify exactly which adversarial cases have passed; no untested vulnerability claim is published.

## Non-goals

- Copying another gateway's implementation or assuming its CVE maps directly to FerroGate.
- Treating prompt guardrails as the boundary for tool side effects.
- Adding a generic fuzzing platform before the named invariants are covered.
- Replacing #570 protocol conformance or #571 decision/settlement evidence work.

## Verification

Focused bounded-body/parser tests, deterministic async session isolation tests, MCP/AI ingress integration tests, the named `ferrogate-test` contract scenario, static gates, clippy, and full workspace tests. Each assertion must name a concrete mutation that makes it fail.

body:
Related to #488.

## Problem

The site-domain verification endpoint increments `attempt_count` but no decision reads it. An `admin.write` credential can therefore drive unbounded outbound DNS-over-HTTPS requests from the admin request path. This traffic is outside the governed egress path and can consume resolver capacity or amplify a compromised tenant.

## Scope

- Define a persisted per-tenant/per-host verification cooldown or bounded attempt window.
- Refuse before constructing or sending the DNS request when the limit applies.
- Return a typed retryable response with a bounded retry time.
- Record the refusal in audit/metrics without leaking another tenant hostname.
- Use an injected clock and deterministic tests; no timing sleeps.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Repeated verify calls hit a documented limit before outbound DNS.
- [ ] Limits are scoped by tenant and hostname.
- [ ] Successful proof and elapsed cooldown reset or advance state explicitly.
- [ ] Restart does not silently erase the enforced limit when durable storage is configured.
- [ ] Tests prove the resolver is not called on the refused path.

## Non-goals

- Moving DNS verification into a long database transaction.
- Replacing DNS-over-HTTPS.
- A global rate limit that lets one tenant block another.

Refs #488.

title: [assets][security][P2] Rate-limit site-domain verification before outbound DNS

body:
Related to #488.

## Problem

Site-domain bind reads the hostname and later performs an unconditional upsert. Two tenants can race: tenant B observes no binding, tenant A verifies and writes, then B overwrites A with the stale decision. Cross-tenant theft is blocked only when the earlier read sees the row; the write itself has no compare-and-set contract.

This is an availability and ownership-integrity defect introduced by treating a security decision as a read followed by an unrelated write.

## Scope

- Add a narrow conditional site-domain claim operation to the storage contract.
- Implement identical semantics for memory, Postgres, and D1.
- Allow create-if-absent and same-tenant replacement; reject a different current tenant.
- Make the bind handler map the conflict to the existing non-leaking ownership response.
- Add deterministic concurrency coverage using barriers/channels, not sleeps.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Two tenants racing for one hostname cannot overwrite each other.
- [ ] Memory, Postgres, and D1 expose the same conditional-write result.
- [ ] A stale preflight read cannot authorize the final write.
- [ ] Same-tenant update remains supported.
- [ ] The losing request leaves inspectable rejected audit evidence.

## Non-goals

- Long transactions around DNS resolution or other external work.
- Global serialization of unrelated hostnames.
- Changing the ownership proof format.

Refs #488.

labels.description: Validated follow-up; do not pull ahead of P0/P1

title: [assets][security][P2] Make site-domain claim a cross-backend conditional write

body:
Related to #519.

## Problem

The managed external-action authorization path resolves the real project for a workspace, but it emits timeline and guardrail evidence only. It never calls the quota resolver for spend, writes a billing event, or emits a metering row. Therefore #519 can prove that its producer context binds the shared quota resolver, but cannot prove which project an external-action spend lands on because no such spend record exists.

Calling the existing producer test a billing or spend proof would be false: there is no downstream row to inspect.

## Scope

- Define which managed external actions are billable and at what settlement point.
- Carry the resolved tenant/project/workspace attribution into the billing event.
- Persist a metering row with request, run, action, and project identity.
- Make retries idempotent and keep non-billable/refused actions out of spend.
- Add a cross-component or harness scenario that starts from a real external action and asserts the durable metering row.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A successful billable managed external action emits exactly one metering row.
- [ ] The row carries the project resolved from the workspace, never the workspace id in the project field.
- [ ] Refused and non-billable actions emit no spend.
- [ ] Retry/replay does not double-settle.
- [ ] A real external-action request proves the producer-to-metering chain end to end.

## Non-goals

- Rewriting pre-#519 append-only audit evidence.
- Treating every external action as billable without an explicit product rule.
- Replacing the shared quota or billing repositories.

Refs #519.

body:
## Problem

The documented Supabase Storage S3 endpoint form is https://<project>.supabase.co/storage/v1/s3, but the current asset SigV4 path treats the endpoint path as part of the signed Host header while building the canonical request path only from /<bucket>/<key>.

That produces an illegal Host value containing /storage/v1/s3 and signs a URI that disagrees with the actual endpoint prefix. Configuration can load successfully, so the failure is deferred to an opaque request-time signature or transport error.

## Observe

Configure the S3 asset backend with a Supabase endpoint carrying /storage/v1/s3, then inspect the signed request: the Host contains the path prefix while the canonical URI omits it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Endpoint authority and base-path prefix are represented separately.
- Host contains only host[:port].
- The base-path prefix is included exactly once in both the request URL and SigV4 canonical URI.
- Runtime/config agreement coverage uses the actual signed request rather than restating parser grammar.
- Existing bare-host S3/R2 behavior remains unchanged.

Discovered during #485 code review; deliberately tracked separately from that narrow R2 validation rework.

## Problem

parse_r2_endpoint validates the R2 host shape but does not validate the parsed scheme. As a result, http://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com is accepted as a valid R2 endpoint and passes the region/host guards even though Cloudflare R2 is not served through this plaintext endpoint form.

The invalid configuration therefore fails only on the live asset request path instead of failing closed at config load with an actionable error.

## Observe

parse_r2_endpoint("http://abc123.r2.cloudflarestorage.com") currently returns a valid R2 endpoint.

## Acceptance criteria

- R2 endpoint validation accepts HTTPS only, case-insensitively.
- Plaintext HTTP R2 endpoints fail Config::validate with an actionable, credential-free diagnostic.
- Generic S3 HTTP endpoints remain available for explicit local/mock deployments.
- Config/runtime agreement coverage includes the plaintext R2 row and proves the load-time rejection.

Discovered during #485 code review; deliberately tracked separately from the scheme-case parsing rework.

body:
Parent: #285
Related: #57, #199, #293, #294, #300
Research: `docs/design/ai-gateway-trend-research-2026-07-28.md` sections 3.3, 3.5, and 5.3

## Problem

FerroGate has the pieces of an explainable gateway, but no single contract proves the product claim across the complete agent path:

`identity -> model route -> provider attempt/fallback -> model tool call -> governed tool/action -> side effect/outcome -> usage/cost settlement`

#57 extracted the AI request decision pipeline and #199 built the investigation surface. Current tests prove many stages separately (`gateway-billing-chain`, Guardrail investigation, agent timelines, MCP/tool governance), but no cross-component scenario requires every material decision and correlation key to survive the whole path. A future change can therefore leave `decision_reason` empty, lose the run/trace link at a model-to-tool boundary, silently fall back to an incompatible provider, or settle cost under a detached attempt while the existing isolated suites remain green.

This is P0 because FerroGate's stated Secure Agent Gateway wedge is not credible unless an operator can explain the full model-and-tool chain from durable runtime evidence. This issue is a narrow contract and missing wiring fix, not another observability rewrite.

## Required evidence contract

For one managed agent request, durable/Admin-visible evidence must preserve:

- authenticated tenant, project/workspace, key/user, and agent/run identity;
- requested/logical model and required capabilities;
- route candidate set, each exclusion reason, selected provider/provider-model, config or policy revision, and the evidence used for the choice;
- every provider attempt, retry/fallback reason, pre-first-token versus post-first-token failure boundary, and final provider outcome;
- canonical tool/action identity and fingerprint, delegated subject, policy/guardrail/approval decision and non-empty machine-readable reason;
- actual side-effect outcome, including denial, definite failure, cancellation, or outcome-unknown where applicable;
- provider-reported or gateway-estimated usage, provider-attempt identity, billing/ledger settlement, and reconciliation state;
- one joinable request/trace/agent-run chain exposed through the existing investigation/Admin API.

Do not add a parallel evidence store if existing request logs, audit events, agent-run events, Guardrail evaluations, billing events, and investigation joins can carry the contract. Add a new type or repository only where it removes a demonstrated ambiguity.

## Scope

- Define the required fields and typed reason codes at the existing decision-stage boundaries.
- Make provider capability filtering explicit before dispatch. A fallback lacking required tool, structured-output, streaming, context, or modality capability is excluded with evidence; it is never tried and then silently adapted.
- Preserve correlation from the model response/tool call into the governed execution chokepoint and onward to billing/settlement.
- Expose the joined result through the existing investigation/Admin surface; no raw-log archaeology.
- Add one deterministic cross-component harness scenario with local provider/tool doubles.
- Keep prompts, tool arguments, secrets, and response bodies out of durable evidence by default; store fingerprints and bounded metadata.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A deterministic managed-agent scenario routes to provider A, records a retryable pre-first-token failure, falls back to compatible provider B, receives a tool call, executes one governed side effect, and settles model/tool usage exactly once.
- [ ] The Admin investigation for its request ID, trace ID, or agent-run ID reconstructs the same ordered chain and shows non-empty typed reasons for route selection, provider fallback, tool authorization, execution outcome, and settlement.
- [ ] Every row/event that represents the chain carries enough canonical correlation to join without timestamps, fuzzy text, or implementation-specific log parsing.
- [ ] An incompatible cheaper/healthier provider is present in the candidate registry but is excluded before dispatch because it lacks a required capability; the exclusion and capability are operator-visible.
- [ ] Removing one required capability filter makes the scenario red by observing that the wrong peer received a request; asserting config text is not coverage.
- [ ] Removing or blanking each required decision/correlation field makes a focused assertion red. At minimum cover selected route reason, fallback reason, action fingerprint/delegated subject, provider-attempt identity, and settlement link.
- [ ] A streaming failure after the first emitted token does not silently replay the request or duplicate the tool side effect; the terminal evidence states the actual partial/unknown outcome.
- [ ] Tenant-scoped Admin/RBAC tests prevent cross-tenant reconstruction of the chain.
- [ ] Metrics remain low-cardinality; request, trace, user, tool, and run identifiers stay in traces/durable evidence rather than metric labels.
- [ ] `ferrogate-test` exposes the scenario as a named cross-component chain and documents the exact mutation each assertion is intended to catch.

## Non-goals

- Adding an opaque LLM classifier or semantic router.
- Rebuilding the investigation UI completed by #199.
- Persisting raw prompts, tool arguments, secrets, or full response bodies.
- Adding providers, MCP Apps/Tasks, A2A, or payment protocols.

## Verification

Focused decision-stage unit/invariant tests, async streaming and duplicate-side-effect tests, the named `ferrogate-test` cross-component scenario, Admin API/RBAC integration coverage, static gates, clippy, and full workspace tests. No live Supabase performance/load testing.

labels.name: priority:p0
labels.description: Must be addressed before the product claim is credible

title: [gateway-core][P0] Enforce one routing-to-tool-to-settlement decision-evidence contract

body:
Parent: #286
Follow-up to: #277
Research: `docs/design/ai-gateway-trend-research-2026-07-28.md` section 5.2

## Problem

FerroGate currently claims MCP `2026-07-28` support in the roadmap and product overview, but the runtime implements only the version string and `Mcp-Method` / `Mcp-Name` routing headers. The wire flow is still the legacy handshake:

- `crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/http_client.rs` sends `initialize` with `protocolVersion: 2026-07-28`;
- `crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/server/mcp_rpc.rs` negotiates `2026-07-28` inside `initialize_result`;
- no `server/discover` dispatch exists;
- outbound HTTP requests do not carry `MCP-Protocol-Version`;
- JSON-RPC requests do not carry per-request `_meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/{protocolVersion,clientInfo,clientCapabilities}`;
- fallback skips the immediately preceding `2025-11-25` revision and drops to `2025-06-18`.

The `2026-07-28` protocol removes `initialize` / `initialized` and protocol-level sessions. A modern client discovers server capabilities through `server/discover`, then sends self-describing requests. A version string echoed through a removed handshake is not protocol support.

This is P0 because the public product claim is false and a conforming modern client/server pair cannot use the claimed flow. It is the same failure class as a control-plane value that writes successfully but is never read at runtime.

## Required protocol truth table

| FerroGate side | Peer | Required behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| client | modern server | `server/discover`, then per-request metadata; no `initialize` or session id |
| client | legacy server | downgrade only on a definitive legacy signal; negotiate an initialize-capable version |
| ingress | modern client | accept stateless self-describing requests and reject missing/inconsistent required metadata with the specified typed error |
| ingress | legacy client | preserve the supported legacy initialize/session behavior without advertising a modern version through it |

Implementation must re-read the final official schema/changelog before coding. If the final release is still absent, pin the exact RC artifact and say so; do not infer the contract from a blog post.

## Scope

- Implement `server/discover` and modern per-request metadata on client and ingress paths.
- Emit and validate `MCP-Protocol-Version` on Streamable HTTP.
- Preserve `Mcp-Method` / `Mcp-Name` body consistency checks and per-operation metrics.
- Add explicit modern-to-legacy probing/downgrade; support `2025-11-25` as the direct legacy predecessor unless the final spec says otherwise.
- Keep transport stateless for modern requests: no `Mcp-Session-Id`, sticky-route assumption, or cached client capability inferred from an earlier request.
- Downgrade README, roadmap, and product-overview claims in the same change until the external conformance path passes; restore the claim only with evidence.
- Record negotiated/downgraded protocol evidence without logging credentials or high-cardinality client identifiers in metrics.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Modern client -> FerroGate ingress calls `server/discover`, lists tools, and calls a tool without `initialize` or `Mcp-Session-Id`.
- [ ] FerroGate client -> modern server uses `server/discover`, sends `MCP-Protocol-Version` and all required per-request `_meta`, and completes `tools/list` / `tools/call`.
- [ ] Modern client -> legacy server and legacy client -> modern-capable FerroGate cover the documented downgrade paths without claiming `2026-07-28` inside `initialize`.
- [ ] At least one official Tier 1 SDK or its unmodified protocol fixture is used as an external opponent; self-written mocks alone do not satisfy conformance.
- [ ] Missing protocol metadata, unsupported version, and header/body mismatch fail with the specified JSON-RPC/HTTP contract and leave attributable audit evidence.
- [ ] A modern request never creates or requires protocol session state; two consecutive requests can land on different gateway/server instances in the test fixture.
- [ ] Existing governed tool auth, approval, guardrail, metering, and per-tool metric paths remain active for both modern and legacy requests.
- [ ] `ferrogate-test` gains a contract/compliance scenario for the four-way matrix; changing `server/discover` back to `initialize` or removing one required metadata field makes it red.
- [ ] Product docs state exactly which protocol revisions and modes the runtime has proven, with no RC/final ambiguity.

## Non-goals

- MCP Apps, Tasks, A2A, sampling, roots, or logging feature expansion.
- Rewriting `ferrogate-mcp` around a new SDK without first proving that the dependency removes more compatibility code than it adds.

## Verification

Focused unit and async transport tests, MCP crate integration tests, the new `ferrogate-test` contract scenario, static gates, clippy, and full workspace tests. The external SDK fixture must run locally; GitHub Actions are not a fallback.

body:
## Problem

The control-plane client has three whole-registry sweeps for HTTP method/effect, mutation receipts, and action identity. All three were introduced into a tree that already contained the four-segment `asset-channels set` verb, while their shared prober tried only three, two, one, then zero segments. The sweeps therefore failed before reaching their assertions and had never completed successfully.

This was not a four-day regression and the crate was not absent from the workflow matrix:

- #363 added `asset-channels set` on 2026-07-23.
- #505 introduced the method and receipt sweeps on 2026-07-27 at 04:32 UTC.
- #548 introduced the identity sweep on 2026-07-27 at 13:13 UTC.
- `rust-cli-tooling-tests.yml` had selected the crate since #360 / `265555a` on 2026-07-23.
- The actual CI gap is that the composing `ci.yml` is `release: published` only, and no release after those tests were introduced executed them.

## Root Cause

The prober guessed accepted arities from builder behavior. That was circular: permissive builders accepted junk trailing segments, under-guarded builders accepted incomplete composite keys, and the fixed ceiling made a valid four-segment verb unconstructable.

The audit also found live under-addressing holes:

- quota-policy item verbs accepted only `scope_type` while the key is `scope_type/scope_id`;
- `tenant-roles bind` accepted no tenant path segment;
- `tenant-roles unbind` accepted fewer than the required tenant/role pair.

## Scope

- Derive exact probe arity from the enforced OpenAPI operation path and required query parameters.
- Declare any CLI positional query value explicitly in verb metadata.
- Make composite item builders reject incomplete keys.
- Accumulate failures with the owning group and verb name.
- Keep registry-family disappearance covered by the independent OpenAPI-to-CLI parity gate; keep request-shape correctness covered by these sweeps.

## Acceptance

- [ ] All registered API verbs build at their contract-required shape.
- [ ] Every addressed verb rejects one positional segment fewer.
- [ ] Arity coverage includes representative zero-, one-, two-, three-, and four-segment verbs.
- [ ] Method/effect, receipt, and identity sweeps name the failing verb and reach every registered verb.
- [ ] Quota-policy and tenant-role builders reject incomplete target keys.
- [ ] Review/test lanes execute the previously born-red sweeps and mutation checks.

Refs #363, #505, #548, #561.
