body:
Found while diagnosing a load average of **308.93** on an 8-core box during a routine dev-loop cycle.

## What was there

**106 orphaned `ferrogate run` processes**, every one `PPID=1` (reparented to init), every one launched by a test:

```
267195  14:05:47  /home/dev/rev518/target/debug/ferrogate run --config /tmp/.tmphLnUiO/ferrogate.toml
267197  14:05:47  /home/dev/rev518/target/debug/ferrogate run --config /tmp/.tmpC2Uuq7/ferrogate.toml
...
2434355  02:18:06  ...
```

- **Oldest: 14 hours 5 minutes.** Youngest: 2 hours 18 minutes. None was younger than two hours, so none belonged to a test running at the time.
- Every config path is a `/tmp/.tmpXXXXXX/ferrogate.toml` temp dir — the shape `crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/support/` writes.
- **No systemd unit exists**, so nothing was ever going to reap them.
- Combined: **~10.6% of system memory** and, at ~0.8% CPU each plus context-switching, the bulk of a load average that peaked above 370.

**This is not a today problem.** A large share came from `/home/dev/rev518/target/debug/ferrogate` — a *different checkout entirely*. The leak accumulates across sessions and across working trees.

## Why it matters beyond the load

- A wedged box makes every concurrent slice slower and, at 300+, unreliable. One agent in this cycle **died mid-run** with `Connection closed mid-response` while the load was at its peak.
- Each orphan holds a listening port. Port exhaustion or a bind collision would present as a *flaky test*, not as a leak — which is how this stays invisible.
- `/tmp` fills with config dirs that outlive their process.

## Where the gap is

`start_ready_gateway` / `start()` in `crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/support/mod.rs` spawn the binary. A `Drop` impl that kills the child covers the normal path, but **not**:

- a test that panics before the guard is constructed;
- `cargo test` being killed (Ctrl-C, a `timeout`, the harness's own fail-fast) — Rust runs no destructors on `SIGKILL`, and on `SIGTERM` only if a handler exists;
- a test binary that exits while the child is still starting.

Every one of those leaves the child alive and reparented.

## What would actually fix it

Not a better `Drop` — the cases above are exactly the ones `Drop` cannot reach. Options worth weighing:

1. **Kill the process group.** Spawn with `setsid`/`process_group(0)` and signal the group, so a child that outlives the harness still dies with it.
2. **`PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`** on Linux — the kernel kills the child when its parent dies. Precise, and it covers `SIGKILL` of the parent, which nothing in userspace can.
3. **A reaper the suite invokes at start** — sweep `ferrogate run --config /tmp/` processes older than N minutes before spawning. Ugly, but it also cleans up the backlog from previous runs, which 1 and 2 do not.
4. Make the temp dir's `Drop` refuse to unlink while its child lives, so a leak becomes a visible failure rather than a silent one.

1 or 2 is the real fix; 3 is worth having anyway because the backlog is already 106 deep on any machine that has run this suite for a day.

## Reproducing

```
ps -eo pid,ppid,etime,args | awk '$2==1 && /target\/debug\/ferrogate run/'
```

on any box that has run `cargo test -p ferrogate-cli` a few times.

**Cleanup, for anyone hitting this now** — note `pkill -f 'ferrogate run --config /tmp/'` **matches its own shell's command line and kills the shell** (exit 144). Collect PIDs first:

```
ps -eo pid,args | awk '/target\/debug\/ferrogate run/ && !/awk/ {print $1}' > /tmp/fg_pids.txt
xargs -r kill -TERM < /tmp/fg_pids.txt ; sleep 4 ; xargs -r kill -KILL < /tmp/fg_pids.txt
```

That took the load from 308 to 4.5.

Refs #561, #564.

body:
## What

Three tests in `crates/agent-worker` branch on `crate::docker_backend::docker_backend_readiness()` — a bare `docker version --format {{.Server.Version}}` probe:

- `docker_backend_test.rs:96` — `docker_backend_runs_full_lifecycle_against_real_container` (prepare, start, exec write, exec read, snapshot, cleanup against a real container)
- `management_test.rs:272` — `provision_fails_closed_when_docker_backend_enabled_but_daemon_unreachable` (skips when a daemon IS present)
- `management_test.rs:918` — `docker_backend_provisions_and_execs_through_management_api_when_enabled`

They do **not** gate on `AGENT_WORKER_ENABLE_DOCKER_BACKEND`; two of the three set it themselves, so the daemon probe is the real discriminator.

## Why it matters

The suite therefore runs a *different set of assertions* depending on whether the host has Docker, with nothing recording which set ran. On a developer box without a daemon you get the fail-closed assertion and two skips; on `ubuntu-latest` you get two live-container runs and lose the fail-closed one.

#561's rework pinned `AGENT_WORKER_DOCKER_BIN` to a nonexistent binary in `rust-platform-crate-tests.yml`'s `agent_worker` slice and in `run_platform_crates`, so CI runs the branch that was actually watched locally rather than a branch nobody has ever seen. That is the right call for a CI-wiring commit — it makes the workflow honest — but it leaves the real hole visible and unclosed:

**Nothing in CI exercises the Docker isolation backend end to end.** `IsolationBackendKind::Docker` is a shipped tier; its lifecycle is proven by a test that skips wherever it is run.

## Acceptance

1. A job (or an explicitly-opted-in leg of the existing one) that runs the live-Docker lifecycle on a runner with a daemon, so the result exists somewhere.
2. The three probes made deterministic: a test that self-skips should say so in a way a run log records, and the choice of branch should be an input, not an accident of the host. `AGENT_WORKER_ENABLE_DOCKER_BACKEND` is the existing opt-in and is documented as "must never be selected by accident just because a daemon happens to be running" — the tests should honour the same doctrine the backend registry does.
3. `provision_fails_closed_when_docker_backend_enabled_but_daemon_unreachable` should be runnable on a Docker host (point the probe at an unreachable binary rather than skipping), so the fail-closed assertion is not the one that disappears exactly where a daemon exists.

## Evidence the pin works, and that the branch really does flip

Observed locally on a box with no daemon:

```
AGENT_WORKER_DOCKER_BIN=echo    -> probe reports ready; docker_backend_runs_full_lifecycle_against_real_container
                                   takes the LIVE branch and panics at docker_backend_test.rs:129
AGENT_WORKER_DOCKER_BIN=agent-worker-docker-absent
                                -> "skipping docker lifecycle test: docker daemon not available", test passes
cargo test -p agent-worker --all-features (under the pin) -> 5 targets, 342 passed, 0 failed
```

Refs #561
title: [ci][agent-worker][P3] agent-worker's live-Docker lifecycle is exercised by no job, and its gate is a daemon probe rather than the opt-in

body:
## What

`scripts/check-secret-scan.sh` exits 1 on `main` at `3487459`:

```
==> high-confidence secret scan (engine: rg)
secret scan coverage: 1545/1545 tracked files are line-scannable
secret scan matched: private key material
Potential secrets found:
workers/agent-gateway/test/git-credential.test.ts:776:      GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY: "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----\nnot-a-key\n-----END PRIVATE KEY-----",
```

The literal is a deliberate *non*-key: the string body is `not-a-key`. It is a fixture for the git-credential broker's GitHub App path (landed with #475, last touched by #501).

## Why it matters

`run_quality` in `scripts/local-test-modules.sh` runs `scripts/check-secret-scan.sh`, and `set -euo pipefail` means the module aborts there — so every gate *after* it in that function (`scripts/test-check-secret-scan.sh`, `scripts/check-kubernetes-examples.sh`) is unreachable locally until this is resolved. `rust-quality.yml` reaches the same scan through `scripts/security-check.sh` with `FERROGATE_SECURITY_REQUIRE_TOOLS=1`.

This is the failure mode #525 was about, one step on: the scan now runs, and the first thing it found is a false positive nobody has adjudicated.

## What needs deciding

Not "silence it" — that is the choice that makes the next real match invisible. Two honest options:

1. **Make the fixture not look like a key.** The test does not need a PEM-shaped string; if the code under test only checks for the header, a shorter marker with no `-----BEGIN` may do. Cheapest, and leaves the scan with no exceptions surface at all.
2. **Give the scan a narrow, reviewed exception**, in the shape `scripts/check-audit-exceptions.py` already models for the audit gate — file + line + a reason, so an exception is a statement someone made rather than a pattern that quietly widens.

Whichever is chosen, `scripts/test-check-secret-scan.sh` should carry a case that fails if the mechanism starts exempting a *real* key.

## Not in scope of the finder

Found while reworking #561 (CI crate coverage). Untouched there: it is pre-existing on `main`, and `workers/` is not that slice's area.
title: [ci][P2] The secret scan is red on main: a not-a-key PEM literal in a Worker test fails scripts/check-secret-scan.sh

body:
## Why this exists

#500 proposed five things and landed **one** — item 4, the *"an assertion must be
able to fail"* standard in `AGENTS.md` + `docs/testing/testing-architecture.md`.
That slice is done and gate-passed. Items 1–3 are deferred **with a documented
reason**, but the deferral lives only in a doc, and #500 is closing. This issue
puts it on the board so it is not dropped.

Filed by the test gate on closing #500.

## What is deferred, and the reason given

`docs/testing/testing-architecture.md:304-325`:

> `cargo-mutants` is **not adopted yet** and is not installed on the dev boxes.
> […] Deliberately unresolved until someone runs it: the per-mutant test timeout
> on a suite this slow, whether each mutant should run the whole workspace suite
> or only the owning crate's, and therefore whether a `.cargo/mutants.toml` is
> worth having at all. No config is committed, because a filter config nobody has
> run `--list` against can silently examine nothing — which is the exact defect
> class this section exists to prevent.

That reasoning is sound and should be preserved: **do not commit a
`.cargo/mutants.toml` before running `--list` against it.** A mutants config that
silently examines nothing is the same shape as the suites #500 was filed about.

## Items 1–3, restated from #500

1. **Adopt `cargo-mutants`** for the crates carrying money, security and scheduling logic — `ferrogate-storage`, `ferrogate-runtime`, `ferrogate-cloudflare`, `agent-worker`, and the x402 modules. Report-only first, to establish a baseline rather than blocking day one.
2. **Set a floor on the load-bearing surfaces first** rather than chasing a global score: wallet/settlement, the egress-enforcement path, the due-scan filter, and every deny/allow decision. A surviving mutation on those is a bug, not a metric.
3. **Cover the Worker layer.** `vitest-pool-workers` boots these Workers offline in workerd (no Docker, no CF account), so this is reachable today — and as of `d2dc34f` the whole `agent-gateway` suite terminates again (7 files, 109 tests), which it did not when #500 was written.

## First step, concretely

Run `cargo mutants -p ferrogate-cloudflare --list` and time one real run on the
smallest of the four crates. That answers the three questions the doc leaves
open — per-mutant timeout, crate-scoped vs workspace-scoped test command, and
whether a config is worth having — with a measurement instead of a guess. Only
then decide about CI, where the bar is `AGENTS.md` → CI Workflow Structure.

## Acceptance

- [ ] One crate has a real `cargo mutants` run recorded — command, wall time, and the surviving-mutant count — in this thread.
- [ ] The three open questions in `testing-architecture.md:315-318` are answered from that run, and the doc updated.
- [ ] A floor is set on at least one load-bearing surface, with the surviving mutations on it either killed or filed as bugs.
- [ ] The Worker layer has at least one mutation-verified surface, or a stated reason it is not reachable yet.
- [ ] No `.cargo/mutants.toml` is committed without a `--list` run proving it examines what it claims to.

body:
#561's second gap, measured. `cargo test -p ferrogate-cli` is never run unfiltered anywhere — every workflow names individual `--test` targets, and 50 of the 63 targets in `crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/` are selected by nothing. Running it for the first time shows why that matters.

## Measurement

    CARGO_TARGET_DIR=... cargo test -p ferrogate-cli --all-features --no-fail-fast -j4 -- --test-threads=4

on `21f1495`, Linux aarch64, test binaries pre-built:

**65 test binaries, 352 passed, 13 failed, 0 ignored, 104s wall.** No hangs — every target terminated. `--no-fail-fast` is required to see this at all: without it cargo stops at `agent_jobs_e2e`, the first failing target alphabetically, and reports nothing about the other 60.

## The 13, by target

- `ai_proxy_dispatch_errors::streaming_pipeline_has_no_blocking_thread_shim` — `failed to read crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/dispatch.rs: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
- `control_cli_crud_round_trip_e2e` (5): `access_policy_crud_round_trip_pins_every_leg`, `project_crud_round_trip_pins_every_leg`, `quota_policy_crud_round_trip_pins_the_composite_key`, `tenant_account_crud_round_trip_pins_every_leg`, `workspace_crud_round_trip_pins_every_leg` — the mutation receipt's `target.resource_id.absent_reason.code` is `response_names_no_resource_id` or `null`; the test expects `collection_scoped_mutation`
- `tenant_isolation_admin_api::project_and_workspace_update_delete_are_tenant_scoped_and_reject_if_referenced` — the renamed project reads back `Null`, expected `"Renamed Project A"`
- `tenant_isolation_admin_api::tenant_scoped_admin_key_cannot_change_its_own_plan_or_status` — `tenant must not change its own account status: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request`
- `vpc_offline_loop_e2e::data_plane_survives_control_plane_interruption_on_last_known_good_snapshot` — `control-plane publisher failed to issue api key vpc-client-v2: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request`
- `agent_jobs_e2e::an_agent_job_is_submitted_idempotently_observed_collected_and_cancelled` — `Bool(true) != false`
- `asset_visibility_promotion_e2e::pending_scan_asset_is_promoted_visible_and_quarantined_with_audit_evidence` — `push failed: HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted`
- `asset_withheld_listing_e2e::withheld_listing_surfaces_pending_and_quarantined_with_evidence_scoped_and_paginated` — same shape
- `tenant_suspension_e2e::a_tenant_can_re_enable_the_project_it_disabled` — panics on `secret`

None of these need docker, a live Supabase DSN or a cloud credential; they are hermetic in-process e2e suites. The genuinely credential-bound targets (`supabase_storage_s3_live`, `vertex_provider_e2e`, `bedrock_provider_e2e`) all **passed** — they self-skip cleanly, so they are not the reason the unfiltered run is unwired.

## Two families are visible without deep triage

1. **#553 fallout.** `ai_proxy_dispatch_errors` reads `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/dispatch.rs` by hard-coded path; #553 stage 3b (`a772842`) moved that whole tree to `crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/server/`. Same defect class as the three `asset_bucket.rs` source-scan allow-lists #561 fixes: a structural guard that silently stopped looking at anything when the directory moved.
2. **HTTP 400 on admin mutations** in `vpc_offline_loop_e2e` and `tenant_isolation_admin_api`, in the same week #540 made an API key declaring neither `organization_id` nor `platform_operator` a hard refusal. Not confirmed. The other two families (`control_cli_crud_round_trip_e2e`'s receipt reasons, the asset `202 Accepted` pair) look unrelated to either.

## Consequence for #561

#561 wires CI slices only for suites it watched pass, so it does **not** add an unfiltered `cargo test -p ferrogate-cli` job — a job that is red on arrival gets disabled by the next person. The 50 unselected targets stay unselected until these 13 are resolved. That is the deferral this issue tracks.

Refs #561, #553, #540, #500

body:
Found while doing #561's triage: running `cargo test -p ferrogate-gateway --all-features` for the first time (the crate is compiled by CI and executed by no job) leaves four failures after the #553 path-rename fallout is fixed.

## The failures

`cargo test -p ferrogate-gateway --all-features` on `21f1495` + #561's allow-list fix: **1063 passed, 4 failed, 0 ignored, 2.4s.**

    state::state_quota_and_policy::state_quota_and_policy_test::signed_shared_snapshot_verifies_activates_and_rejects_forgery
    state::state_quota_and_policy::state_quota_and_policy_test::signed_snapshot_replay_floor_advances_on_local_publish
    state::state_quota_and_policy::state_quota_and_policy_test::signed_snapshot_replay_floor_persists_across_restart
    state::state_quota_and_policy::state_quota_and_policy_test::unsigned_shared_snapshots_are_unaffected_by_the_persisted_replay_floor

All four panic in the same place, on `cfg.validate().expect("config valid")`:

> refusing to start: these API keys declare neither organization_id nor platform_operator, so they have no tenant identity to authorize against and would be refused at authentication (tenant_identity_required)

## Cause

`crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/state_quota_and_policy_test.rs:2307`:

```rust
fn signed_snapshot_test_api_key(id: &str) -> ferrogate_config::ApiKey {
    serde_json::from_value(serde_json::json!({
        "id": id,
        "name": id,
        "key": format!("{id}-secret"),
        "scopes": ["chat.completions"],
    }))
    .expect("valid test api key")
}
```

It declares neither `organization_id` nor `platform_operator`. #540 (`0c4493c`, "Make platform root something a config says, never something it omits") made exactly that shape a hard `Config::validate()` refusal. The fixture was not updated, and nothing noticed, because nothing has ever executed this crate's suite.

## Why this is not fixed here

The fix is one field on the fixture, but *which* field is a call about what #540 means for a cluster-snapshot node key. `platform_operator = true` reproduces the pre-#540 behaviour these tests were written against and is what #540's own error text recommends for preserving it; `organization_id = "tenant-a"` matches `cfg.cluster.snapshot_tenant_id`, which those tests already set. Those are not the same test. The four tests are about replay floors and signature verification, so the tenancy of the key is incidental to them — but "incidental" is the sort of judgement that belongs to whoever owns #540, not to a CI-wiring slice.

## Until then

#561 lands a `ferrogate-gateway` CI slice that runs the other 1,063 tests and carries four `--skip` filters naming these tests and this issue. Delete the skips with the fix.

Refs #561, #540

body:
## Problem

`cargo test -p ferrogate-gateway` is red on `main` (`8adfc3d`): **1060 passed, 7 failed**.

```
server::asset_bucket::tests::the_buffering_bucket_read_is_only_called_from_the_bounded_chokepoint
server::asset_bucket::tests::every_inlined_asset_entry_forwards_its_charge_to_the_response
server::asset_bucket::tests::uncharged_buffers_are_only_minted_on_the_inline_content_paths
state::state_quota_and_policy::state_quota_and_policy_test::signed_shared_snapshot_verifies_activates_and_rejects_forgery
state::state_quota_and_policy::state_quota_and_policy_test::signed_snapshot_replay_floor_advances_on_local_publish
state::state_quota_and_policy::state_quota_and_policy_test::signed_snapshot_replay_floor_persists_across_restart
state::state_quota_and_policy::state_quota_and_policy_test::unsigned_shared_snapshots_are_unaffected_by_the_persisted_replay_floor
```

Both groups were last touched by `a772842` — *(#553 stage 3b) Move the gateway
trunk and the state it runs on out of the CLI* — i.e. the crate split, not by any
behaviour change.

## Why the asset_bucket ones are the interesting half

They are **source-scanning guards** (the `#480`/`#526` family), and the split
moved the files out from under their path assumptions. The failure output is the
tell — the scanner now reports the chokepoint's own file as a violation of
itself:

```
these call the buffering bucket read outside the bounded chokepoint --
route them through asset_bucket::read_object_bounded …
server/asset_bucket.rs:360: match bucket.get_object(key, declared_size_bytes).await {
server/asset_bucket.rs:394: self.as_ref().get_object(key, max_bytes).await
server/asset_bucket.rs:585: self.get_object_if_present(key, max_bytes)
server/asset_bucket.rs:2206: .get_object("tenant-a:cli_tool:liar:1.0.0", 64 * 1024)
```

Line 2206 is inside a `#[cfg(test)]` fixture. So the scan is not finding real
violations; its notion of "which file is the chokepoint" and "which lines are test
code" did not survive `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/` →
`crates/ferrogate-gateway/src/server/`.

That matters more than an ordinary red: these guards are the repo's answer to
#500, and a guard that fails for a path reason teaches people to ignore it. The
fix is to re-derive the paths (or the exemptions) from the new layout, **not** to
add the reported lines to an allowlist.

## Reproduce

```
cargo test -j4 -p ferrogate-gateway --locked
```

`-j4`, not `-j8` — `-j8` OOM-kills this box.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `cargo test -p ferrogate-gateway` is green.
- [ ] The asset_bucket scans are fixed by correcting their path/`cfg(test)` derivation, not by exempting the sites they now report — state which was wrong.
- [ ] Mutation-verify each repaired scan still bites: an actual unbounded `get_object` call outside the chokepoint must still fail the test after the repair.
- [ ] Say what the four `state_quota_and_policy` signed-snapshot failures were — if they are also path/fixture drift from the split rather than a signing regression, record that, because "signed snapshot verification broke" reads much worse than it is.

Found by the test gate while gating #543 (whose own tests are green and unaffected).

title: [gateway-core][P1] main is red: 7 ferrogate-gateway tests fail after the #553 crate split, including three source-scanning guards that now report their own chokepoint

body:
Found while reworking #553. Not a #553 regression by itself, but #553 created the crate that makes it severe, so it is filed rather than left in a doc comment.

> **Corrections, 2026-07-27 (#553 rework 2).** Every count below was one high, because the survey grepped `#[test]` unanchored and its own text contained the string in backticks; the baseline line count was the *published* figure for a different commit rather than a re-measurement at `8adfc3d`; the title said 1,066 while the body said 1,069; and `agent-worker` belonged on the list and was missing. All four are fixed in place below. The re-derivation used `^\s*#\[test\]\s*$` and `^\s*#\[tokio::test` against `git ls-tree -r 8adfc3d`.

## The gap

No GitHub workflow selects `-p ferrogate-gateway`. Parsing every `package:` matrix key and every `-p <crate>` selector across `.github/workflows/*.yml`, the workspace members that **no** workflow ever names are:

- `ferrogate-gateway`
- `ferrogate-cloudflare`
- `ferrogate-payments`
- `ferrogate-secrets`
- `ferrogate-sync-bridge`
- `agent-worker` — reachable only from `firecracker-boot-validation.yml`, which is `workflow_dispatch`-only and needs a KVM self-hosted runner, and even there only via `--test firecracker_boot_validation`. So it is not CI coverage, and the other 341 tests ran nowhere.

Measured on `main` at `8adfc3d`:

| crate | `.rs` lines | `#[test]` | `#[tokio::test]` | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ferrogate-gateway` | 136,215 | 962 | 105 | 1,067 |
| `agent-worker` | 34,953 | 342 | 0 | 342 |
| `ferrogate-cloudflare` | 6,833 | 115 | 0 | 115 |
| `ferrogate-payments` | 3,560 | 47 | 0 | 47 |
| `ferrogate-secrets` | 2,770 | 50 | 0 | 50 |
| `ferrogate-sync-bridge` | 80 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

So **1,067 tests in the largest crate in the workspace (136,215 of 431,719 `crates/` lines, 31.6%) are compiled by CI and executed by no job.** That includes `auth_test.rs`, `server/rbac_test.rs`, `server/guardrail_policies_test.rs`, `auth_admission_test.rs` and `tenant_scope_reads_fault.rs` — the tenant-scope and RBAC enforcement tests.

`scripts/local-test-modules.sh`, which mirrors the CI slices for local runs, has the same gap: `run_cli_tooling` omits both the `cli_e2e` and the control-plane-client slices that `rust-cli-tooling-tests.yml` has, and no function names `ferrogate-gateway` or `ferrogate-guardrails`.

## The more severe half: `ci.yml` runs on `release: published` and nothing else

This was unstated in the original filing and it changes what every number above is worth. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` declares:

```yaml
on:
  release:
    types: [published]
```

No `push`, no `pull_request`, no `workflow_dispatch`. `rust-quality.yml` and the per-slice test workflows are reusable workflows reachable from nothing else, so:

- no Rust test runs in CI on any commit, only when a release is cut;
- `ferrogate-gateway` has never been compiled or tested by CI at all, because it was created after the last release;
- the gate this issue asked for (`scripts/check-ci-crate-coverage.py`) is likewise a release-time backstop plus a local habit, not a per-commit check;
- "compiles in CI" claims written in doc comments about this crate are optimistic.

The trigger is a deliberate runner-spend decision, recorded in `ci.yml`'s own comment and in `AGENTS.md`. It is recorded here because "a workflow selects the crate" and "the crate is tested" are two different statements, and only the first has been fixed.

## Second, related gap: most of `ferrogate-cli`'s integration corpus is unselected

`cargo test -p ferrogate-cli` is never run unfiltered; every workflow names individual `--test` targets. Counting those selectors at `8adfc3d`: **13 of the 63 targets in `crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/` are selected (14,224 lines); 50 targets and 26,571 lines are selected by no workflow**, including `asset_presign_e2e` (3,278), `tenant_isolation_admin_api` (1,663), `control_cli_crud_round_trip_e2e` (1,399) and `config_catalog_scope_admin_api` (1,291).

Some of those legitimately cannot run on a hosted runner as written (`supabase_storage_s3_live`, `vertex_provider_e2e`, `bedrock_provider_e2e` need live credentials). That explains part of the list; it does not explain `tenant_isolation_admin_api`.

## Why it was not fixed in place

Adding a `ferrogate-gateway` slice is a two-line change to `rust-cli-tooling-tests.yml` (or a new workflow), but nobody had executed that suite in CI, so landing the job as part of an unrelated rename slice would be asserting a green run no one has seen — exactly the #500 failure mode. It needed someone to run the tests, triage what is red or environment-dependent, and land the job with that answer in hand.

## Suggested shape, and what has landed

1. ~~Run `cargo test -p ferrogate-gateway --all-features` and triage.~~ **Done** — 1,067 passed, 0 failed, 0 filtered out, after #563 removed the four `--skip` filters the first attempt needed.
2. ~~Add a gateway slice plus slices for `ferrogate-cloudflare`, `ferrogate-payments`, `ferrogate-secrets`.~~ **Done** — `rust-platform-crate-tests.yml`, which also covers `ferrogate-sync-bridge` and `agent-worker`.
3. Triage the 50 unselected `ferrogate-cli` targets into "runnable in CI" and "needs live credentials", and mark the second group explicitly (a feature gate or `#[ignore]` with a reason) so the distinction is visible rather than inferred from a workflow's absence. **Still open — this is what is left of this issue.**
4. ~~Re-sync `scripts/local-test-modules.sh` with the workflow matrices, and add a gate that fails when a workspace member is named by no slice.~~ **Done** — `scripts/check-ci-crate-coverage.py`.
5. **Added by #553 rework 2:** the same gate now also fails when a `cargo test` *name filter* matches no test. Step 4 alone could not have caught `governed-decision-conformance.yml` running `cargo test -p ferrogate-cli --bin ferrogate governed_decision` after #553 moved the file to `ferrogate-gateway` — `ferrogate-cli` *is* named by that line, so the crate-level check was satisfied while libtest exited 0 having run nothing. Three filters in the tree were in that state.

Item 4 was the durable fix for "a new crate appears and nothing points at it"; item 5 is the durable fix for "a file leaves a crate and the filter that named it stays behind".

Refs #553, #500, #560
title: No workflow runs ferrogate-gateway's 1,067 tests, and 50 of ferrogate-cli's 63 test targets are selected by nothing

body:
Raised by the dev agent that executed #553 stage 3b (`a772842`), in its own words:

> **`ferrogate-gateway` is now the blob, renamed.** `server/` holds the Pingora proxy *and* a ~50-resource Admin API surface in one directory; `state` is one `AppState` with 20+ `state_*` submodules. **This slice bought the crate boundary, not the decomposition.**

Filed separately because it is a new issue's worth of work, not a stage of #553. #553's acceptance is met and should close on its own terms.

## Measured on `main` = `d40c7b9`

| | files | lines |
|---|---|---|
| `ferrogate-gateway/src/server/` | **82** | **72,677** |
| `ferrogate-gateway/src/state*.rs` | **44** | **41,838** |
| whole crate | 161 | 135,087 |

Largest files:

```
11,842  server/local.rs
 7,475  state.rs
 4,706  state_agent_runtime.rs
 4,235  server/chat.rs
 3,916  server/asset_bucket.rs
```

## Why this is worth its own issue rather than "it's fine now"

#553's diagnosis was that **`ferrogate-cli` had no API boundary, so nothing ever forced a decision about what was public, so the crate absorbed every new subsystem.** That is fixed: `ferrogate-gateway` has a stated 22-item public surface and `ferrogate-cli` is 5,629 lines.

But the *internal* structure that let 154k lines accumulate travelled intact. Two things in particular:

1. **`server/` mixes two subsystems.** The Pingora data plane and the Admin API control surface are in one directory with no boundary between them — `local.rs` alone is 11,842 lines and carries the Admin API. Every concurrent slice in this repo's dev loop collides there; during one session `local.rs` was touched by four slices (#515, #535, #519, #528).
2. **`state` is one `AppState` with 44 files hanging off it.** `state_*.rs` keep their flat prefix at the crate root — deliberately, to preserve every `#[path]` attribute and `crate::state::` path during the move — but the result is a 44-file god object whose submodules are related only by sharing a struct.

`scripts/check-module-layout.py` exists precisely because entry files grow unbounded here. It passes today only because `lib.rs` is 211 lines: the mass moved into `server/mod.rs` and `state.rs`, which carry their own submodule declarations.

## What a first slice should probably do

Not a big-bang. The staging discipline from #553 worked and should be reused:

- **Separate the Admin API from the data plane inside `server/`.** They have different callers, different auth posture, and different change cadence. This is the split with the highest collision-relief value.
- **Ask whether `AppState` should be one type.** 44 submodules on one struct is the same "nothing forces a decision" shape one level down. A first step could be identifying which `state_*` groups have no cross-references.
- **Keep it move-only per slice**, with the public surface derived from compiler errors rather than declared — that method produced 22 `pub` items out of 1,301 in stage 3b and is worth keeping.

## Explicit non-goal

Behaviour change. Same rule as #553: a refactor that also fixes things is a refactor nobody can review, and this repo's review lane reads diffs without building them.

## Note on sequencing

There is no urgency that competes with correctness work. #553 took the crate boundary because the *cross-crate* edges were what blocked parallel development; the intra-crate ones are cheaper to live with. This should be scheduled when it is the most valuable thing available, not ahead of open P1s.

Refs #553, #505.
title: [architecture][P2] ferrogate-gateway bought a crate boundary, not a decomposition — server/ is 82 files in one directory and state is one AppState with 44

body:
## Problem

`npm test` in `workers/agent-gateway` **never terminates**. Any test that drives
`POST /control/destroy` hangs the vitest-pool-workers runner indefinitely, taking
the whole Worker's suite with it.

Observed at `1ec7e25`. Isolated with a single-test filter, which is what makes the
cause unambiguous:

```
vitest run test/destroy-alarm.test.ts -t "predates the compatibility date"
    -> 1 passed | 2 skipped, exits in seconds        (does NOT touch destroy)

vitest run test/destroy-alarm.test.ts -t "no alarm survives"
    -> killed at 300s, exit 124                      (drives POST /control/destroy)
```

Same file, same runner, same node_modules. The discriminator is the destroy route.

## Mechanism, in workerd's own words

```
uncaught exception; exception = workerd/api/actor-state.c++:1178:
  failed: broken.outputGateBroken; jsg.Error: destroyed
```

(5 occurrences in one `lifecycle.test.ts` run before the timeout.)

`destroyRun` ends in the Agents SDK's `destroy()`, whose final step is
`ctx.abort("destroyed")` (`src/index.ts:395-408` documents this deliberately).
Aborting the Durable Object breaks its **output gate**; workerd then raises the
uncaught exception above repeatedly and the pool never settles, so vitest waits
forever instead of finishing the file.

`await this.destroy()` landed in `e3ed951` (#414). Before it, `deleteAll()` alone
left the object intact and the runner terminated.

## Blast radius

Three of the seven test files in this Worker cannot run:

- `test/destroy-alarm.test.ts` — 2 of 3 tests (this is #482's guard; #482 was gate-rejected because of it)
- `test/control.test.ts` — hangs
- `test/lifecycle.test.ts` — hangs

`test/git-credential.test.ts` (24 passed, 1.9s), `git-credential-egress` and
`git-credential-leak` (14 passed) are fine and DO reach the Durable Object via
`runStub`, so this is not "the DO cannot boot in workerd" — it is specifically the
abort.

`scripts/check-workers.sh` runs `npm test` for every Worker with a
`vitest.config.ts`, so this hangs that gate too — it does not fail, it *hangs*,
which is worse: a CI job that never returns reads as "still running", not as red.

## Environment caveat, stated plainly

The corrupted `~/.npm/_cacache` (`Unknown system error -117`) and the #468
out-of-sync lockfile forced me to reinstall this Worker's `node_modules` with
`npm install --legacy-peer-deps --cache /tmp/...` during the #501 gate, so the
dependency set is not pristine. I cannot fully exclude that a correct install
handles the abort gracefully. What argues against that reading: the same
node_modules runs 38 tests across three other files, including ones that exercise
the Durable Object, and the single-test discriminator above localizes the hang to
the destroy path rather than the toolchain.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `npm test` in `workers/agent-gateway` terminates, and the three affected files run.
- [ ] `POST /control/destroy` is exercised by a test that *completes* — the destroy semantics must stay covered, not be deleted to make the runner terminate.
- [ ] Say which side was changed and why: the test harness (e.g. isolated storage per test, or asserting the abort-rejection without leaving the pool waiting) or the abort itself. Do not disable `ctx.abort()` in production code purely to satisfy the runner without saying so.
- [ ] Verify by inverting: with the fix in place, a destroy that fails to abort must still be caught by something.

title: [cloudflare][ci][P1] agent-gateway npm test never terminates: ctx.abort("destroyed") breaks the DO output gate and hangs vitest-pool-workers

body:
Found by the dev agent while reworking #482 (`0b3d16c`), each confirmed by reading the pinned `agents@0.0.109` bundle. Filed together because they share one root: **the scheduler never consults run lifecycle state, and nothing ever calls `deleteAlarm()` except `destroy()`.**

## (a) `cancel` is #482 for a different verb

`"stopped"` is not in `TERMINAL_STATUSES`, and `dispatchScheduledTask` reads no run status at all. So a **cancelled** run's schedules keep firing: the alarm re-arms, the Durable Object wakes, and work runs for a run the caller explicitly cancelled and paid to stop.

This is the same shape as #482 (a destroyed run waking itself), and closely related to #551's finding that a cancel must guarantee the work *stops* rather than that a particular dispatch exists.

## (b) Destroy is not a latch

`scheduleCreate` never checks `state.runId` or `state.status`. So a `POST /schedule/create` **after** `/control/destroy` arms a fresh alarm on a `cleaned_up` instance name — resurrecting an instance that was explicitly torn down. #482 closed the path where destroy *left* an alarm behind; this is the path where a caller can *add* one afterwards.

## (c) `scheduleCancel` on the last schedule leaves an armed alarm

`_scheduleNextAlarm()` (`agents@0.0.109`, `dist/chunk-3IQQY2UH.js:863-875`) only ever calls `setAlarm()` — it never calls `deleteAlarm()`. So cancelling the final schedule leaves the previously-armed alarm in place. The DO wakes once with nothing to do.

Least severe of the three (one spurious wake, no work executed), but it is the mechanism that makes (a) and (b) persistent rather than self-healing, and it is why #482's fix had to be `destroy()` rather than `deleteAll()`.

## Suggested scope

- Have `dispatchScheduledTask` consult run lifecycle state, and decide deliberately which statuses suppress a fire — `TERMINAL_STATUSES` currently omits `"stopped"`, which looks like an oversight rather than a decision.
- Make `scheduleCreate` refuse on a destroyed/cleaned-up instance.
- Call `deleteAlarm()` when the last schedule is cancelled.

## Test bar

The #482 rework is the cautionary tale here: its schedule-count assertion **greens on the broken implementation**, because `deleteAll()` wipes the SQL tables and the Agent constructor's `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` rebuilds them empty — so `count: 0` is satisfied either way. That test is now named to say so.

For all three items above, assert on **alarm state** (`ctx.storage.getAlarm()`) and on **whether the task actually fired**, not on a schedule-row count. A row count cannot distinguish "cleaned up" from "wiped and recreated empty". Per #500, state the mutation each new assertion catches.

Refs #482, #426, #413, #551.
title: [cloudflare][agent-worker][P2] Three more agent-gateway schedule/lifecycle leaks in the #482 family

body:
Split out of #471. The prevention half of #471 is observed by an offline workerd
suite (`workers/agent-gateway/test/container-egress.test.ts`), which stops at the
platform boundary by design: workerd has no container engine, so it can pin the
posture the platform is handed and what Cloudflare's own decision function does
with it, and nothing beyond that.

Everything below needs a real Cloudflare account, a bound `CONTAINER_SANDBOX`,
and a running container. Until it is run, `docs/cloudflare-container-isolation.md`
states plainly that FerroGate does **not** have first-party proof that a process
inside the container cannot reach a provider directly.

## Gate items

1. **Sealed instance cannot reach a provider.** Start sealed, `exec`
   `curl -sS https://api.anthropic.com/v1/models`. Must fail (520 / connection
   refused), not return a provider response.
2. **Tethered instance cannot reach a provider.** `CONTAINER_GOVERNED_EGRESS_HOSTS`
   set to only the gateway host. The gateway host must be reachable and
   `api.anthropic.com` must still fail — proving `setDeniedHosts` overrides the
   allowlist.
3. **Non-HTTP sockets are denied.** Raw TCP on e.g. 8443, and a UDP send.
4. **HTTPS interception actually filters rather than breaking.** #471 pins
   `AgentSandbox { interceptHttps = true }` (the pinned
   `@cloudflare/containers@0.3.7` defaults it **false**, and
   `@cloudflare/sandbox@0.12.4` never sets it, which would have left the provider
   denylist bound to plaintext HTTP only). Confirm on the deployed image that:
   the container trusts `/etc/cloudflare/certs/cloudflare-containers-ca.crt`;
   HTTPS to the governed gateway host still works; HTTPS to a provider is
   refused. **If the image does not trust the CA, HTTPS breaks entirely** —
   fail-closed and loud, but it would take the tether down with it.
5. **In-container bypass of `enableInternet = false`.** The evidence table marks
   "can code inside the container turn egress back on?" as **assumed** — Cloudflare
   does not state it in the negative and we have never tried. As root inside the
   container, attempt to defeat the filter: rewrite `/etc/resolv.conf`, add
   routes, bind a raw socket, drop the injected CA, talk to the proxy sidecar
   directly, and reach a provider IP literal without DNS. Record what happens.
   This is the single assumption the whole tier rests on.
6. **HTTPS from a client that does NOT trust the interception CA.** Undocumented
   by Cloudflare. We assume TLS validation fails (fail-closed) rather than the
   connection passing through uninspected. Settle it.
7. **Sealed reuse.** Start instance name `N` tethered, then start `N` sealed, then
   `exec` a request to the previously allowed gateway host from inside. It must
   fail. (`allowedHostsOverride` is persisted to DO storage; #471's rework resets
   both lists on the sealed path, and this is the live counterpart of the offline
   test.)
8. **Attestation.** `/container/start` with `enableInternet: true` returns 422,
   and a start response missing the `egress` attestation fails the Rust-side start.

Refs #471, #415, #404.

body:
Split out of #471 as an **explicit deferral**, so acceptance item 3's detection
half is tracked rather than silently unmet.

## Where #471 left it

`crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/cloudflare_container_tether_audit.rs` lands the
typed seam and nothing else calls it: `grep -rn "TetherAuditor\|tether_audit"
crates/` returns only the module, its own tests, three doc-comment cross
references, and the re-export at `lib.rs:97`. Because no provider usage source is
wired, **every run reconciles to `Unattested`** — which is honest (`Unattested`
is a distinct verdict and never a pass, and `is_proven_tethered()` is `true` only
for `Tethered`) but it means the detection path has never fired in anger.

#471 therefore ships prevention that is observed by tests and detection that is
only a type. `docs/cloudflare-container-isolation.md` states this in the residual
risk section; this issue is the work that removes it.

## Why it was deferred rather than faked

Each provider has its own usage/billing API, its own attribution key, and its own
reporting lag. Wiring one is not a line of glue: it is a credential path, a
polling window, a reconciliation tolerance, and a false-positive budget per
provider. Wiring a stub that always returns zero would manufacture a false
total-bypass alarm; wiring one that returns the gateway's own numbers would
manufacture a false pass. Both are worse than `Unattested`.

## Scope

- Implement `RunUsageSource` over at least one real provider usage API, with the
  attribution key that ties provider-side usage back to a FerroGate run.
- Call `TetherAuditor::audit` on run completion for the CF container tier and
  persist/emit the `TetherReconciliation`.
- Alarm on `Breached` (severity critical) and surface `Unattested` distinctly, so
  "we could not check" is never rendered as "we checked and it was clean".
- A test that makes the detection path **fire**: a scripted provider source
  reporting tokens the gateway never metered must produce `Breached` end to end,
  through the wiring, not only through the module's own unit tests.
- Update the residual-risk item (6) in `docs/cloudflare-container-isolation.md`
  and the #428 budget note once a run can reconcile to `Tethered`.

Refs #471, #428, #404.

body:
Found by the dev agent while landing #542 (`909c70a`); deliberately not wired in that slice because it needs its own design.

## The gap

#542 added `lifecycle::ensure_auth_posture_is_declared(&config)`, called from `gateway::serve` before anything binds. It refuses two configurations:

1. auth required with **no credential source** (no `[[api_keys]]`, no enabled `[auth_service]`, no durable Postgres/Supabase `[storage]`) — exits non-zero with a message naming `[auth]\ndisabled = true`;
2. the contradiction — `[auth] disabled = true` **alongside** a declared static credential.

`state.rs:796` `reload_process_local` does **not** run that gate. So the contradiction case can be introduced at runtime through `POST /admin/v1/config/reload`, even though startup refuses it.

## Why it was not simply wired in

`reload_from_source_path` merges the durable control plane into `candidate.api_keys` (`state.rs:786`). So by the time the candidate config reaches the point where the gate would run, it carries keys that did not come from the file — and the startup contradiction check misfires against them. Reusing the startup predicate verbatim would reject legitimate reloads on any deployment with durable keys. The gate needs a reload-specific formulation that distinguishes file-declared credentials from control-plane-merged ones.

## Severity: the dangerous direction is already closed

Worth stating plainly so this is not read as a live auth bypass. Reload can only reach the **open** posture by carrying the named switch `[auth] disabled = true` — never by omission. The predicate is `!self.auth.disabled` and reads one field, so an operator cannot accidentally reload into an unauthenticated gateway. What can be reached is the *contradiction* state (open posture declared while static credentials exist), which startup would have refused. That is a consistency defect, not a privilege escalation.

## Ask

- [ ] Decide the reload-time formulation of the auth-posture check, given that `candidate.api_keys` contains control-plane-merged entries by that point — most likely by checking the file-declared set before the merge.
- [ ] Apply it in `reload_process_local`, so a config startup would refuse cannot be introduced by reload.
- [ ] A test that a reload carrying the contradiction is rejected, and one that a legitimate reload on a durable-key deployment still succeeds — the second is what makes the first non-trivial.

Refs #542.
title: [gateway-core][auth][P2] Config reload bypasses the #542 auth-posture startup gate

body:
Found by the dev agent while landing #542 (`909c70a`); deliberately left out of that slice to keep it narrow.

## The problem

`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth_test.rs` has roughly 15 durable-key tests carrying `api_keys: vec![decoy_yaml_key()]`. The decoy is not an input under test — it exists **solely to make `auth_required()` return true** under the old predicate `auth_service.enabled || !api_keys.is_empty()`.

That convention is exactly what hid #542 for as long as it existed: every durable-key test passed while the predicate was broken, because each one silently supplied the static key that switched authentication on. The single test that omitted it (#515's `durable_virtual_key_is_never_platform_root`) went red immediately, which is how the defect was finally found.

## Why it still matters after #542

#542 changed the predicate to `!self.auth.disabled`, so the decoy no longer *does* anything. But it is now worse than dead weight: these tests present the durable secret and would pass either way, **and the decoy would keep `auth_required()` true if someone reverted to credential-counting.** So the fixtures actively mask a revert of the fix.

`durable_virtual_key_is_never_platform_root` had its decoy removed in #542 and now reds if the old predicate returns. The rest did not.

## Ask

- [ ] Drop `api_keys: vec![decoy_yaml_key()]` from the remaining durable-key fixtures in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth_test.rs`, so each one pins the #542 predicate rather than compensating for its absence.
- [ ] Confirm by mutation: restoring `auth_service.enabled || !api_keys.is_empty()` should red these tests, not leave them green.
- [ ] If any test genuinely needs a static key as an *input* (rather than as an auth-required switch), keep it and say so in a comment, so the next reader can tell the two uses apart.

This is the #500 defect shape — a green suite that does not hold the code — in its fixture-convention form. Refs #542, #515, #500.
title: [auth][testing][P3] Remaining decoy_yaml_key() durable fixtures would mask a revert of #542

body:
Owner directive, 2026-07-27: *"抽出 ferrogate-gateway(数据面 + Admin API + 控制面状态),让 ferrogate-cli 回归为二进制入口 + 命令装配。"*

## The measurement that prompted it

| crate | LOC | files |
|---|---|---|
| **ferrogate-cli** | **154,329** | **200** |
| ferrogate-storage | 65,694 | 75 |
| ferrogate-runtime | 39,821 | 67 |
| agent-worker | 31,984 | 34 |
| ferrogate-cli-core | 17,021 | 51 |
| … | | |
| **ferrogate-core** | **215** | **1** |

`ferrogate-cli` is **42% of the workspace**. Inside it: `gateway/` with 93 modules (the data plane — `chat.rs`, `local.rs` at 11,821 lines carrying the Admin API, `asset_bucket.rs`, `virtual_keys.rs`), `state.rs` at 7,442 lines (control-plane state), plus `config/`, `acme.rs`, `dashboard.rs`.

**`ferrogate-core` being small is not the defect.** 215 lines, 10 public items (`RequestContext`, `TenantContext`, `WorkspaceScope`, `ToolDef/Call/Result`, `GatewayError`), and **nine crates depend on it**. It is the shared vocabulary that lets storage, auth, runtime, providers, billing and mcp agree on the same types *without depending on each other*. A vocabulary crate should be small; the question to ask of it is whether it is missing types that belong at that layer, not why it is short.

## The structural cause, and why it matters more than the line count

**`ferrogate-cli` is a bin-only crate.** No `lib.rs` — just `main.rs` with ~30 `mod` declarations, everything `pub(crate)`.

So **nothing has ever forced a decision about what is public.** There is no API boundary to violate, therefore none was ever designed, therefore the crate absorbed every new subsystem. The 154k lines are a symptom; the absent boundary is the cause.

Corroborating evidence: **#505 had to create `ferrogate-cli-core` (17,021 lines) to hold the CLI command machinery.** The actual CLI was extracted *out of* `ferrogate-cli`. When X needs an `X-core` to hold X, the name has stopped describing the contents.

## The cost is already being paid

- Every subagent brief in the current dev loop has to hand-fence `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/*`, because unrelated slices collide there. `local.rs` alone was touched by four concurrent slices (#515, #535, #519, #528) in one session.
- With the parallel-agent ceiling raised to 6, the throughput bottleneck is no longer agent slots — it is **how many slices land in the same oversized crate**.
- `scripts/check-module-layout.py` exists precisely because entry files grow unbounded here (`ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs` sits under an 18,600-line cap).

## Design

**Target shape**

- `ferrogate-gateway` (new) — the Pingora data plane, the Admin API surface, and control-plane state. Everything currently under `gateway/`, plus `state*.rs`.
- `ferrogate-cli` — binary entry, argument parsing, command wiring, `ctl`, and the operator-facing subcommands. What the name says.
- `ferrogate-core` — unchanged in role; see the open question below.

**Staging.** This must not be one atomic 154k-line move. Rebase conflicts on moved files are brutal, and this repo has 3-6 slices in flight at any moment.

**Stage 1 — create the boundary, move nothing.** Give `ferrogate-cli` a `lib.rs`; `main.rs` becomes a thin binary over it. Nearly free (the crate is unchanged, so every `pub(crate)` stays valid) and it is the change that makes every later step mechanical: from then on, moving a module is a visibility question with a compiler answer, not a judgement call.

**Stage 2 — extract leaf subsystems first**, in dependency order, one slice each: the ones with no inbound edges from the rest of `gateway/`. Each stage is a `git mv` plus a visibility pass, and each must land green before the next starts.

**Stage 3 — the trunk**: `local.rs`, `state.rs`, `chat.rs`. These are the collision-heavy files; schedule them when the board is quiet, not alongside feature work.

**Stage 4 — delete the seam**: `ferrogate-cli` keeps only entry + wiring; anything left that is neither is a finding.

**Rule for new code, effective immediately and worth more than any single stage:** new gateway-shaped code goes to `ferrogate-gateway`. The extraction competes with feature work for time; the rule does not.

## Open question to settle in stage 1, not later

Which types belong in `ferrogate-core`? `AuthContext` and `CallerScope` currently live in `ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs`, and #515's whole lesson was that **tenant identity must have exactly one interpreter**. If the gateway crate and the CLI crate both need to reason about a caller's scope, that type is vocabulary and belongs one layer down. Decide this in stage 1 — moving it later means moving it twice.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `ferrogate-cli` has a `lib.rs` and a thin `main.rs`; `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` green.
- [ ] `ferrogate-gateway` exists with a stated, documented public surface — not a mechanical re-export of everything that used to be `pub(crate)`.
- [ ] Each stage lands green and separately; no stage bundles a behaviour change with a move. A move-only commit must be verifiable as move-only.
- [ ] `ferrogate-cli`'s LOC drops below `ferrogate-storage`'s, as an objective stop condition rather than a feeling.
- [ ] The `ferrogate-core` question above is answered in writing, either way.
- [ ] `check-module-layout.py` still passes, and the new crate's entry file is under the cap by construction rather than by exception.

## Explicit non-goal

Behaviour change. Every stage is a move plus the minimum visibility edits to compile. A refactor that also fixes things is a refactor nobody can review — and this repo's review lane reads diffs without building them.

Refs #505.

body:
Split out of #505, whose acceptance box 5 half (a) is structurally unreachable and has been carried through three review rounds as a disclosure rather than an artifact.

## The box, as written on #505

> - [ ] E2E: mutate a guardrail policy revision, then follow the receipt's audit id and rollback pointer to **(a) locate the audit row** and (b) reverse the change, with no identifier typed by hand.

Half (b) is landed and good: `tools/ferrogate-test/src/cli_mutation_receipt.rs:196-228` executes the receipt's `rollback.command` argv verbatim and reads the reversed revision back from the server.

Half (a) cannot be satisfied, and the reason is not a gap in the CLI.

## Why it is unreachable

**No mutating operation in the Admin API contract returns an audit id.** `crates/ferrogate-cli-core/src/receipt_test.rs` re-derives this from `docs/openapi/admin-api.openapi.json` on every run (`no_mutating_operation_in_the_contract_returns_an_audit_id`): it resolves `$ref`s, walks all 135 mutating operations, and asserts none declares an `audit*` property in a resolved 2xx schema. It carries a `mutating.len() > 100` non-vacuity guard, so it cannot pass by finding nothing.

So `MutationReceipt.audit_id` is permanently `null` with `NO_AUDIT_ID_IN_CONTRACT`, and the harness takes the `None` branch at `cli_mutation_receipt.rs:261` and prints a note. That is honest, and it is the correct behaviour for the CLI given the contract — but it means the box can never be ticked by work on the CLI.

## Ask

- [ ] Decide whether a mutating Admin API operation should return the id of the audit row it wrote. The receipt already reserves the field and documents the absence reason, so the CLI side needs no change if the answer is yes.
- [ ] If yes: pick the operations (guardrail-policy activate/rollback is the natural first, since that is what #505's E2E exercises), add the field to their 2xx schemas, regenerate `admin-console/src/lib/api-types.generated.ts` **in the same commit**, and have the handler populate it from the audit write it already performs.
- [ ] If no: record why on this issue — and note that `no_mutating_operation_in_the_contract_returns_an_audit_id` then becomes a deliberate invariant rather than an observation, so it should say so in its own doc comment.
- [ ] Either way, edit #505's box 5 so it matches what was decided. It cannot stay as an unreachable checkbox.

## Verification

- [ ] If the field is added: an E2E that mutates a guardrail policy revision, reads `audit_id` off the receipt, and fetches the audit row by that id with **no identifier typed by hand** — which is what #505's box asked for and what `cli_mutation_receipt.rs` is already shaped to do (the `None` branch at `:261` becomes the `Some` branch).
- [ ] State the mutation that reds it. Per #500, a green suite is not evidence on its own.
- [ ] The derivation test above must be updated in the same change, or it will correctly go red the moment the first operation declares an audit id.

## Notes

`approval_id` has the same shape and is worth deciding at the same time: `receipt.rs` looks for `approval_id`/`tool_approval_id`, and those keys appear in no 2xx schema — only in `AssetPresignCommitRequest`, a request body — so it too is permanently absent-with-reason.

Filed by the code-review agent at #505's pass.
title: [api-contract][P3] No mutating Admin API operation returns an audit id, so a receipt can never locate its audit row (split from #505)

body:
## Problem

`ferrogate-test agent-jobs-api` fails deterministically (3/3) on `main` (`ee81f23`):

```
Error: worker never leased a cancel_run dispatch for job-247cf43603bff35b4cfd3443e6b817ee;
       last poll: 204 (no dispatch offered)
```

The cancel itself succeeds — `POST /v1/agent-jobs/{id}/cancel` answers 200 and the
run terminalizes to `cancelled`. What no longer happens is the next step the
harness has asserted since #474:

```rust
// ...and it must have reached the RUNTIME, i.e. a cancel_run dispatch is
// now leasable by the worker for that run.
let cancel_lease = lease_action_for(.., "cancel_run")?;
```

## Which side is wrong is a product decision, so I did not pick one

`b67cb40` — *(#502) Make a job's own settlement free the slot and return the rows* —
rewrote this path and changed the documented meaning of the cancel result:

```
-/// `true` when a `cancel_run` dispatch was handed to the runtime transport.
+/// `true` when a `cancel_run` dispatch was handed to the runtime transport,
+/// `false` here means "nothing was executing it", not "the cancel did not ..."
```

So there are two readings, and they need different fixes:

1. **The new behaviour is intended** — a job no worker has leased has nothing to
   cancel at the runtime, so no `cancel_run` dispatch is minted. Then #502 changed
   a contract #474 established and left its E2E proof asserting the old one. The
   harness box needs rewriting to assert the *new* contract (cancel of an unleased
   job withdraws the start dispatch; cancel of a **leased** job still produces
   `cancel_run`) — and the second half is the part that must keep real coverage.
2. **It is a regression** — a cancelled job's runtime is never told, so a worker
   that leases the start dispatch afterwards runs work the caller already
   cancelled and paid to stop.

I deliberately did **not** relax the harness assertion. As the gate I own
`tools/ferrogate-test` and would normally just fix it, but weakening this
particular assertion is indistinguishable from deleting the only proof that
cancellation reaches the runtime — the exact failure mode #500 is about. Tell me
which reading is right and I will write the corresponding coverage.

## Reproduce

```
cargo build -j4 -p ferrogate-cli -p ferrogate-test --locked
./target/debug/ferrogate-test agent-jobs-api
```

Fails 3/3, and takes `ferrogate-test ci` red with it. `-j4`, not `-j8`.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `ferrogate-test ci` is green again.
- [ ] The issue states explicitly which of the two readings above is the contract, and the doc comment on the cancel path says the same thing.
- [ ] Whichever it is, a **leased** job's cancel still provably reaches the runtime transport — verified by mutation: suppressing the `cancel_run` enqueue must turn the scenario red.
