title: [agent-worker][security][P1] Worker records raw response headers into event metadata and stdout, leaking credentials

body:
## Problem

`scripts/security-check.sh:48` runs the secret scan through `rg`:

```bash
rg "${rg_common[@]}" -- "$pattern" "${tracked_secret_scan_files[@]}" >>"$scan_file"
```

**`rg` is not installed on this box** (`which rg` → nothing), so the script errors out at that section and the secret scan **never runs**. Found while landing #344, which needed the script to confirm that a previously-binary file is now scannable.

## Why this matters more than a missing tool

This is the fourth instance this session of a gate that is believed to be running and is not:

- #499 — `scripts/check-workers.sh` never invoked by CI
- #506 / #509 / #513 — the repo's own clippy gate red on `main` (now fixed)
- #508 — Node off-`PATH`, admin-console gate silently skipped
- this one

The pattern is identical and the failure mode is the worst kind: **nothing announces that the check did not happen.** In #344's case the fix made `admin-console/src/pages/assets.tsx` greppable again after two NUL bytes had made git and every grep-based tool skip it silently — but the claim that it is *now scanned* rests on the greppability gate, because the actual scan could not be observed.

## Scope

- Install `ripgrep` on the dev/CI box, or make the script fall back to `git grep -I` (which handles the tracked-file list natively) when `rg` is absent.
- Whichever route: **the script must fail loudly and by name** when its scanner is unavailable — `secret scan did NOT run: ripgrep not found` and a non-zero exit — rather than erroring out mid-section in a way that reads like an unrelated failure.
- Add a test or CI assertion that the script exits non-zero when the scanner is missing, so this cannot silently regress.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `bash scripts/security-check.sh` completes end to end on a clean checkout, secret scan included.
- [ ] With the scanner removed from `PATH`, the script exits non-zero with a message naming the missing tool.
- [ ] A test asserts that behaviour.
- [ ] The scan is confirmed to cover `admin-console/src/pages/assets.tsx` (the #344 file), now that it is text to git again.

labels.name: priority:p2
labels.description: Validated follow-up; do not pull ahead of P0/P1

title: [ci][infra][P2] scripts/security-check.sh cannot complete — ripgrep is not installed, so the secret scan never runs

body:
## Requirement (founder, 2026-07-26)

A user who publishes a static website — or static **markdown** content — must get a **public preview URL** that anyone can open, backed by Cloudflare R2.

This is additive. The gateway path `GET /sites/{tenant}/{site}/{path...}` remains the default serving mode (#523); this issue adds a public, CDN-served address on top of it.

## The constraint that shapes the whole design

**R2 buckets are private by default and Cloudflare gives you no usable public URL for free.** There are exactly two exposure mechanisms:

| Mechanism | Shape | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Managed `r2.dev` subdomain | `https://pub-<hash>.r2.dev/<key>` | ⛔ **Not usable.** Cloudflare rate-limits it and documents it as development-only. Already recorded in this repo at `gateway/asset_bucket.rs:63` and `docs/cloudflare-integration.md:195`. |
| Custom domain attached to the bucket | `https://<our-domain>/<key>` | ✅ The production path. Requires a domain in a Cloudflare zone we control. |

So this feature requires **a FerroGate-owned public domain** (e.g. `preview.token4ai.cloud`). There is no zero-config option.

## Topology decision — must be made before implementation

**Option A — one shared domain, key-prefixed path**
`https://preview.token4ai.cloud/{tenant}/{site}/index.html`
One DNS record, one certificate, trivial mapping to R2 keys. **But every tenant shares one origin**, so tenant A's page JS can same-origin `fetch()` tenant B's content and read B's `localStorage`/`IndexedDB`. This is the same isolation weakness as the gateway path, relocated rather than fixed.

**Option B — per-tenant subdomain** *(recommended if user-authored HTML/JS is ever served)*
`https://{tenant}.preview.token4ai.cloud/{site}/...`
Wildcard DNS + wildcard certificate + a small routing Worker mapping `Host` → R2 key prefix. Gives each tenant a real origin boundary.

Recommendation: **B**. The moment a customer's static site stores anything client-side, a shared origin is a cross-tenant leak, and migrating origins later breaks every published URL. Option A is defensible only if content is guaranteed inert.

## Markdown is a separate problem, not a detail

Browsers do not render markdown. An `.md` object served from R2 with `Content-Type: text/markdown` will display as plain text or download. So "public preview of static markdown" requires an explicit decision:

- **render to HTML at publish time**, storing the rendered artifact alongside the source (preferred: keeps serving inert and static), or
- ship a viewer page that fetches and renders client-side (adds JS, and on a shared origin compounds the isolation problem).

If rendering, the markdown→HTML step is untrusted-input handling and needs sanitization — raw HTML embedded in user markdown is an XSS vector on whatever origin it lands on.

## What is lost by going public — must be explicit, not discovered

Content served directly from R2 **does not pass through FerroGate at all**. That means no `assets.read` gating, **no audit trail of reads, no request logs, no egress guardrails, and no per-request billing attribution.** Publishing is therefore a deliberate change of access-control posture, not a convenience toggle.

⚠️ **Scan-state interaction — the sharpest correctness risk.** `AssetVisibility` (`ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:11526`) exists precisely to withhold bytes that are `PendingScan` or `Quarantined` from consumers. That gate is enforced *by the gateway*. A public R2 URL bypasses the gateway, so unscanned or quarantined bytes could become world-readable. Publishing must be gated on `Visible`, **and a later quarantine must actively take down already-public objects** — the existing state machine has no such reach today.

## Scope

- [ ] **1. Decide and record the topology** (A vs B above), the public domain, and the certificate/DNS model.
- [ ] **2. Public-publish action** — opt-in per site, refused unless the site is already `manifest.public == true` (`gateway/sites.rs:98`, set via `x-site-public` at publish). A site that is authenticated-only through the gateway must not silently become world-readable.
- [ ] **3. Gate on scan state** — publish only `AssetVisibility::Visible` objects; wire quarantine to trigger takedown + cache purge of anything already public.
- [ ] **4. Version-addressed URLs + stable alias** — bundles are immutable and channel-versioned (#397), so address the public URL by bundle version and provide a stable alias that re-points on channel move. This designs most cache-invalidation away instead of fighting it.
- [ ] **5. Takedown that actually takes down** — unpublish must delete *and* purge CDN cache. A takedown that leaves cached copies served is a compliance failure, not a bug.
- [ ] **6. Security response headers** — serving user-authored HTML publicly makes `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a default CSP **mandatory**. The repo currently sets **no** security headers on any asset/site response (verified: repo-wide grep for `Content-Security-Policy` / `X-Content-Type-Options` / `X-Frame-Options` returns nothing). Deliverable via Transform Rules or the routing Worker.
- [ ] **7. Markdown rendering decision + sanitization** per the section above.
- [ ] **8. Per-tenant accounting and abuse controls** — public URLs are hotlinkable. R2 egress is free, but Class A/B operations are billed, so account ops per tenant and rate-limit. Decide the behaviour when a tenant's quota is exhausted.
- [ ] **9. Surface the URL** — return the public URL from the publish response and show it in the console alongside published/stale state.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Publishing a public static site yields a URL that renders correctly in a browser from a clean profile with no credentials.
- [ ] The same content is byte-identical to what the gateway path serves for that bundle version.
- [ ] A site with `public == false` cannot be published to the public URL — typed error.
- [ ] An object that is `PendingScan` or `Quarantined` is never publicly reachable; quarantining an already-published object removes it and purges cache, proven by test.
- [ ] Unpublish makes the URL stop serving, cache included.
- [ ] Responses carry `nosniff` and a CSP.
- [ ] Markdown content is viewable as rendered output, not raw text or a download.
- [ ] `r2.dev` is not used anywhere in the production path.

## Out of scope

- Changing the default gateway serving mode.
- Cloudflare Pages publishing — that is #523, a different target with a different URL model (`<project>.pages.dev`).

Related: #523 (opt-in Pages publish), #411 (`AssetObjectStore` trait — Part A landed), #410 (R2 backend), #258 (static-site serve), #397 (immutable channel-versioned bundles), #366 (asset scan visibility), #488 (site-domain DNS proof), #404 (Cloudflare epic).

title: [cloudflare][assets] Public preview URLs for static sites and markdown, served from R2 on a FerroGate-owned domain

body:
## Decision (founder, 2026-07-26)

Static asset access **stays as it is**: served by FerroGate over the gateway path, `GET /sites/{tenant}/{site}/{path...}` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/sites.rs`, #258), with optional customer-owned custom domains bound through `StoredSiteDomain` + DNS-proof verification (#488) and ACME TLS.

**Publishing a static website to Cloudflare Pages becomes an explicit, opt-in user action** — not the default, and not a change to how assets are served.

## Why this framing matters (and why it is not a repeat of the #411 failure)

#411's Part A — the `AssetObjectStore` trait with the S3/R2 impl behind it — **is landed and passed review**: `asset_bucket.rs:166-193` defines the trait, `state_assets.rs:289` hands out `Option<Box<dyn AssetObjectStore>>`, and all 16 non-test call sites funnel through that accessor.

Part B — the Workers Static Assets publish flow — **failed code review** and was bounced back to Ready, with the finding that "as wired it breaks the asset store it is plugged into."

That failure is instructive: it came from treating a Cloudflare *publish target* as an `AssetObjectStore` **backend**, sitting in the asset store's read/write path. This issue deliberately does not do that.

> **Publish is an export action, not a storage backend.** The bundle in FerroGate remains the single source of truth; publishing pushes a copy outward. Nothing in the asset read/write path changes, and `AssetObjectStore` gains no Pages implementation.

## Scope

- [ ] **1. Publish action** — an explicit, authenticated trigger (e.g. `POST /admin/v1/sites/{tenant}/{site}/publish` with a `cloudflare_pages` target). Off by default; a site that is never published behaves exactly as today.
- [ ] **2. Source the ACTIVE bundle, not the mutable marker** — resolve through the `serving` asset channel per #397 (bundles are retained and immutable, keyed by bundle version). Publishing must not read the legacy mutable `__site_manifest__` path except for pre-#397 sites, and should say so when it does.
- [ ] **3. Pages deployment** — per-tenant Pages project; `POST /accounts/{account_id}/pages/projects/{project}/deployments`. Per #411's research the raw per-file negotiation is under-documented, so plan for `wrangler pages deploy` as the fallback mechanism and record which path was taken.
- [ ] **4. Record the deployment** — project name, deployment id, preview URL, production alias, source bundle version, publisher identity, timestamp — persisted and surfaced so the console can show "published / not published / stale relative to the active bundle".
- [ ] **5. Idempotency** — republishing an unchanged bundle version must not create a duplicate deployment.
- [ ] **6. Credentials** — the Cloudflare API token resolves through `SecretResolverRegistry` (`env://`, `cf://`), never plaintext config. Follows the pattern used for the collector token in #520.

## Design decisions that must be made explicitly (not discovered during implementation)

1. **⚠️ Custom-domain conflict.** A hostname bound via `StoredSiteDomain` is served by *our* gateway with *our* ACME certificate. A hostname attached to a Pages project is CNAME'd to Cloudflare and served with *their* certificate. **The same hostname cannot be both.** Define which wins and make the illegal combination unrepresentable — publishing to Pages while a verified FerroGate binding exists for the same hostname should fail with a clear error, or explicitly hand the hostname over. This is the sharpest edge in the whole feature.
2. **Rollback semantics.** The channel model already has rollback (#367/#397/#345). Does a channel rollback in FerroGate re-publish to Pages, leave the Pages deployment stale, or refuse? A silently-stale published site is the worst of the three and must not be the default.
3. **What governance is lost on publish.** Content served from Pages does **not** pass through FerroGate — no `assets.read` gating, no per-site anonymous-access opt-in, no audit of reads, and no request logs. Publishing a non-public site to Pages therefore changes its access-control posture. The action must refuse, or at minimum require explicit acknowledgement, for any site that is not already anonymously readable.
4. **Tenancy on the Cloudflare side.** One Pages project per tenant, in a single FerroGate-owned Cloudflare account. Verify the per-account Pages project cap and per-deployment file-count/size limits against current Cloudflare docs before committing to the model — **do not assume**; if the cap is low relative to tenant count, the design needs a different partitioning.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A site that is never published serves identically to today over `/sites/{tenant}/{site}/{path...}` — proven by the existing `static_site_serve.rs` and `site_custom_domain.rs` suites passing unchanged.
- [ ] Publishing an active bundle produces a reachable Pages deployment whose content byte-matches what the gateway path serves for the same bundle version.
- [ ] Republishing the same bundle version is a no-op.
- [ ] Publishing a site whose hostname is already verified-and-bound to the FerroGate gateway fails with a typed, actionable error rather than producing a split-brain hostname.
- [ ] Publishing a non-anonymous site either fails or requires an explicit acknowledgement flag; the access-control change is stated in the response.
- [ ] The Cloudflare token never appears in config, logs, or `Debug` output.
- [ ] `AssetObjectStore` has no Pages implementation and the asset read/write path is untouched — verified by diff.

## Explicitly out of scope

- Changing the default serving mode. The gateway path stays authoritative.
- Making Cloudflare Pages an `AssetObjectStore` backend (this is what broke in #411).
- The Workers Static Assets publish flow — that remains #411's bounced Part B and is a separate decision.

Related: #411 (`AssetObjectStore` trait — Part A landed, Part B bounced), #258 (static-site serve mode), #397 (immutable channel-versioned bundles), #488 (site-domain DNS proof), #345 (console rollback), #175-#179 (asset hosting v1), #404 (Cloudflare epic).

body:
## Architectural decision (founder, 2026-07-26)

Observability closes at the **gateway layer**, not inside the customer's agent.

All agent traffic — LLM calls, tool calls, and MCP calls — transits the FerroGate AI Gateway. Therefore the gateway alone can reconstruct the full chain. The agent's only obligation is to **declare an action id**; FerroGate does not require, and will not attempt, instrumentation of customer agent internals, because how a customer's agent runs is outside our control.

### What this decision retires

This **supersedes scope item 7 of #520** ("cross-boundary trace propagation") and retires the framing, recorded earlier in `docs/cloudflare-observability.md`, that missing W3C `traceparent` propagation into MCP / sandboxes / agent-workers makes the chain "not actually full-link". Propagating W3C trace context into an uninstrumentable third-party agent is now an explicit **non-goal**. Correlation is achieved by funnelling, not by propagation.

Note this also removes the dependency on Cloudflare's unshipped external `traceparent` propagation (roadmap, not delivered as of the 2026-05-07 changelog) — the design no longer needs it.

## What already exists — do NOT rebuild

Issues #305/#306 already delivered exactly this model:

| Capability | Where |
|---|---|
| The correlation triple `{request_id, trace_id, agent_run_id}` on every governance artifact | `crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/correlation_join_e2e.rs` |
| Action identity: `ActionIdentity`, `action_fingerprint` (`canonical_target_sha256`, `sha256:<64hex>`) | `crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/action_identity.rs:216`, `:234` |
| Parent linkage across handoffs via `x-ferrogate-parent-action-fingerprint` | `action_identity.rs:101`, `is_canonical_action_fingerprint` `:105` |
| Client-declared run id via `x-ferrogate-agent-run-id` | `gateway/agent_runs.rs:43`, `:474` |
| Untrusted-input hardening on that header: visible ASCII/UTF-8, **≤128 chars**, charset `[A-Za-z0-9_-.:]` | `gateway/local.rs:10235-10255` |
| End-to-end proof that approval record + timeline rows + audit rows all join on one triple, and the #199 investigation view finds approvals by `agent_run_id` alone with no related-id back-fill | `correlation_join_e2e.rs:31-161` |
| Persistence + indexes: `request_logs(agent_run_id)`, `audit_events` partial index on `agent_run_id` (#231), `agent_runs`, `agent_run_events` | `sql/001_init_postgres.sql` |

## The actual gaps

Coverage of `agent_run_id` across the governed surfaces (occurrence count in each handler):

| Surface | Status |
|---|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions` (32), `/v1/messages` (11), `/v1/embeddings` (5), `/v1/images` (5) | ✅ |
| `/v1/agent-runs` (13), reverse proxy path (28), A2A ingress (`local.rs:10229`) | ✅ |
| **MCP JSON-RPC (`gateway/mcp_rpc.rs`)** | ⛔ **1 occurrence — and it is `agent_run_id: None` hardcoded at `mcp_rpc.rs:541`** |
| **Asset endpoints (`gateway/assets.rs`)** | ⛔ **0 occurrences** |

### 1. ⛔ MCP drops the correlation id on the floor
`mcp_rpc.rs:541` sets `agent_run_id: None` unconditionally. MCP is one of the three traffic classes this architecture names as in-scope, so today an agent's MCP tool call cannot be joined to the agent run that issued it. This is the single highest-value fix in this issue.

### 2. ⛔ Asset traffic carries no run correlation
`gateway/assets.rs` has no `agent_run_id` at all. Asset fetch/put is a governed agent action under the asset-hosting pillar (#175-#179) and should join the same chain.

### 3. The declaration is optional everywhere
Every ingress treats `x-ferrogate-agent-run-id` as an optional declaration. For a customer agent we cannot instrument, "optional" means a chain silently breaks whenever the agent omits it, and the gap is invisible — the records still write, they just do not join. Needs either a per-tenant "require action id on governed surfaces" policy, or an explicit, measured degradation (a counter for unjoinable governed actions) so the hole is observable rather than silent.

### 4. Client-declared ids need tenant namespacing
The run id is untrusted client input. Validation today is purely **syntactic** (length + charset). Reads are tenant-filtered (`enforce_tenant_filter`), but nothing documented prevents tenant A from *writing* records under an id that collides with tenant B's chain — polluting B's investigation view. Confirm the write path is tenant-namespaced; if it is not, make it so.

## Scope

- [ ] **1. Thread the correlation triple through MCP** — replace the hardcoded `agent_run_id: None` at `mcp_rpc.rs:541`; accept `x-ferrogate-agent-run-id` on the MCP ingress using the same validated parser as the other surfaces (do not duplicate the validation).
- [ ] **2. Thread it through the asset surface** — `gateway/assets.rs`.
- [ ] **3. Unjoinable-action metric** — count governed actions that arrive with no declared action id, per tenant and per surface, exposed on `/metrics`. Makes the coverage hole measurable instead of invisible.
- [ ] **4. Optional per-tenant enforcement** — a config/policy switch that rejects governed agent traffic lacking an action id, default off.
- [ ] **5. Confirm/enforce tenant namespacing** of client-declared run ids on the write path; add a test that tenant A cannot inject into tenant B's chain.
- [ ] **6. Document the contract for customers** — one page: which header to send, on which endpoints, what the id may contain (≤128 chars, `[A-Za-z0-9_-.:]`), how parent linkage works via `x-ferrogate-parent-action-fingerprint`, and exactly what they get back (investigation view, joins). This is the customer-facing half of the decision and currently exists only as scattered code comments.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An agent that declares one action id and then performs an LLM call, a tool call, an MCP call **and** an asset fetch produces artifacts that all join on that id — extend `correlation_join_e2e.rs` to cover the MCP and asset legs, which it does not today.
- [ ] The investigation view selected by `agent_run_id` alone returns the MCP and asset legs.
- [ ] A governed request with no declared action id increments the unjoinable counter, and is rejected when per-tenant enforcement is on.
- [ ] Tenant A declaring tenant B's run id cannot cause records to appear in B's investigation view.
- [ ] No W3C `traceparent` propagation into customer agent processes is added — this is a non-goal, and existing inbound `traceparent` handling (`gateway/mod.rs:144`) is unchanged.

## Explicitly out of scope

- Instrumenting customer agent internals (the whole point of the decision).
- W3C trace-context propagation to MCP servers, sandboxes, or agent-workers.
- Anything requiring Cloudflare's unshipped external `traceparent` propagation.

Related: #305 / #306 (correlation triple + shared action identity), #199 (investigation view), #231 (audit `agent_run_id` index), #520 (Cloudflare observability backend — item 7 superseded), #294.

body:
## Requirement

A customer's own agent should be able to define its **own** guardrails through the FerroGate gateway at runtime, so that the safety envelope is not a fixed, platform-authored set.

## Verdict after a codebase investigation: feasible, and most of the plane already exists

This is **not** a greenfield build. The versioned guardrail enforcement plane from the (closed) epic #193 already delivers runtime authoring — it is simply not reachable by an agent, and a tenant is currently boxed into a narrow slice of it.

### Already built — do NOT rebuild

| Capability | Where |
|---|---|
| Runtime create / list / get / archive / **activate** / **rollback** / dry-run | `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/guardrail_policies.rs:123-724` |
| Immutable revisions + `generation` CAS + conflict metric + audit event | `sql/001_init_postgres.sql:1619-1627`; `guardrail_policies.rs:1029-1056` |
| Atomic activate → runtime reload → **auto-restore on reload failure** | `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:4521+` |
| Multi-check composition; `all`/`any`/`threshold`; sequential or parallel | `crates/ferrogate-guardrails/src/policy.rs:717-747`, `:862-916` |
| Actions: block / redact / record / shadow / require_approval / quarantine | `policy.rs:607-628`; dispatch at `gateway/local.rs:3612-3665` |
| Scope binding to tenant / org / project / workspace / api-key / service-account / gateway-config / model / provider / managed-action | `policy.rs:62-91`, `:100-164` |
| Tenant isolation on read, write **and** activate (incl. anti-squatting on `policy_id`) | `guardrail_policies.rs:795-885`, `:364-376` |
| DB-backed per-action RBAC (`guardrails.policy.*`) | `guardrail_policies.rs:36-54`, `:923-955` |
| Per-check evidence, investigation timeline, **fail-closed when evidence cannot be written** | `sql:454-516`; `state_quota_and_policy.rs:641-643` |
| Customer-owned HTTP detector, SSRF-safe with bulkhead + circuit breaker | `crates/ferrogate-guardrails/src/custom_http.rs` |
| Streaming semantics: `buffer_and_enforce` / `shadow_after_complete` / `reject_streaming` | `policy.rs:35-40`; `state_quota_and_policy.rs:650-676` |
| Typed, permission-checked redaction patches (detectors cannot rewrite identity/route/tool fields) | `crates/ferrogate-guardrails/src/envelope.rs:742-880` |
| **No DDL needed for new detector kinds** — `policy_json JSONB` | `sql/001_init_postgres.sql:421-429` |

So the honest framing: the requirement is ~70% delivered. This issue is about the remaining 30%, which is where the hard problems are.

## What is actually missing

### 1. No agent-native surface (the literal ask)
There is no MCP tool and no `/v1`-side self-service endpoint for guardrail management. The built-in tool registry is one tool: `builtin_tools.rs:39-41` is `vec![fetch_asset_tool()]`. `crates/ferrogate-mcp/` is FerroGate acting as an MCP *client*, not a server exposing guardrail tools. `GovernedAgentToolDispatcher` (`ferrogate-runtime/src/agent.rs:199`) is the surface guardrails are *applied to*, never a surface for *managing* them.

Today an agent can only manage guardrails by holding a real admin API key with `admin.write` plus the DB-backed RBAC action, and calling the same REST endpoints a human would.

### 2. ⛔ Tenant-scoped secrets — the blocking dependency
`SecretResolverRegistry::from_env()` (`state.rs:6234`) resolves against the **host's** env/Vault/Cloudflare-Secrets-Store with **no tenant scoping**. Because of that exfiltration risk, `authorize_guardrail_secret_refs` (`guardrail_policies.rs:860-885`) returns 403 for *any* org-scoped author whose detector dereferences a host secret.

Consequence: of the five detector kinds, a tenant can use **two** — `Local`, and `CustomHttp` **without authentication**. Presidio, LlmGuardPromptInjection and WorkersAiLlamaGuard all require `fingerprint_secret_ref` and are therefore platform-operator-only. A customer cannot even put a bearer token on a call to their *own* detector endpoint.

This must land before "customers bring their own detectors" is真 self-service. Relates to the Secrets Store work in #417/#418.

### 3. Detector *kinds* are a closed Rust enum
`DetectorDefinition` (`policy.rs:260-372`) has exactly five variants, with compiler-enforced exhaustive matches at `policy.rs:391-588`, `state.rs:6285-6299`, `state.rs:6300-6510`, `guardrail_policies.rs:735-783`, `:833-850`. `Arc<dyn GuardrailDetector>` is only ever produced by the `match` in `build_guardrail_detector` — there is no registry, no name→constructor map, no plugin loading.

So "custom guardrail" today means **custom parameters**, not custom logic. Notably absent: an LLM-judge kind (`{ model, system_prompt, threshold }`) routed through FerroGate's own provider layer — which is the shape most agentic customers will actually ask for, and which needs no new secret plumbing because the provider layer already holds the credentials.

### 4. No authorship quotas — and an agent loop is exactly the trigger
There is a body-size cap and a per-policy `deadline_ms ≤ 30s`, but **no cap on policies-per-tenant, checks-per-policy, or the aggregate latency budget across all matching policies**. All matching policies are evaluated additively (`state_quota_and_policy.rs:411-415`, `:620` — not first-match-wins), so every policy an agent creates adds hot-path latency to **every request in that tenant**. A human admin creates policies at human rates; an agent in a loop does not. This stops being theoretical the moment agents can author.

### 5. Dry-run gives an agent no signal
`dry_run_check` (`guardrail_policies.rs:735-773`) returns `"not_executed"` for all four non-`Local` kinds, and even for `Local` when `json` / `request` / `secret_patterns` are set. An agent iterating toward a working guardrail gets nothing back to iterate on.

### Supporting gaps (smaller)
- `SecretPattern` is 3 hardcoded values (`deterministic.rs:143-146`) — customers can approximate with raw regex but lose the category taxonomy and default redact semantics.
- No policy **diff / impact estimate** before activation, though specified at `docs/design/guardrail-security-architecture-2026-07.md:334`.
- No shadow-rollout sampling by subject/request hash, also specified (`:336`).
- `reload_process_local` is process-local; fleet propagation rides `cluster_sync` (`state.rs:1016-1060`), so there is an eventual-consistency window.
- `guardrail_policy_revisions` / `_bindings` have **no `tenant_id` column and no RLS** — tenancy is application-level only, unlike `guardrail_evaluations` which has both.
- The D1/Cloudflare backend does not implement the CAS transitions at all (`sql/d1/001_init_d1.sql:540-543`, issue #449).

## Security constraints this design must not violate

1. **No request-inline enforcing hooks.** `docs/design/guardrail-security-architecture-2026-07.md:459` explicitly forbids the requester submitting raw enforcing hooks that bypass versioning and audit. An agent-authored guardrail must still become a normal versioned, audited policy revision — the agent surface is a *client* of the existing plane, never a side door into it.
2. **Authoring enforcement policy is a privilege-escalation surface.** An agent that can author guardrails scoped to its own tenant can also author a *permissive* one. Deciding what an agent may author is the core design question, not an implementation detail — see open questions.
3. **The existing tenant guards must be reused verbatim**, not reimplemented: `require_guardrail_auth`, `authorize_guardrail_scope`, `authorize_guardrail_secret_refs`, and the anti-squatting check in `create_guardrail_revision`.
4. **Fail-closed on evidence** must survive: `state_quota_and_policy.rs:641-643`.

## Scope

- [ ] **1. Agent-facing guardrail tools** — `guardrail.list_policies` / `create_revision` / `dry_run` / `activate` / `rollback`, exposed through the MCP tool surface and `builtin_tools.rs`, each delegating to the existing handlers so RBAC, scope authorization and audit are shared rather than duplicated.
- [ ] **2. Meta-governance** — an agent's guardrail-authoring call is itself a managed action. Decide and implement its `ManagedActionClass` (`Rest`? a new class?) so it can be guardrailed, approval-gated and audited like any other agent action. This is what stops the recursion from being a hole.
- [ ] **3. Per-tenant authorship quotas** — max active policies/tenant, max checks/policy, and an aggregate per-request guardrail latency budget with a defined behaviour on exceed (reject authorship vs. shed at evaluation). Without this, item 1 is a tenant-wide DoS lever.
- [ ] **4. `DetectorDefinition::LlmJudge`** — model + system prompt + threshold, routed through FerroGate's provider layer. Highest-value new kind, and it sidesteps blocker #2 because the provider layer already owns the credentials.
- [ ] **5. Executable dry-run** for non-`Local` detectors, so an agent can iterate before activating.
- [ ] **6. Policy diff + impact estimate on activate** (`design doc:334`) — matters far more when the author is an agent than when it is a human reviewing its own change.
- [ ] **7. (Dependency) tenant-scoped secret resolution** — `resolve_for_tenant(tenant_id, ref)`, then relax `authorize_guardrail_secret_refs` accordingly. Coordinate with #417/#418. **Until this lands, tenants stay limited to `Local` + unauthenticated `CustomHttp`.**

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A tenant-scoped agent, holding only its own credentials, can create → dry-run → activate a guardrail policy scoped to its own tenant, and see it enforced on the next request.
- [ ] That same agent **cannot**: author a global or cross-tenant policy, read another tenant's policy, dereference a host secret, or squat a `policy_id` owned by another tenant. Each has a test.
- [ ] The agent's authoring call appears in the audit timeline as a managed action, and is itself subject to guardrail evaluation.
- [ ] Exceeding the per-tenant policy or latency-budget quota fails with a typed error, and the existing hot path is unaffected when no agent-authored policy exists.
- [ ] An `LlmJudge` detector authored by a tenant evaluates through the tenant's own configured provider, with cost attributed to that tenant.
- [ ] `ferrogate-test` green; no regression in the 1236-test CLI suite.

## Open questions (need a decision before implementation)

1. **May an agent author a policy that is more permissive than the one it currently runs under?** Recommendation: no — an agent-authored policy may only *narrow* the effective envelope, with widening reserved for a human admin. This needs a defined lattice over `PolicyAction`, which does not exist today.
2. Should agent-authored policies be forced into `PolicyMode::Shadow` first, with promotion to enforce requiring either a human or a clean shadow record?
3. Does an agent-authored policy bind to the authoring agent's service account by default, or to the whole tenant? Default-narrow (service account) seems right; `service_account_ids` is already a scope dimension (`policy.rs:75-76`).

Parent: #269. Related: #200 (managed-action guardrails), #201 (semantic adapters), #417/#418 (Secrets Store + multi-tenant caps), #449 (D1 CAS gap), #422/#430 (Workers AI Llama Guard).

body:
## Decision (founder, 2026-07-26)

FerroGate's observability backend switches **entirely to Cloudflare infrastructure**. Vector and ClickHouse are retired — no third-party observability backend is retained.

Research: `docs/cloudflare-observability.md` (this issue supersedes its "layered" recommendation with a full switch).

## The one hard constraint that shapes the design

**Cloudflare has no observability ingest endpoint anywhere on the platform.** No OTLP receiver, no Workers Logs write API, and Analytics Engine's `writeDataPoint()` is a Worker binding only (its sole HTTP API is read/SQL). A Rust process in a container cannot write to Cloudflare directly.

So "switch to Cloudflare" is realised through **a collector Worker we deploy** — exactly the fronting-Worker pattern already established by #413 for agents (CF has no first-party REST API for the primitive, so a Worker we own fronts it). FerroGate POSTs OTLP/HTTP+JSON to that Worker; the Worker fans out into CF-native storage over bindings.

Favourable existing seam: `dispatch_otlp_request` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/telemetry.rs:1221`) is the single chokepoint for all telemetry HTTP egress, already speaks OTLP/HTTP+JSON (`state_observability.rs:150`), and `OtlpHttpRequest` already carries a generic `headers: Vec<(String,String)>` escape hatch (added in #228, reused by `budget_alerts.rs:120`) — that is where collector auth goes. No new transport is needed on the Rust side.

## Target architecture

```
FerroGate (container, anywhere)
  └─ dispatch_otlp_request  ──OTLP/HTTP+JSON + Bearer──▶  workers/telemetry-collector (CF Worker)
                                                             ├─ writeDataPoint()  ▶ Analytics Engine   (metrics / aggregates, 3-month)
                                                             ├─ console.log(JSON) ▶ Workers Logs       (searchable, 7-day, query API)
                                                             └─ (Logpush workers_trace_events) ▶ R2    (long retention, cheap)
workers/{gateway-front,agent-gateway,mcp-server,d1-proxy}
  └─ native Workers Traces  ──OTLP──▶  same collector / same datasets   (one correlated trace)
```

## Scope

- [ ] **1. `workers/telemetry-collector`** — new Worker. OTLP/HTTP+JSON ingest for traces/metrics/logs; Bearer auth resolved from CF Secrets Store (reuse the `cf://` resolver from #417); per-tenant routing; batching within the 250-data-points-per-invocation cap. Single-concern modules per the #429 standard.
- [ ] **2. `ObservabilityProvider::Cloudflare`** — new variant in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs:1869` + config fields (collector URL, token via the `clickhouse_url_env`-style env indirection, never plaintext). Auth headers injected through the existing `OtlpHttpRequest.headers`.
- [ ] **3. Analytics Engine schema** — dataset layout for `GatewayMetricsSnapshot`. **`index` = tenant** (only 1 index per data point is allowed, and it is the sampling axis, so it must be the tenancy key). Respect: 20 blobs / 20 doubles / 16 KB combined blobs / 96 B index / 250 points per invocation.
- [ ] **4. Workers Logs path** — structured JSON for `request_logs` / `audit_events` / `billing_metering_events` exports. Set `invocation_logs = false` (halves billable events). Respect the 256 KB per-line cap.
- [ ] **5. Logpush `workers_trace_events` → R2** — long retention beyond the 7-day Workers Logs window. `$5` Workers Paid is sufficient (this dataset is the documented Enterprise carve-out). Accept the ~1-minute delivery floor and the no-backfill property.
- [ ] **6. Worker-side native traces** — `observability.traces.enabled = true` on all five Workers (note `gateway-front/wrangler.toml` has no `[observability]` block at all today), OTLP destination pointed at the same sink so CF-side and FerroGate-side spans land in one store.
- [ ] **7. Cross-boundary trace propagation** — CF does **not** yet propagate W3C `traceparent` to non-CF origins (explicitly roadmap, not shipped, per the 2026-05-07 changelog). So `gateway-front`/`agent-gateway` must set `traceparent` on the origin-bound `fetch()` themselves; record `cf-ray` as a span attribute as a join fallback (⚠️ CF states Ray IDs are **not guaranteed unique** — join key only, never a trace id).
- [ ] **8. Retire Vector + ClickHouse** — delete `deploy/vector/`, `sql/clickhouse/`, `docs/analytics-warehouse.md`, the `ObservabilityProvider::Vector` / ClickHouse analytics paths (`telemetry.rs:61` `start_analytics_background_sender`, `:282` `CLICKHOUSE_ANALYTICS_TABLES`, `:290` `clickhouse_insert_url`) and their config surface.
- [ ] **9. Admin surface** — `GET /admin/v1/observability` (`gateway/local.rs:442`) reports the Cloudflare provider, health, and backpressure. Existing route group, so no new console-coverage obligation.

## Explicitly NOT in scope

**The Postgres evidence chain stays.** `request_logs`, `audit_events`, `billing_metering_events` are the **billing and audit authority**, not telemetry. They cannot move to Analytics Engine: AE samples on both write and read (`SUM(_sample_interval)` weighting is mandatory, exact counts unavailable at volume), retains only 3 months, and Cloudflare's own docs state these datasets "should not be used as a measure for usage that Cloudflare uses for billing purposes." Moving the *control-plane store* to Cloudflare is a separate, already-filed track: #419 (extract `ControlPlaneStore` trait) → #420 (per-tenant D1) and #410 (R2).

This issue switches the **telemetry/analytics backend**. The third-party components being removed are exactly Vector and ClickHouse.

## Cost envelope ($5/mo Workers Paid, per account — not per Worker)

| Requests/mo | Base compute | Workers Logs | Analytics Engine | Logpush→R2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1M | $5.00 | $0 | $0 | $0 |
| 10M | $5.00 | $0 | $0 | $0 |
| 100M | $35.40 | $48.00 (invocation logs off) | $22.50 (**currently unbilled**) | ~$4.50 |

Included allowances: 10M requests + 30M CPU-ms; **20M log events/mo** (+$0.60/M, 7-day retention, shared with traces); **10M AE data points + 1M read queries/mo** (+$0.25/M, +$1.00/M, 3-month retention); **10M `workers_trace_events` Logpush records/mo** (+$0.05/M, billed post-sampling). Head sampling (`head_sampling_rate`) is the cost lever — there is no tail-based sampling anywhere on CF.

⚠️ **Verify before budgeting:** CF docs contradict themselves on the included log/trace pool — the Traces page says 10M/mo, the Workers Logs and Workers pricing pages say 20M/mo, for the same shared pool.
⚠️ AE pricing page currently states "you will not be billed for your use of Workers Analytics Engine" — rates are published for forecasting and will start applying without much notice.

## Known limits to design against

1. **1 index per AE data point** — determines the sampling axis; must be the tenant key.
2. **250 AE data points per Worker invocation**; 16 KB combined blobs per point; 96 B index.
3. **Workers Logpush truncates `logs`+`exceptions` at a combined 16,384 characters** — far tighter than the 256 KB Workers Logs line cap.
4. **5 billion logs/account/day** → forced 1% head sample for the remainder of the day (silent quality cliff).
5. **Logpush cannot backfill**; ~1-minute delivery floor regardless of batch tuning.
6. CF's OTLP export is **JSON only — binary protobuf is not supported**; Worker **metrics** export is not supported at all (hence writing AE directly).
7. Workers Traces is still **open beta**, and `observability.enabled = true` does not turn it on — `observability.traces.enabled = true` is separate. Requires Workers Paid; unavailable on Free.
8. The Workers Observability query API and the AE SQL API have **no published rate limits** — design for undocumented throttling.
9. The collector Worker must be reachable from wherever FerroGate runs, and FerroGate-off-Cloudflare pays a public-internet hop per export batch (today: one batch per 5 s, `OTLP_EXPORT_INTERVAL`).

## Pre-existing gaps this work will expose

- Export is a **5-second polling thread over Postgres** that synthesises spans at export time (`telemetry.rs:32`, `stable_trace_id` at `:1408`) — not SDK instrumentation. Any new sink inherits that latency floor and cursor model.
- **Metrics are counters/gauges only — no histograms**, so there are no latency distributions to ship to AE.
- **No `traceparent` propagation to MCP, sandboxes, or agent-workers** (`crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/`, `ferrogate-runtime/src/`, `agent-worker/src/` have zero hits) — "full-link" is not actually full-link today.
- `ObservabilityPlugin` (`ferrogate-observability/src/config.rs:125`) validates config but has **no export method**, and `ObservabilityExporterKind` is a closed enum — adding a Cloudflare kind is a breaking enum edit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With `[observability] provider = "cloudflare"`, a governed request produces a queryable record in Analytics Engine (via the SQL API) and in Workers Logs (via the telemetry query API), with the tenant as AE `index`.
- [ ] A trace originated at FerroGate and passing through `gateway-front` appears as **one** correlated trace, with the CF-side spans nested under the FerroGate-side parent.
- [ ] `GET /admin/v1/observability` reports `provider = "cloudflare"`, health, last success, and drop/backpressure counters.
- [ ] `deploy/vector/`, `sql/clickhouse/` and the ClickHouse/Vector code paths are gone; no config key references them; `ferrogate-test` is green.
- [ ] Collector auth token is resolved through `SecretResolver`, never plaintext in TOML.
- [ ] Docs updated: `docs/cloudflare-observability.md` reflects the switch; `docs/analytics-warehouse.md` removed or replaced.

Parent epic: #404. Related: #294 (Metrics, tracing, and analytics), #413 (fronting-Worker pattern), #417 (Secrets Store resolver), #428 (CF agent observability & cost governance).

organization_id: Some(session.tenant_id.clone()),

body:
Found by a test-gate audit, **confirmed by live probe**.

`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/rbac.rs:369` authenticates and then **discards the `AuthContext`**:

```rust
Ok(_) => match state.list_roles()
```

Same shape at `:44`, `:131`, `:435`.

Probe: a **tenant-a-scoped** key called both endpoints:

```
GET /admin/v1/permissions  → 200, full global catalog
GET /admin/v1/roles        → 200, every role including its permission_keys
```

Every tenant can therefore read the platform's complete entitlement model — role names, permission keys, and how they are composed.

## Why it is P2 and not P1

It is disclosure, not mutation: `POST /admin/v1/roles` from the same key is correctly refused with `403 platform_operator_required`. But it hands every tenant a map of the authority model, which is exactly the reconnaissance step before an escalation attempt.

## Ask

- Decide whether the RBAC catalog is public-to-tenants by design. If it is, say so in the OpenAPI description so it stops looking like an oversight.
- If not, scope the list to what the caller may see, and add a test that goes red when the `AuthContext` is discarded again.

body:
Found by a test-gate audit.

`sql/001_init_postgres.sql:886` declares four membership tiers:

```sql
CHECK (role IN ('owner','admin','member','viewer'))
```

Grep for `"viewer"` in Rust: **zero** matches. Every comparison in the codebase is `!= "owner"` — 11 sites across `ferrogate-auth/src/admin_console.rs:698,764,827,898,933,976,1008`, `sso.rs:164,338,386`, `scim.rs:73`. So the model is binary: **owner, or not-owner**. `member` and `viewer` are indistinguishable from `admin`.

## The consequence

`provision_gateway_api_key` (`ferrogate-auth/src/admin_console.rs:1084-1089`) mints

```
["admin.read", "admin.write", "assets.read", "assets.write"]
```

for **every console session, regardless of role**. A user invited as `viewer` receives a gateway key with `admin.write`.

## Two aggravating factors

1. `sql/d1/001_init_d1.sql:140` — the D1 twin has **no CHECK constraint at all**, so on that backend the column accepts anything.
2. `handle_admin_team_change_role` (`admin_console.rs:802`) validates only **non-emptiness** — any string is an acceptable role.

## Ask

- Decide whether the four tiers are real. If they are, implement them and make `provision_gateway_api_key` derive scopes from the role. If they are not, drop them from the schema and the UI rather than advertising authority levels that do not exist.
- Validate the role value against the accepted set on write, in code — not only in a Postgres CHECK that one backend lacks.
- A test per tier asserting the scopes minted, each going red if the mapping is flattened.

body:
Found by a test-gate audit, triggered by the #340 bounce. **This is the entity-model contradiction behind that bounce.**

## Five sites state mutually exclusive things about one field

| Site | Claim |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/ferrogate-core/src/lib.rs:41,83` | `organization_id` **IS** `tenant_id` — `tenant.organization_id = Some(self.tenant_id.clone())`; doc: *"the top-level tenant/billing boundary"* |
| `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/api_key_tenancy.rs:160,170` | a **foreign key** to `tenants.id` — `if project.tenant_id != organization_id { TenantMismatch }` |
| `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs:227-237` | the **authorization identity** — `authorize_tenant_scope` denies on `caller != target` |
| `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/local.rs:122-124` | *"free-form attribution, **not a foreign key**"* |
| `admin-console/src/resources/api-keys.ts:138-144` | *"**not guaranteed to be** admin-console tenant/user rows"* → shipped as free text |

**Both halves are true, and that is the defect.** The last two describe the *write* path accurately; the first three describe the *read* path accurately. `organization_id` is an **unvalidated tenant claim that is load-bearing for authorization**.

On the same admin form, `project_id` and `workspace_id` are typed entity pickers while **the parent of both is free text**.

## Is `organization_id == tenant_id`? — *Sometimes*, which is the finding

**Always equal** on the durable/virtual-key path: `ferrogate-auth/src/api_key.rs:170`, `ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:9543`, `virtual_keys.rs:2147`.

**Not guaranteed** on the native/static-config path: `auth.rs:484` and `local.rs:10731` copy the caller's value **verbatim with no lookup**. And `config/loader.rs:214` sets `organization_id: None` for env-derived keys — which is **platform operator**.

## Why that last point is the sharp edge

`organization_id: None` does not mean "no access". It means **all access**:

```rust
auth.rs:231  _ => Ok(())            // scope check: no org ⇒ allow
auth.rs:250  None => rows           // list filter: no org ⇒ every tenant's rows
auth.rs:325  None => requested      // forced ?tenant= : no org ⇒ whatever was asked
auth.rs:276  let Some(..) else { return Ok(()) }
```

Probe: an operator key (`organization_id` unset) read **all four tenants'** projects and `GET /admin/v1/tenant-roles/tenant-b` → 200.

So **a typo silently creates a new tenant; an omission silently creates root.** The only thing standing between "tenant admin" and "platform root" is `require_platform_operator` (`auth.rs:372`) on the api-key routes — one guard, protecting a field the console describes as free text. That guard *is* mutation-proven (removing it turns 5 tests red) and probe-confirmed 403, so this is latent rather than trivially exploitable — but the margin is one function.

## Ask

Pick a side and make the whole stack agree:

- **(a)** `organization_id` is an FK to `tenants.id` → validate it on every write path, make the console an entity picker (this also fixes #340 box 1), and delete the "free-form attribution" doc comments; **or**
- **(b)** it is genuinely free-form attribution → then it **must not be** the authorization identity, and `authorize_tenant_scope` needs a different, validated input.

Either way: **`organization_id: None` meaning "platform root" must become explicit opt-in**, not the default an omitted config field lands on (`config/loader.rs:214`).

Refs #340.

---

## Scope amendment, 2026-07-27 (dev agent, at the code-review agent's direction)

The review of `c597ddf` accepted side **(a)** and the `CallerScope` mechanism, but correctly held that the non-negotiable above — *"must become explicit opt-in, not the default an omitted config field lands on"* — **is not delivered**: `TenancyConfig::default()` keeps `implicit_platform_operator: true`, `config/loader.rs` still emits `organization_id: None, platform_operator: None`, and the probe in this issue still reproduces out of the box.

The reviewer offered two resolutions: flip the default and take the fixture churn, or split it so the acceptance text matches what shipped. **Split taken — the flip is #540.** Nothing is being weakened by amendment: the original text stands above, unedited, and #540 carries that exact sentence as its own acceptance.

So this issue's remaining scope is the mechanism and its wiring:

- the `Option<bool>` round-trip hazard on `AdminApiKey::platform_operator` (a `GET` → `PUT` of an unchanged document currently bricks a legacy root key);
- converting the ~8 remaining consumers that still spell root as `organization_id.is_none()`, or dropping the defence-in-depth claim;
- pinning the wiring — that the write path calls the validator, and that `Config::validate` calls the startup warning.

**#540 is what closes the non-negotiable.** This issue must not be read as having closed it.

body:
Found by a test-gate audit of the org/RBAC entity model. **Confirmed by live probe against a running gateway**, and by a static sweep.

## `status` is a decorative column

```
$ grep -rn '"suspended"' --include=*.rs crates/ | grep -v '_test\.rs|/tests/' | wc -l
0
```

**Zero** non-test comparison sites in the entire Rust codebase. `check_api_key_tenancy` never reads `StoredProject.status` or the tenant's status.

## Live probe — suspension changes nothing

Suspended a tenant, its project **and** its workspace (all `200 OK`), then:

| Action after full-chain suspension | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Pre-existing virtual key → `GET /v1/models` | **200 OK** |
| Same key → `POST /v1/chat/completions` | `400 model_not_found` — i.e. **passed auth** |
| Mint a **new** virtual key under the suspended chain | **201 + live secret** |
| `POST /admin/v1/api-keys {"project_id":"proj-susp"}` | **201** |
| `POST /admin/v1/projects {"tenant_id":"tenant-susp"}` | **201** |

## Failure scenario

An operator suspends a non-paying or compromised tenant. The console shows `suspended`. Every existing key keeps serving traffic and billing, and anyone can mint fresh credentials under the suspended chain. **Suspension is a billing and abuse control; a control that only the UI honours is not a control.**

## The one subsystem that does honour it

MCP identity (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/mcp_identity.rs:511, 1395, 2182`) filters `status='active'` and returns `WorkspaceInactive`. That outcome has **zero test references** — so even the one correct implementation is unprotected against regression, and it is Postgres-only SQL.

## Ask

1. Decide the semantics of each lifecycle state (`suspended`, `disabled`, `deleted`) at **both** seams: attach-time (can a suspended row be referenced?) and **request-time** (does an existing key stop working?). Request-time is the one that matters for billing.
2. Enforce it in one place per seam, so it holds for every caller and every storage backend — not per-handler.
3. Cover both seams in the harness. `assert_api_key_tenancy_enforcement` (landed in `0e78beb`) is the natural home for the attach-time half.
4. Give `WorkspaceInactive` a test.
5. Every check must go **red** when removed. An enforcement with no failing test is an untested assumption.

## Not yet determined

All probes ran the **in-memory** control-plane store. The `status='active'` filters found are Postgres-only, so backend behaviour may differ — this needs a run against the live Supabase project before anyone concludes Postgres is safe.

Supersedes the narrower #512 (attach-time only).

body:
Found by the test gate while gating #340. Established by **probing a live gateway**, not by reading code.

`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/api_key_tenancy.rs` validates that referenced rows belong to the same tenant, but it never inspects the target's `status`/`enabled` field. So a suspended project or tenant can still be attached to a brand-new api key:

```
POST /admin/v1/projects        {"id":"p-susp","status":"suspended"}   -> 201
POST /admin/v1/api-keys        {"project_id":"p-susp",...}            -> 201   <- accepted
POST /admin/v1/tenant-accounts {"id":"t-susp","status":"suspended"}   -> 201
POST /admin/v1/projects        {"tenant_id":"t-susp"}                 -> 201   <- accepted
```

## Why this was not a #340 bounce

#340's box 5 reads *"Disabled/deleted targets are **visibly marked** and **cannot be newly selected**"* — worded in UI terms, and the console half genuinely works (deleting the `selectOption` guard turns the component test red). Its box 4, the one that says *"rejected authoritatively by the API"*, is about **cross-tenant** pairs, and that IS enforced and mutation-proven.

So the API-side status check falls in the gap between the two boxes. Filing it rather than stretching #340's acceptance to cover it.

## Why it matters

The console guard is the only thing stopping this today. Any non-console caller — CLI, script, another service, or a console with a stale cache — can attach a suspended tenant or project to a new key. Suspension is a billing/abuse control; a control that only the UI honours is not a control.

## Ask

- Decide the intended semantics for each lifecycle state (`suspended`, `disabled`, `deleted`) on the **reference** side: refuse the attach, accept-but-inert, or accept with a warning.
- Enforce it in `check_api_key_tenancy` (or wherever the reference-validation seam belongs) so it holds for every caller, not just the console.
- Cover it in the harness. `assert_api_key_tenancy_enforcement` already exists in the `admin-api` scenario (landed in `0e78beb` for #340's box 4) and is the natural home — extend it rather than adding a parallel path.
- The test must go **red** when the status check is removed. An enforcement with no failing test is an untested assumption.

## Reproduction

Start a gateway, then run the four requests above in order. Both marked lines should be refused and are not.

Refs #340.

body:
## Problem

`expect_supabase_schema_migrations` in `tools/ferrogate-test/src/storage.rs` (~:1307) asserts the latest applied migration is `50:050_bucket_backed_asset_size_constraint`. `sql/001_init_postgres.sql` now reaches **58** (`058_site_domain_verifications`).

`ferrogate_storage::POSTGRES_SCHEMA_VERSION` / `POSTGRES_SCHEMA_NAME` are also still pinned at 50, despite an in-code comment claiming they are the harness's authority for the expected schema.

**Consequence: `ferrogate-test supabase-restart` bails on that assertion before it reaches anything else.** The scenario is effectively dead — it cannot exercise the durability coverage it exists to prove, and every slice that adds a table to the Supabase verified set inherits a scenario that fails for an unrelated reason.

Found while landing #352's restart/durability coverage (`45628b6`). Independent of that slice: the Postgres restart scenarios do not call this assertion, so #352's coverage is unaffected — but it means #352's Supabase leg cannot be exercised until this is fixed.

## Why it is the same defect class as #499 / #509 / #510

A stale pin that hard-fails a scenario is indistinguishable, in practice, from the scenario not existing. It is the third guard found this session that is believed to be running and is not actually holding anything.

## Scope

- Bump `POSTGRES_SCHEMA_VERSION` / `POSTGRES_SCHEMA_NAME` to the real latest migration and update the two schema tests that pin them.
- Fix `expect_supabase_schema_migrations` to assert against that constant rather than a second hard-coded literal, so the two cannot drift again.
- Decide whether the assertion should be "latest == N" or "latest >= N"; an exact pin means every migration must touch this file, which is what let it rot. If exact is deliberate, add a test that fails when `001_init_postgres.sql` grows past the pin, so the rot is caught at the source.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `ferrogate-test supabase-restart` proceeds past the schema-migration assertion.
- [ ] `POSTGRES_SCHEMA_VERSION` and the harness assertion derive from a single source of truth — grep proves no second hard-coded migration literal remains.
- [ ] A test fails if a new migration is added without updating that source of truth.
- [ ] #352's Supabase restart leg (payment attempts + wallet links) is exercised once this clears.

## Note

`cargo clippy --all-targets` is separately red on `crates/ferrogate-storage/examples/d1_live_456_wallet_ops_probe.rs` (2 `uninlined_format_args`) — small, unrelated, mentioned here only so it is not rediscovered as new.

body:
## Problem

Two admin-console gates are red on `main`, independent of any in-flight slice. Verified by me on `467f5f4` in a clean worktree with a fresh `npm ci`.

### 1. `npx tsc -b` fails

```
src/pages/agent-jobs.tsx(85,43): error TS2345:
  Argument of type '{ input: string; idempotency_key: string | undefined; }'
  is not assignable to parameter of type
  '{ input: string; idempotency_key?: string | null; framework_adapter?: string | null;
     required_capabilities: string[]; workload_ref?: string | null; }'.
  Property 'required_capabilities' is missing.
```

The generated API types require `required_capabilities`, and the page's submit call does not pass it. Related: `npm run check:api-types` reports the generated types are stale against `docs/openapi/admin-api.openapi.json`, which is very likely the same root cause — the spec grew the field and the call site was never updated.

### 2. Seven `vitest` failures, all one root cause

```
src/pages/assets.test.tsx        13 tests | 2 failed
src/pages/static-sites.test.tsx  29 tests | 5 failed
```

All seven fail with `object.stream is not a function` — a Node 22.17 `Blob`/undici incompatibility in the upload paths (presigned register-intent → PUT → commit, and zip-bundle publish), not a product defect in the pages themselves.

Full run on `467f5f4` + `f7178ff`: **487 passed, 7 failed, 74 of 76 files passing.**

## Why file it

`scripts/check-admin-console.sh` cannot pass while either of these is red, so the gate is permanently failing and everyone learns to skip it — the same defect class as #499, #500 and #509. A red gate that everyone ignores is indistinguishable from no gate.

## Scope

- Fix the `agent-jobs.tsx` call site to pass `required_capabilities` (and re-run `npm run generate:api` so `check:api-types` is clean — this also clears the drift #351 left behind).
- Fix the `object.stream` failures: either polyfill/adapt the `Blob` the tests construct, or update the upload code to the API surface Node 22.17's undici actually provides. Do not delete or skip the seven tests — they cover the presigned-upload and zip-publish paths that #368 and the static-site work depend on.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `cd admin-console && npx tsc -b` exits 0.
- [ ] `npm run check:api-types` exits 0 with no uncommitted generated diff.
- [ ] `npx vitest run` exits 0 — 494/494.
- [ ] `scripts/check-admin-console.sh` exits 0 end to end.
- [ ] No test is deleted, skipped or `.only`'d to reach the above.

## Note on the toolchain

Node is installed but **off `PATH`** at `$HOME/toolchain/node/node-v22.17.0-linux-x64/bin`, and `admin-console/node_modules` is absent from a fresh checkout (`npm ci` takes ~5s). See #508 — do that first or you will conclude the toolchain is missing, as I did.

body:
## Problem

`cargo +1.88.0 clippy -p ferrogate-cli --all-targets -- -D warnings` **fails on `main`** with 6 errors. The clippy gate is red, so every agent and every CI consumer that runs it gets a failure that is not theirs, and the natural response — "pre-existing, not mine, moving on" — means the gate stops gating.

## Reproduction

Verified on a **pristine `origin/main` checkout** (`e64377a`) in a throwaway worktree, before cherry-picking anything:

```
$ git worktree add -f --detach /tmp/wt origin/main
$ cd /tmp/wt && cargo +1.88.0 clippy -p ferrogate-cli --all-targets -- -D warnings
error: consider using `sort_by_key`
error: the `Err`-variant returned from this function is very large
error: redundant closure
error: redundant closure
error: doc list item overindented
error: doc list item overindented
error: could not compile `ferrogate-cli` (bin "ferrogate") due to 6 previous errors
error: could not compile `ferrogate-cli` (bin "ferrogate" test) due to 6 previous errors
```

Sites:

- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/agent_jobs.rs:1180`
- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/chat.rs:2605`, `:2668`, `:2670`
- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/site_domains.rs:559`, `:562`

Independently reported by three separate dev agents this session (#340, #351, #360), each correctly declining to fix it because the files belong to other in-flight slices and touching them would only manufacture cherry-pick conflicts.

Attribution from the code-review thread on #360: last touched by `a950b3a` (#488) and `1748b9d` (#470).

## Why it matters beyond the six lints

`cargo clippy … -D warnings` is one of the repo's local gates. A permanently-red gate trains every agent to skip it, which is exactly how a *new* lint slips in unnoticed. Same class as #499 (`check-workers.sh` never invoked) and #508 (no Node toolchain, admin-console gate silently skipped): **a gate believed to be running that is not actually holding the code.**

## Scope

- Fix all six lints. They are mechanical: `sort_by_key`, boxing a large `Err` variant, two redundant closures, two overindented doc list items.
- Do it as one small commit touching only those three files, so it does not collide with the in-flight slices that own their surrounding code.
- Confirm no other workspace crate is red: run `cargo +1.88.0 clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` and either fix or file what it surfaces.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `cargo +1.88.0 clippy -p ferrogate-cli --all-targets -- -D warnings` exits 0 on `main`.
- [ ] `cargo +1.88.0 clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` exits 0, or every remaining failure has its own filed issue linked here.
- [ ] The `Err`-variant fix does not change any public error type's semantics — only its representation.

body:
## This issue was filed on a false premise — retitled and rescoped

I filed this claiming "there is no Node toolchain on the dev box". **That is wrong.** Node is installed, just not on `PATH`:

```
$ export PATH=$HOME/toolchain/node/node-v22.17.0-linux-x64/bin:$PATH
$ node -v && npm -v && npx -v
v22.17.0
10.9.2
10.9.2
```

My original evidence (`command -v node`, scanning `PATH` entries, looking for nvm/volta/asdf) only ever proved Node was *not on `PATH`*. I read that as *absent*. I have since run the full admin-console gate myself — see https://github.com/lianluo-esign/ferrogate/issues/340#issuecomment-5082183640 — and the #340 agent's reported results reproduce exactly (`vitest` 487 passed / 7 failed).

## The real problem, which is narrower but still real

The gate is **runnable but not discoverable**, and that cost something concrete today: because I believed the gate could not run, I pushed #351 without it and **shipped a regression** — three new `/admin/v1/x402-spend-policies*` operations with no console surface and no reviewed exclusion, breaking the #313 acceptance-box-1 guard in `admin-api-coverage.test.ts` (13/13 at `3064f3c` → 2 failures at `467f5f4`). Fixed in `f7178ff`. A discoverable gate would have caught it before the push.

Three concrete gaps:

1. **Node is off-`PATH` and nothing says where it is.** Every agent must independently rediscover `$HOME/toolchain/node/node-v22.17.0-linux-x64/bin`. Because `npm`/`npx` are shebang scripts, invoking them by absolute path fails with `env: 'node': No such file or directory` — an error that reads like "node is missing" and actively misleads.
2. **`admin-console/node_modules` is absent from a fresh checkout**, so the first `npx vitest` an agent tries fails on missing deps and reinforces the "toolchain is broken" reading. (`npm ci` succeeds in ~5s from the canonical registry — the registry is reachable.)
3. **`scripts/check-admin-console.sh` does not fail loudly when the toolchain is unreachable.** A gate that can be silently not-run is the same defect class as #499 and #500.

## Scope

- Put Node on `PATH` for every shell that runs repo tooling (append to the existing `~/.local/tcbin/rust-env.sh`, which is already auto-sourced from `~/.bashrc`, so one edit fixes both interactive shells and subagents).
- Document the path in `AGENTS.md` next to the Rust toolchain note, including the shebang gotcha, so the misleading error never costs another agent an hour.
- Make `scripts/check-admin-console.sh` exit non-zero with `admin-console gate did NOT run: node not found on PATH` rather than skipping or reporting success.
- Decide and document whether `admin-console/node_modules` should be pre-installed on the box or whether `npm ci` is a required first step, and have the script run it rather than failing obscurely.
- Install the Playwright browsers (or make `test:e2e` fail with an actionable message) — dev writes the spec, the gate runs it, and the gate cannot today.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `node -v` and `npm -v` succeed in a plain non-login shell with no manual `export`.
- [ ] `cd admin-console && npm run typecheck && npx vitest run && npm run lint && npm run build` all *execute* from a fresh checkout (pass or fail on their merits).
- [ ] `scripts/check-admin-console.sh` fails loudly and by name when Node is unreachable, with a test or CI job asserting that behaviour.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` documents the Node path and the `env: 'node': No such file or directory` shebang gotcha.

## Still separately true

`npx tsc -b` is red on `main` at `src/pages/agent-jobs.tsx(85,43)` (`required_capabilities` missing), and 7 `vitest` failures persist in `assets.test.tsx`/`static-sites.test.tsx` (`object.stream is not a function`, Node 22.17 Blob/undici). Both are real, both are pre-existing, and neither is what this issue is about — filing separately.

body:
Found by the test gate while gating #469. **Pre-existing — not introduced or worsened by #469**, which is why #469 was not held for it.

## The defect

`WalletStore::settle_wallet_reservation` flips an expired reservation to `released` **and persists it**, and only then returns `Conflict` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/wallet.rs:1183-1191`):

```rust
if reservation.expires_at_unix <= now_unix {
    reservation.status = WALLET_RESERVATION_RELEASED.to_string();
    reservation.updated_at_unix = now_unix;
    self.wallet_reservations
        .insert(reservation.id.clone(), reservation);   // <-- the release is COMMITTED
    return Err(StorageError::Conflict(format!(
        "wallet reservation {reservation_id} expired; cannot settle"
    )));
}
```

On the reconciler side, `is_unresolved` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state_x402_settlement.rs:869-877`) matches only `OperationCommitOutcomeUnknown` / `OperationDeadlineExceeded` / `OperationCancelled` — **not `Conflict`**. So the caller takes the "terminal edge failed (isolated)" branch and logs *hold retained* (`state_x402_settlement.rs:576-606`).

## Impact

The money is confirmed on-chain and the merchant keeps it, the hold has actually been **released**, and the operator-facing log says the opposite — so the tenant is never charged and the log actively misdirects whoever investigates. Identical for exact and overpaid transfers.

This is squarely #400/#401 hold-TTL-floor territory: the TTL floor makes the expiry window rare, it does not make the branch correct, and the log line is wrong regardless of how often it fires.

## Ask

- Decide the intended semantics for "hold expired between reserve and settle" and make the code and the log agree. Either the release should not be committed on the error path, or the caller must recognise `Conflict` as a *terminal, hold-already-released* outcome and say so.
- Whichever way it goes, the attempt must not be left in a state where confirmed funds are never captured and nothing surfaces it.
- A test must cover the expired-hold settle path on both the exact and the overpaid branch, and must go red if the log/branch mismatch is reintroduced.

## Reproduction

Open a paid-egress attempt, let the wallet reservation pass `expires_at_unix`, then drive a reconciler tick with a confirmed on-chain transfer. Observe the reservation row is `released` while the log claims the hold was retained.

Refs #469, #400, #401.

title: [tooling][P1] The repo's own clippy gate is red on main — security-check.sh cannot pass

body:
Parent: #358. Depends on #360, #361–#364.

Raised externally on #362 by @hegu-1 after that issue closed, so it has no home. Triaged: the other two suggestions from the same reviewer are already implemented and were **not** opened as issues — action identity by `crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/action_identity.rs` (#303/#304), and cost receipts by `AgentCostReceipt` / `BudgetDecision` / the burn ledger in `crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/cloudflare_agent_cost.rs` (#428). This one is a real gap.

## Problem

The CLI has the *inputs* of a governed surface but not the *output contract*:

- `crates/ferrogate-cli-core/src/output.rs` is 125 lines — `OutputFormat`, `Table`, `render_json`. There is no mutation-result envelope of any kind.
- `dry-run` exists, but only as a per-resource verb invented ad hoc (`ops config validate`, `guardrail-policy dry-run`), not as a uniform property of every mutation.
- Idempotency keys are threaded on some resources (`billing`, `agent submit`) and absent on others.
- Nothing in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/ctl/` references `audit_id`, `approval_id`, or a rollback pointer.

So a CLI mutation returns success text (or a raw JSON body) and the operator cannot tell, from the CLI, which policy decision permitted it, which audit row records it, what exact object version it changed, or how to reverse it. The runtime already has the canonical vocabulary for all of this — `ActionIdentity`, `ActionDecision` (`allow`/`deny`/`ask`/`degrade`), `action_fingerprint` — and the CLI simply does not surface it. That makes the CLI a privileged side channel next to the UI/API rather than another view onto the same governance plane.

#364 asks for audit identifiers on the *operator-action and evidence* command groups specifically. This issue is the cross-cutting contract: every mutating command in every group, enforced by a shared type rather than per-command discipline.

## Scope

- A single `MutationReceipt` envelope in `ferrogate-cli-core`, rendered for every mutating verb in every format (`table` and `json`), carrying:
  - actor identity (resolved principal + context/tenant that authorized the call)
  - target object identity and version/fingerprint, reusing the runtime `action_fingerprint` contract rather than inventing a CLI-local one
  - policy decision and approval id where the mutation crossed a governance gate
  - `dry_run: true|false` — explicit on every mutation, never inferred from the verb name
  - rollback pointer where the resource has revisions (guardrail policies, routing, gateway config)
  - immutable audit id
- Fields the API does not return are `null` with a stated reason, not silently omitted — an absent audit id is itself a finding.
- Registry-level enforcement: a verb marked mutating cannot render a bare body.

## Non-goals

- No new server-side audit emission. If a control-plane endpoint returns no audit id today, this issue records the gap (and files a follow-up); it does not add the write path.
- No change to the invocation-level approval fingerprint in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/approval.rs`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `MutationReceipt` lives in `ferrogate-cli-core` and is the only sanctioned return shape for a mutating verb; a unit test enumerates the command registry and fails if any mutating verb can render without one.
- [ ] `--dry-run` is accepted and echoed by every mutating verb; a dry run provably issues no state-changing request (test asserts on the transport, not on output text).
- [ ] The CLI's `action_fingerprint` for a given target byte-matches `CanonicalCapabilityTarget::fingerprint` for that same target — asserted by a test, not by convention.
- [ ] `--output json` receipts are machine-parseable and stable enough to pipe into an audit query; a test round-trips one.
- [ ] E2E: mutate a guardrail policy revision, then follow the receipt's audit id and rollback pointer to (a) locate the audit row and (b) reverse the change, with no identifier typed by hand. _(#552, 2026-07-30: YES decision taken — guardrail-policy activate/rollback now return a real `audit_id` (`114f18ef`), so half (a) is reachable; the harness None→Some wiring is tracked on #552 in the test-agent lane.)_
- [ ] Endpoints returning no audit id are enumerated in the issue thread on close.

title: [cli][P2] Mutating CLI commands return no decision receipt — no actor, target fingerprint, policy decision, dry-run flag, rollback pointer, or audit id

body:
Found by the code-review agent while passing #474's rework. Disclosed by the dev
as `Scope-risk: medium` in `928e82c` and bounded to a single tenant, so it was
recorded rather than blocking — filing so it is tracked.

## The gap

`apply_worker_reported_run_state` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state_agent_runtime.rs:1610-1640`)
is the bridge that lets a self-hosted worker terminalize a run and attach its
`output`. It checks that the reporting worker's **tenant** matches the run's
tenant — using `registration.tenant`, which is correctly server-derived
(`state_agent_runtime.rs:842`), not a worker-supplied claim.

What it does **not** check is that this worker holds, or ever held, a **lease** for
the run it is reporting on.

## Impact

Any worker registered to tenant A can name **any** non-terminal `agent_runs` row in
tenant A and:

- flip it to a terminal state, and
- attach arbitrary `output` to it, which `/v1/agent-jobs/{id}/result` will then
  serve as the run's real output.

That includes runs the worker never leased, and runs created by other surfaces
entirely — the synchronous `/v1/agent-runs` harness path and
`gateway/external_actions.rs`, neither of which involves a worker lease at all.

The blast radius is one tenant, which is why this is P2 rather than P1: it is not
cross-tenant. But within a tenant it means a compromised or buggy worker can
fabricate the recorded outcome of work it never performed, and the audit trail
will show that outcome as the run's genuine result.

## How to observe

1. Register worker W in tenant A.
2. Create a run through `/v1/agent-runs` (the synchronous path — no dispatch, no
   lease).
3. From W, `POST /v1/self-hosted-workers/events` naming that run id with
   `{"state":"completed","output":"anything"}`.
4. `GET /v1/agent-jobs/{that run id}/result` returns `200` with that output.

## Suggested fix

Bind the report to the lease rather than to the tenant: require that the run has a
dispatch leased to this `worker_id` (or that `assigned_worker_id` matches), and
reject otherwise. `durable_self_hosted_dispatch_for_run`
(`state_agent_runtime.rs:1580`) already resolves the dispatch for a run, so the
lookup exists; it is the check that is missing.

Runs with no dispatch at all — the `/v1/agent-runs` and `external_actions` cases —
should be rejected outright, since no worker can legitimately report on them.

Refs #474
