Parent: #295.
Related product coverage epic: #313.

Origin: operator review of the local Admin Console on 2026-07-21.

## Problem

The dashboard cannot truthfully act as a global control plane because no endpoint exposes an authorized, consistent overview of the system. `admin-console/src/pages/dashboard.tsx` currently combines status, provider health, approvals, recent request logs, and the latest usage report. Its token value is the latest tenant/month report, not global total consumption, and there is no MCP server count, static asset count/storage usage, agent-run count, resource utilization/reference summary, or consolidated error signal.

Making the browser fetch every list endpoint and count rows is not a fix: it creates a large request fan-out, truncates at pagination boundaries, duplicates aggregation rules, and can mix snapshots or authorization scopes.

## Scope

- Add a typed read-only Admin API endpoint, `GET /admin/v1/overview`, backed by bounded repository aggregation rather than loading every record into memory.
- Define "global" as all resources visible to the authenticated admin context. Never leak counts across an unauthorized tenant or scope.
- Return explicit time/scope semantics for token, request, and cost totals. At minimum expose lifetime and current-calendar-month token totals; do not relabel a latest report as a lifetime total.
- Return resource inventory counts for tenants, projects, workspaces, providers/models, API or virtual keys, policies/guardrails, MCP servers, static assets, agent runs, and self-hosted workers.
- Return meaningful state breakdowns where applicable: enabled/disabled, healthy/unhealthy, active/succeeded/failed, referenced/unreferenced, storage bytes/quota, and pending approvals. Use nullable/not-applicable fields rather than fake zeros.
- Return a bounded critical-alert summary for unhealthy providers, failed requests/runs, quota pressure, pending approvals, and stale/draining workers, with evidence links/identifiers and timestamps.
- Include `generated_at_unix`, the effective visibility scope, section freshness, and explicit unavailable/error state. A failed section must not silently report zero.
- Register the route in the runtime contract and generated OpenAPI client.

## Acceptance

- [x] One request returns the authorized overview without N+1 queries or browser-side list counting.
- [x] Token totals are proven against durable usage/ledger data and distinguish lifetime from current month.
- [x] MCP server, static asset, and agent-run totals match their repositories for both in-memory and Postgres backends.
- [x] Asset storage-**bytes** usage exposed with documented semantics. _(Per-scope asset storage **quota** + referenced/unreferenced breakdown re-scoped to #458 — quota is a per-scope admission override with no single global number.)_
- [x] Critical alerts (unhealthy providers, failed requests/runs, stale/draining workers) include evidence identifiers/links and remain bounded. _(Quota-pressure + pending-approval alerts/counts re-scoped to #458.)_
- [x] Tenant/RBAC tests prove no cross-scope count leakage; partial storage failure never becomes a false zero.
- [x] OpenAPI/schema checks and focused contract/integration tests pass.

> **Re-scoped 2026-07-24 (before lane move, per lane-entry contract):** guardrail/quota/policy inventory counts, enabled/disabled virtual-key breakdown, and the asset-quota/approval/quota-pressure sub-parts above are tracked in follow-up **#458** (guardrail revisions carry no tenant column; asset quota is per-scope). The amended #339 acceptance above is fully delivered + tested; commit `c2a6ef0`.

## Non-goals

- Analytics-warehouse time series or arbitrary BI queries.
- Returning full resource collections inside the overview response.
- A dashboard UI; that is a dependent issue.

Parent: #295.
Related: #176, #259, #260, #263.

Origin: static-resource UI audit on 2026-07-21.

## Problem

The runtime has substantially more asset-management behavior than its OpenAPI contract exposes. `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/assets.rs` implements manifest, channel list/move/delete, yank/unyank, semver/variant resolution, and concrete version operations. `asset_presign.rs` implements upload-intent, commit, and download URL flows for large bucket-backed objects. The Admin OpenAPI currently declares only list-by-type and concrete get/put/delete routes.

As a result the console hand-defines a reduced `AssetSummary`, uses only inline `PUT`, and cannot safely build a typed management module for versions, variants, channels, or large assets.

## Scope

- Add runtime-contract/OpenAPI entries for:
  - `GET /v1/assets/{asset_type}/{name}/manifest`
  - `GET /v1/assets/{asset_type}/{name}/channels`
  - `PUT|DELETE /v1/assets/{asset_type}/{name}/channels/{channel}`
  - `POST|DELETE /v1/assets/{asset_type}/{name}/{version}/yank`
  - presigned upload-intent, commit, and download URL routes.
- Publish schemas for manifest versions/variants, channel summaries/mutations, presign requests/responses, upload constraints, and typed error responses.
- Make variant and yank state discoverable through the list/manifest contract without leaking bucket object keys.
- Expose an authoritative asset storage usage/quota summary suitable for the console; stop requiring client-side summation of a potentially paginated list.
- Document auth/RBAC, checksum/size/content-type requirements, inline-vs-presigned selection rules, expiry, idempotent commit behavior, and failure cleanup semantics.
- Regenerate the TypeScript client and remove asset endpoint drift from the contract checks.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Every asset lifecycle route implemented by the runtime is represented in the enforced contract or explicitly removed from runtime.
- [ ] Generated TypeScript types cover manifests, channels, yank state, variants, and presigned transfer responses; the console needs no hand-written duplicate response shape.
- [ ] Storage usage/quota comes from an authoritative backend result, not list-page summation.
- [ ] Contract tests prove route/method/auth parity and typed 4xx responses.
- [ ] Integration tests cover inline upload and presign intent -> upload -> commit -> typed list/manifest -> download.
- [ ] `scripts/check-openapi.py` and generated-client drift checks pass.

## Non-goals

- Redesigning the asset storage engine.
- Building the registry or static-site UI.

Origin: operator review of project/workspace and other Admin Console forms on 2026-07-21.

## Problem

The control plane models relationships, but the UI exposes them as strings. `admin-console/src/lib/resource-config.ts` supports text/number/boolean/static select/textarea/json/csv fields only; `ResourceForm` therefore asks operators to type foreign IDs and comma-separated ID lists. Bespoke pages repeat the same failure.

Examples include project -> tenant, workspace -> project, API key -> organization/project/workspace, role -> permissions, quota/policy -> scope/model/provider, workflow -> tenant/project/key, schedule -> tenant/workspace, and site domain -> tenant/static site. This is error-prone and makes valid relationships undiscoverable.

## Scope

- Extend resource field metadata with explicit single-entity and multi-entity reference types: target resource, value key, primary/secondary labels, query key, search/pagination behavior, and optional dependency on another selected entity.
- Build shared shadcn-based async combobox and multi-select primitives with server search/pagination, selected-value hydration, keyboard navigation, clear/remove, loading/empty/error states, and accessible names/descriptions.
- Display human labels plus a compact/copyable ID; continue sending canonical IDs in API payloads.
- Support dependent selectors such as tenant -> project -> workspace and clear invalid descendants when a parent changes.
- Cache/deduplicate lookups through TanStack Query. Do not preload every entity or issue duplicate per-row/per-field requests.
- Preserve unknown or deleted existing IDs as an explicit "unresolved reference" state so editing never silently drops data.
- Provide an escape hatch for legitimately opaque references, but raw free-text ID entry must not remain the default relationship control.
- Add a small registry/adapter layer so generated forms and bespoke forms reuse the same lookup contracts.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A generated form can declare and render a typed single or multi entity reference without page-specific fetch code.
- [ ] Tenant -> project -> workspace cascading works and never submits an entity outside the selected parent scope.
- [ ] Existing values hydrate to labels; missing/deleted values remain visible as unresolved instead of disappearing.
- [ ] Search is debounced, paginated, cached, and race-safe; large collections are not loaded in one initial request.
- [ ] Keyboard and screen-reader flows cover open/search/select/remove/error/focus restoration.
- [ ] Unit tests cover serialization and dependent clearing; Playwright covers single and multi selection at mobile and desktop widths.
- [ ] No new relation field is implemented as CSV or raw JSON when the target has a list/get API.

## Non-goals

- Migrating every current form in this foundation issue.
- Changing backend relationship identifiers or storage schemas.

Origin: admin-console UI audit on 2026-07-21.

## Problem

The shared resource table and several bespoke operations tables are desktop tables squeezed into a phone viewport, not responsive operator interfaces.

The same risk exists across request logs, audit/billing events, workers, approvals, schedules, and other bespoke tables.

Parent: #295.
Depends on: #331.

Origin: admin-console build and React performance audit on 2026-07-21.

## Problem

admin-console/src/App.tsx eagerly imports every auth, resource, guardrail, agent, billing, worker, operations, and long-tail page before the router renders one route.

Current production build evidence:

- One application JS asset: 716.70 kB minified / 197.05 kB gzip.
- Vite emits the over-500-kB chunk warning.
- A login visit pays parse/compile cost for all protected control-plane pages.
- Rarely used operations editors and heavy dialog/table code cannot be cached or fetched independently.

This is exactly the route-level bundle failure the React best-practices audit flags; changing chunkChunkSizeWarningLimit would hide the symptom and is not a fix.

## Scope

- Convert page routes to React.lazy/dynamic imports with intentional Suspense boundaries.
- Keep the shell, auth/session gate, router, query provider, and small shared primitives in the initial graph.
- Group only routes that share meaningful runtime code; do not create one giant manual vendor chunk.
- Add a usable route-loading fallback that preserves shell dimensions and does not flash/shift navigation.
- Add route import failure handling with an operator-visible retry/reload path.
- Record before/after Vite build output and add a deterministic size-budget check to the local admin-console gate.
- Extend Playwright coverage to prove direct deep links load their lazy chunk and navigation does not cause a full document reload.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Login/register do not download protected feature page chunks.
- [ ] Production build emits no chunk larger than 500 kB and no Vite chunk-size warning.
- [ ] The initial entry chunk is at most 300 kB minified; before/after gzip sizes are recorded in the issue.
- [ ] Direct deep links to representative resource, guardrail, billing, and operations routes render after a loading state.
- [ ] Chunk-load failure is explicit and recoverable.
- [ ] No new runtime dependency is added solely for code splitting.

Parent: #285. Follow-up to #309 (which removed the hot-path bridged WRITES). The read-side counterpart remains: several per-request quota/budget reads still park a Pingora worker thread on synchronous Postgres via `block_on_sync_bridge`/`block_in_place`.

## Sites (all on the request hot path)
- `state_quota_and_policy.rs:222` `resolve_effective_quota` — bridges 4 sequential `get_quota_policy` reads + `resolve_tenant_plan` per request; reached from the sync `finalize_auth` gate (#221 explicitly deferred this as the hard case).
- `state_quota_and_policy.rs:263` `api_key_total_tokens_used` — bridges `usage_aggregates()` which loads the ENTIRE table then filters in memory per request (a full-table scan on the hot path — also a #231-class efficiency bug). Should push the api_key filter + sum to SQL.
- `state_wallets.rs:152` `wallet_balance_exhausted`, `state_agent_runtime.rs:33` `workflow_run_started_at` (full-table gating reads) — same bridge pattern per request.

## Scope (follow the #309 approach)
- Where the caller chain is already async and shallow, propagate async to the storage read and drop the bridge.
- Where the sync-ness is imposed only by the AppState wrapper on a hot path reachable from an async handler, add an async variant the handler `.await`s (keep the sync wrapper for genuine sync/thread callers like finalize_auth if it can't be made async cheaply — assess and document).
- `api_key_total_tokens_used`: add a storage method that filters+sums by api_key_id in SQL (`WHERE api_key_id = $1`) instead of loading the whole table; keep an in-memory equivalent for the memory backend.
- Do NOT weaken any budget/quota enforcement; preserve exact semantics and ordering. Cold/thread callers may stay bridged.

## Acceptance

Parent: #287. Follow-up explicitly deferred by #305 and #307 (and anticipated in-code: `self_hosted_worker.rs:312` "the dispatch's correlation keys ride the lease so the worker can [stamp them]").

## Gap
The dispatch lease now carries `request_id`/`trace_id`/`agent_run_id` (#305) and `parent_action_fingerprint` (#307) — `SelfHostedRunLease` at `crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/self_hosted_worker.rs:297`, populated verbatim from the dispatch (`:1064-1069`). But NOTHING in `crates/agent-worker/src/` reads those fields: when the self-hosted worker executes a leased run and reports evidence/events back to the gateway, that evidence is NOT stamped with the lease's correlation identity. So the self-hosted-worker leg is the one governance layer that doesn't natively emit the shared action identity (hegu-1's #267 framing) — the gateway can only back-fill it from the run, and parent→child A2A/dispatch handoff evidence from the worker isn't correlated by fingerprint.

## Scope
- The worker's run-execution path (where it consumes a lease and produces `NormalizedFrameworkEvent`s / run results / heartbeats/telemetry) threads the lease's correlation keys onto the evidence it reports back over the worker transport.
- The gateway's worker-transport ingestion (self-hosted heartbeat/checkpoint/artifact/event/run-result endpoints in `state_agent_runtime.rs` + the framework-event recording in `gateway/agent_runs.rs`/`external_actions.rs`) records worker-reported evidence with the lease's `{request_id, trace_id, agent_run_id}` + `parent_action_fingerprint` when present, so it joins the #199 investigation view + `action_correlations` (#306/#307) by the same keys/fingerprint instead of relying on gateway-side back-fill.
- Absent keys stay None (report-only / keyless dispatches) — never fabricated.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A self-hosted worker run started from a correlated dispatch produces evidence rows carrying the same {request_id, trace_id, agent_run_id} triple + parent_action_fingerprint as the lease (integration/e2e, following the correlation_join_e2e / tenant_isolation patterns; in-memory backend acceptable in-sandbox).
- [ ] Keyless dispatches record NULL, not fabricated ids.
- [ ] Wire-compatible + backward compatible (older workers/gateways that don't send the fields still work).

body:
A read-only pre-release correctness/robustness review of the two security-sensitive surfaces landed 2026-07-20 (#315 admin-api reverse proxy, #326 project/workspace update+delete). **No security defect found** — no open-proxy path (auth gate precedes every forward), no read→write scope escalation, fail-closed startup guard sound, ownership checks on every verb with structural tenant/project immutability, reject-if-referenced counts children across all tenants. The reportable items are robustness/consistency:

1. **[FIXED in follow-up commit] Storage errors on load-before-mutate collapsed to 404.** #326's PUT/PATCH/DELETE handlers loaded the row with `.ok().flatten()` (`virtual_keys.rs` ~863/961/1391/1493), mapping a transient storage error AND a genuine miss both to 404 — inconsistent with the GET arm which returns 503 `storage_unavailable`. A brief pool outage during an update told the operator "no project with id X" (implying deletion) and defeated 5xx-keyed retry. Fixed by matching the GET arm's three-way Ok(Some)/Ok(None)→404/Err→503.

2. **Chunked / missing-Content-Length request bodies silently dropped, not rejected** (admin-api + pre-existing in the auth service HTTP parser). `read_http_request_bounded` derives body length only from `content-length` (default 0); no `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` handling. A chunked POST through the proxy parses body.len()==0, passes the 413 cap, and forwards an empty body → gateway 400. No request-smuggling (fresh upstream conn, explicit CL, Connection: close). Fix: reject chunked/unknown-length with 411/400 at the parser.

3. **Parse cap can sit below a configured per-family `[limits]` cap** → connection reset instead of clean 413 (non-default config only). `MAX_PROXY_REQUEST_BYTES` ≈10MB is applied before the per-path cap; raising a per-family cap (e.g. guardrail_policy_body_max_bytes) above 10MB makes a mid-size request Err out of the parser and drop the connection with no HTTP response. Fix: validation guard that the parse cap ≥ max configured family cap, or raise it.

4. **Reject-if-referenced delete is TOCTOU, not atomic.** The child-count and the DELETE are separate non-transactional round-trips; a child created in the window is missed and then `ON DELETE CASCADE` destroys it. Low likelihood (admin traffic). Fix: check+delete in one transaction, or DB-level `ON DELETE RESTRICT`.

Minor (not tracked separately): 502 request-id not correlated with the gate's id (observability); tenant-scoped 403-vs-404 existence oracle on opaque ids.

Finding 1 is fixed in the follow-up commit that references this issue; 2–4 remain open here.
title: [security][P3] Pre-release robustness review findings: admin-api proxy + project/workspace CRUD (mostly correctness, no security defect)

body:
Surfaced by the post-#324 full-workspace release-gate run: `ferrogate-mcp` `lib_test::http_client_adopts_2026_07_28_when_server_echoes_it` failed once under `cargo test --workspace` (92/92 other suites green). Passes 3/3 standalone. Same load-sensitive family as #234/#235/#240/#324 but a distinct test/helper not in #324's scope.

## Suspected root cause
`capture_one_http_request` (`crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/lib_test.rs:790`) spawns a one-shot TCP server thread that `accept()` → reads until `\r\n\r\n` → `write_all` the canned response → returns the request; the client runs on the main thread via `client_call`, then `handle.join().unwrap()`. Under CPU contention the `HttpMcpClient` request likely hits its timeout, drops the connection, and the server thread's `write_all`/`flush` then fails with EPIPE → thread panics → `join().unwrap()` propagates. (The listener is bound before `client_call`, so unlike #324 this is NOT a free_addr TOCTOU — the socket is held.)

## Fix direction
- Make the server thread tolerant of a client that gave up: don't `unwrap()` the final `write_all`/`flush` (ignore broken-pipe), and have `join()` not hard-panic on a benign thread error.
- If the client-side timeout is the real trigger, give the test client a generous request timeout (test-only config, not production default).
- Verify under simulated load (concurrent copies + `yes` workers), like #324.
- Shared helper: applies to all `capture_one_http_request` / `post_http_*` tests in this file — harden the helper once.

Non-blocking per the established flake policy (passes standalone; documented here for the evidence chain). Release gate treated green modulo this documented standalone-passing flake.

Parent: #313. User directive 2026-07-20: the admin console must be served by its OWN dedicated API service module — not mixed with the core system's API surface.

## Current state
The console calls two things: the auth service (`/v1/admin/register|login|refresh|logout|me`, #157/#232 sessions) and the GATEWAY's `/admin/v1/*` surface with a minted virtual key — i.e. admin control-plane traffic rides the same process/listener/route-table as the AI data plane.

## Scope
- New service module `ferrogate admin-api serve` following the established decomposition pattern (`ferrogate auth serve` / `ferrogate billing serve`: same binary, own HTTP listener, own config section, optional durable Supabase backend): a dedicated admin-console API process.
- Path-compatible `/admin/v1/*` surface so the console (and UI slices in this epic) only change base URL (`GATEWAY_ADMIN_BASE_URL` → `ADMIN_API_BASE_URL` in env-config, keeping backward compat).
- Implementation strategy — explore then choose, documenting the trade-off: (a) mount the existing admin route-group handlers on the new service's listener sharing `ferrogate-storage` repositories (preferred if the handlers' AppState dependencies are separable), or (b) an authenticated reverse proxy to the gateway's admin routes as a first slice with handler extraction as follow-up. Either way: admin scope enforcement + tenant scoping (#185/#186/#232 lessons) must be identical — reuse, don't reimplement.
- The gateway's own `/admin/v1/*` surface stays for operators/back-compat this slice (removal/gating = follow-up decision), but the console switches to the new service.
- Deployment: admin-console Docker/K8s/Helm updated to point at the new service; docs updated.

## Acceptance
- [ ] `ferrogate admin-api serve` runs the admin surface standalone; console works against it end to end (login → resource CRUD) with the data plane process untouched.
- [ ] Scope + tenant enforcement proven identical (reuse the existing tenant-isolation test patterns against the new listener).
- [ ] E2E: console-shaped flows against the new service in ferrogate-test or a --test bin.

Parent: #285. Origin: Pingora integration audit 2026-07-20. Complements #310 (which gives /v1/messages parity on the existing shim; this issue de-blocks the shared shim both ingresses use).

## Problem
Streaming provider responses cross from reqwest to the Pingora session via a blocking bridge: `ProviderBodyReader::read` (`gateway/dispatch.rs:39-73`) calls `runtime.block_on(response.chunk())` inside a synchronous `Read`, driven by `task::spawn_blocking` + `mpsc(8)` in `responses.rs:2005-2043`. Every concurrent SSE stream permanently occupies one blocking-pool thread for its whole lifetime — a hard scalability ceiling. Pingora's async body streaming has no such cost.

## Scope
- Replace the sync `Read` + spawn_blocking pipeline with an async pipeline: `reqwest::Response::bytes_stream()` consumed in the async task, chunks written to `session.write_response_body` directly (respecting the existing per-chunk caps in `dispatch.rs:110-128` and cancellation/timeout semantics).
- Both chat completions and (post-#310) /v1/messages inherit the async path.
- Preserve the RAII token-budget reservation lifetime semantics (#round-7 fix: reservation held through the stream) and usage extraction at stream end.

## Acceptance
- [ ] No `block_on`/`spawn_blocking` per active stream; concurrent streams bounded only by async resources (test with N concurrent mock streams asserting blocking-pool usage does not scale with N, or structural assertions on the removed shim).
- [ ] Backpressure/cancellation: client disconnect aborts the upstream read promptly (existing behavior preserved, test).
- [ ] Streaming E2Es + perf smoke (openai_chat_streaming_concurrent_dispatch_debug_perf_smoke) green.

Parent: #285. Origin: Pingora integration audit 2026-07-20.

## Problem
The Anthropic-native `/v1/messages` endpoint does not actually stream. Even for streaming requests it calls `dispatch_provider_streaming_request` then `read_streaming_body_to_vec` (`gateway/messages.rs:1101-1147`), which collects the ENTIRE provider SSE stream into a `Vec<u8>` (up to max_body_bytes) before returning — the client receives the whole body at once and loses token-by-token delivery. Chat completions (`chat.rs`) already does true incremental streaming via `write_streaming_response`; the two ingresses are inconsistent.

## Scope
- Route `/v1/messages` streaming responses through the same incremental streaming path chat completions uses (`write_streaming_response` machinery), preserving the endpoint's guardrail/usage-extraction semantics (note #305/#213 lessons: streaming usage extraction for the Responses normalizer had a dedicated fix — verify /v1/messages usage settlement still reads the right shape when streamed incrementally).
- Keep buffered mode for non-streaming requests unchanged.
- Regression: streaming guardrail enforcement + billing settlement on the streamed path (mirror the chat.rs test patterns).

## Acceptance
- [ ] A streaming /v1/messages request delivers SSE events incrementally (test asserts multiple write calls / chunk boundaries, not one buffered body).
- [ ] Usage/billing settlement identical to the buffered path for the same stream (regression vs recorded usage).
- [ ] Guardrail streaming semantics preserved; existing messages tests green.

Parent: #285. Origin: Pingora integration audit 2026-07-20.

## Problem
`block_on_sync_bridge` (`gateway/mod.rs:357-379`) uses `tokio::task::block_in_place(|| handle.block_on(...))` and is reachable from async Pingora request hooks on the HOT PATH: `record_request_log`/`append_request_log` (`state_billing_metering.rs:446`), billing-event writes (`:316,:333,:360,:425`), `append_audit_event` (`:517`), the `state_agent_runtime.rs` surface, and `managed_action_guardrail.rs:167`. Each such call parks a Pingora worker thread on synchronous DB I/O during request handling; under load this throttles the whole proxy. This is the clearest anti-pattern an experienced Pingora user would flag.

## Context / prior art
#221 deliberately kept these AppState wrappers sync+bridged (275 call sites; sync consumers incl. the telemetry thread senders and the unix-socket authorizer thread) — full async propagation was correctly rejected then. This issue is NOT that: scope is the REQUEST HOT PATH only.

## Scope
- Identify the hot-path writes (request logs, billing events, audit events, guardrail evidence written per-request) and make them non-blocking from the handler's perspective: enqueue into a bounded async writer (channel + dedicated writer task with backpressure policy + drop/overflow accounting), or propagate async where the caller chain is already async and shallow.
- Cold paths (admin mutations, startup, authorizer thread, telemetry thread) stay bridged — they are not per-request.
- Preserve ordering guarantees where correctness depends on them (e.g. audit row order within one request — see #304's ordering-sensitive chokepoint rows); document any relaxation.
- Fail-safe: writer overflow must never drop billing events silently (billing has the outbox/dead-letter pattern — reuse it) and must surface metrics.

## Acceptance
- [ ] No `block_in_place`-backed DB write remains on the per-request path for request-log/billing/audit/guardrail-evidence (verified by grep + a call-graph note in the PR/commit).
- [ ] Ordering-sensitive audit sequences (chokepoint success/redacted/withheld rows) remain in-order (regression test).
- [ ] Billing events cannot be lost silently under writer backpressure (test with a stalled writer).
- [ ] Existing suites green: cli-bin, guardrail E2Es, correlation/action-identity E2Es, agentic_lite.

The capability layer's `action_fingerprint` — documented in-code as the "stable exact-action contract consumed by approval/Guardrail layers" (`capability_boundary.rs:124-127`) — is computed then thrown away: `FrameworkEventTimelineRecord` (`gateway/framework_adapter.rs:466-472`) keeps only `{event_id, run_id, kind, target, outcome, message}`, and `StoredAgentRunEvent` (`ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:932`) has no fingerprint or decision column. Audit events (`StoredAuditEvent`, `lib.rs:10914`) likewise have free-text `outcome`/`message` only. Net effect: the identity meant to bind capability → approval → guardrail is unqueryable, and #199's investigation view must reverse-engineer `final_outcome` from HTTP status codes (`state_guardrail_evidence.rs:308-328`).

## Scope
- Additive migration (045+): `action_fingerprint`, structured `decision`, `output_disposition` columns on `agent_run_events` and `audit_events` (nullable, backward compatible).
- Thread `CapabilityAuthorizationEvidence` → `FrameworkEventTimelineRecord` → `StoredAgentRunEvent` without loss; emit the same fields from the tool-execution chokepoint (`local.rs:3263 execute_tool_request_with_governance`) audit drafts.
- `validate_schema` + harness assertions updated; live-DSN gated schema-routing test per the established pattern.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A governed action's fingerprint + canonical decision + output disposition are queryable columns on its timeline and audit rows (not prose).
- [ ] Capability-authorizer evidence survives persistence end to end (regression test: authorize → timeline row carries identical fingerprint/decision).
- [ ] Backward compatible: pre-migration rows (NULL columns) still render in existing views.

Parent: #267. Origin: community architecture suggestion by @hegu-1 on #267 — every governance layer should produce the SAME action identity so budgets, approvals, and microVM execution audit as one state transition instead of separate logs.

## Current state (audited 2026-07-20)
`CapabilityAuthorizationEvidence` (`ferrogate-runtime/src/capability_boundary.rs:110-133`) is the only struct that already carries all six tuple elements (capability+canonical target, subject/tenant/worker, session/run/request/trace ids, decision, action_fingerprint) — but it exists only on the self-hosted authorizer path and is discarded on persistence. Decisions live in four disjoint vocabularies (`CapabilityAuthorizationDecision{Allowed,Denied}`, `ApprovalStatus{Pending,Approved,Denied,Expired}`, guardrail `verdict`+`action`+`enforcement_status`, free-text audit `outcome`) and **`degrade` is unrepresentable anywhere**. Output disposition (returned/redacted/withheld) exists only as English prose in `AdminAuditEventDraft.message` (`gateway/local.rs:3633,3653`).

## Scope
Define, in `ferrogate-runtime` (new module, promoted from `CapabilityAuthorizationEvidence`), the canonical model every seam will emit:
- `ActionIdentity`: requested capability/tool (canonical target string, one format), acting principal (actor api key / subject + tenant + optional worker/delegated user), context (request_id, trace_id, agent_run_id, workflow_id/version/node_id, session/lease where applicable), single `action_fingerprint` contract (extend the existing `canonical_target_sha256` scheme, `target_capability.rs:292`).
- `ActionDecision` enum: `Allow / Deny / Ask / Degrade` with structured reason + lossless mappings from the four existing vocabularies (document each mapping; `Ask` = approval-pending, `Degrade` = explicit fallback e.g. non-KVM microVM degradation).
- `ActionReceipt`: what actually executed + structured output disposition enum (`returned/redacted/withheld/errored`), replacing prose-only messages.
Model + serde + mapping/unit tests only — persistence and seam wiring are follow-ups (see sub-issue chain on #267).

## Acceptance
- [ ] One struct/enum set expresses all six tuple elements incl. `Degrade`; serde snake_case locked by tests.
- [ ] Lossless documented mappings from all four existing decision vocabularies, with round-trip tests.
- [ ] Fingerprint contract documented (relationship to approval Blake2b args-binding fingerprint stated explicitly: target-level identity vs invocation-level binding).
- [ ] No behavior change to existing paths yet (model-only slice).

labels.name: priority:p1
labels.description: High-value enterprise capability after P0 foundations

title: [agentic][P1] Canonical ActionIdentity model: one action-identity tuple + allow/deny/ask/degrade decision enum

body:
Follow-up from the #260↔#258 merge.

## Context
#258 added conditional caching (`ETag`/`Last-Modified`/`Cache-Control` → 304, `Range` → 206) to the `/v1/assets/*` pull path via `responses::write_cacheable_response`. #260 then rewrote the pull path for registry resolution (channels/semver/variants/yank), serving through `write_asset_body` → `write_raw_response_with_headers` so it can attach `x-ferrogate-asset-*` resolution metadata + the yank `warning` header.

Result: the registry pull path currently serves with metadata/yank headers **but not** 304/Range conditional caching. (Caching is still fully applied on the static-site serve mode, and the pure cache logic — `evaluate_conditional_request` — remains unit-tested.)

## Fix
Combine both on the `/v1/assets` pull response: extend `write_cacheable_response` to accept an `extra_headers: &[(&'static str, String)]` slice (insert them in each of its 4 arms), thread the request `HeaderMap` into `write_asset_body`, and have it build `AssetCacheHeaders` from the resolved asset + call `write_cacheable_response` with the `x-ferrogate-asset-*`/yank headers. Update the one other caller (`sites.rs`) to pass `&[]`.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A conditional GET (`If-None-Match`) on `/v1/assets/{type}/{name}/{version}` returns 304; `Range` returns 206 — AND the response still carries `x-ferrogate-asset-resolved`/`-version` (+ yank `warning` when applicable).
- [ ] Tests cover the combined path; fmt + clippy clean.

Low priority (P3): the pull path is fully functional today; this restores the re-pull 304 optimization #258 introduced.
title: [assets][P3] Unify HTTP caching (304/Range) with registry-metadata headers on the /v1/assets pull path

Parent: #268 · files the roadmap 'Next' item surfaced by the x402/AP2 spike (docs/design/x402-ap2-spike-2026-07.md, ref #191)

## Summary
`adjust_wallet_balance` is check-then-proceed with no hold: two concurrent spends can both pass the balance check. Any exact-amount, irreversible spend decision (agent-initiated x402 payments — a direction Cloudflare's Monetization Gateway just validated — or future hard-guaranteed budgets) is unsafe without a reservation mechanic.

## Scope
- `reserve → settle|release` lifecycle on wallets: a hold row with TTL reduces available (not actual) balance atomically (single SQL statement or SELECT FOR UPDATE); settle converts to a ledger charge idempotently; expiry auto-releases via sweeper (billing-outbox sweeper pattern).
- Admin API: list/inspect holds per tenant; metrics for active/expired holds.
- Wire the agent-run graph budget (workflow-budget issue under the agent epic) and future x402 flows to reserve up front.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Concurrency test: N parallel reserves against a wallet that can afford N-1 of them → exactly N-1 succeed (no oversell), proven with the deterministic harness.
- [ ] Crash between reserve and settle: hold expires and releases; settle after release is rejected idempotently.
- [ ] Ledger entries reference their originating hold for evidence.

labels.name: priority:p1
labels.description: High-value enterprise capability after P0 foundations

Parent: #267

## Summary
`ferrogate-mcp` pins protocol version 2025-06-18. The MCP 2026-07-28 revision (final spec published 2026-07-28; RC available) is the largest since launch and is explicitly gateway-friendly: a stateless core that scales on plain HTTP, and required `Mcp-Method`/`Mcp-Name` headers on Streamable HTTP so gateways/load-balancers can route and rate-limit per operation **without parsing bodies**. As an MCP gateway, FerroGate should exploit exactly that.

## Scope
- Client side (`crates/ferrogate-mcp`): negotiate 2026-07-28 with fallback to 2025-06-18; emit the new headers on outbound Streamable HTTP.
- Ingress side (`/v1/mcp`, `gateway/mcp_rpc.rs`): accept both versions; use inbound `Mcp-Method`/`Mcp-Name` for scope-gating, per-tool rate limits, and metrics **before** body parse where possible.
- Track rmcp SDK version bump; note any stateless-session implications for `McpManager` reconnect logic.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Version negotiation matrix test (new↔new, new↔old, old↔new) passes; no regression in existing MCP E2Es.
- [ ] Ingress rejects a tools/call whose body method mismatches the Mcp-Method header (fail closed, audited).
- [ ] Header-based per-tool Prometheus metrics present.

## Summary

## Scope
- Per logical model: canary route with percentage + sticky hashing (by api_key/tenant) and independent health/latency accounting; shadow route that mirrors requests (sampled, budget-capped) to a secondary provider without affecting the client response, results logged for comparison.
- Shadow traffic must be marked in metering (not billed to the tenant by default) and excluded from provider circuit-breaker state unless opted in.

## Acceptance
- [ ] 10% canary split measured within tolerance over N requests (deterministic seed in tests); flipping canary to primary is a config-only change.
- [ ] Shadow mirror never alters client responses, never double-bills, and its cost is capped by config (E2E).

Ran `ferrogate-test component-compliance-supabase` against live Supabase (the release-gate verification recommended after #254). It bailed with `ferrogate-billing process exited before readiness check: exit status: 1`.

NOT the cause: `ferrogate billing serve --supabase-init-schema` and `ferrogate auth serve --supabase-init-schema` both start cleanly against the same live DSN (verified standalone); live ferrogate_control is complete (58 tables, v37).

So the failure is inside the scenario's fault-injection harness (it deliberately breaks the provider-attempt migration, starts billing expecting a controlled failure/rollback, runs a concurrent-initializer pair + v29->v30 upgrade). The billing child's stderr is not captured, so the failing start + reason is opaque from outside.

Suggested: emit the billing child's stderr on a readiness failure; determine environmental (Supabase pooler connection limits under the concurrent pair) vs a real robustness bug. Not blocking — individual services start fine against live.

**Priority: P3** · pillar: asset hosting (epic #175 follow-on) · slice 7/7

## Summary

There is no lifecycle management for stored assets: versions accumulate forever, deleting registry rows can strand bucket objects, and tenant offboarding has no cascade story. The codebase audit also found the gap is system-wide: **no retention/TTL/purge engine exists anywhere** — `request_logs`, `audit_events`, `metering_events` grow unbounded too (only OAuth tokens have natural expiry). This slice builds the asset-scoped engine in a shape that generalizes.

## Scope

1. **Version retention policies**: per `{asset_type}/{name}` (with tenant/plan defaults) keep-last-N-versions and/or max-age rules; pruning respects channel pins and yank state (slice 4) — a version referenced by a channel is never pruned.
2. **Unreferenced-blob GC**: background sweeper (follow the `state_scheduler.rs` / billing-outbox sweeper patterns: batched, resumable, multi-instance-safe) reconciling bucket objects against the registry; orphans (failed presigned commits from slice 3, deleted rows) grace-period then delete. Dry-run mode reporting what would be deleted.
3. **Tenant cascade**: tenant/project deletion enqueues asset+blob cleanup with audit evidence of what was purged.
4. **Generalizable contract**: express retention rules through a `retention_policies` shape not hard-coded to assets, so request_logs/audit_events TTL (filed separately if needed) can adopt the same engine. Purge actions themselves emit audit events (compliance evidence of deletion).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] keep-last-2 policy on a name with 4 versions prunes the 2 oldest unpinned versions (registry rows + bucket objects) and leaves channel-pinned versions untouched.
- [ ] GC dry-run lists an orphaned bucket object; live run deletes it after the grace period; multi-instance run does not double-delete (lease/idempotency proven like the dispatch queue).
- [ ] Tenant deletion leaves zero bucket objects and zero registry rows for that tenant, with an audit trail of the purge.
- [ ] Storage-quota accounting is reconciled after pruning (freed bytes returned to the tenant's quota).
- [ ] Sweeper is off by default, enabled via config, with Prometheus metrics for scanned/pruned/failed.

## Out of scope

Applying the engine to request_logs/audit_events/metering (separate issue once the contract proves out); legal-hold semantics.

**Priority: P2** · pillar: asset hosting (epic #175 follow-on) · slice 6/7

## Summary

The billing pipeline (`crates/ferrogate-billing` price book → ledger → outbox → wallets) and quota engine (`crates/ferrogate-policy/src/quota.rs`) are token-denominated only. Asset traffic is governed for storage bytes at rest (`asset_storage_quota_bytes`) but downloads are unmetered, unbilled, and (pull-side) under-audited. Static/tool hosting cannot be commercialized without an egress dimension.

## Scope

1. **`asset_egress` metering events**: emit per-download metering (tenant/key/asset/version/bytes) through the existing metering + billing-outbox path; add egress pricing to the `PriceBook` (`price per GB` alongside token prices) so ledger charges and wallet settlement work unchanged. Presigned direct downloads (slice 3) meter at URL issuance using object size.
2. **Egress quota**: extend `quota_policies`/`plans` with monthly egress byte budgets + download RPM, enforced in `resolve_effective_quota` with the same nearest-overrides-capped-by-ancestor semantics; deny fail-closed with a distinct error code.
3. **Pull-side audit**: audit events for asset downloads and presigned-URL issuance (actor key, tenant, asset, version, bytes) — push/delete already audit; make pull symmetric.
4. **Guardrail scan at publish**: run text-bearing asset types (`static_site` html/md, `config_file`, `skill_bundle` text) through the existing `ferrogate-guardrails` detector chain (secret patterns, PII/Presidio) at push time; block/redact/monitor per bound guardrail policy, with findings in `guardrail_evaluations` evidence like inference traffic.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Downloading an asset produces a metering event and a priced ledger entry; wallet balance decreases by size × egress rate (E2E through the billing outbox, idempotent under retry).
- [ ] Exceeding the monthly egress budget denies further downloads fail-closed; budget alert webhooks fire at configured thresholds (reuse `budget_alerts.rs` tiers).
- [ ] Pull audit events are queryable via `/admin/v1/audit-events` filtered by asset target.
- [ ] Pushing a `config_file` containing a known secret pattern (e.g. AWS key) is blocked/redacted per policy mode, with a guardrail evaluation record and no matched-text leakage in evidence.
- [ ] Prometheus counters for asset egress bytes + denials added to `ferrogate-observability`.

## Out of scope

CDN/edge cache billing reconciliation; per-request cost response headers (could ride along if trivial).

**Priority: P2** · pillar: asset hosting (epic #175 follow-on) · slice 5/7 · continues #179 (its scan is explicitly a stand-in)

## Summary

`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/asset_security.rs` self-documents its limits: the EICAR check is a "does the scanning step run" placeholder, not an AV engine, and there is no signing story. FerroGate distributes content another tenant's agent will execute (CLI binaries, skill scripts, MCP manifests) — the trust bar must be higher than for proxied LLM text. The repo already runs an SBOM/cosign pipeline for its own releases (#189); the same trust chain should extend to tenant-published assets.

## Scope

1. **Real scanner integration**: pluggable scan backend behind the existing `validate_asset_content` seam — ClamAV (clamd TCP) and/or a hosted-scanner HTTP adapter; configurable fail-closed vs quarantine. Async scan for large objects (pairs with slice 3 commit step: asset stays `pending_scan`, invisible until clean).
2. **Signatures**: accept a detached signature (cosign/minisign) at push, store alongside the blob, verify against publisher-registered public keys; expose signature + sha256 via a verification manifest endpoint so agents verify before executing. Unsigned publishes allowed per-tenant policy (default: allowed but labeled), signed-only mode enforceable per plan/tenant.
3. **SBOM/provenance attachments**: optional attachment slots per version (`sbom`, `provenance`), returned in the manifest.
4. **Publish approval gate**: before an asset becomes visible outside its publishing tenant (public sites, shared catalogs), require an explicit approval — reuse the `tool_approvals` pattern (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/approval.rs`, durable `tool_approvals` storage) with immutable approval evidence + audit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] EICAR push is rejected by the real scanner path (not the inline stand-in); a clean binary passes; scanner-unavailable behaves per configured fail-closed/quarantine policy — all three proven by tests (mock scanner acceptable in sandbox per local E2E policy).
- [ ] Tampering with a stored blob (hash mismatch vs manifest) is detectable by a client following the documented verify flow; signed-asset verification E2E passes with a minisign/cosign test key.
- [ ] Cross-tenant-visible publish without approval is fail-closed; approval produces immutable evidence retrievable via Admin API.
- [ ] Admin API exposes scan status, signature status, and approval state per asset version; dashboard shows them.

## Out of scope

Full sigstore/Rekor transparency-log integration; automated malware-family intelligence feeds.

labels.description: Validated follow-up; do not pull ahead of P0/P1

**Priority: P2** · pillar: asset hosting (epic #175 follow-on) · slice 4/7

## Summary

Assets are only addressable by exact `{asset_type}/{name}/{version}` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/assets.rs`). An agent that wants "the latest ripgrep build for my platform" has to list-and-guess. For binary `cli_tool` distribution the registry needs package-manager semantics.

## Scope

1. **Channels/tags**: mutable pointers `latest` / `stable` / `canary` (and free-form tags) per `{asset_type}/{name}`, resolvable at pull time (`GET .../{name}/latest`). Tag moves are audited.
2. **Semver resolution**: optional semver-range resolution (`^1.2`, `~2.0`) for assets whose versions parse as semver.
3. **Platform/arch variants**: one logical version can carry multiple artifacts keyed by target triple (e.g. `linux-x86_64`, `darwin-arm64`, `windows-x86_64`); pull selects by explicit query param or `User-Agent`-style hint. Each variant keeps its own sha256/size.
4. **Immutability + yank**: a published `{name}/{version}` blob is immutable (re-PUT of same version rejected unless explicitly deleted); `yank` marks a version un-resolvable via channels/ranges while exact pulls still work with a warning header (cargo semantics).
5. **Manifest endpoint**: `GET /v1/assets/{asset_type}/{name}/manifest` returning versions, channels, variants, hashes — the single document an agent needs to self-serve. Surface the same data through slice 1's MCP resources metadata.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Publish 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 with two platform variants each; `latest` + variant selector returns the right artifact + hash for each platform.
- [ ] Yanking 1.1.0 makes `latest`/`^1.0` resolve to 1.0.0 while exact `1.1.0` pull still succeeds with a deprecation/warning header.
- [ ] Re-PUT of an existing version is rejected (409) — immutability proven by test.
- [ ] Channel moves and yanks emit audit events; schema migration for tags/variants lands through the normal migration path (see #254 lesson: live DB must run app migrations).
- [ ] CLI (`ferrogate assets`) gains `--channel`/`--platform` flags for push/pull.

## Out of scope

Delta updates, dependency graphs between assets, cross-registry mirroring.

**Priority: P1** · pillar: asset hosting (epic #175 follow-on) · slice 3/7

## Summary

Two coupled problems:

1. `MAX_ASSET_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024` in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/assets.rs` and the whole request body is buffered in memory (`read_request_body`). Binary CLI tools routinely exceed 10MB; buffering large bodies in the Pingora hot path is not acceptable.
2. The live Supabase `ferrogate` storage bucket is `public: true`. Tenant isolation is enforced at the gateway API layer but is bypassable at the storage layer for anyone holding an object path. This is a security gap, not just a feature gap.

## Scope

1. **Presigned direct path**: gateway endpoints that authorize + meter + audit, then issue short-TTL S3 presigned upload/download URLs (Supabase Storage S3 endpoint, client already in `gateway/asset_bucket.rs`) so bytes bypass the gateway hot path. Push flow: register-intent → presigned PUT → commit (gateway verifies size + sha256 via HEAD before the asset becomes visible; supply-chain checks from `asset_security.rs` still run — for large objects run them against the committed object, fail closed by deleting on violation).
2. **Per-plan size limits**: replace the hard 10MB constant with a plan/quota-driven limit (`plans` / `quota_policies` already carry `asset_storage_quota_bytes`; add per-object ceiling). Small objects (< threshold) may keep the inline path for simplicity.
3. **Private bucket migration**: flip `ferrogate` bucket to private; all reads go through gateway-issued presigned GETs or gateway-proxied streams. Include a migration note/runbook for existing objects. (`dev-migration` bucket: review whether it must stay public.)
4. Download side returns sha256 alongside the URL so agents can verify (pairs with slice 5 signing).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Push and pull of a 100MB binary succeeds end-to-end via presigned URLs with gateway RSS staying flat (no full-body buffering), proven by an E2E or measured harness run.
- [ ] Commit step rejects an object whose sha256 or size differs from the registered intent; the orphaned object is cleaned up.
- [ ] Direct unauthenticated fetch of a bucket object URL (without a presigned signature) returns 4xx after the private-bucket flip.
- [ ] Presigned URL TTL is bounded and configurable; issuing one produces an audit event with key/tenant/asset identity.
- [ ] Storage quota accounting remains correct for presigned uploads (counted at commit).

## Out of scope

Resumable/multipart chunk protocol beyond what S3 presigned multipart gives for free; CDN layering.

**Priority: P1** · pillar: asset hosting (epic #175 follow-on) · slice 2/7

## Summary

`static_site` assets today are only reachable through the authenticated pull API (`handle_asset_pull` in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/assets.rs`), one blob at a time. That is artifact download, not website hosting. `assets.rs` sets no HTTP caching semantics at all (no `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Cache-Control`, no `Range` support), which also penalizes agents that repeatedly re-pull tools.

## Scope

1. **Serve mode**: a browseable site surface, e.g. `GET /sites/{tenant}/{site}/{path...}` (route registered in `gateway/route_groups.rs`), resolving `index.html` for directory paths, optional SPA fallback, per-file `Content-Type` from the stored metadata. Anonymous access is per-site opt-in (default: authenticated); visibility otherwise reuses key/plan gating.
2. **Site bundles**: publishing a multi-file site as one unit — accept a zip/tar `static_site` push and either unpack into per-file bucket objects or serve-from-archive; site manifest records the file tree.
3. **HTTP caching semantics** on all asset GET paths (both `/v1/assets/*` pull and the new serve mode): strong `ETag` from the stored sha256, `Last-Modified`, configurable `Cache-Control`, `304 Not-Modified` handling, and `Range`/`206` for partial content.
4. **Custom domains (stretch, may split)**: bind a site to a hostname using the existing ACME HTTP-01/DNS-01 + graceful-upgrade machinery.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Pushing a zip containing `index.html` + `style.css` + `docs/readme.md` then fetching `/sites/{tenant}/{site}/` returns the rendered index with `text/html`, and `/sites/{tenant}/{site}/style.css` returns `text/css`.
- [ ] Conditional GET with `If-None-Match` returns 304; `Range: bytes=0-99` returns 206 with correct `Content-Range`.
- [ ] Anonymous fetch of a non-public site returns 401/404 (fail closed); enabling public mode is an explicit admin/config action with an audit event.
- [ ] Serve-mode requests produce request logs + metering events like any other gateway traffic (feeds slice 6 egress billing).
- [ ] E2E in `crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/` (extend `assets_api.rs` / `asset_bucket_e2e.rs` patterns).

## Out of scope

Presigned direct-download URLs and >10MB uploads (slice 3), egress billing dimension (slice 6).

**Priority: P1** · pillar: asset hosting (epic #175 follow-on) · slice 1/7 of the asset closed-loop plan

## Summary

`POST /v1/mcp` JSON-RPC ingress (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/mcp_rpc.rs`) implements only `initialize` / `ping` / `tools/list` / `tools/call`. There is no `resources/list` / `resources/read`, so an MCP client agent has no native way to discover or fetch assets published through `/v1/assets/*`. This is the missing key of the publish → govern → agent-consume closed loop: assets exist (#176–#179) but agents can't find them without a proprietary client.

## Scope

1. Implement `resources/list` and `resources/read` on the native `/v1/mcp` ingress, backed by the stored-asset registry (`ferrogate-storage` `StoredAsset`, `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state_assets.rs`).
2. Map each visible asset to a resource URI `asset://{asset_type}/{name}/{version}` with metadata (content_type, size_bytes, sha256).
3. Visibility must reuse the exact same virtual-key auth + StoredPlan entitlement + tenant scoping as `handle_asset_list`/`handle_asset_pull` — no new authz path.
4. Add a built-in `fetch_asset` tool exposed via `tools/list`/`tools/call` so tool-only MCP clients get the same closed loop; it must flow through the existing governed tool-execution chokepoint (approval gate + managed-action guardrails + audit), same as other tools.
5. `resources/read` of large/binary assets may return a downloadable reference (URL + sha256) instead of inline base64 — align with slice 3 (presigned URLs) when it lands; inline is acceptable for this slice under the current 10MB cap.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resources/list` returns only assets the calling key is entitled to see; a key without `assets.read` scope gets a JSON-RPC error, not an empty list masking a 403.
- [ ] `resources/read` on `asset://cli_tool/{name}/{version}` returns content whose sha256 matches the stored `stored_asset_id` fingerprint.
- [ ] `fetch_asset` tool call produces an audit event and (if configured) passes the approval gate, proven by an E2E in `crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/` alongside `mcp_jsonrpc_tool_governance_e2e.rs`.

## Fix

## Problem

`build_supabase_repositories` (crates/ferrogate-cli/src/service_storage.rs:43) opens the auth-service and billing-service Supabase repositories with:

```rust
pool_acquire_timeout_millis: 1_000,
```

The first pool acquisition includes the full TCP/TLS handshake to a (often remote) Supabase pooler, which regularly exceeds 1s. This is the **exact** failure #250 already fixed for the migration tool — `storage.rs:46` uses `30_000` with a comment explaining a 1s deadline 'made the tool fail against real Supabase poolers before the first query ran'. The auth/billing path never got the same fix.

### Observed
While migrating live `ferrogate_control` via `ferrogate auth serve --supabase-init-schema` (#254), the run failed with `storage operation initialize schema exceeded its deadline during pool acquisition` (wait_micros≈1001884 ≈ the 1s cap) and only succeeded on retry when the handshake happened to finish <1s. So auth/billing service startup against remote Supabase is flaky/unreliable.

## Fix

Raise the side-service pool-acquire timeout to match the migration tool's generous value (30s); the per-statement `statement_timeout_millis` (30s) still bounds each operation. Same rationale as #250.

## Acceptance
- [ ] auth/billing Supabase repository init uses a >= a few-seconds pool-acquire timeout (not 1s).
- [ ] Rationale comment references the remote-pooler handshake (mirrors storage.rs).
- [ ] Build + storage tests green.
title: [storage][P2] auth/billing side-service Supabase init uses a 1s pool-acquire timeout that flakes against remote Supabase

## Finding (2026-07-19 read-only column audit, follow-up to #253)

After #253 fixed the missing `wallet_settlements` **table**, a full column-level audit of live `ferrogate_control` vs the schema contract (`sql/001_init_postgres.sql`, 58 tables / 609 columns) found **7 tables missing columns** — all from **migrations 30-33, which were never applied to live**.

### Smoking gun: ledger gap
```
live ferrogate_control ledger versions = 1..29, 34, 35, 36, 37
                                          ^^^^^^ MISSING 30, 31, 32, 33
```
The schema was hand-assembled by applying migrations piecemeal (1-29 then 34-37) and **skipping 30-33**. The app's `initialize_schema` migration path has evidently **never run against this database** (if it had, 30-33 would be present).

### Missing columns (billing-critical)
| table | missing columns | migration |
|---|---|---|
| `metering_events` | `billing_event_id`, `event_json`, `provider_attempt_id`, `provider_attempt_index` | 30 |
| `metering_event_routes` | `billing_event_id` | 30 |
| `metering_event_usage` | `billing_event_id` | 30 |
| `billing_ledger` | `provider_attempt_id`, `provider_attempt_index` | 30 |
| `guardrail_policy_bindings` | `generation` | 32 |
| `usage_metadata_rollups` | `organization_id` | 33 |
| `self_hosted_worker_registrations` | `token_secret` | (base ALTER) |

Migration 30 (`030_provider_attempt_settlement_identity`, issue #213) also **rewrites primary keys**: `metering_events`/`_routes`/`_usage` PK moves `request_id` → `billing_event_id` with FKs. These are the provider-attempt billing-idempotency guarantees — **without them, billing writes from current code would fail** against this DB.

### Impact
Deploying current (v37) code against this live DB would hit `column does not exist` on metering/billing writes. Latent production-breaking, but currently masked because the DB holds only test data (metering tables = 1 row, billing_ledger = 0).

### Remediation (self-healing — recommended)
Because 30-33 are **absent from the ledger**, the app's own idempotent `initialize_schema` will apply them on the next migration run (the self-gating `DO … INSERT version … IF FOUND THEN <ddl>` blocks fire when the version is missing). Verified mechanism: the `live_initialize_schema_provisions_the_configured_schema_not_public` test provisions a fresh schema with the **complete** v37 contract incl. 30-33.

**Options:**
1. **Deploy the app / run its migration** against this DB with `postgres_schema=ferrogate_control` and migration enabled → self-heals 30-33 (idempotent; near-empty tables ⇒ trivial backfill). **Preferred.**
2. I can apply migrations 30-33 manually via SQL, pinned to ferrogate_control. Held back autonomously because migration 30 does PK/FK rewrites on **billing** tables — wanted explicit sign-off despite the tables being near-empty.

### Prevent recurrence
- Gate releases on the live-Supabase compliance suite (`component-compliance-supabase`, which checks these columns) — it would have caught this; it wasn't run against this DB (same note as #253).
- Consider a startup assertion that fails if any table is missing an expected column (not just missing tables), since a ledger row can lie about what physically exists.

Root cause is shared with #253: the live schema predates/​bypassed the app's pinned migration path. Filing P1 because it blocks a correct production deploy.
title: [storage][P1] Live Supabase ferrogate_control is missing migrations 30-33 (billing idempotency columns + PK/FK) — hand-built schema never ran the app migration path

## Finding (surfaced 2026-07-19 during a live schema-readiness check)

The live Supabase project (`wpgzljfyunypmuacyesv`) carries the FerroGate control-plane schema in **two** namespaces:

- `ferrogate_control` — the **active** schema (the app pins `search_path` here post-#250). Now at **v37** (just applied `037_agent_schedules`; see below).
- `public` — a **stale full duplicate**: **58 tables** including `storage_schema_migrations` (ledger at **v36**), `admin_users`, `tenants`, `control_plane_replay_floors`, etc. Almost certainly created during the pre-#237/#250 era when `initialize_schema` ran DDL **unpinned** so tables landed in `public`.

### Why it matters
Post-#250 the app fails closed onto `ferrogate_control`, so the `public` copy is inert **as long as every path pins search_path**. But it is:
- latent correctness risk — any unpinned query would silently read/write the stale `public` copy (exactly the class #237/#238/#239/#250 hardened against), and
- confusing + space-consuming duplicate that drifts (public ledger is already a version behind at v36 vs ferrogate_control v37).

### Recommended action (needs a human decision — destructive)
Drop the `public` control-plane duplicate once confirmed unused, e.g. per-table `DROP TABLE public.<t>` for the 58 control-plane tables (NOT any genuine Supabase/PostgREST `public` objects — audit first), or `DROP SCHEMA`-scoped cleanup after a backup. **Not done autonomously**: dropping 58 production tables is irreversible and requires explicit owner sign-off + a backup/snapshot.

### Acceptance
- [ ] Confirm no code path reads/writes the `public` copies (search_path is always pinned).
- [ ] Snapshot/backup taken.
- [ ] `public` control-plane duplicate removed (or a documented decision to keep it with an enforcement guard).
- [ ] A guard (test/CI) that fails if control-plane tables appear in `public` on a fresh init.

### Note
Separately, the live `ferrogate_control` schema was **behind main** (v36) until this check — `037_agent_schedules` (#246: `agent_schedules` + `agent_schedule_fires` + indexes) had never been applied to live. Applied today (idempotent DDL, pinned to `ferrogate_control`, verified no public leak: public ledger still v36). Live control plane is now v37, in sync with main.
title: [storage][P2] Live Supabase: stale full duplicate of the control-plane schema in public (pre-#250 unpinned-DDL era)

body:
## Problem

FerroGate can execute agent runs today, but only when something external asks for one: `POST /v1/agent-runs` (synchronous trigger) or a dispatch seeded at self-hosted worker registration (`SelfHostedWorkerDispatchRuntime::seed_run`, `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:3768`). There is **no way to run an agent on a recurring schedule** ("every night at 02:00 run the compliance-report agent"). Every comparable platform ships this as a first-class trigger (Dify Schedule Trigger, n8n Schedule Trigger, Inngest cron functions, Windmill/Hatchet Postgres-backed schedules), and it is the standard entry point for unattended enterprise agent workloads.

## Design decision (from architecture survey)

Two candidate shapes were considered:

1. **Scheduler = pure trigger**: a timer that, on fire, kicks an agent execution.
2. **Scheduler = task-state table**: a managed task list with state transitions that agents pull from.

**Decision: hybrid — build (1), reuse the existing infrastructure for (2).** FerroGate already has the pull-side task-state machine: the self-hosted dispatch lease queue (`InMemorySelfHostedRunQueue`, `crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/self_hosted_worker.rs:899`) with `queued → leased (lease_id, lease_expires_at_unix, attempt++) → acknowledged` transitions, persisted write-through to `self_hosted_run_dispatches` (schema v36, `sql/001_init_postgres.sql:341`) and polled by workers via `POST /v1/self-hosted-workers/runs/poll` / `.../ack`. Building a second task-state system would duplicate it. The scheduler is therefore a **control-plane trigger layer**: schedule definitions + a tick loop that, when a schedule is due, **enqueues a dispatch into the existing lease queue** (self-hosted pull path) or creates an agent run via the existing `handle_agent_run_create` path (managed/synchronous path), plus an idempotent fire-history record. This matches the Postgres-scheduler pattern used by Windmill and Hatchet (transactional enqueue, `SKIP LOCKED`/advisory-lock single-firer, durable fire history).

## Scope

### 1. Schema (bump to v37 in `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:508` + append to `sql/001_init_postgres.sql`)

- `agent_schedules`: `schedule_id` PK, `tenant_id`, `workspace_id`, `name`, `enabled`, `spec_kind` (`cron` | `interval`), `cron_expr`, `timezone` (IANA, default UTC), `interval_secs`, `target_kind` (`self_hosted_dispatch` | `agent_run`), `target_json` (agent/workflow ref, framework_adapter, required capabilities, input payload template), `overlap_policy` (`skip` | `allow`), `catchup_policy` (`skip_missed` | `fire_once`), `jitter_secs`, `next_fire_at_unix`, `last_fire_at_unix`, `created/updated_at_unix`, `revision`.
- `agent_schedule_fires`: fire history + idempotency — `schedule_id`, `scheduled_fire_at_unix`, `fired_at_unix`, `node_id`, `outcome` (`dispatched` | `skipped_overlap` | `skipped_disabled` | `error`), `dispatch_id` / `run_id` FK-ish reference, **`UNIQUE (schedule_id, scheduled_fire_at_unix)`** so a lost multi-instance race cannot double-trigger (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`).
- Storage repo methods in `ferrogate-storage`: schedule CRUD, `list_due_schedules(now)`, `insert_schedule_fire` (idempotent), following the existing upsert conventions (`upsert_self_hosted_run_dispatch`, lib.rs:6558).

### 2. Cron support

- Add a cron-parsing crate to `[workspace.dependencies]` (recommend `croner` or `cron`; none exists in the tree today). 5-field standard syntax + explicit IANA timezone field; compute `next_fire_at_unix` on create/update and after each fire. Also support plain `interval_secs` schedules without cron syntax.

### 3. Scheduler tick loop (in `ferrogate-cli`)

- Model on the billing outbox sweeper (`start_billing_outbox_sweeper`, `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/mod.rs:411`): always-spawn thread + `Arc<AtomicBool>` stop flag + `Drop` join, re-reads `state.current()` each tick so config hot-reload applies, no-ops when `scheduler.enabled = false`. Handle held in `run()` (`gateway/mod.rs:189`). Default tick interval ~5s (minute-level firing precision is the contract; document this).
- **Multi-instance single-firer**: per tick, take `pg_try_advisory_lock` on a scheduler key (precedent: `initialize_schema`, `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:1297-1305`) — if not acquired, skip the tick. Inside the lock: `list_due_schedules`, and for each due schedule insert the `agent_schedule_fires` row (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`); only the winning insert proceeds to trigger. Stamp `node_id` (`resolve_cluster_node_id`, state.rs:6192) for attribution. This is belt-and-braces: advisory lock for efficiency, unique fire row for correctness.
- **Fire action**: `target_kind = self_hosted_dispatch` → enqueue via the dispatch runtime (generalize `seed_run`/`enqueue_run` into a schedule-originated `StartRun` dispatch carrying `schedule_id` + `scheduled_fire_at` in its payload) + write-through persist, exactly like the poll/ack handlers (`state_agent_runtime.rs:564`). `target_kind = agent_run` → invoke the existing agent-run create path. Either way the run shows up in `agent_runs`/`agent_run_events` observability.
- **Overlap policy**: `skip` (default) checks whether the previous fire's dispatch/run is still unacked/active and records `skipped_overlap` instead of firing (prevents the pile-up failure mode). **Catch-up policy**: on startup/downtime, `skip_missed` (default, n8n semantics) advances `next_fire_at`; `fire_once` fires a single catch-up for the most recent missed slot (bounded — never replay every missed tick).

### 4. Admin API (in `ferrogate-cli`, contract-driven routing)

- `/admin/v1/agent-schedules` CRUD + `POST .../{id}/run-now` + pause/resume (via `enabled`), `GET .../{id}/fires` history. Register per the three-part pattern: path patterns + group in `docs/openapi/runtime-api-contract.json`, `RouteGroup::AgentSchedule` variant + `from_contract_name` + `try_agent_schedule_routes` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/route_groups.rs:33,125`), `handle_admin_agent_schedule_*` in `gateway/local.rs` (mirror `handle_admin_agent_workflows`, local.rs:1208). Same auth/scope machinery as other admin routes; tenant/workspace-scoped.

### 5. Config

- `scheduler: SchedulerConfig` on `Config` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs:19`): `enabled` (default false), `tick_interval_secs`, `max_catchup_fires`, `default_timezone`. Documented in `config/ferrogate.example.toml`.

### 6. Tests + docs

- Unit: cron next-fire computation (incl. timezone/DST edge), overlap/catch-up policy state transitions, fire idempotency.
- Storage integration: schedule CRUD round-trip, `list_due_schedules`, fire-row conflict dedup (two concurrent inserters → one winner). Live-Postgres tests follow the hermetic schema-routing conventions from #241.
- E2E (local-process backend per sandbox closure policy): create schedule with a short interval → tick loop fires → dispatch appears in `self_hosted_run_dispatches` → worker poll leases it → ack → fire history shows `dispatched` with linked dispatch_id; restart gateway mid-schedule → no duplicate fire for the same slot.
- Docs: scheduler section in `docs/agentic-gateway-architecture.md` + admin API additions to `docs/openapi/`.

## Non-goals (this issue)

- DAG/workflow orchestration between scheduled runs (compose later with agent workflows).
- Event/webhook triggers (separate trigger-kind follow-up; schema's `spec_kind` leaves room).
- Sub-second or exactly-at-boundary firing guarantees; contract is at-most-once per (schedule, slot), minute-level precision.
- Replaying the full backlog of missed fires after long downtime (bounded catch-up only).

## Acceptance criteria

1. Schema v37 lands with `agent_schedules` + `agent_schedule_fires` and idempotent DDL, following the single-file embedded-schema convention.
2. A cron schedule (`*/1 * * * *` equivalent or `interval_secs`) targeting a self-hosted dispatch fires on time, produces exactly one dispatch per slot with two gateway instances running against the same database (proven by an integration test using the fire-row unique constraint).
3. Worker poll/ack consumes schedule-originated dispatches unchanged (no worker-protocol change required for report-only execution).
4. Admin CRUD + run-now + fire history endpoints pass contract-routing tests; schedules are tenant-scoped.
5. Overlap `skip` policy demonstrably prevents a second fire while the previous dispatch is unacked; gateway restart does not duplicate or silently lose the current slot beyond documented catch-up semantics.
6. `scheduler.enabled = false` (default) results in zero behavior change; loop no-ops like the billing sweeper when disabled.

## References

- Existing dispatch lease queue: `crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/self_hosted_worker.rs:899-1100`, persistence `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:6558`, handlers `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state_agent_runtime.rs:534-591`.
- Loop template: `start_billing_outbox_sweeper` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/mod.rs:411`).
- Advisory-lock precedent: `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:1297`.
- Community patterns surveyed: Windmill schedules, Hatchet (Postgres queue + cron), Inngest cron triggers (catch-up semantics), n8n Schedule Trigger (skip-missed semantics), Dify Schedule Trigger.

- [ ] Make each test hermetic: unique schema name (add a per-test nonce beyond process::id), avoid shared `public` shadow tables (or uniquely name/namespace + guaranteed cleanup incl. on panic), and ensure the store-under-test's pool doesn't leak `search_path` across tests.

## Problem
`crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/ai_proxy_perf.rs::openai_chat_streaming_concurrent_dispatch_debug_perf_smoke` fails intermittently on the assertion at line ~370:
```
assert!(end_rss <= start_rss + 32 * 1024, "gateway RSS grew too much: start={start_rss}KB end={end_rss}KB");
```
Observed **3/6 standalone** and 1/1 under full-`cargo test --workspace` parallelism, with growth ranging 33–53MB against the 32MB (32*1024 KB) budget:
- start=51916KB end=86220KB (+34MB)
- start=51832KB end=93672KB (+41MB)
- start=51556KB end=104260KB (+52MB)

## Root cause (suspected)
RSS-growth is an inherently noisy signal for a concurrent-streaming workload: the system allocator retains freed arenas (RSS doesn't shrink after the burst), so a hard `+32MB` post-burst threshold is measuring allocator retention, not a leak. It's timing/scheduling-sensitive, hence the ~50% flake. Discovered by a full-workspace cumulative integration run (2026-07-18); the test file was not touched by recent work — pre-existing.

## Fix directions (pick the honest one)
- If the intent is a **leak guard**: measure growth AFTER an allocator trim / settle (e.g. drop connections, sleep, `malloc_trim` on glibc) and/or compare steady-state across two bursts rather than start-vs-immediately-after-burst; raise the budget to a documented, headroomed value backed by observed steady-state.
- If the intent is a **perf smoke**: keep the latency/p95 assertions hard, but make the RSS check a warn-with-headroom (or median-of-N) so it doesn't hard-fail CI on allocator noise.
- Either way: document what the number guards and why it's stable.

## Acceptance
- [ ] The test passes 20/20 standalone and under `cargo test --workspace`.
- [ ] The RSS assertion (if kept) is robust to allocator retention with a documented rationale, and still catches a real unbounded leak.

body:
## Problem
3 tests in `crates/agent-worker/src/external_actions_target_test.rs` fail on hosts where Ubuntu ships **uutils coreutils** (e.g. Ubuntu resolute / WSL2, 2026-07-18 dev box):

- `bound_cli_cwd_fd_survives_path_replacement_after_binding`
- `sealed_cli_snapshot_executes_authorized_bytes_after_source_mutation`
- `governed_cli_execution_uses_the_fingerprinted_empty_environment`

## Root cause (reproduced without project code)
`/usr/bin/env` under uutils coreutils is a multi-call binary that dispatches on `argv[0]`. The sealed-exec path executes the binary as `/proc/self/fd/N`, so coreutils sees `argv[0]=N` and exits 1 with `unknown program 'N'`. GNU coreutils' standalone env does not care about argv[0], which is why these tests pass on classic hosts and in CI.

## Fix directions
Either set `argv[0]` explicitly to the original program name when execing the sealed `/proc/self/fd/N` snapshot (faithful: sealed exec should preserve argv[0] anyway), or make the tests use a helper binary that ignores argv[0]. Preserving argv[0] in the sealed-exec path is likely the real product fix — argv[0]-sensitive multi-call binaries (busybox, uutils) are common.

## Evidence
Pre-existing on clean `main` baseline (56a4fa0), independently reproduced with a pure-Python probe; discovered during #227 verification (2026-07-18).

## Summary
Round-13 audit (skeptic-confirmed LOW). The provider AI response cache stores the response body already redacted under the Response-stage guardrail rules in effect at STORE time (`chat.rs` ~1919, stored ~1962). On a cache HIT the body is returned raw via `write_raw_response` (`chat.rs` ~554) with **no Response-stage guardrail re-evaluation**, and the cache key (`ai_response_cache_key`, `state_routing.rs`) does not include a guardrail-policy revision.

## Impact
If an operator TIGHTENS response guardrails after an entry is cached (adds a new PII/secret redaction rule, or one that now matches this content), every cache hit within the TTL keeps serving the pre-tightening, un-redacted body until the entry expires — a data-leak window a policy update does not close. LOW: requires a guardrail policy change after a matching response was cached, bounded by the cache TTL.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A tightened Response-stage guardrail policy takes effect on cache hits immediately, not after TTL expiry — either by re-running Response-stage guardrails on cache-hit bodies before serving, or by including a guardrail-policy revision in the cache key (so a policy bump misses stale entries), or flushing/invalidating the response cache on guardrail-policy reload.
- [ ] Regression test.

## References
- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/chat.rs` (cache-hit branch ~515-561; store ~1960)
- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state_routing.rs` `ai_response_cache_key`
