body:
## Summary
Round-13 adversarial audit found several multi-tenancy scoping gaps in the admin-console/SCIM/RBAC surface (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs`) that share one root cause: **admin accounts, roles, and refresh tokens are GLOBAL, while memberships and SCIM/SSO trust are per-tenant** — and the two are not consistently reconciled. The most severe item (cross-tenant SSO account takeover) is already fixed in `56a4fa0`; these remaining items need a small storage-schema change and/or a per-tenant role model, so they are tracked here rather than rushed.

## Confirmed findings (skeptic-verified)

### 1. Refresh re-issues a session for `memberships.first()`, not the token's tenant (MED)
`StoredAdminUserRefreshToken` has no `tenant_id`, so `handle_admin_refresh` (lib.rs:1429) issues the new session for `memberships.first()` — the user's OLDEST membership (`ORDER BY id ASC`), which may be a different tenant/role than the session the token was minted for. A user who is a member of multiple tenants can thus be silently refreshed into the wrong tenant/role.
**Fix:** add `tenant_id` (and role) to `StoredAdminUserRefreshToken` (schema + migration), stamp it in `issue_session`, and re-issue for that tenant on refresh.

### 2. SCIM deactivate/delete globally disables a shared account (MED, cross-tenant DoS)
`handle_scim_user_patch(active=false)` / `handle_scim_user_delete` are gated only by membership-in-the-token's-tenant, but call `deactivate_admin_user`, which sets the GLOBAL `disabled_at_unix` (lib.rs:2274) and `revoke_all_admin_user_refresh_tokens` across ALL tenants (lib.rs:2281). Combined with `handle_scim_user_create` attaching a membership to any pre-existing global account by email (lib.rs:2243), any tenant owner can disable any user system-wide by knowing their email.
**Fix:** SCIM deactivation must be tenant-scoped — remove/disable only the token-tenant's membership and revoke only that tenant's sessions; only set the global `disabled_at_unix` when the user has no remaining active memberships elsewhere. (Depends on per-tenant refresh-token revocation from #1.)

### 3. Global role catalog is tenant-writable (MED, cross-tenant RBAC tamper)
Roles are one global `Vec<Role>` keyed by id; `handle_rbac_role_upsert` (lib.rs:1786) requires only *any* valid session (no owner/tenant check), so a member of tenant B can overwrite a role id that tenant A's owner-gated bindings resolve to — escalating A's subjects to wildcard permissions or stripping them (DoS). `GET /v1/rbac/roles` now requires a session (fixed in 56a4fa0) but still returns the global catalog.
**Fix:** make roles tenant-owned (namespace per tenant; `authorize()` resolves a binding's role only within the binding's tenant), gate `handle_rbac_role_upsert` on owner + caller tenant, and return only the caller's tenant's roles from the listing.

## Why tracked, not fixed inline
#1 needs a `StoredAdminUserRefreshToken` schema/migration change and #3 a role data-model change; both should be validated against a real Postgres/Supabase (not available in the current sandbox), and #2 depends on #1. The already-shipped SSO fix (`56a4fa0`) closes the account-takeover chain, so these are integrity/DoS scoping gaps rather than an active takeover.

Found by round-13 adversarial security audit, skeptic-verified (2× MED cross-tenant + 1× refresh-scoping).

Round-11 adversarial audit (skeptic-confirmed MEDIUM). Several self-hosted-worker / agent-run stores are driven by an authenticated but customer-hosted worker over endpoints with no per-worker count/rate cap, and the hot write/read paths load whole tables.

## Confirmed scope (verifiers refined the original claim)
- **Already bounded (no action):** `self_hosted_worker_heartbeats` and `self_hosted_worker_telemetry_events` are retention-capped in-memory (`ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:8023-8028`, `with_retention_limit(audit_event_retention_records)`).
- **Unbounded growth remains:**
  - `agent_run_events` — `InMemoryAppendRepository::new()` (no cap) at `lib.rs:8007`.
  - `self_hosted_worker_artifacts` / `self_hosted_worker_checkpoints` — keyed `InMemoryRepository` (no eviction); a worker can create unbounded **distinct** ids for its own rows.
  - **No Postgres-side pruning/retention** exists for any of these tables (the in-memory `with_retention_limit` only bounds the in-memory backend; the durable path grows without limit).
- **O(n) full-table load on the hot path:** every worker heartbeat/telemetry/artifact/checkpoint write calls `self_hosted_worker_record(worker_id)` → `self_hosted_worker_records()` (`state_agent_runtime.rs`), which loads ALL heartbeats + telemetry + artifacts + checkpoints + registrations and filters in memory; `self_hosted_run_timeline` and `agent_run_summaries` likewise load whole tables. This degrades to full scans as tables grow and affects other tenants' admin reads sharing the process.

## Impact
Self-amplifying memory/CPU DoS from a single registered worker; MEDIUM (requires an authenticated worker; no cross-tenant data disclosure).

## Acceptance
- [ ] Bound `agent_run_events` and give the keyed artifact/checkpoint stores a distinct-id cap (or per-worker cap) with oldest-eviction, matching the heartbeat/telemetry pattern — mindful that `agent_run_events` feed run timelines, so pick a bound/semantics that doesn't silently truncate an active run's timeline.
- [ ] Add Postgres-side retention/pruning for these tables (the durable path currently has none).
- [ ] Push `worker_id`/`run_id` filtering + `LIMIT` into SQL for `self_hosted_worker_record`, `self_hosted_run_timeline`, `agent_run_summaries` instead of loading whole tables and filtering in memory.
- [ ] Validate the Postgres path (needs a real Postgres/Supabase — not available in the current sandbox).

## References
- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state_agent_runtime.rs` (`self_hosted_worker_records`, `record_*` writers)
- `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:8007,8023-8028` (store construction + retention)

Found by round-11 adversarial security audit, skeptic-verified MEDIUM.

## Summary
A **tenant-scoped admin key** (one whose `organization_id` is set) could escalate its own entitlements by editing its own tenant account.

`PATCH`/`PUT /admin/v1/tenants/{id}` (`handle_admin_tenant_account_by_id`) accepted `plan_id` and `status` changes from any caller with `admin.write` on that tenant — including the tenant's own scoped key. A tenant could therefore:
- self-upgrade its `plan_id` (e.g. to an enterprise plan with higher rate/token/wallet limits), or
- flip its own `status` (e.g. reactivate a `suspended` account).

Only a **platform-operator key** (`organization_id: None`) should be able to change a tenant's plan or status; a tenant may only self-service non-entitlement fields (name, etc.).

## Impact
Entitlement / privilege escalation across the billing + rate-limit control plane. Severity: **HIGH**.

## Acceptance
- A tenant-scoped admin key that PATCHes its own `plan_id` or `status` is rejected `403 platform_operator_required`.
- Non-entitlement fields (name) remain editable by the tenant (`200`).
- A platform-operator key can still change plan/status (`200`).
- Regression test covering all three.

Found by round-10 adversarial security audit (admin-entitlement-mutation surface), skeptic-verified HIGH.

body:
Two LOW-severity findings from the round-9 adversarial audit, tracked here (the round's HIGH + MEDIUM are already fixed: 89589e5 embeddings token estimate; 1aa804a agent-run cross-tenant overwrite). Filed as P2 (both are LOW severity; label p3 does not exist in this repo).

## 1. Budget-alert webhooks are delivered with no signature (forgeable alerts)

`dispatch_budget_alert_webhook` (crates/ferrogate-cli/src/budget_alerts.rs:64-77) builds an `OtlpHttpRequest` with method/url/content_type/body only; the shared transport `send_otlp_http_request` (telemetry.rs) emits no Authorization / X-Signature / HMAC. `OtlpHttpRequest` (ferrogate-observability/src/lib.rs) has **no field to carry a header**, so there is structurally no signing hook, and `BillingAlertsConfig` (config/types.rs) exposes only `webhook_url` + `webhook_timeout_secs`. A receiver therefore cannot authenticate an alert.

**Fix (feature-add, spans 3 crates):**
- Give `OtlpHttpRequest` / `send_otlp_http_request` a way to carry extra headers.
- Add a `webhook_signing_secret` to `BillingAlertsConfig`; when set, emit `X-FerroGate-Signature` = HMAC-SHA256(body + timestamp) using the existing blake2b/HMAC pattern, plus a timestamp header so receivers can reject replays.
- Optionally require `https://` for `billing_alerts.webhook_url` and document that receivers must verify the signature.

LOW: requires reaching the operator-configured receiver URL; impact is spoofed alerts, not data theft.

## 2. Workflow run-gating reads span tenants (no tenant scope)

The three gating readers in crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state_agent_runtime.rs (`workflow_run_started_at`:30, `workflow_run_last_successful_node_id`:71, `workflow_edge_transition_error`:126) filter `request_logs`/`audit_events`/`metering_events` only by `(workflow_id, workflow_version, agent_run_id)` — **no tenant/org compared**. `agent_run_id` is client-supplied and not tenant-namespaced; these feed the create-time workflow authorization gate (agent_runs.rs:562/609, chat.rs:3054/3092). For a workflow usable by multiple tenants (empty organization_ids/api_key_ids), one tenant referencing another's agent_run_id could have its edge-transition/start-timestamp/timeout gating computed from the other tenant's logs.

**Fix:** thread the caller's organization_id into the three readers and add `log.tenant.organization_id` to each filter (the boundary the read path enforces, issue #185). ~3 signatures + ~5 call sites. NOTE: touches the workflow-gating path, which has a known approval-timing flake — validate carefully.

LOW: requires a cross-tenant-usable workflow + knowing another tenant's agent_run_id; impact is gating confusion.

Found by round-9 adversarial security audit, skeptic-verified LOW.

## Problem

`configure_and_start_firecracker` (crates/agent-worker/src/backends.rs) attaches the shared host rootfs image with `is_read_only: false` and boots `root=/dev/vda rw`, contradicting the declared `IsolationFilesystemPolicy.read_only_rootfs = true` (crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/isolation.rs).

Every microVM boots from the **same** backing file (`AGENT_WORKER_FIRECRACKER_ROOTFS`, resolved once, no per-VM templating — no `fs::copy`/overlay/CoW anywhere in `backends.rs`/`lifecycle.rs`; the only `is_read_only` literal is `false`). Consequences:

- **Concurrent** microVMs write through to the shared image → ext4 corruption of the image every other tenant then boots from.
- **Sequential** boots carry filesystem state across tenants.
- **Latent escalation**: once the guest RPC start entrypoint (currently hardcoded `not_implemented`, backends.rs ~244) is wired to run tenant workloads, a malicious workload can write directly to `/dev/vda` and persist a backdoor into the shared rootfs image all future tenants' microVMs boot from — a cross-tenant persistence/escape.

Found by round-6 adversarial security audit (isolation-backend-escape surface), skeptic-verified MEDIUM (latent; not exploitable until guest execution lands).

## Why not fixed inline now

Attaching the rootfs read-only (`is_read_only: true` + `root=/dev/vda ro`) breaks the systemd guest boot unless a writable workspace/overlay is provided, and a per-VM CoW/copy of the rootfs needs design (disk/perf) — both require a **real Firecracker host** to validate the guest actually boots, which the current sandbox cannot provide. Shipping an unvalidated boot-critical change would risk breaking all microVM provisioning. A `SECURITY / ISOLATION (tracked)` comment has been added at the code site (backends.rs) warning that guest execution must not be wired until this is fixed.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Each microVM has an isolated rootfs: either (a) rootfs attached `is_read_only: true` + a per-VM writable workspace/overlay drive (matching the declared `read_only_rootfs_with_prepared_workspace` policy), or (b) a per-VM CoW/reflink copy of the rootfs image.
- [ ] Guest boot validated on a real Firecracker host with the new layout.
- [ ] A test asserts the rootfs drive config enforces the declared `IsolationFilesystemPolicy.read_only_rootfs`.
- [ ] Concurrent microVMs no longer share a writable backing file.

## References
- Code site: `crates/agent-worker/src/backends.rs` (`configure_and_start_firecracker`, `/drives/rootfs`)
- Policy: `crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/isolation.rs` `IsolationFilesystemPolicy.read_only_rootfs`

## Context

Follow-up to the round-4 security fix `ea1040b` (`fix(usage-reports): restrict cross-tenant metadata breakdown to operators`).

`/admin/v1/usage-reports?group_by=metadata.<key>` is served from `usage_metadata_rollups`, an aggregation keyed on `(period_month, metadata_key, metadata_value)` with **no tenant/org column**. That containment removes a feature a tenant admin arguably should have: seeing **their own** metadata breakdown.

- Migration/backfill consideration for existing rollup rows (their tenant is not recoverable post-aggregation; document that pre-migration rows stay operator-only).

- [ ] Regression test covers both the tenant-scoped (own-only) and operator (global) paths.

body:
## Problem

#200 delivered managed-action guardrail enforcement: managed MCP/Tool/CLI/etc actions are evaluated against managed-action guardrail policies at the external-action authorizer and the tool-governance chokepoint, input and output, fail-closed. The `ActionKind` model gained `RequireApproval` and `Quarantine` (commit f571c90), but the enforcement seams do not yet treat them distinctly from `Block`/`Redact`:

- `state_quota_and_policy.rs:1350` collapses `RequireApproval → GuardrailEffect::Deny` and `Quarantine → GuardrailEffect::Redact`. `GuardrailMatch` carries only `effect`, not the originating `ActionKind`, so a seam cannot tell an approval-gate from a hard block.
- A `RequireApproval` managed-action guardrail therefore hard-denies instead of routing through the existing tool-approval subsystem (`approval.rs`, already wired into `execute_tool_request_with_governance`) to create an approval request and allow on approval.
- A `Quarantine` output match fully withholds the tool result instead of applying the detector's redaction `content_patches` to return a redacted-but-usable result.

Current behaviour is fail-closed and directionally correct (approval-required denies, quarantine withholds); this issue is about the richer, distinct semantics — not a security gap.

## Scope

- [ ] Add `action_kind: GuardrailActionKind` to `GuardrailMatch` and populate it at all construction sites in `state_quota_and_policy.rs` (guardrail_enforcement, shadow candidates, evidence-unavailable) — additive; `effect` semantics unchanged for the model-content path.
- [ ] `RequireApproval` at the tool-governance chokepoint: route through the existing tool-approval subsystem (request/verify approval, deny until approved) instead of a plain deny, reusing the `ApprovalPolicy::Always` machinery already in `execute_tool_request_with_governance`.
- [ ] `Quarantine` on output: apply the match's `content_patches` to produce a redacted result rather than full withhold; full withhold remains the fallback when no safe redaction evidence exists (mirror the `guardrail_invalid_redaction` fail-closed path).
- [ ] Distinct audit/response codes per kind (`guardrail_approval_required`, `guardrail_quarantined`, `guardrail_blocked`).

## Acceptance

- [ ] A `RequireApproval` managed-action guardrail creates a pending approval and the action is allowed only after approval is granted (E2E through the chokepoint).
- [ ] A `Quarantine` output match returns redacted content (patches applied), not a full withhold, when redaction evidence is available.
- [ ] `Block` behaviour and all model-content guardrail behaviour are unchanged (regression).
- [ ] Unit + crate-integration coverage for each kind; the E2E harness closes the loop.

## Non-goals

- Changing the model-content (chat/responses/embeddings) guardrail path.
- New detector types or policy schema beyond surfacing the existing `ActionKind`.
- Isolation/sandbox backends (tracked separately).

## Problem

Issue #221 migrated **all runtime/production** PostgreSQL access (the `ferrogate-storage` control-plane storage layer) from the synchronous `postgres` crate to async `tokio-postgres` + `deadpool-postgres`, and deleted the sync driver + dropped the `postgres` dependency from `ferrogate-storage` (commit a95197e; `cargo tree -p ferrogate-storage -i postgres` is empty).

The **only** remaining user of the synchronous `postgres` crate in the workspace is the standalone compliance/verification CLI `tools/ferrogate-test`, which connects to a live/local Postgres to independently validate the deployed schema, RLS, and migration state (an out-of-band oracle, not runtime code). It is exercised only by the separate `rust-supabase-storage-tests` / `rust-cli-tooling-tests` workflows, not the main blocking gate.

## Scope

Migrate `tools/ferrogate-test` off the sync `postgres` crate to async `tokio-postgres`, so `postgres` can be dropped from the entire workspace:
- ~85 sync `Client` call sites across `src/{mcp_identity.rs (31), compliance.rs (29), guardrails.rs (19), supabase_schema.rs (4), target_capability.rs (2)}`.
- Single connect entry point `supabase_schema.rs::connect_live_supabase(...) -> Client`; clients are held as struct fields (`self.client`).
- **4 transaction blocks** (`self.client.transaction()? ... commit()?`): 3 in `mcp_identity.rs` (~2008/2047/2071), 1 in `compliance.rs` (~1078) — these need async-transaction handling.
- Remove `postgres` (+ `postgres`/`postgres-native-tls` as needed) from `tools/ferrogate-test/Cargo.toml`; keep the async stack.

Two viable shapes: (a) a thin sync wrapper over `(tokio::runtime::Runtime, tokio_postgres::Client)` exposing `query/execute/batch_execute/transaction` that `block_on`s internally (minimizes call-site churn, but transactions need care since they borrow the client across awaits), or (b) make the command handlers async and thread `&tokio_postgres::Client`.

## Acceptance

- `tools/ferrogate-test` builds with `--locked`, `cargo clippy -p ferrogate-test --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean, `cargo fmt --check` clean, `cargo test -p ferrogate-test` green.
- `cargo tree -i postgres` reports the sync `postgres` crate is **no longer anywhere in the workspace**.
- Compliance/verification SQL + semantics unchanged (this tool is the independent DB oracle — no behavioral drift).
- The `rust-supabase-storage-tests` / `rust-cli-tooling-tests` CI workflows still pass.

Closes the last thread of the #221 sync-driver removal.

body:
## Problem

`crates/ferrogate-cli/tests/agentic_lite.rs::tool_approvals_bind_fingerprint_and_fail_closed` intermittently fails under `cargo +1.88.0 test --workspace --all-features` (cross-binary scheduler contention), not in isolation and not when running the `agentic_lite` suite alone. Discovered while verifying #222 (a separate, already-fixed flake in `proxy_runtime.rs`).

Root cause: the test's `approval_mcp_config` set `tool_approval_timeout_secs = 1`, which has to satisfy two conflicting needs in the same test:

1. The mismatch/approve/deny cases need the pending approval to stay alive until the admin decision HTTP request lands. `decision()` in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/approval.rs` checks terminal-state, then expiry, then fingerprint, in that order — so under scheduler stall a 1s TTL let the approval auto-expire *before* the admin request arrived, and `decision()` returned `tool_approval_terminal` (Expired) instead of `tool_approval_fingerprint_mismatch`.
2. The test's final case has no admin decision at all — it deliberately relies on the approval failing closed via TTL auto-expiry, bounded by the client's read timeout in `support::http_request` (was 3s).

These two constraints only both hold within a narrow window (TTL <= 3s in isolation, but a 1s TTL is too tight under full-workspace load).

## Scope

- Do not add blind retries or weaken any assertion.
- Decouple the two constraints instead of picking a single point value: raise `support::http_request`'s client read timeout (only bounds a genuinely hung request, never changes a response) so raising the TTL is safe, then raise `tool_approval_timeout_secs` in `approval_mcp_config` comfortably above worst-case decision latency and comfortably below the new client timeout.
- Keep the test bodies and TTL rationale documented inline so a future change to either timeout doesn't silently reopen the race.

## Acceptance

- [x] Root cause identified precisely (order of terminal/expiry/fingerprint checks in `approval.rs::decision`, plus the shared TTL serving two conflicting needs).
- [x] Fix decouples client read timeout from approval TTL without retries or weakened assertions.
- [x] Verified stable in isolation (5/5) and across repeated full-workspace runs.

## Evidence source

Discovered while verifying #222 (proxy_runtime flake fix).

body:
Related: #217, #220

## Decision

FerroGate will migrate the entire workspace PostgreSQL stack to `tokio-postgres` plus `deadpool-postgres`. The synchronous `postgres` client, custom Condvar pool, and database `spawn_blocking` adapters are transitional debt and must be removed, not retained alongside the async stack.

This is an explicit SQL migration, not an ORM rewrite.

## Scope

- Add pinned workspace dependencies for `tokio-postgres` and `deadpool-postgres` with current Rustls/TLS behavior.
- Convert PostgreSQL repository contracts and implementations to async end to end.
- Migrate every PostgreSQL-backed repository: control plane/auth/RBAC, Guardrails, MCP identity, billing/ledger, assets/quota, provider/config state, audit/evidence, startup schema/migration/validation, admin/runtime handlers, and `ferrogate-test`.
- Replace the custom synchronous pool with deadpool async acquisition.
- Remove all database `spawn_blocking` use and all direct workspace dependency/use of the synchronous `postgres` crate.
- Keep SQL explicit and simple: short indexed CRUD/CAS; transaction-local RLS/timeout setup plus the minimum irreducible mutation; immediate commit.
- Configure bounded Rust-side pool acquisition plus PostgreSQL connect, TCP user, statement, and fail-fast lock timeouts.
- Preserve tenant RLS, arbitrary DB-backed RBAC, TLS modes, migrations, schema validation, audit/metrics, restart behavior, and repository contracts.
- Do not add an ORM, SQL DSL, stored procedure orchestration, database retry loops, advisory locks, `FOR UPDATE`, or long transactions.

## Correctness Contract

Async cancellation does not prove COMMIT rollback. Every mutation crossing a timeout must carry operation/lease ID plus version/generation fencing and use the explicit states `PreCommit`, `CommitInFlight`, `KnownSuccess`, `KnownFailure`, and `OutcomeUnknown`. A stale reread while COMMIT remains unresolved never proves failure.

## Acceptance

- [ ] No workspace production or test-harness crate directly depends on or imports synchronous `postgres`.
- [ ] No database repository call is wrapped in `spawn_blocking`.
- [ ] The custom `PostgresClientPool`/Condvar implementation is deleted.
- [ ] All PostgreSQL repository traits and call sites are async without a hidden blocking compatibility adapter.
- [ ] Deadpool acquisition has an explicit short Rust-side timeout and emits pool wait/timeout metrics.
- [ ] All mutations retain explicit SQL, RLS, fencing, indexed predicates, and short transaction boundaries.
- [ ] Guardrail binding activation/archive contains no advisory lock or `FOR UPDATE`.
- [ ] Deterministic barrier/channel tests cover pre-commit cancel, COMMIT in flight plus stale reread, ACK-lost success, revoke/takeover, pool timeout, and explicit outcome-unknown; no sleep-based race tests.
- [ ] TLS disable/prefer/require/verify-ca/verify-full behavior retains focused coverage.
- [ ] Startup migration, restart/durability, Admin/OpenAPI, gateway runtime, and `ferrogate-test` suites pass on the async implementation.
- [ ] Bounded unique-schema Supabase contract/durability suites pass with exact cleanup; no load, stress, lock injection, or performance traffic reaches Supabase.
- [ ] Local isolated PostgreSQL carries concurrency/fault verification.
- [ ] `cargo tree -i postgres` proves the synchronous driver is absent from the shipped workspace graph, unless a transitive non-runtime dependency is explicitly documented and has no FerroGate call site.

## Delivery Plan

Land this as dependency-ordered, reviewable slices under this issue, but do not close it while the workspace has mixed synchronous/asynchronous PostgreSQL runtime paths:

1. async connection/TLS/pool foundation and repository contract;
2. MCP identity and Guardrail CAS paths;
3. remaining control-plane, billing, assets, audit, and provider repositories;
4. startup migrations/schema validation and all callers;
5. `ferrogate-test`, live contracts, deletion of sync driver/pool, final workspace verification.

body:
Parent: #193

## Problem

The PostgreSQL Guardrail policy activation and archive paths currently coordinate with `pg_advisory_xact_lock` and `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside multi-statement transactions. This makes Supabase carry wait semantics and violates the project rule that database coordination must be short indexed CRUD/CAS while Rust owns retry/backoff.

Affected runtime paths:

- `activate_guardrail_policy_revision`
- `archive_guardrail_policy_revision`

## Required Design

- Read the immutable revision and current binding without acquiring a database wait lock.
- Compute the desired binding transition in Rust.
- Persist with one short conditional version/generation CAS statement.
- On a CAS conflict, return an explicit conflict or perform bounded Rust-side reread/backoff; never wait/retry inside PostgreSQL.
- Keep a fail-fast lock/statement timeout and indexed predicates.
- Preserve rollback-only validation, archived revision ordering/deduplication, transition evidence, RLS, and arbitrary DB-driven RBAC.
- Do not add stored procedures, advisory locks, `FOR UPDATE`, `pg_sleep`, or long transactions.

## Acceptance

- [ ] No production Guardrail policy activation/archive SQL contains `pg_advisory_xact_lock` or `FOR UPDATE`.
- [ ] Binding rows carry an explicit optimistic version/generation and mutations compare the expected value.

- [ ] Activation, rollback, and archive semantics retain focused unit and repository integration coverage in dedicated test files.
- [ ] Bounded live Supabase functional/contract proof uses a unique schema, sequential requests, exact cleanup, and no load, stress, lock injection, or performance testing.
- [ ] Metrics/audit evidence makes a CAS conflict observable without leaking policy content.

## Constraint

Supabase never serves as a waiting mechanism. Database operations remain simple, short, indexed CRUD/CAS; business orchestration, retry, wait, and backoff remain in Rust.

body:
Related: #216

## Problem

The MCP refresh heartbeat uses async owner and renewal deadlines, but repository operations run through `spawn_blocking`. Dropping the async future does not cancel the blocking task. The PostgreSQL pool also waits indefinitely on a Condvar when no client is available.

A timed-out renewal or completion may therefore execute later. Existing version, authorization-generation, lease-ID, and revocation fencing prevents stale writes after takeover or revoke, but the operator-visible timeout currently bounds only the response wait, not the underlying storage operation.

## Risk

- A response can report owner/renewal timeout while a detached completion later persists the credential.
- A detached renewal can extend the lease after its caller stopped awaiting it, delaying takeover.
- Pool starvation can accumulate blocking tasks and make timeout telemetry disagree with durable state.
- Tests that only assert async future cancellation give false confidence.

## Scope

- Add a bounded PostgreSQL pool acquisition API using a real deadline.
- Make MCP claim/renew/complete/release operations carry an operation deadline or cancellation/fencing token checked before SQL and before mutation.
- Use one short conditional CAS SQL mutation per refresh coordination operation; Supabase must never be used as a waiting mechanism.
- Bound SQL execution with a matching statement timeout and short lock timeout.
- Keep wait, backoff, retry, timeout observation, and external IdP work in the Rust async layer outside database operations.
- Reconcile an ACK-lost mutation with a bounded authoritative reread, or explicitly record an unknown outcome when durable state cannot be proven.
- Preserve exact version, authorization-generation, lease-ID, expiry, and revoke fencing.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A focused local deterministic test exhausts the pool and proves acquire returns by the declared deadline with no later SQL side effect.
- [ ] Claim, renewal, completion, and release use single short conditional CAS mutations without long transactions, lock waits, `pg_sleep`, or database-side retry loops.
- [ ] A renewal that times out cannot extend the lease later; an ACK-lost successful renewal is recovered by bounded authoritative reread.
- [ ] A completion that times out cannot silently persist later, or returns a reconciled success with explicit evidence.
- [ ] Revoke/takeover still reject stale renewal and completion.
- [ ] Metrics/logs distinguish response deadline, storage cancellation, reconciled late success, and explicit outcome-unknown.
- [ ] Live Supabase proof uses only normal bounded two-caller CAS behavior, durable state/fencing, and exact per-run schema cleanup.
- [ ] No Supabase live scenario performs pool exhaustion, deliberate row-lock waits, `pg_sleep`, load, stress, throughput, or high-concurrency testing.

## Evidence

Discovered during read-only review of #216. `PostgresClientPool::acquire` currently loops on `Condvar::wait` without a deadline, while MCP storage calls are wrapped in `spawn_blocking`.

Acceptance was corrected on 2026-07-13 by explicit operator directive: Supabase never carries wait semantics. Deliberate contention and delayed-commit faults are local-only proofs.

body:
## Problem

Live `ferrogate-test mcp-identity-supabase` exposed duplicate OAuth refresh grants under concurrent load. Six callers target one expired credential, but the mock IdP observed two refresh grants.

The runtime refresh lease is fixed at 10 seconds while waiters remain active for 12 seconds. If live Supabase plus the IdP call takes longer than 10 seconds, another caller can claim the expired lease and issue a second grant before the first refresh completes.

Observed on 2026-07-11:

```text
Error: concurrent MCP refresh expected one IdP grant, observed 2
```

The isolated failure-path schema was cleaned successfully, so this is not cross-scenario row pollution.

## Risk

Duplicate refresh grants can rotate or invalidate refresh tokens, create avoidable IdP load, and make concurrent MCP requests fail nondeterministically. A fixed lease that can expire while its owner is still performing external IO is not a valid single-flight guarantee.

## Scope

- Make refresh ownership survive slow but valid IdP/Supabase operations, using a bounded lease renewal/heartbeat or another explicit single-flight design.
- Preserve crash recovery so a dead owner cannot hold the credential forever.
- Keep authorization generation, revocation, and version checks fail closed.
- Emit inspectable evidence for claim, renewal/takeover, completion, timeout, and conflict outcomes.
- Do not solve this with blind test retries or an arbitrarily huge static lease.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A focused async concurrency test holds the IdP response beyond the original 10-second lease and still observes exactly one refresh grant.
- [ ] All waiting callers receive the same persisted refreshed credential or a precise bounded failure.
- [ ] Owner crash/stall permits safe takeover after the renewed lease expires.
- [ ] Revocation during refresh still supersedes the lease and prevents credential resurrection.
- [ ] `ferrogate-test mcp-identity-supabase` passes against live Supabase under concurrent load.
- [ ] Tests live in dedicated test files, not the business-logic module.

## Evidence

Discovered while implementing #212. Related to the MCP identity runtime and live Supabase contract.

Related: #210

## Problem

The reusable provider settlement contract now proves OpenAI-compatible success, exact pricing, fallback, and streaming/non-streaming terminal errors with reported usage. It does not enumerate Anthropic, Gemini, Grok/xAI, OpenRouter, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, or Vertex.

A new adapter can therefore be added to ProviderAdapterRegistry without adding a runtime usage/cost compliance case. That does not satisfy the binding rule that every provider adapter must prove what it reports is what billing and telemetry settle.

## Scope

- Expose one canonical supported-adapter registry that the runtime and compliance matrix share.
- Add one runtime contract fixture per canonical adapter family, including its real request and usage response shape.
- Fail the suite when a canonical adapter has no compliance case or a case names an unsupported adapter.
- For every adapter, assert provider/model attribution, provider-reported usage, exact configured cost, status, request/trace attributes, and standalone billing ledger settlement.
- Cover streaming where the adapter supports provider-reported streaming usage.
- Keep credentials local and deterministic through mock providers; retain opt-in live provider scenarios as additional evidence, not replacements.

## Acceptance

- [ ] The compliance matrix and ProviderAdapterRegistry have exactly the same canonical adapter families.
- [ ] OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Gemini, Grok/xAI, OpenRouter, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, and Vertex each pass the shared settlement contract.
- [ ] Removing any adapter case fails ferrogate-test before runtime E2E is considered green.
- [ ] Adding a new canonical adapter without a case fails the suite.
- [ ] Each case proves exact usage/cost and required telemetry through gateway and billing ledger.
- [ ] Dedicated tests live outside business-logic files.

## Non-goals

- Calling paid external providers in the deterministic local gate.
- Treating transport failures without reported usage as billable.
- Solving multi-attempt ledger identity; tracked separately in #213.

Related: #210

## Problem

BillingEvent and LedgerEntry idempotency are keyed only by trace_id + request_id. A logical request can dispatch multiple provider attempts through retry/fallback. If both a failed primary attempt and the successful fallback report billable usage, their ledger_entry_id values collide; the second insert becomes an idempotent no-op and one provider charge is silently lost.

The #210 provider compliance slice can safely prove a fallback whose failed primary reports no usage, but cannot honestly prove multi-attempt settlement until attempt identity is part of the billing contract.

## Scope

- Add a stable provider-attempt identity to the request execution and BillingEvent/LedgerEntry contracts.
- Include attempt identity in ledger/outbox idempotency keys while preserving retry idempotency for replay of the same attempt.
- Settle reported usage for every provider attempt, including retryable failures followed by fallback success.
- Expose provider, provider_model, attempt index, status, usage, and cost through billing/admin evidence.
- Add local and live Supabase migration/round-trip coverage.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A failed primary response with reported usage plus a successful fallback response produces two distinct ledger entries.
- [ ] Re-delivering either attempt is idempotent and does not double-charge.
- [ ] Retry, fallback, streaming, and non-streaming attempt identities are stable and inspectable.
- [ ] Usage/cost rollups equal the sum of all settled attempts.
- [ ] ferrogate-test provider compliance includes the multi-attempt case against local and live Supabase storage.

## Non-goals

- Charging transport failures or provider errors that report no usage.
- Replacing logical request_id as the cross-service correlation identifier.

body:
## Problem

`AGENTS.md` and `docs/dynamic-workflow.md` both document a fallback verification path: when Docker/network access blocks local Docker-backed and live-Supabase E2E proof, push and rely on GitHub Actions CI (`rust-ci` quality gate + GHCR image build + E2E jobs), then pull the exact CI-built image locally with `ferrogate-test`.

That fallback does not currently exist. `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s only trigger is:

```yaml
on:
  release:
    types: [published]
```

Every module workflow it calls (`rust-quality.yml`, `rust-e2e-harness.yml`, `rust-supabase-storage-tests.yml`, etc.) is `workflow_call`-only, invoked solely by `ci.yml`. Confirmed live: pushing directly to `main` (`b583f95`, the #202 integration) produced no new run in `gh run list` — the most recent runs on `main` are all `workflow_dispatch` or old `push`-triggered runs from before commit `874a3b4` ("ci: gate ci.yml and package.yml on release tag push, not per-commit") changed this trigger.

This means: every commit landing on `main` between releases currently gets zero automated CI verification. The repo's branch protection also reports "Required status check 'rust-ci' is expected" on push, but no workflow run ever produces that check outside of a release — so the required check is permanently pending/bypassed rather than actually gating anything.

## Scope

- Restore a `push`-to-`main` (or PR) trigger for the `rust-ci` quality gate at minimum (`rust-quality.yml`'s fmt/clippy/metadata/openapi-contract checks), separate from the release-only image build/package/E2E jobs if those are intentionally kept release-scoped for cost reasons.
- If keeping the full E2E/image-build pipeline release-only is intentional (e.g. cost), say so explicitly in `AGENTS.md`/`docs/dynamic-workflow.md` and correct the documented fallback instructions, since they currently promise CI-backed proof that does not happen per-commit.
- Reconcile branch protection's "rust-ci" required check with whatever trigger is chosen so it isn't permanently non-blocking.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A push (or PR) to `main` triggers at least the static/quality gate automatically, visible in `gh run list`.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` / `docs/dynamic-workflow.md` accurately describe what CI proof is actually available per-commit vs. release-only.
- [ ] Branch protection's required check corresponds to a workflow that actually runs on the events it gates.

## Non-goals

- Not asking to make the full Docker/live-Supabase E2E suite run on every commit if that's a deliberate cost tradeoff — just to make the documentation and required-check configuration match reality.

Surfaced while integrating #202: pushed a large, security-relevant change to `main` expecting the documented CI-fallback proof and found none was triggered.

Related: #112 (full-business-coverage), #188 (asset-quota-scope failure mode)
Design reference: docs/testing/testing-architecture.md ("Open work"), AGENTS.md -> Testing Architecture

## Problem

FerroGate's test system is layered, but the Contract/compliance layer began as point scenarios: `ferrogate-test api-contract`, `gateway-billing-chain`, and `guardrail-supabase`. Without a reusable contract, a new component can ship a green suite while silently violating a cross-cutting runtime contract.

This is how #188 passed review: a quota value was writable and readable through the Admin API, but the runtime did not consistently consume the declared scope. "Interface tested green" is not "behaves as claimed".

## Scope

- Add a shared compliance module to `tools/ferrogate-test`: a per-component-class contract plus a single runner that owns write, read, runtime exercise, verification, and cleanup.
- Encode write-path == read-path == runtime behavior first for tenant/project/workspace/key quota scopes.
- Keep asset storage quota tenant-only because stored assets and cumulative usage are tenant-owned; reject project/workspace/key asset values at API and DB boundaries instead of accepting write-only configuration.
- Provider-adapter contract: emits usage/cost telemetry with required attributes; billing cost equals configured settlement for adapter-reported usage; fallback and reported-usage error paths settle correctly.
- Guardrail contract: block and allow paths emit auditable evidence; blocked content produces durable, queryable evidence.
- Wire compliance assertions into `ferrogate-test ci` and matching release-only reusable workflows.

## Acceptance

- [x] A reintroduced #188-style regression fails the compliance assertion. Proven by temporarily disconnecting the tenant asset runtime read: the contract observed status 200 instead of the required quota block.
- [x] Every generic scope the Admin API accepts is asserted read-back at runtime; unsupported narrower asset scopes fail explicitly at write time.
- [ ] A new provider adapter cannot pass the suite without emitting required usage/cost telemetry and settling billing to the configured cost. OpenAI-compatible success, exact GPT-5.5 pricing, fallback, and streaming/non-streaming terminal errors with reported usage are implemented; the exhaustive adapter registry matrix remains #214.
- [x] A new Guardrail cannot pass the live suite without emitting auditable evidence on both block and allow paths.
- [x] The quota/provider compliance layer runs in `ferrogate-test ci`; live Supabase quota and Guardrail forms are wired into the release-only Supabase workflow and therefore into `rust-ci`.
- [x] `docs/testing/testing-architecture.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `ferrogate-test-strategy` describe the implemented contracts and keep the provider-matrix gap explicit.

## Current status

The reusable executor and quota component class run locally and against live Supabase. The provider class now drives gateway -> billing service settlement for success, exact GPT-5.5 pricing, fallback, and reported-usage errors in streaming and non-streaming paths. The Guardrail class writes/reads a DB-backed policy and verifies allow/block evaluation, per-check, audit, and request-log evidence directly in live Supabase.

#213 tracks distinct billing identities when multiple attempts in one logical request each report usage. #214 tracks mechanical coverage of every canonical provider adapter family. This issue stays open until #214 makes the provider acceptance enforceable.

## Non-goals

- A generic plugin/marketplace contract before the internal contract survives real provider and Guardrail adapters.
- Replacing existing point commands; they become callers of the shared contract.
- Coverage-percentage targets; this layer proves behavior, not line count (#112).

Parent: #194

## Decision to validate

FerroGate's sellable wedge is a customer-boundary Secure Agent Gateway: one identity/policy/Guardrail/approval/isolation/egress/billing/evidence chain for model and Agent traffic. This must be tested with buyers before broadening the roadmap.

## Research plan

- Interview at least five platform/security buyers operating or actively piloting MCP/Agent systems in enterprise environments.
- Collect a recent concrete incident or blocked rollout, current architecture, data boundary, identity model, approval/isolation needs, investigation workflow, procurement blockers, and willingness to pay.
- Do not count generic interest, open-source stars, or “security is important” as validation.
- Recruit two technical design partners only after confirming the same painful workflow in at least three interviews.
- For one partner, run a time-boxed VPC pilot with real but scoped Agent/MCP traffic and an agreed security success test.
- Keep facts, buyer quotes approved for use, assumptions, and FerroGate preferences separate in the issue updates.

## Falsifiable gates

- [ ] 5 qualified interviews completed with role, environment, date, and evidence notes.
- [ ] At least 3 report a recent identity/action-control/data-boundary/investigation problem severe enough to block or delay deployment.
- [ ] At least 2 accept a technical design-partner plan with named owner, workload, timeline, and success criteria.
- [ ] At least 1 runs real traffic in its VPC through the identity-to-evidence chain.
- [ ] At least 1 enters a concrete paid contract/support/SLA discussion; free experimentation does not satisfy this gate.
- [ ] Detector, protocol, deployment, and UI priorities are reordered from observed evidence rather than competitor feature counts.

## Stop condition

If fewer than three interviews confirm the pain, or no design partner will run scoped real traffic, pause the Secure Agent Gateway wedge and revisit the target segment. Do not compensate by adding generic gateway features.

## Non-goals

- Inventing TAM, price, or conversion numbers before evidence exists.
- Using vendor case studies as customer validation.
- Promising certifications, SLAs, or detector accuracy not yet delivered.

Self-hosting alone does not provide the enterprise hybrid operating model validated by Portkey: sensitive traffic and logs remain in the customer VPC while a managed control plane distributes policy safely. Parent: #194

## Problem

FerroGate has isolation abstractions and targeted adversarial tests, but an enterprise sandbox claim requires repeatable evidence against a real backend and the same governed action path shipped to customers. A mock or class-level policy test does not prove filesystem, network, process, resource, and secret containment under production wiring.

## Scope

- Select one supported production isolation backend and threat model; state kernel/runtime/deployment prerequisites.
- Run Agent worker execution through target-level capability policy, Guardrail/approval where applicable, isolation, governed egress, billing, and evidence.
- Add adversarial fixtures for filesystem escape, symlink/hardlink races, process spawning, namespace escape attempts, resource exhaustion, network/metadata access, DNS rebinding, secret exfiltration, and cancellation/timeout cleanup.
- Capture backend identity/config digest, policy revisions, image digest, and action fingerprints in evidence.
- Define fail-closed behavior when the requested backend or isolation feature is unavailable; never downgrade silently.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A real rootless container/gVisor-class backend (chosen explicitly) passes the documented adversarial suite in CI or an approved security runner.
- [ ] Network egress reaches only target-level allowed destinations and cannot reach cloud metadata by default.
- [ ] Filesystem access cannot escape the mounted workspace through traversal, symlink, or race fixtures.
- [ ] CPU/memory/process/time limits terminate work and settle billing/evidence predictably.
- [ ] Backend unavailable/misconfigured requests fail before executing unisolated work.
- [ ] Docker/CI evidence records exact image digest, backend version/config, commands, and results.
- [ ] Security docs separate proven controls, environmental assumptions, and residual risk.

## Non-goals

- Declaring the sandbox universally secure from one CVE-shaped fixture.
- Maintaining several nominal backends without production evidence for one.

Parent: #194
Required by the Agent action Guardrail slice under #193.

## Problem

The capability boundary distinguishes broad classes such as Filesystem, NetworkEgress, and McpTool, but does not consistently constrain concrete targets. A grant can therefore authorize more paths, hosts, methods, tools, or arguments than the operator intended.

Class-level authorization is not a credible least-privilege claim.

## Scope

- Define typed target selectors:
  - MCP: server, tool, read/write risk, argument schema/field rules.
  - Filesystem: workspace-relative path glob and read/write/execute operation.
  - Network/REST: scheme, host, port, method, path and DNS/IP rebinding controls.
  - Secret: secret reference and allowed adapter/action destination; never plaintext.
  - CLI: executable, argv rules, cwd and resource bounds.
- Evaluate selectors against canonical normalized targets, not caller strings.
- Make grants additive and deny/fail closed on ambiguous target resolution.
- Produce normalized decision evidence and an action fingerprint consumable by exact-action approval and Guardrails.
- Provide migration behavior for existing class-only policies; do not silently reinterpret them as narrow grants.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A policy can allow one path/host/tool/method while denying a sibling target in the same capability class.
- [ ] Path traversal, symlink escape, alternate host notation, redirects, DNS rebinding, and argument-shape bypasses have adversarial tests.
- [ ] Secret grants cannot expose resolved values or inject them into an unapproved target.
- [ ] Approval and execution compare the same canonical action fingerprint.
- [ ] Policy decision evidence states subject, selector, canonical target, policy revision, outcome, and request/trace/run ids.
- [ ] Admin API/OpenAPI and Docker E2E cover MCP, filesystem, network, secret, and CLI decisions.

## Non-goals

- Using Guardrail content classification as authorization.
- Granting all paths/hosts because an older policy names only the capability class without an explicit migration mode.

Related: #51, #62, #86, #190.

Parent: #194

## Problem

Runtime routes for projects, workspaces, quota policies, plans, wallets, usage reports, assets, and other control-plane resources are not all represented in the current OpenAPI completeness gate. `scripts/check-openapi.py` validates a hand-selected method set, so a green check does not prove that the public runtime contract is complete.

Enterprise SDK generation, RBAC review, compatibility, and change management cannot depend on reading Rust route branches.

## Scope

- Create one structured source or extraction contract for public/admin runtime route + method + operation identity.
- Make CI compare every in-scope runtime route/method against OpenAPI and fail on undocumented or stale operations.
- Classify internal/debug/health routes explicitly rather than silently omitting them.
- Add the missing Project, Workspace, Quota Policy, Plan, Wallet, Usage Report, Asset, Guardrail, and other live schemas and errors.
- Define compatibility rules for operation ids, path/field removal, enum changes, pagination, auth, and error envelopes.
- Wire the check into the smallest CI workflow module and retain `rust-ci` as the aggregate gate.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Adding a runtime route or method without OpenAPI fails CI.
- [ ] Removing/renaming a documented route or incompatible schema fails a compatibility check or requires an explicit reviewed baseline update.
- [ ] Every exposed route is classified as public/admin/internal and has auth/RBAC/error documentation where applicable.
- [ ] Generated client smoke tests compile against representative Project, Quota, Wallet, Guardrail, and Asset operations.
- [ ] `python3 scripts/check-openapi.py` no longer relies on an incomplete manually selected subset.
- [ ] Existing OpenAPI consumers retain stable operation ids unless a migration is documented.

## Non-goals

- Documenting private implementation helpers as public API.
- Treating schema formatting as proof of runtime behavior.

Related: #20, #96.

body:
Parent: #194

## Problem

`McpAuthType` declares `oauth`, `per_user_oauth`, and `per_user_headers`, but runtime dispatch does not branch on `auth_type`; `HttpMcpClient` resolves only static headers. Config can therefore claim a user-isolated identity mode while every caller uses shared or missing credentials.

This is a product-truth and tenant-isolation defect, not a documentation gap.

## Scope

- Immediately reject unimplemented auth modes during config/Admin API validation until their E2E path exists.
- Implement per-user OAuth/OIDC as the first identity path, including authorization-code flow where applicable, token storage, refresh, revocation, subject binding, and server/workspace scope.
- Support explicit upstream identity modes: original bearer passthrough and FerroGate-signed short-lived JWT. Do not accept a caller-supplied claims header as trusted identity.
- Strip identity-forwarding headers from inbound traffic and regenerate them from authenticated tenant context.
- Persist credentials/tokens through an encrypted secret/token repository; never expose tokens through config reads, logs, audit, debug, or OpenAPI examples.
- Record subject, workspace, MCP server, tool, credential source, decision, request/trace id, and revocation outcome.

## Acceptance

- [x] Unsupported modes fail config and Admin API validation with an exact error until implemented.
- [x] Two OIDC users calling the same MCP server receive distinct upstream identities and policy outcomes.
- [x] Forged identity headers and cross-user token substitution fail closed.
- [x] Token refresh, expiration, logout/revocation, IdP outage, and MCP 401 behavior are covered.
- [x] Workspace/user removal prevents subsequent dispatch without waiting for process restart.
- [x] Static header mode remains backward compatible and clearly named as shared identity.
- [x] OpenAPI, Admin visibility, audit, metrics, and local-container E2E use a real OIDC mock plus MCP server.

## Non-goals

- Pretending client-credentials OAuth provides per-user identity.
- Storing refresh tokens in plaintext config.
- Trusting raw identity claims supplied by the client.

Related: #17, #27, #108.

Parent: #193
Commercial validation parent: #194

## Problem

Partner count is not a security outcome. A vendor adapter is useful only when its credential, payload, verdict, transformation, failure, version, and accuracy behavior fit the common contract and can be evaluated on relevant traffic.

## Scope

- Publish a narrow adapter contract and conformance suite for external semantic detectors.
- Require descriptor metadata: supported stages/segments, transformation capability, data residency, maximum payload, detector/config version, credential type, and failure modes.
- Build a versioned evaluation corpus and runner that reports precision, recall, false-positive/negative examples, latency distribution, and errors. Keep sensitive customer examples out of the repository.
- Select exactly two initial native integrations from design-partner requirements: one DLP/PII path and one prompt-injection/content-security path. Do not choose by logo count.
- Run integrations in deterministic shadow sampling before enforcement, with a documented promotion/rollback decision.
- Document deployment locality: customer-VPC detector, provider SaaS, and what content leaves the boundary.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A third adapter can be implemented without editing core policy semantics.
- [ ] Conformance tests cover pass/fail/error/timeout/transform, sanitized evidence, and version reporting.
- [ ] Both selected integrations have reproducible fixtures and a documented known-limitations/accuracy report.
- [ ] Shadow results can be compared to human labels and promoted by scope to enforcement with rollback.
- [ ] Data-flow documentation states every field sent to each vendor and where it is processed.
- [ ] No marketing accuracy or compliance claim is emitted from integration existence alone.

## Non-goals

- Marketplace/SDK before the internal contract has survived two real adapters.
- Building FerroGate-native semantic classifiers without training/evaluation ownership.

Depends on the async detector runtime, policy/evidence model, and design-partner signal.

Parent: #193
Roadmap parent: #194

## Problem

Model-content Guardrails do not govern the more consequential Agent side effects: MCP tools, CLI, filesystem, REST calls, secret injection, and network egress. Capability policy answers whether a subject may attempt a target; Guardrail must inspect the concrete arguments/result and risk before and after execution.

## Scope

- Extend `GuardrailTarget` and `ContentSegment` to MCP server/tool, tool arguments/result, CLI argv/cwd, filesystem path/operation, REST method/host/body, secret reference destination, and network target.
- Order the decision path: authenticated identity -> target-level capability policy -> input Guardrail -> optional exact-action approval -> isolated execution -> output Guardrail -> billing/evidence.
- Bind approval to a canonical action fingerprint after Guardrail transformations so “approve A, execute B” is impossible.
- Add actions appropriate to tools: block, redact arguments/results, require approval, quarantine, record. Never retry non-idempotent actions automatically.
- Ensure the external detector payload is minimized and never includes resolved secret values unless a dedicated, explicitly approved detector contract requires it.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A policy scopes a check to one MCP server/tool and specific argument fields without affecting unrelated tools.
- [ ] A high-risk argument requires approval bound to the exact post-transformation action fingerprint.
- [ ] Revocation between approval and execution fails closed.
- [ ] Blocked input produces no MCP/tool/network side effect and no erroneous usage charge.
- [ ] Tool-result redaction happens before model/client consumption and before normal logs.
- [ ] Non-idempotent actions are never retried by a Guardrail action.
- [ ] E2E covers at least MCP and one additional managed action type with audit, billing, and evaluation evidence.

## Non-goals

- Replacing target-level capability authorization with content classification.
- Treating approval as a substitute for isolation.

Depends on the target-level capability policy and MCP identity issues under #194, plus the policy/evidence slices under #193.

Also contributes to the investigation requirement in #194.

## Problem

Current Guardrail observability is aggregate counters plus generic deny/redact audit events. Operators cannot retrieve every check verdict, detector error, policy revision, latency, transformation, and enforcement status for a request. Existing request, audit, billing, approval, and agent-run records are separate surfaces.

## Scope

- Add a durable `GuardrailEvaluationRepository` with one overall evaluation and per-check records.
- Persist request/trace/agent-run ids, subject and scope, target/stage/mode, policy revision, detector/version/config digest, pass/fail/error/skipped, action, latency, finding categories/counts, transformation flag, and input fingerprint.
- Do not store matched PII/secret text by default. Any future forensic payload store is separately encrypted, RBAC-protected, short-retention, and out of scope here.
- Add paginated/filterable Admin API by ids, scope, subject, policy/revision, detector, category, verdict, action, error, and time.
- Add low-cardinality Prometheus/OTLP evidence and detector-health views.
- Extend the Admin console request/action investigation view to join Identity, Route, Policy, Guardrail, Approval, Provider/Tool execution, Usage/Cost, and final outcome in one unframed timeline.

## Acceptance

- [x] An operator can start with request id, trace id, or agent run id and find all relevant decisions without querying raw database tables.
- [x] Every check distinguishes fail from detector error and states whether it was enforced or shadow-only.
- [x] Evidence survives restart on supported durable backends and retention is configurable.
- [x] API/RBAC tests prevent cross-tenant and unauthorized forensic access.
- [x] Sanitizer tests prove prompts, PII, secrets, auth headers, and detector credentials are absent by default.
- [x] Metrics avoid high-cardinality policy/user/request labels.
- [ ] Given a failed request, a security engineer unfamiliar with the implementation can answer who, why, target, action, and cost in under 10 minutes during a usability test.
- [x] local-container ferrogate-test E2E joins a Guardrail block and a Guardrail-redacted successful request to their audit and billing evidence.

## Non-goals

- Storing all raw prompts as “observability.”
- A separate decorative dashboard that does not use runtime evidence.

Parent: #193

## Problem

FerroGate has keyword, regex, and byte-length checks, but enterprise policies also need deterministic structure, request-parameter, tool, metadata, and high-confidence secret controls. Adding each as a special branch in `match_guardrail` would preserve the current first-match architecture and create inconsistent transformation behavior.

## Scope

- Implement built-in detectors behind the same contract: regex/contains/size compatibility, JSON parse/schema, required/forbidden keys, request/tool parameter constraints, endpoint/model/metadata constraints, and high-confidence secret patterns.
- Add typed `ContentPatch` validation and application. A patch may touch only detector-declared content segments and allowlisted paths.
- Ensure transformations cannot modify identity, tenant scope, route/provider/model selection, tool allowlists, budget, approval fingerprint, or credential fields.
- Return multiple sanitized findings with category, severity, confidence when meaningful, segment/range, and HMAC fingerprint.
- Treat broad PII entity recognition, prompt injection, jailbreak, toxicity, grounding, and hallucination as semantic/external detector concerns until accuracy is measured.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Every detector has pass, fail, error, and boundary tests; mutating detectors also have transformation tests.
- [ ] JSON Schema and request/tool parameter checks operate on structured fields, not serialized substring matching.
- [ ] Secret detection catches versioned fixture patterns without logging or persisting the secret value.
- [ ] Property/adversarial tests prove a patch cannot modify protected fields or escape its segment/path.
- [ ] Existing keyword/regex/max-input config behavior remains compatible.
- [ ] E2E proves input block, output redact, and a protected-field patch rejection with evidence.

## Non-goals

- Calling a regex pack “complete DLP.”
- Shipping an unmeasured in-house prompt-injection classifier.
- Adding a new external dependency without documenting why a structured standard-library/existing-workspace option is insufficient.

Depends on the policy and envelope slices in #193.

body:
Parent: #193

## Problem

Guardrails currently inspect serialized body text and cannot reliably identify system/developer/user content, tool schemas, tool arguments, results, or attachments. Streaming behavior is safe only because guarded output is buffered, but this contract is not modeled or operator-visible.

Portkey checks only the last input message and treats post-stream output checks as informational. FerroGate must state exactly what was inspected and whether enforcement happened before any byte escaped.

## Scope

- Define immutable `GuardrailEnvelope` and typed `ContentSegment` with source, segment id, protocol location, content type, and fingerprint.
- Add Chat Completions and Responses adapters that extract system, developer, user, assistant, tool schema/arguments/result, metadata, and supported text attachments without leaking auth headers.
- Define output streaming modes: `buffer_and_enforce`, `shadow_after_complete`, and `reject_streaming`.
- Keep `buffer_and_enforce` bounded by maximum bytes and time; overflow/error follows explicit policy and cannot silently switch to pass-through.
- Mark shadow output evaluations `not_enforced`; they may never emit a blocked outcome after content was sent.
- Return stable standard HTTP errors for blocked/unsupported modes; keep typed internal outcomes instead of using nonstandard 246/446 orchestration statuses.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Findings identify a stable segment and byte range across UTF-8 and multi-part content.
- [ ] Tests prove that system/developer/user/tool content are inspected according to detector declarations, not only the last message.
- [ ] Buffered SSE catches a secret split across chunks and sends no unsafe first byte.
- [ ] Shadow SSE remains pass-through and records `not_enforced`, never `blocked`.
- [ ] Buffer byte/time overflow follows configured error action and emits sanitized evidence.
- [ ] Unguarded and shadow-only streams retain a pass-through path with measured regression limits.
- [ ] Chat and Responses streaming/non-streaming paths have Docker E2E coverage.

## Non-goals

- Claiming real-time output blocking for pass-through streams.
- Audio/image classification before a supported media extraction contract exists.

Depends on the versioned policy model in #193.

Parent: #193

## Problem

`GuardrailRule` currently mixes scope, a single matcher, and effect. Evaluation is first-match-wins, policy history is not immutable, and there is no activation/rollback contract. This cannot support enterprise inheritance, multiple checks, shadow rollout, or reliable incident reconstruction.

## Scope

- Add a narrow Guardrail domain model: immutable `PolicyRevision`, `CheckBinding`, `Action`, execution mode, aggregation (`all|any|threshold`), streaming mode, deadline, and explicit pass/fail/error actions.
- Support draft, active, and archived states. Updating creates a revision; activation and rollback are audited atomic state changes.
- Merge scopes additively: organization/tenant enforced + project/workspace enforced + assigned key/service account + approved profile. A lower scope cannot remove an enforced policy.
- Add `ferrogate-storage` repository contracts and durable implementations for policy revisions and active bindings; in-memory remains a test/development backend.
- Add Admin CRUD, revision, activate, rollback, and dry-run endpoints with RBAC and audit.
- Compile static TOML config into the same domain model. Preserve the current simple config through a documented compatibility compiler; do not maintain two evaluators.
- Publish the complete schemas in Admin OpenAPI.

## Acceptance

- [x] A revision is immutable and every runtime decision records its exact policy revision.
- [x] Lower-scope config and request headers cannot weaken an organization-enforced policy.
- [x] `all`, `any`, `threshold`, sequential, and parallel semantics have deterministic truth-table tests including detector errors and disabled checks.
- [x] Activate and rollback survive restart on each supported durable control-plane backend.
- [x] Dry-run returns selected checks/actions and sanitized results without dispatching a provider or external action.
- [x] Existing simple Guardrail config has regression coverage through the compatibility compiler.
- [x] Admin API, RBAC, audit, OpenAPI, config reload, and local-container ferrogate-test E2E cover one policy from creation to enforced request.

- A general workflow language.
- Request-supplied raw enforcing hooks.
- A policy-authoring visual canvas in this slice.

body:
Parent: #193

## Problem

`custom_http` Guardrail evaluation currently calls `ferrogate_secrets::http_post`, which uses blocking `TcpStream`/rustls I/O, directly from the AI request path. A slow or unavailable detector can pin a Pingora runtime worker. The response contract also collapses the detector result to `match + matched_text`, so timeout, overload, invalid response, and policy violation are indistinguishable.

This is a correctness problem before it is a feature gap.

## Scope

- Introduce a narrow async `GuardrailDetector` contract with descriptor, bounded deadline, typed result, typed error, detector version, findings, and optional constrained content patches.
- Move `custom_http` to a pooled async client; do not reuse the synchronous secret-resolution helper.
- Add per-detector timeout, semaphore/bulkhead, health state, and circuit breaker. Retry is off by default and may occur at most once within the parent deadline.
- Make `on_error = block | record | fallback_detector` explicit in compiled policy. Enforcing security policies default to block; shadow policies record.
- Resolve credentials through `secret_ref`; sanitize debug, audit, metrics, and detector error surfaces.
- Protect the endpoint against SSRF, redirects to disallowed targets, cloud metadata access, and DNS/IP rebinding. Private endpoints require explicit operator allowlisting.
- Compile existing `provider = custom_http` config into the new runtime so existing supported behavior does not split into a permanent second engine.

## Acceptance

- [ ] No synchronous socket or blocking HTTP helper executes in the Guardrail request path.
- [ ] Contract tests cover pass, fail, typed transformation, timeout, malformed JSON, 401, 429, 5xx, oversized payload, and circuit recovery.
- [ ] `on_error=block`, `record`, and `fallback_detector` produce distinct runtime outcomes and evidence.
- [ ] A detector timeout cannot consume more than the configured parent Guardrail deadline.
- [ ] Concurrent slow detector calls are bounded without stalling an unguarded request path.
- [ ] SSRF tests reject localhost, link-local/cloud metadata, redirect escape, and DNS rebinding by default.
- [ ] Existing `custom_http` allow/deny behavior remains config-compatible or fails validation with a precise migration error.
- [ ] Docker-backed `ferrogate-test` proves detector outage behavior, metrics, audit, and that the provider was or was not called as expected.

## Non-goals

- Native integrations for every security vendor.
- A general plugin ABI.
- Secret fetching on every hot-path evaluation.

References: #164, `docs/design/guardrail-security-architecture-2026-07.md` sections 2, 3.3, and 4.3.

## Decision

Build a versioned Guardrail enforcement plane, not a larger list of regex rules.

The architecture must separate Policy, Check, Detector, Action, and Evaluation; preserve FerroGate's fail-closed and buffered-streaming behavior; and extend enforcement from model input/output to MCP and Agent actions.

Design source: `docs/design/guardrail-security-architecture-2026-07.md` (committed 2026-07-10).

## Why

Portkey demonstrates a commercially mature `Check -> Action -> Config -> Evidence` product structure, including deterministic, native, partner, and custom detectors. FerroGate currently has useful request/response deny/redact behavior, but the runtime is still first-match, lacks versioned composition and per-check evidence. The blocking `custom_http` defect was closed by #195.

We will learn the product structure without copying unsafe semantics:

- Enforcing policies never silently fail open.
- Pass-through streaming output inspection is shadow-only; blocking requires buffering before first byte.
- Detectors return findings and constrained patches, not authority to replace identity/routing/permission fields.
- Organization-enforced policies cannot be weakened by a lower scope or request header.

## Outcome

An enterprise operator can create an immutable policy revision, dry-run it, enforce it by scope, inspect every check and failure, roll it back, and apply the same evidence model to model, MCP, Tool, and Agent action paths.

- [x] #200 — P1: MCP, Tool, and managed Agent action Guardrails.

on #196/#197; #200 additionally depends on #202/#204; #201 depends on #195/#196/#199 and
design-partner evidence from #209.

- [x] Versioned policy/check/action domain and durable repository exist.
- [x] Deterministic and external detectors use the same async contract and explicit error policy.
- [x] Streaming modes state whether output is truly enforceable.
- [x] Every evaluation produces queryable, sanitized per-check evidence.

body:
## Summary

The user has given an explicit direction: MySQL is no longer an allowed storage backend for FerroGate going forward. Only Supabase/PostgreSQL are permitted. This issue tracks formally retiring the MySQL storage provider (`RuntimeControlPlaneBackend::Mysql`, `MySqlControlPlaneStore`, `storage.provider: mysql` config) from the codebase, following the same removal pattern already used for Turso/libSQL in #94.

`docs/roadmap.md`'s "Storage And Analytics Boundary" section currently still describes MySQL as a "compatibility path until their separate hardening or removal issues close" (tracked loosely under #68/#94) -- this issue is the concrete removal issue that section refers to, and the roadmap text should be updated once this closes.

## Why it matters

Surfaced by #189's CI-runner migration: dispatching `ci.yml` on a working `ubuntu-latest` runner (run 28999350268, commit d12e77c) exposed that `ferrogate-test ci`'s `mysql_restart`/`mysql_tls_restart` scenarios hit `GET /admin/v1/status` -> `finalize_auth` -> `resolve_effective_quota` -> `Repositories::get_quota_policy`, which hard-fails with `quota_resolution_unavailable` (503) for *any* authenticated request when the backend is MySQL, because quota-policy records are Supabase/Postgres-only by design (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:4419-4423`, `quota_policies_supabase_only_error()`). This was never exercised on a working CI runner before (the self-hosted runner was offline through most of #189's history), so the incompatibility went unnoticed until now.

Given MySQL is being retired rather than hardened, the correct interim fix (this session) was to drop `run_mysql_restart`/`run_mysql_tls_restart` from `ferrogate-test ci`'s default sequence (`tools/ferrogate-test/src/main.rs`) rather than spend effort making quota-policy resolution MySQL-compatible for a backend on its way out. The standalone `ferrogate-test mysql-restart`/`mysql-tls-restart` subcommands and the MySQL storage provider itself are untouched by that fix and still exist in the codebase.

## Current Code Touchpoints

- `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs`
  - `RuntimeControlPlaneBackend::Mysql`
  - `MySqlControlPlaneStore`, `MySqlStorageConfig`
  - `quota_policies_supabase_only_error()` and other `*_supabase_only_error()` call sites gated on `RuntimeControlPlaneBackend::Mysql`
- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs` / `validate.rs` -- MySQL DSN/TLS config fields
- `tools/ferrogate-test/src/cli.rs` -- `MysqlRestart`/`MysqlTlsRestart` subcommands
- `tools/ferrogate-test/src/main.rs` -- `mysql_restart`/`mysql_tls_restart` dispatch wiring (no longer called from `ci`, still standalone)
- `tools/ferrogate-test/src/storage.rs` -- `run_mysql_restart`, `run_mysql_tls_restart`, `run_control_plane_mysql_restart`, `start_mysql_container`
- `docs/roadmap.md` -- "Storage And Analytics Boundary" section's MySQL mention
- `README.md:247,310` -- MySQL mentioned as a control-plane storage option

## Required Design

- Decide final scope: full removal (matching #94's Turso precedent) vs. read-only/deprecated mode with a clear migration error.
- Remove MySQL config, migrations, and repository adapters once no compile path depends on them.
- Provide migration guidance from `storage.provider: mysql` to `supabase`.
- Update `docs/roadmap.md` and `README.md` to drop MySQL as a supported control-plane backend.

## Acceptance Criteria

- No CI workflow or default `ferrogate-test` entrypoint exercises a MySQL-backed scenario.
- Config validation rejects or deprecates `storage.provider: mysql` with a clear migration message once removal is active.
- `docs/roadmap.md`'s Storage And Analytics Boundary section no longer lists MySQL as a compatibility path.
- `cargo metadata --locked` and Rust CI pass without dead MySQL references, or any remaining reference is explicitly documented as intentionally retained.

## Out of Scope

- Any change to the Supabase/PostgreSQL production storage path.
- Turso/libSQL (already tracked and closed under #94).

Related: #189, #68, #94
title: Retire MySQL as a durable storage provider (compatibility path only per roadmap, now explicitly disallowed)
