**Severity: Medium** · category: billing/agentic-gateway · from 2026-07 market research (docs/design/ai-gateway-market-research-2026-07.md §2, §4.3)

## Summary

FerroGate already has a real prepaid-credit wallet system (issue #169: prepaid-credit wallet + auto-recharge orchestration, issue #168: sellable plans) that answers "who is authorized to spend how much" for the gateway's own internal AI-request billing. The emerging x402 protocol (x402 Foundation, formerly coinbase/x402) is an open HTTP-layer "pay-per-request" standard — no API key or credit card required, buyer/seller (including AI agents) settle via wallet-based stablecoin payment (e.g. USDC), built around a "trust-minimizing" design where a facilitator cannot unilaterally move funds, only execute what the client authorized. AP2 (google-agentic-commerce/AP2) is a complementary Google-led protocol with Python/Go/Android SDKs for verifiable agent-initiated payment flows.

## Why it matters

2026-07 research found no evidence any competitor (Bifrost, Portkey, LiteLLM, Kong, agentgateway, Cloudflare AI Gateway, etc.) has shipped AP2/x402 support as of this writing — this is a genuinely open space, not a "catch up to competitors" feature. A real market signal exists: an HN Show-HN project ("Lexiso") is already building an "AP2-compliant agent payment authorization layer" as a standalone product, meaning the market believes a gateway/middleware is a plausible place for this authorization+audit function to live — independent of FerroGate's own judgment.

FerroGate's existing wallet/plan/quota infrastructure already does the exact function x402/AP2 needs at the protocol layer: authorizing spend against a bounded budget and leaving an auditable evidence trail (wallet ledger, billing events). This issue is scoped as a **spike**, not a full implementation — per SOUL.md 事上磨练, this needs a small, falsifiable proof before any larger investment, not a big-bang integration.

## Suggested scope (spike, time-boxed)

- Read the x402 protocol spec (github.com/x402-foundation or successor) and the AP2 reference implementation to understand the actual wire protocol (HTTP 402 handshake + wallet-based settlement).
- Prototype: can an incoming x402 HTTP 402 payment-required challenge be intercepted at the FerroGate policy/billing layer and authorized against an existing tenant's prepaid-credit wallet balance, with a corresponding billing/audit event recorded — for a single narrow scenario (e.g. an agent invoking an external x402-priced API through FerroGate's egress path)?
- Explicitly out of scope for this issue: production wallet-to-wallet cryptocurrency settlement, custody of stablecoins, any actual on-chain transaction signing. The spike is about the *authorization and audit* role a gateway can plausibly play, not about FerroGate becoming a crypto wallet custodian.
- Deliverable is a short design note (docs/design/ or a GitHub issue comment) stating: is this technically coherent with FerroGate's existing billing/policy boundary, what would a real implementation need (new crate? extension of ferrogate-billing?), and a go/no-go recommendation — not working production code.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A design note answers, with evidence (protocol spec citations + a concrete walk-through against FerroGate's actual billing/policy code paths): can FerroGate plausibly sit in an x402/AP2 payment-authorization flow without becoming a custodial wallet provider?
- [ ] The note gives an explicit go/no-go recommendation for further investment, with the reasoning stated (not just a verdict).
- [ ] If go: the note identifies the smallest first E2E slice (per AGENTS.md dynamic-workflow.md) that would prove the integration in running code.
- [ ] If no-go: the reason is recorded so this does not get proposed again without new information.
title: [billing][medium][agentic-gateway] Spike: x402/AP2 agent-payment authorization — can FerroGate's wallet/policy layer plausibly gate agent-initiated payments?

**Severity: High** · category: security/agentic-gateway · from 2026-07 market research (docs/design/ai-gateway-market-research-2026-07.md §3, §4.1)

## Summary

FerroGate already ships a substantial agent-sandbox security boundary in ferrogate-runtime: isolation.rs (multi-backend abstraction over Firecracker microVM / Kata Containers / gVisor / rootless Docker), capability_boundary.rs (gateway-mediated capability boundary covering Tool/McpTool/Cli/Skill/Filesystem/Browser/Rest/Secret/MemoryRead/MemoryWrite/NetworkEgress — ten distinct capability classes, explicit "a sandbox is an execution boundary, not an authorization boundary" design), and function_egress.rs (fail-closed per-tenant allowlist governance for gateway-brokered function/tool invocation, issue #117). Combined this is 6,600+ lines across managed_worker.rs, self_hosted_worker.rs, isolation.rs, capability_boundary.rs, function_egress.rs.

None of this is documented externally, and none of it has been validated against a real published attack class. It is currently an unverified internal claim, not a provable product differentiator.

## Why it matters

2026-07 market research found the MCP ecosystem has a continuous, multi-point stream of real CVEs, not isolated incidents: CVE-2025-53967 (Figma MCP Server RCE, CVSS 8.0, unauthenticated attacker injects shell commands via malicious HTTP POST — network access to the MCP interface alone is sufficient), CVE-2025-47274 (ToolHive, MCP container secret leakage to local config file), CVE-2026-56274 (Flowise MCP RCE, Metasploit module already exists). NVD returns 54 CVEs for "Model Context Protocol". Palo Alto Networks acquiring Portkey (2026-04/05, ~$140M) to fold it into Prisma AIRS is a market signal that "gateway = agent security control plane" is where acquirers and buyers are putting money — not raw routing throughput.

FerroGate has real, shipped capability-boundary infrastructure that plausibly blocks this exact attack class (an MCP tool trying to reach a filesystem/network target outside its granted CapabilityAction would be denied by capability_boundary.rs + function_egress.rs fail-closed logic) but nobody outside the repo knows that, and it has never been proven against a concrete attack scenario.

## Suggested scope

Two deliverables, sequenced:

1. **Red-team regression test** (engineering-first, must land before any external claim): write a ferrogate-test scenario that reproduces the *shape* of CVE-2025-53967 (an MCP tool call attempting to execute an out-of-scope shell/filesystem/network action without a corresponding granted CapabilityAction) and asserts the gateway denies it fail-closed with an auditable evidence trail (request log / audit event). This is the acceptance-grade proof, not the marketing artifact.
2. **Technical documentation** (only after #1 passes): a docs/security/agent-sandbox-model.md explaining the isolation + capability_boundary + function_egress design, written for a security buyer audience, referencing the regression test in (1) as reproducible proof rather than asserting safety unverified.

Do not publish (2) without (1) passing — an unverified security claim is worse than no claim; SOUL.md 致良知 standard applies directly here.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A new ferrogate-test scenario proves a simulated CVE-2025-53967-shaped attack (unauthorized tool-triggered shell/filesystem/network action) is denied fail-closed by the existing capability_boundary + function_egress machinery, with an audit/evidence record left behind.
- [ ] The scenario is wired into the relevant CI workflow slice (rust-agentic-gateway-tests.yml or equivalent) so it runs on every change to isolation.rs/capability_boundary.rs/function_egress.rs.
- [ ] docs/security/agent-sandbox-model.md exists, documents the real architecture (not aspirational), and links to the regression test as its evidence.
- [ ] No claim in the new doc goes beyond what the regression test actually proves.
title: [security][high][agentic-gateway] Prove agent-sandbox capability boundary against real MCP CVE attack shape (CVE-2025-53967-class), then document it

**Severity: High** · category: security/release · from 2026-07 market research (docs/design/ai-gateway-market-research-2026-07.md §2, §4.2)

## Summary

FerroGate publishes container images to GHCR (.github/workflows/package.yml, .github/workflows/ci-image.yml) with no cryptographic signing, no SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation, and no build provenance attestation. deny.toml + cargo-deny/cargo-audit (.github/workflows/rust-quality.yml) already cover dependency-level supply-chain risk (license/advisory scanning), but the *artifact* a customer actually pulls (ghcr.io/.../ferrogate:vYYYY.MM.DD) carries no verifiable proof of what went into it or that it was not tampered with between build and pull.

## Why it matters

2026-03 market research (docs/design/ai-gateway-market-research-2026-07.md §2) documents a real, recent incident: LiteLLM (BerriAI) suffered a PyPI supply-chain attack — a hijacked maintainer account published v1.82.7/v1.82.8 with a malicious .pth file that exfiltrated SSH keys, AWS/K8s credentials, and env-var API keys on interpreter import (GitHub issue #24512, 487 comments). Developers publicly stated on Hacker News they were evaluating alternatives specifically because of this. FerroGate is a static Rust binary with no interpreter-import attack surface, but that architectural advantage is currently just an unverified claim — no signed release, no SBOM, no attestation a security-conscious buyer could check.

This is not a "nice to have" — Kong, TrueFoundry and others already sell governance/trust as the core AI-gateway value proposition (§2 of the report); a security buyer will ask "how do I verify this image is what you say it is" and today the honest answer is "you can't."

## Suggested scope

- Add SBOM generation to the image build (e.g. syft or docker buildx --sbom=true) and publish the SBOM alongside each GHCR tag.
- Sign published images with cosign (keyless OIDC signing via GitHub Actions identity is the simplest path — no key management burden) in both ci-image.yml and package.yml.
- Add GitHub Actions build provenance attestation (actions/attest-build-provenance) for the published image digest.
- Document the verification command (cosign verify ...) in README or a new docs/security/supply-chain.md so operators can actually check it — a signature nobody knows how to verify does not move the needle on trust.
- Do not block the existing manual-dispatch package.yml release flow; add signing/SBOM as additional steps in the same job, fail the job if signing fails (fail-closed, not silently skip).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Every image published via package.yml has a corresponding SBOM artifact and a cosign signature verifiable against the GitHub Actions OIDC identity.
- [ ] ci-image.yml (per-commit CI images) also produces SBOM + signature, not just release images.
- [ ] A documented cosign verify (or equivalent) command exists and was actually run once against a real published tag as proof it works end-to-end.
- [ ] No new long-lived signing secrets are introduced (keyless OIDC signing preferred over stored private keys).
title: [security][high] Release supply-chain hardening: no artifact signing, SBOM, or provenance attestation

**Severity: Medium** · category: assets/billing · from founder product feedback (monetization lever)

## Summary

`StoredPlan.default_asset_storage_quota_bytes` (crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:6099-6101, issue #178) sets a per-PLAN default cumulative asset storage cap, already admin-console-editable via the Plans page (admin-console/src/resources/plans.ts:78-81) and enforced at push time in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/assets.rs:270-315` via `AppState::tenant_asset_storage_bytes_used` (state_assets.rs:33-40). This is a *shared* default — every tenant on the same plan gets the same allowance.

The repo already has a proven per-tenant/project/workspace/key override mechanism for exactly this kind of quota: `StoredQuotaPolicy` (lib.rs:6294-6319), with a full CRUD admin API (`/admin/v1/quota-policies/{scope_type}/{scope_id}`, crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/quota_policies.rs) and admin-console UI (admin-console/src/resources/quota-policies.ts) — but it only covers `rpm_limit`/`tpm_limit`/`monthly_budget_usd`/`model_allowlist`. There is no `asset_storage_quota_bytes` field on it, and `assets.rs:270`'s cumulative check reads only `plan.default_asset_storage_quota_bytes`, with no tenant-scope override lookup.

## Why it matters

Asset storage quota is a monetization lever: negotiated/enterprise deals need a tenant-specific allowance without editing the shared plan (which would affect every other tenant on that tier) and without inventing a one-off plan per customer. Every other quota dimension (rpm/tpm/budget) already supports this exact per-tenant override; asset storage is the one gap.

## Suggested scope

- Add `asset_storage_quota_bytes: Option<u64>` to `StoredQuotaPolicy` (lib.rs:6294-6319), following the existing `rpm_limit`/`tpm_limit` pattern exactly (struct field, Postgres column + SELECT/INSERT/ON CONFLICT SQL, `quota_policy_from_row` mapping, in-memory backend gets it for free via the struct).
- Add the SQL column via an idempotent `ALTER TABLE quota_policies ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS asset_storage_quota_bytes BIGINT` (sql/001_init_postgres.sql), mirroring how `alert_threshold_pcts_json` was added.
- Thread the field through the admin API: `AdminQuotaPolicy`/`AdminQuotaPolicyMutation` (responses.rs:1260-1296), `admin_quota_policy()` mapper and both upsert branches (merge vs replace) in quota_policies.rs.
- Expose it in the admin console's existing quota-policies editor (admin-console/src/resources/quota-policies.ts) as a new form field — no new page needed, this resource already handles tenant/project/workspace/key scoping generically.
- Wire enforcement: `assets.rs:270`'s cumulative check should look up `state.get_quota_policy(QuotaScopeKind::Tenant, &tenant_id)` and prefer its `asset_storage_quota_bytes` (when the policy is `enabled` and the field is set) over `plan.default_asset_storage_quota_bytes`, falling back to the plan default when no override exists.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `StoredQuotaPolicy` round-trips `asset_storage_quota_bytes` through both the in-memory and Postgres backends.
- [ ] `PUT`/`PATCH /admin/v1/quota-policies/tenant/{id}` can set/clear the override; `GET` reflects it.
- [ ] A tenant with a `StoredQuotaPolicy` override gets that value enforced at `/v1/assets/*` push time instead of their plan's default (test both a tighter and a looser override than the plan default).
- [ ] A tenant with no override still falls back to the plan default exactly as today (no regression).
- [ ] Admin console's quota-policies form can set the new field.
title: [assets][medium] Add per-tenant asset storage quota override — StoredQuotaPolicy has no asset_storage_quota_bytes field

body:
## Summary

Follow-up from #186's audit (List B): MCP servers, gateway configs, agent workflows, skill packages, prompt templates, plugins, guardrail policies, agent upstreams, and sellable plans (`StoredPlan`) are all structurally global config resources — none carry a tenant-ownership field, they're deployment-wide by design. Their `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` admin handlers only check `admin.write` scope, never whether the caller is a platform operator (`organization_id: None`) or a tenant-scoped admin-console key (`organization_id: Some(_)`). Confirmed with the user: any tenant-scoped `admin.write` key can currently create/edit/delete these platform-wide resources, affecting every other tenant (e.g. reconfiguring a shared MCP server, deleting another integration's plugin, flipping a feature flag on the shared `free` plan).

## Decision

Restrict mutation (not read) of these resources to platform-operator keys only, via the `require_platform_operator` helper added in #186 for `/admin/v1/api-keys*`. Read access (`GET`/list) is unaffected — tenant users can still see the platform's available MCP servers/plugins/gateway-configs/etc., matching how models/providers/tools catalogs already work.

## Scope

- MCP servers: `handle_admin_mcp_server_upsert`, `handle_admin_mcp_server_delete`
- Gateway configs: `handle_admin_gateway_config_upsert`, `handle_admin_gateway_config_delete`
- Agent workflows: `handle_admin_agent_workflow_upsert`, `handle_admin_agent_workflow_delete`
- Skill packages: `handle_admin_skill_package_upsert`, `handle_admin_skill_package_delete`
- Prompt templates: `handle_admin_prompt_template_upsert`, `handle_admin_prompt_template_archive`
- Plugins: `handle_admin_plugin_upsert`, `handle_admin_plugin_delete`
- Guardrail policies: `handle_admin_policy_upsert`, `handle_admin_policy_delete`
- Agent upstreams: `handle_admin_agent_upstream_upsert`, `handle_admin_agent_upstream_delete`
- Sellable plans (`plans.rs`): `handle_admin_plan_create`, `handle_admin_plan_upsert_at_id`

## Acceptance

- [ ] A tenant-scoped `admin.write` key is denied (403) on every mutation handler listed above.
- [ ] A platform-operator key (`organization_id: None`) retains full function on all of them, unaffected.
- [ ] Read access (`GET`/list) for all these resources is unchanged for both key types.
- [ ] Regression test covering at least one representative resource end-to-end.
- [ ] Full existing test suite passes unchanged.
title: [auth][medium] Restrict global platform config mutation to operator-only keys

body:
## Summary

A follow-up audit after #185 found the same vulnerability class (and one worse variant) in admin surfaces #185's fix didn't touch: self-hosted workers, tool approvals, managed-worker sessions, the tenant roster, and — most severe — the static config API-key CRUD endpoint.

### Most severe: `/admin/v1/api-keys*` lets a tenant-scoped key mint a platform-operator credential

`handle_admin_api_key_upsert` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/local.rs:6878`) / `api_key_from_mutation` (`local.rs:8776`) build a new static `ApiKey` entirely from caller-supplied JSON: `scopes: payload.scopes.unwrap_or_default()` and `organization_id: payload.organization_id` are copied verbatim, with no cap and no check against the caller's own identity. Any key with `admin.write` scope (including a tenant-scoped admin-console session key, `organization_id: Some(_)`) can:

```
POST /admin/v1/api-keys
{"id":"pwn","name":"pwn","key":"pwn-secret","scopes":["admin.read","admin.write"],"organization_id":null}
```

`organization_id: null` is the exact "platform-operator/root key" shape every #185 tenant-scope check exempts unconditionally. This mints a brand-new credential that bypasses every tenant boundary in the system — a straight escalation path from "any signed-up tenant" to "full platform operator," strictly worse than #185's cross-tenant IDOR. Confirmed the admin-console frontend never calls this endpoint (`/app/api-keys` in the UI is wired to `/admin/v1/virtual-keys`, the tenant-safe surface #185 already fixed) and no existing test exercises it with a tenant-scoped key — so this is a dead/unintended capability for tenant users, not a designed one.

### List A — genuine tenant-scoped resources with no tenant-ownership check (same class as #185)

1. **Self-hosted workers** (`local.rs`, `handle_admin_self_hosted_workers` and sub-handlers) — `StoredSelfHostedWorkerRegistration`/heartbeat/telemetry/artifact/checkpoint all carry `tenant: TenantContext`, but every op resolves by bare `worker_id`/`id` with no tenant check:
   - Register a worker attributed to an arbitrary tenant via `payload.tenant` (`local.rs:5016`).
   - Read any tenant's worker record (`local.rs:4905`), rotate any worker's identity fingerprint — a takeover primitive (`local.rs:5267`).
   - Inject heartbeats/telemetry/artifact/checkpoint metadata onto any tenant's worker (`local.rs:5406,5553,5740,5887`).
   - Read any tenant's telemetry event stream (`local.rs:5566`).
   - List every tenant's worker records unfiltered (`local.rs:6035`).
2. **Tool approvals** (`handle_admin_tool_approvals`, `local.rs:6529`) — `ToolApprovalRecord` carries `tenant: TenantContext`; a tenant-scoped caller can list/read every tenant's pending approvals and approve/deny/expire another tenant's tool-execution gate.
3. **Managed worker sessions** (`handle_admin_managed_worker_sessions`, `local.rs:4139`) — read-only leak, `StoredManagedWorkerSession` carries `tenant` but the page is unfiltered.
4. **Tenant roster** (`handle_admin_tenants`, `local.rs:7489`) — a tenant-scoped `admin.read` key enumerates every tenant on the platform.

### List B — structurally global config resources (separate concern, NOT a bug to silently fix)

MCP servers, gateway configs, agent workflows, skill packages, prompt templates, plugins, guardrail policies, agent upstreams, and `StoredPlan` (`plans.rs`) have no tenant-ownership field at all — they're deployment-wide config by design. Any `admin.write` key, including a tenant-scoped one, can currently mutate these, affecting every tenant (e.g. a tenant user flipping `mcp_enabled` on the shared `free` plan, or deleting another integration's MCP server config). This is architecturally a different question — "should tenant self-service admins have platform-operator-level config power at all" — not resolvable by applying the #185 pattern, and needs a product decision before any lockdown. Documenting here for visibility; not in this issue's fix scope.

## Suggested scope

- Deny `/admin/v1/api-keys*` entirely to tenant-scoped callers (`organization_id: Some(_)`) — this surface is operator-only in practice already.
- Apply the same `authorize_tenant_scope`/`filter_by_tenant_scope` pattern from #185 to every self-hosted-worker handler, tool-approvals, managed-worker-sessions, and the tenant roster.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A tenant-scoped `admin.write` key cannot create/update/delete/read any static API key via `/admin/v1/api-keys*` (platform-operator key still can, unaffected).
- [ ] A tenant-scoped key cannot read, register-as-another-tenant, rotate, heartbeat, or attach telemetry/artifacts/checkpoints to another tenant's self-hosted worker; bulk worker list is filtered to the caller's own tenant.
- [ ] A tenant-scoped key cannot read or approve/deny/expire another tenant's tool-approval record.
- [ ] Managed-worker-sessions list and tenant roster are filtered to the caller's own tenant for tenant-scoped keys.
- [ ] Full existing test suite passes unchanged; new regression tests cover the exploit scenarios above.
title: [auth][critical] More cross-tenant IDOR + tenant-scoped key can mint a platform-operator credential

body:
## Summary

`authenticate()` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs:95-205`) only checks whether a presented API key has a required *scope* (e.g. `admin.read`/`admin.write`) — it never checks whether the key's own tenant (`AuthContext.organization_id`) matches the tenant/resource a request actually targets.

`ferrogate-auth::provision_gateway_api_key` mints an `admin.read`+`admin.write`-scoped virtual key, tied to the logging-in user's own `organization_id`, on **every** admin-console login/registration/SSO callback, for **any** tenant member (not just `owner`). This is the live, real credential shape every admin-console user actually holds today — not a theoretical edge case.

**Confirmed live** against a running gateway (two tenants `org_a`/`org_b` bootstrapped via a platform-operator key, then accessed with an `org_a`-scoped `admin.read`+`admin.write` key):
- `GET /admin/v1/wallets/org_b` → 200, returns `org_b`'s wallet.
- `GET /admin/v1/tenant-accounts/org_b` → 200, returns `org_b`'s tenant record.
- `GET /admin/v1/tenant-accounts/org_b/resolved-defaults` → 200, returns `org_b`'s plan/quota.
- `POST /admin/v1/wallets/org_b/adjust {"delta_credits":999999}` → 200, **actually credited `org_b`'s real wallet balance** — a full cross-tenant financial write, not just a read leak.

This is not isolated to wallets — it's systemic across essentially every `/admin/v1/*` resource family: tenant-accounts, projects, workspaces, virtual-keys, quota-policies, RBAC tenant-role-bindings, payment-methods. A second, related class: several bulk-list endpoints (`GET /admin/v1/tenant-accounts`, `/projects`, `/workspaces`, `/virtual-keys`, `/wallets`, `/quota-policies`) and several read-only audit/log endpoints (`request-logs`, `audit-events`, `agent-runs`, `self-hosted-runs`, `metering-events`, `usage-aggregates`, `usage-reports`, `billing-outbox-dead-letters`, `request-log-exports`) return **every tenant's** data with zero filtering regardless of the caller's own tenant.

## Why it matters

Any signed-up admin-console user at any tenant can read and financially/operationally mutate **every other tenant's** wallet balance, virtual keys, quota policies, RBAC bindings, and tenant configuration — full horizontal privilege escalation across the entire platform's tenant base. This is the actual attack surface the admin console (a multi-tenant SaaS product surface, per #157/#168/#178's own framing) presents to any registered user today.

## Suggested scope

- Add `authorize_tenant_scope(auth: &AuthContext, target_tenant_id: &str) -> Result<(), AuthError>` (or equivalent) to `auth.rs`: a platform-operator key (`organization_id: None` — the existing "root/bootstrap key manages everything" pattern this codebase's entire test suite already relies on) stays unrestricted; a tenant-scoped key is denied when `target_tenant_id` doesn't match its own `organization_id`.
- Apply it to every handler that reads/writes a specific tenant's resource, resolving the target tenant either directly (path segment already is a tenant_id) or via a lookup (project→tenant, workspace→tenant, virtual-key→tenant, quota-policy scope_type→tenant).
- Filter (or deny outright for tenant-scoped keys) the bulk-list and read-only audit/log endpoints enumerated above.

## Acceptance

- [ ] The exact live-verified scenario above (cross-tenant wallet read + adjust) is denied and covered by a regression test.
- [ ] Every directly tenant_id-scoped single-resource admin endpoint denies cross-tenant access for a tenant-scoped key while remaining fully functional for a platform-operator key (no organization_id).
- [ ] Bulk-list and read-only audit/log endpoints no longer leak other tenants' data to a tenant-scoped key.
- [ ] Full existing test suite (which predominantly uses platform-operator-style keys) passes unchanged.
title: [auth][critical] Cross-tenant IDOR across /admin/v1/*: admin.read/admin.write never checks tenant ownership

body:
## Summary

Issue #183 found and fixed a privilege-escalation bug: `/v1/tools/execute` (Extension backend) bypassed the plan/RBAC entitlement gate (`mcp_enabled`/`extension_tools_enabled` + `mcp.execute`/`extensions.execute` permission) that `/v1/mcp/tool/execute` (Mcp backend) enforced. A follow-up audit for other instances of the same failure class found a third, still-unfixed sibling: the `/v1/mcp` JSON-RPC transport's `tools/call` method (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/mcp_rpc.rs:158-373`, invoked from `handle_mcp_rpc` in `local.rs`) executes the exact same MCP tools via `AppState::execute_mcp_tool`, but never checks the tenant's plan `mcp_enabled` flag or the `mcp.execute` role permission at all — only a generic `"tools.execute"` API-key scope check via `authenticate()`.

Concretely: a tenant whose plan has `mcp_enabled = false` (and no `mcp.execute` role grant) is correctly blocked from `POST /v1/mcp/tool/execute`, but can execute the identical tool by sending `POST /v1/mcp` with a JSON-RPC body `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"...","arguments":{...}}}`.

## Why it matters

Same risk as #183: a tenant on a plan that doesn't include MCP tool execution can still run arbitrary MCP-registered tools by using a different (spec-compliant, fully supported) transport for the same operation, defeating the entitlement/RBAC boundary entirely for that capability.

## Fix

`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/local.rs`'s `tool_execution_entitlement_denial` — the plan/RBAC gate logic previously inlined only in `handle_tool_execute_with_backend` — was extracted into a shared, `pub(super)` free function, and `mcp_rpc.rs::tools_call` now calls it (as `ToolExecuteBackend::Mcp`) before doing any tool lookup or execution, converting a denial into a JSON-RPC error response. This centralizes the gate so any future third call site reaching `execute_mcp_tool` is forced through the same check rather than needing to remember to reimplement it — the exact mechanism that let this and #183 both happen.

## Acceptance

- [x] `/v1/mcp` JSON-RPC `tools/call` denies execution for a tenant whose plan disables MCP and has no `mcp.execute` role grant, matching `/v1/mcp/tool/execute`'s behavior.
- [x] Regression test proving this end-to-end against a real gateway process.
title: [auth][high] /v1/mcp JSON-RPC tools/call bypasses the plan/RBAC tool-execution gate

**Severity: High** · category: security/authz · discovered while auditing which business modules still lack RBAC/plan gating (post-#182)

## Summary

`handle_tool_execute_with_backend` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/local.rs:2796`) serves both `/v1/mcp/tool/execute` (`ToolExecuteBackend::Mcp`) and `/v1/tools/execute` (`ToolExecuteBackend::Extension`) through the same function. The plan/permission gate added for issue #182 (`local.rs:2846`) is explicitly scoped to `backend == ToolExecuteBackend::Mcp` only — the code comment says so directly: "Extension-backend tool execution (/v1/tools/execute) is unaffected -- it isn't MCP."

Extension-backend tool execution runs registered `ExtensionKind::ToolProvider` extensions (external processes/WASM) — the same resource-cost shape as MCP tool execution, just a different registry. A tenant whose plan has `mcp_enabled = false` (or who lacks the `mcp.execute` permission) has zero protection against routing the exact same kind of tool-execution traffic through `/v1/tools/execute` instead of `/v1/mcp/tool/execute`.

## Why it matters

This is a literal bypass of an access-control gate that was deliberately added: an operator who disables MCP tool execution for a tier expects that tier to not execute arbitrary tools through the gateway, full stop — not "MCP tools specifically, but not identically-shaped Extension tools."

## Suggested scope

Add `StoredPlan.extension_tools_enabled: bool` (mirroring `mcp_enabled`) and a new RBAC permission key `extensions.execute`, gating the `ToolExecuteBackend::Extension` branch in `handle_tool_execute_with_backend` with the exact same fail-closed-only-when-a-formal-StoredTenantAccount-exists pattern already used for `mcp_enabled`/`self_hosted_workers_enabled`/`asset_hosting_enabled`.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `StoredPlan.extension_tools_enabled` persists in both in-memory and Postgres/Supabase repositories, with schema-drift/migration coverage.
- [ ] Extension-backend `/v1/tools/execute` is denied when the tenant's plan disables `extension_tools_enabled` and no bound role grants `extensions.execute`, and allowed when either does.
- [ ] Test coverage proving the gate (mirroring `mcp_tool_execution_is_gated_by_plan_then_lifted_by_role` in `tests/rbac_enforcement_gates.rs`).
- [ ] No regression to existing Extension-backend callers whose keys have no formal `StoredTenantAccount` (same fail-open-when-unattributed pattern as the other three gates).
title: [gateway][high] Extension-backend /v1/tools/execute bypasses the mcp_enabled plan gate

**Severity: High** · category: auth/entitlements · requested directly by the project owner (2026-07-07)

## Summary

FerroGate has two separate, non-overlapping authorization concepts, neither of which is "assign a tenant a role and the tenant gets a bundle of product capabilities":

1. **`ferrogate-auth`'s RBAC** (`Permission { action, resource }` -> `Role { permissions: Vec<Permission> }` -> `PolicyBinding { role_id, tenant, subject }`, `crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:106-133`, issue #162): dynamically definable via `/v1/rbac/roles`/`/v1/rbac/bindings`, but `PolicySubject` is `User | ServiceAccount | ApiKey` — **never `Tenant`**. This governs what a human/service-account/API-key may do *within* a tenant (admin-console authorization), not what the tenant itself is entitled to.
2. **`StoredPlan`** (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5984-6012`, issues #168/#176/#177): hardcoded booleans (`mcp_enabled`, `self_hosted_workers_enabled`, `asset_hosting_enabled`) gating product features, one tenant : one plan. Adding a new gated capability requires a new struct field, a migration, and touching every call site that constructs a `StoredPlan` literal — exactly the friction the owner wants removed.

## Requested design

- `Permission`: finest-grained capability unit, string-keyed (e.g. `assets.host`, `mcp.use`), dynamically definable — no code change to add one.
- `Role`: named, horizontally-extensible bundle of permission keys — dynamically definable, no code change to add one.
- `TenantRoleBinding`: many-to-many, a tenant may hold multiple roles; a tenant's effective permission set is the union of its roles' permissions. Granting a capability to a tenant becomes "assign role Y to tenant X" (one write), not "add a new StoredPlan field + migration + redeploy."
- Admin-configurable end to end: an operator can create a permission, create a role bundling permissions, and assign/revoke a role on a tenant, all via the admin API — no code change for new permissions/roles, only for genuinely new enforcement call sites.

## Suggested scope

- `ferrogate-storage`: `StoredPermission`, `StoredRole` (embeds `permission_keys: Vec<String>`, mirroring `StoredPlan.default_model_allowlist`'s JSONB-array pattern), `StoredTenantRoleBinding` (tenant_id + role_id), dual in-memory/Postgres CRUD mirroring the `StoredPlan`/`StoredAsset` pattern (#168/#176).
- `AppState::tenant_has_permission(tenant_id, key) -> bool`: resolves all roles bound to a tenant, unions their permission keys, checks membership.
- Admin API: `/admin/v1/permissions`, `/admin/v1/roles`, `/admin/v1/tenant-roles` (or nested under `/admin/v1/tenant-accounts/{id}/roles`) CRUD.
- At least one real enforcement call site proving the closed loop end to end (not just CRUD) — e.g. gate `/v1/assets/*` (#177) via a permission check in addition to/instead of `StoredPlan.asset_hosting_enabled`.
- E2E test: define a permission, bundle it into a role, assign the role to a tenant, verify the gated endpoint allows/denies correctly, verify the rows landed in a real Postgres-protocol database (mirrors the verification approach used for #176/#177 in `tests/assets_api.rs`).

## Acceptance

- [ ] `StoredPermission`/`StoredRole`/`StoredTenantRoleBinding` persist in both in-memory and Postgres/Supabase repositories with schema-drift guard coverage.
- [ ] A new permission or role can be created via the admin API with no code change.
- [ ] Assigning/revoking a role on a tenant changes that tenant's effective permission set immediately (no redeploy).
- [ ] At least one real request-handling code path enforces a permission check sourced from this system (not just a CRUD demo).
- [ ] Automated test verifies the full loop end to end, including confirming the tenant-role assignment landed in a real database.
title: [auth][high] No tenant-level Permission->Role->Tenant entitlement system — product capabilities are hardcoded StoredPlan booleans

body:
**Severity: Medium** · category: gateway/routing · requested directly by the project owner (2026-07-07)

## Summary

`handlers.rs::handle_request_filter` matched every fixed (non-dynamic-route) API path through one flat, sequential `if path == "..." { ... }` chain — ~55 blocks, ~480 lines, no structural grouping by business entity. Adding a new API surface (e.g. `/v1/assets/*`, #176/#177) meant inserting yet another block into the same growing chain.

## Fix

Refactored into a route-group dispatch model:
- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/route_groups.rs` (new): a `matchit::Router<RouteGroup>` (radix-tree router, https://github.com/ibraheemdev/matchit — pure Rust, zero-copy, the engine underneath `httprouter` and used internally by axum) resolves each path to one of 25 `RouteGroup` enum variants, one per business entity (inference, tools, agent-runs, self-hosted-workers, skills, prompts, assets, quota-policies, tenant-hierarchy, billing, etc.). Each variant's `try_*_routes` method owns that entity's full path/method sub-dispatch and returns `Ok(true)` once it has responded, or `Ok(false)` if it looked at the request and declined (e.g. `/v1/prompts/{x}` that isn't `.../render`), in which case the caller falls through to the dynamic host/path route table exactly as before.
- `handlers.rs::handle_request_filter` now builds one `RequestParts` (owned headers/method/path/query) and makes a single `self.try_route_groups(session, ctx, &parts)` call instead of the flat chain.
- Pure dispatch refactor: every handler call is unchanged (same function, same arguments) — only how a path resolves to that call changed.

## Verification

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`: clean.
- New unit tests in `route_groups.rs`: `route_group_router_builds_without_conflicts` (forces the lazily-built router to initialize, catching any pattern conflict at test time rather than first request) and `every_previously_flat_route_still_resolves_to_a_group` (asserts all ~80 concrete paths from the original chain still resolve).
- Real-process E2E via `ferrogate-test`: `admin-api`, `gateway-api`, `gateway-billing-chain`, `function-egress-api`, `auth-api` all pass — these collectively exercise the large majority of migrated routes (tenants, projects, workspaces, virtual-keys, quota-policies, tool-approvals, mcp-servers, gateway-configs, agent-workflows, skill-packages, prompt-templates, api-keys, policies, providers, managed-workers, models, chat, tools, MCP) through the real Pingora server.
- Full `cargo test --workspace --lib` (all crates) and `cargo test -p ferrogate-cli --bins` (313 tests): pass.

## Acceptance

- [x] Every route from the original flat chain resolves to the correct group (test + real E2E coverage above).
- [x] No behavior change: same handler, same arguments, same fallthrough-to-dynamic-routing semantics.
- [x] New `/v1/assets/*` surface (#176/#177) added as a route group rather than another flat-chain block, validating the pattern for future entities.
title: [gateway][medium] Fixed API routes matched via 478-line flat if-chain, not grouped by entity

body:
**Severity: Medium** · category: correctness/build-breakage · found and fixed within the same working session, filed retroactively for traceability

## Summary

`6be8d9f` ("feat(policy): sellable subscription plans backing tenant quota defaults") landed on `main` with two compile errors, and `git push origin main` bypassed the repo's branch protection (GitHub reported the push "Bypassed rule violations... Required status check \"rust-ci\" is expected" rather than blocking it).

## Failure scenario

Anyone pulling `main` at `6be8d9f` and running `cargo check --workspace` or `cargo test --workspace` gets a hard build failure — the workspace does not compile at all, blocking any other work on the repo until fixed.

## Evidence

- `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:1519` (at `6be8d9f`) — `let admin_console_seats = plan.admin_console_seats.map(saturating_i64);` — `admin_console_seats` is `Option<u32>`, but `saturating_i64` takes `u64` (E0631, type mismatch).
- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:4702` (at `6be8d9f`) — `AppState::resolve_effective_quota` called `ferrogate_policy::quota::resolve_effective_quota(chain, lookup)` with 2 arguments; the same commit added a third required `plan: Option<&StoredPlan>` parameter to that function (`crates/ferrogate-policy/src/quota.rs:68`) but never updated this call site (E0061, missing argument).
- Consequence of the second bug, independent of the compile error: even had it compiled, `StoredPlan` defaults — the entire point of issue #168 — would have been dead code, since `resolve_effective_quota` never loaded or passed the tenant's plan into the merge chain. #168's own acceptance criterion ("`AppState::resolve_effective_quota` incorporates the tenant's plan defaults as the base of the merge chain") was not actually satisfied by `6be8d9f` despite the commit implying the feature was complete.
- `cargo test --workspace --lib` surfaced a third, separate issue only visible once tests compile (not caught by `cargo check` alone, since `cfg(test)` code isn't checked by default): `ferrogate-storage`'s `sample_tenant()` test helper (`lib.rs:9939`) didn't set the newly-required `plan_id` field (E0063).

## Fix

Fixed in `3faaf80` ("fix(policy): repair workspace build broken by the plan/quota commit"):
- `admin_console_seats.map(saturating_i64)` → `.map(i64::from)` (`u32`→`i64` is always lossless, no saturation needed).
- `resolve_effective_quota` (`state.rs`) now resolves the tenant's `StoredTenantAccount` by `organization_id`, looks up its `StoredPlan` by `plan_id`, and passes it through to `ferrogate_policy::quota::resolve_effective_quota`.
- `sample_tenant()` test helper updated with `plan_id: "free".into()`.
- Verified post-fix: `cargo check --workspace` and `cargo test --workspace --lib` (all crates) pass clean.

## Also noted (separate concern, not fixed here)

`git push origin main` for both this fix and the immediately preceding commit reported the branch protection rule as bypassed rather than blocking. The rule exists (`Required status check "rust-ci"`) but did not actually gate either push. Worth a separate look at whether `rust-ci` is wired correctly as a required check, since it would have caught this exact bug before it reached `main`.

## Acceptance

- [x] Workspace compiles and full test suite passes (verified at `3faaf80`).
- [ ] Branch-protection / required-status-check enforcement gap investigated (open question, not resolved by this issue).
title: [policy][medium] 6be8d9f broke the workspace build — two compile errors landed on main (fixed in 3faaf80)

body:
Part of #175. Required before public/customer-facing rollout of any sub-issue above.

**Severity: High** · category: security/assets · from codebase gap analysis (part of epic "Unified agent-asset hosting")

## Summary

Every prior sub-issue in this epic makes FerroGate a *distribution point for executable content* — CLI binaries agents run directly, MCP manifests that (per `ferrogate-mcp/src/lib.rs:681-791`) can point an agent's `Stdio` transport at a command to spawn as a local subprocess, and Skill bundles whose resources are consumed as instructions/scripts by an agent. This is a materially different risk class from FerroGate's existing job of proxying LLM API traffic: today the platform never stores or serves executable payloads on a tenant's behalf — `self_hosted_worker_artifacts` (`sql/001_init_postgres.sql:293-306`) records artifact *metadata* only (`docs/agent-worker-protocol.md:186-188,896-923` confirms no content upload/retrieval endpoint exists), so there is no precedent inside FerroGate for safely hosting arbitrary customer-uploaded bytes that another party's agent will fetch and execute. `crates/ferrogate-runtime/src/capability_boundary.rs`'s `CapabilityAction::McpTool` (line 20/36) and `SimpleCapabilityAuthorizer::authorize` (lines 117-169) are the closest existing governance pattern — they authorize *use* of a capability at execution time, not integrity of a stored artifact — and are not designed for this.

## Why it matters

A tenant-uploaded CLI binary, MCP manifest pointing at a malicious `Stdio` command, or Skill script is malware/supply-chain-attack surface the moment a *different* consumer (another tenant's agent, or a public/unauthenticated fetch if any asset type is ever made publicly listable) downloads and runs it. Unlike proxied LLM traffic, FerroGate would be the origin server vouching for this content. Shipping `/v1/assets/*` (prerequisite sub-issue) without these controls turns a hosting convenience into an unreviewed malware CDN.

## Suggested scope

- Enforce size and content-type allowlists per `asset_type` at the `/v1/assets/*` `PUT` handler (prerequisite sub-issue) — e.g. reject unexpected MIME/extension combinations for `static_site`, reject anything but declared archive formats for `cli_tool`.
- Require and verify `content_hash` (already part of the `stored_assets` schema in the storage sub-issue) on every read, and add a signing step (tenant-scoped signing key or platform-issued signature over the hash) so a `pull` can verify provenance, not just integrity.
- Integrate a content/malware scan step on `push` (e.g. ClamAV or a hosted scanning API) before an asset transitions from "uploaded" to "servable" status in `stored_assets`; reject or quarantine on hit.
- **Enforce tenant bucket/prefix isolation via Supabase Storage's native Row-Level Security (RLS) policies** (per the storage sub-issue), not an app-layer path-prefix convention alone — RLS is scoped to the caller's JWT claims and is enforced at the storage layer itself, including against raw S3-protocol access, so it closes isolation gaps an application-only convention would leave open. Verify with a cross-tenant fetch-denial test that also attempts a direct S3-protocol call using another tenant's credentials, not just a call through FerroGate's own API.
- Explicitly flag `mcp_manifest` assets pointing at `Stdio` command transports as higher risk (they cause a *different agent's* `ferrogate-mcp` client, `lib.rs:681-791`, to spawn an arbitrary local process) — require an extra confirmation/allowlist step or disallow `Stdio`-transport manifests in the initial hosted-asset launch, permitting only `StreamableHttp`/`Sse` manifests until a stronger review model exists.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Size/type limits enforced and tested for every `asset_type`.
- [ ] `content_hash` verified on every read; tamper test (mutate stored bytes, confirm rejection) passes.
- [ ] A scanning step runs on every `push` and a known-bad test payload (e.g. EICAR) is rejected before becoming servable.
- [ ] Cross-tenant fetch attempt against another tenant's asset — via both FerroGate's API and a direct S3-protocol call using another tenant's credentials — is denied and covered by a test.
- [ ] `mcp_manifest` assets with `Stdio` transport are blocked or gated behind an explicit additional control at initial launch.
title: [assets][high] Supply-chain risk: require content scanning/signing/tenant isolation before public asset hosting

body:
Part of #175. Depends on the gateway API sub-issue.

**Severity: Medium** · category: assets/tooling · from codebase gap analysis (part of epic "Unified agent-asset hosting")

## Summary

`ferrogate-cli`'s clap `Commands` enum (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/cli.rs:257-275`) exposes exactly six subcommands — `Run`/`gateway`, `Auth serve`, `Billing serve`, `Storage migrate-to-supabase` (whose only action is a DB-to-Supabase control-plane migration, `cli.rs:91-141`, unrelated to file upload), `Validate`/`check`, `Reload`, `HashKey`. None of them upload, deploy, or fetch arbitrary files — there is no customer-facing "deploy this asset" entry point anywhere in the CLI today. The admin console has an analogous gap: `admin-console/src/resources/mcp-servers.ts` is the closest existing pattern for a CRUD-over-config-object admin UI, but nothing comparable exists for binary/file upload.

Note on naming collision: the CLI/admin surfaces already use "Skill" for a distinct, unrelated concept — "Skill Package," a governance manifest (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs:795`, `/admin/v1/skill-packages` CRUD, `/v1/skills` agent discovery, `docs/openapi/admin-api.openapi.json:3073,3437`) that bundles *references* to existing plugins/tools/MCP servers/prompts under an id+version — it does not hold file bytes. The founder's "Skill" asset class (Claude-Skill-shaped: a `SKILL.md` + resource-file directory) is a different, currently-nonexistent thing; `docs/agentic-gateway-architecture.md:264` lists a real `ferrogate-skills` "SKILL.md progressive disclosure" loader as an explicit "stretch" goal, and line 479 flags it as "a large new attack surface... beyond a gateway's core scope" — not built. This sub-issue's CLI/UI must not conflate the two; suggest `ferrogate-cli` use `assets` (not `skills`) as the subcommand/asset-type namespace to avoid colliding with the existing Skill Package terminology.

## Why it matters

The founder's vision is "a customer deploys these assets once to FerroGate's cloud" — that requires a push path. Without a CLI/UI entry point, the `/v1/assets/*` API from the prerequisite sub-issue is unreachable by anything but raw HTTP calls, which defeats the "deploy once" self-serve goal.

## Suggested scope

- Add an `Assets` variant to the `Commands` enum (`cli.rs:257-275`) with `push`/`pull`/`list` subcommands, following the existing `Storage`/`Validate` subcommand wiring pattern (`cli.rs:91-141`) — `push <path> --type cli_tool|mcp_manifest|skill_bundle|static_site|config_file --name <name> --version <version>`, authenticating with the same virtual-key credential resolution the gateway client paths already use.
- `push` for `asset_type=static_site` should accept a directory and upload it as a versioned bundle (tar/zip) rather than requiring one call per file, since a static site is many files under one asset identity.
- Add an admin console resource module (new `admin-console/src/resources/assets.ts`, mirroring `mcp-servers.ts`'s structure) plus a page for drag-and-drop upload, version history browsing, and quota-usage display (reading the `default_asset_storage_quota_bytes`/current-usage exposed by the prerequisite API sub-issue).
- Document the new subcommand and admin flow in `docs/roadmap.md` (currently has zero mention of static hosting or asset/file distribution) and cross-link from `docs/agentic-gateway-architecture.md`'s P5 roadmap section.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `ferrogate assets push`/`pull`/`list` work end-to-end against a running gateway using an existing virtual key, for at least CLI-tool and static-site asset types.
- [ ] Admin console can upload a file/bundle, see it listed with version/size/content-hash, and delete it.
- [ ] Quota usage (current bytes vs. `default_asset_storage_quota_bytes`) is visible in the admin console.
- [ ] No naming/route collision with the existing Skill Package (`/admin/v1/skill-packages`) surfaces.
title: [assets][medium] Add ferrogate assets push/pull/list CLI subcommand + admin console upload UI

body:
Part of #175. Depends on the object-storage sub-issue.

**Severity: Medium** · category: assets/gateway-api · from codebase gap analysis (part of epic "Unified agent-asset hosting")

## Summary

Once bytes are storable (prerequisite sub-issue), agents need one authenticated endpoint family to fetch/list/push them, reusing the exact virtual-key auth chain already used for inference: `AppState::resolve_workspace_scope` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:4507`) walks workspace→project→tenant into a `WorkspaceScope`, copied into `TenantContext` on `StoredApiKey.tenant` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/virtual_keys.rs:787-804`); `authenticate()` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs:91`) resolves a presented key into an `AuthContext` and calls `finalize_auth` (`auth.rs:250`). Routing is a sequential dispatch chain in `handle_request_filter` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/handlers.rs:19`, table ~lines 84-566); the existing `handle_models` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/local.rs:162-203`) is the template to follow: `authenticate(&state, headers, "<scope>", &ctx.request_id)` → business logic → `write_json_response`/`write_json_error` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/responses.rs`).

Gating must tie into the already-landed `StoredPlan` (#168; `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5844-5863`), which already carries `mcp_enabled`/`self_hosted_workers_enabled`/`admin_console_seats` but **no asset-hosting fields yet**. Note: a real, pre-existing bug that would have blocked any plan-gated feature (`AppState::resolve_effective_quota` never loaded the tenant's plan or passed it into `ferrogate_policy::resolve_effective_quota`, and a separate `u32`/`u64` type-mismatch broke `cargo check -p ferrogate-storage` outright at HEAD) has since been fixed directly — plan defaults now actually reach the quota merge. Neither `mcp_enabled` nor `self_hosted_workers_enabled` has any other reference in `ferrogate-cli` (grep confirms) — no handler yet reads plan feature flags for gating a capability on/off; this sub-issue would be the first to do so.

## Why it matters

Without plan gating wired through, "deploy once, agents fetch through one authenticated, plan/quota-gated endpoint" (the founder's stated goal) degenerates into an ungated free-for-all — every tenant gets unlimited asset storage/bandwidth regardless of plan, exactly the gap issue #168 already identified for MCP/worker features.

## Suggested scope

- Add `asset_hosting_enabled: bool` and `default_asset_storage_quota_bytes: Option<u64>` to `StoredPlan` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5844`), alongside `mcp_enabled`/`self_hosted_workers_enabled`, plus migration/seed updates (`sql/001_init_postgres.sql:763`-adjacent seed block).
- Add `GET /v1/assets/{asset_type}/{name}` (fetch), `GET /v1/assets` (list, tenant/project-scoped), `PUT /v1/assets/{asset_type}/{name}` (push) branches to `handle_request_filter` (`handlers.rs:19`), following the `handle_models` template (`local.rs:162-203`): `authenticate(..., "assets.read"/"assets.write", ...)` → check `asset_hosting_enabled` on the resolved plan (fail closed if absent/false, matching the fail-closed pattern `capability_boundary.rs` uses for `CapabilityAction`) → enforce `default_asset_storage_quota_bytes` against cumulative `stored_assets` size for the tenant → call the storage-layer methods from the prerequisite sub-issue → `write_json_response`/`write_json_error`.
- New API-key scopes `assets.read`/`assets.write`, following the existing `tools.read`/`tools.execute` scope pattern (`gateway/local.rs:2581-2595`).

## Acceptance

- [ ] A unit test shows plan `asset_hosting_enabled=false` causes `/v1/assets/*` to fail closed, and `=true` with quota headroom succeeds.
- [ ] `PUT`/`GET`/list on `/v1/assets/*` work end-to-end against an existing virtual key, respecting tenant/project scoping from `WorkspaceScope`.
- [ ] Exceeding `default_asset_storage_quota_bytes` returns a quota-exceeded error, not a silent accept.
title: [assets][medium] Add /v1/assets/* gateway API gated by StoredPlan

body:
Part of #175.

**Severity: High** · category: assets/storage · from codebase gap analysis (part of epic "Unified agent-asset hosting")

## Summary

FerroGate cannot store a single byte of customer-supplied file content today. `StorageProviderKind` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:42-49`) is `Memory`/`Supabase`/`TursoLibsql`/`Postgres`/`Mysql` — all relational. The `Supabase` variant is a DSN label only: `Self::supabase(...)` (line 6462) calls `Self::postgres_with_provider(StorageProviderKind::Supabase, config, options)` (line 6466), the same `sqlx`/Postgres client used for `Postgres`. There is no `SUPABASE_URL`, no service-role/anon key, no Supabase Storage REST/JS client, and no S3-compatible client anywhere in the repo (confirmed by grep for `bucket`, `S3`, `blob`, `object-storage`, `SUPABASE_URL` across `.rs`/`.toml`/`.md`/`.sql`). `reqwest` is present but wired only for LLM-provider egress (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/dispatch.rs`, `function_egress.rs`). Schema-side, `sql/001_init_postgres.sql` has zero `BYTEA` columns; the nearest analogues are `control_plane_resources` (line 7-15, generic `document_json JSONB`, used for config/policy/plan documents — not files) and `self_hosted_worker_artifacts` (line 293-306, `artifact_name`/`content_type TEXT`/`size_bytes BIGINT`/`artifact_json JSONB` — metadata about an artifact, no bytes column, no bucket/URI reference; per `docs/agent-worker-protocol.md:186-188,896-923` workers report artifact metadata via `POST /v1/self-hosted-workers/artifacts` with no matching content upload/retrieval endpoint).

Confirmed: Supabase Storage is a real, dedicated product (not something to improvise) — an S3-protocol-compatible object store (bucket/object CRUD, multipart uploads), a RESTful API, TUS resumable uploads, a global CDN, and — notably for this sub-issue — **Row-Level Security (RLS) policies enforced at the storage layer, scoped to a caller's JWT claims**, available identically on hosted Supabase and self-hosted deployments. See [Storage docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage) and [S3 compatibility](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/s3/compatibility).

## Why it matters

Every asset class in the parent epic (CLI binaries, MCP manifests, Skill bundles, static sites, config files) is bytes that need durable, tenant-scoped storage and a way to look them up by tenant/project/type/version. Without this, the API/CLI/security sub-issues have nothing to persist to or read from — this is the literal foundation the rest of the epic is blocked on.

## Suggested scope

- Stand up real Supabase Storage (bucket-per-tenant or prefix-per-tenant in a shared bucket) as the primary backend when `storage.provider = Supabase`, using Supabase's Storage REST API (service-role key) — reuse the existing `reqwest` dependency for the HTTP client rather than adding a new one. For non-Supabase deployments (`Postgres`/`Mysql`/`Memory`/`TursoLibsql`), support a pluggable S3-compatible client or local-filesystem fallback so self-hosted operators aren't forced onto Supabase.
- **Model tenant isolation as Supabase Storage Row-Level Security (RLS) policies scoped to the resolved tenant/project claims, not just an app-layer bucket/prefix naming convention.** Since Storage RLS is enforced independently at the storage layer (and also applies to raw S3-protocol access, not only FerroGate's own REST calls), this closes the gap an app-only prefix convention would leave open if a credential or S3 access key ever leaked or was misused directly against Supabase. Issue directly informs the cross-tenant isolation requirement in the security sub-issue below.
- Add a `stored_assets` metadata table (new migration alongside `sql/001_init_postgres.sql`) modeled on the existing `self_hosted_worker_artifacts` shape (line 293-306) but adding the missing pieces: `tenant_id`, `project_id`, `asset_type` (`cli_tool`/`mcp_manifest`/`skill_bundle`/`static_site`/`config_file`), `version`, `content_hash`, `size_bytes`, `content_type`, `storage_uri` (bucket/key or path pointer — the exact reference column `self_hosted_worker_artifacts` is missing today), `created_at`.
- Add the corresponding `ferrogate-storage` repository trait methods (in-memory + Postgres/Supabase impls, mirroring the dual-backend pattern already used for `StoredPlan`/`StoredQuotaPolicy` at `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5844` and `5727`) for create/get/list/delete of asset records, plus content put/get against the bucket client.
- Extend `validate_postgres_schema`/schema-drift guard coverage for the new table, matching the existing pattern for other `Stored*` types.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A byte payload can be written and read back through the new storage-layer methods against both an in-memory backend and a real Supabase Storage bucket in an integration test.
- [ ] `stored_assets` persists in both in-memory and Postgres/Supabase repositories with schema-drift guard coverage.
- [ ] Content hash is verified on read (detects corruption/tampering) and version history for a given tenant/asset_type/name is queryable.
- [ ] A cross-tenant fetch attempt (including via a raw S3-protocol call, not only FerroGate's own API) is denied by the Storage RLS policy, covered by a test.
- [ ] No existing `Supabase`/`Postgres` control-plane codepath (tenant/project/workspace/key CRUD) is altered — this is additive only.

body:
**Severity: Epic** · category: platform/commercialization · from founder product vision + codebase gap analysis

## Summary

Founder's stated vision (verbatim, translated): in an agent-first future, the primitives an agent consumes are (1) CLI tool invocation, (2) MCP tool invocation, (3) Skill usage — plus, per the original ask, (4) static websites and (5) arbitrary config files. FerroGate should host the static files behind all five and unify access through the same authenticated, plan/quota-gated API surface agents already use for model inference, so a customer "deploys" these assets once to FerroGate's cloud instead of scattering them across GitHub releases, npm, self-hosted static sites, etc.

Today none of this exists, and the reason is foundational, not incremental: **FerroGate has zero object/blob storage capability.** `StorageProviderKind` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:42-49`) has exactly 5 variants — `Memory`, `Supabase`, `TursoLibsql`, `Postgres`, `Mysql` — and `Supabase` is not Supabase's Storage/bucket API, it's a DSN label that routes through the identical Postgres/`sqlx` code path (`Self::supabase` at line 6462 calls `Self::postgres_with_provider(StorageProviderKind::Supabase, ...)` at line 6466). There is no `SUPABASE_URL`/service-role key, no Supabase Storage or S3-compatible client, and no `BYTEA` column anywhere in the schema (`sql/001_init_postgres.sql`, zero `bytea` hits). The two closest tables are metadata-only: `control_plane_resources` (`sql/001_init_postgres.sql:7-15`, generic `document_json JSONB`) and `self_hosted_worker_artifacts` (`sql/001_init_postgres.sql:293-306`, records `artifact_name`/`content_type`/`size_bytes`/`artifact_json` but no bytes column and no bucket/URI reference — workers report artifact *metadata* only, per `docs/agent-worker-protocol.md:186-188,896-923`, with no upload/retrieval-of-content endpoint). `reqwest` exists in the workspace only for outbound LLM-provider egress (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/dispatch.rs`, `function_egress.rs`) — not usable as-is for blob storage. Every asset class the founder named needs bytes stored and served somewhere; that "somewhere" must be built from scratch.

Confirmed externally: Supabase's cloud product genuinely includes a dedicated Storage service (not something we'd be improvising) — an S3-protocol-compatible object store with bucket management, multipart/resumable (TUS) uploads, a global CDN, and JWT-scoped Row-Level Security policies enforced at the storage layer, available on both hosted Supabase and self-hosted deployments. That makes it a real, validated backend choice for the sub-issue below rather than a speculative one. See [Supabase Storage docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage) and [S3 compatibility](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/s3/compatibility).

## Why it matters

This closes the gap between "FerroGate serves LLM inference calls" and "FerroGate is the one place an agent goes for everything it needs to act" — CLI binaries, MCP connection manifests, Skill folders, static sites, config — unifying discovery+fetch behind the exact virtual-key auth and `StoredPlan` entitlement model (#168) already built for inference traffic, rather than customers scattering these across GitHub Releases/npm/self-hosted CDNs with no tenant-scoped quota or governance. It also gives the admin console and `ferrogate-cli` (currently limited to `Run`/`Auth serve`/`Billing serve`/`Storage migrate-to-supabase`/`Validate`/`Reload`/`HashKey` — `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/cli.rs:257-275`) a genuinely new product surface, not just another quota knob.

## Explicit non-goal / scope boundary

**Hosting an MCP server's static manifest/package (so an agent can discover and client-side-install a connection to it) is not the same as running arbitrary customer-supplied MCP server processes as a compute service.** `ferrogate-mcp` today is a client, not a host: `McpManager`/`McpSession` (`crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/lib.rs`, doc comment line 7: "MCP host/client manager") dial *out* to externally-hosted servers over `StreamableHttp`/`Sse` (lines 588-1142) or spawn a local `Stdio` subprocess as a peer (lines 681-791) — there is no server-side transport listener anywhere in the crate. `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/mcp_rpc.rs` (routed `/v1/mcp`, `gateway/local.rs:2564-2617`) only re-exports FerroGate's own already-registered tools; it is not a mechanism for tenants to publish their own MCP server code, and neither the admin API (`/admin/v1/mcp-servers`, `admin-console/src/resources/mcp-servers.ts`) nor skill-package `resources.mcp_servers` (`config/validate.rs:1429,2133,2161`) store anything beyond connection parameters (url/command/auth/headers). `docs/agentic-gateway-architecture.md:461` explicitly lists "FerroGate-as-MCP-server" and "MCP registry client" as unbuilt P5 roadmap items. **This epic covers hosting the static manifest/package describing how to reach an MCP server (the thing an agent downloads to know what to dial) — it explicitly does not cover executing arbitrary tenant-supplied server processes on FerroGate's compute.** That is a separate, much larger hosting-compute feature (closer to `agent-worker`'s Firecracker isolation scope) and is out of scope here.

## Founder priority ordering

Per the founder's stated priority, sub-issues below build CLI-tool-package, MCP-manifest, and Skill-file (Claude-Skill-shaped: `SKILL.md` + resources, distinct from FerroGate's existing "Skill Package" governance manifest at `/admin/v1/skill-packages` — real Anthropic-style skills are a documented "stretch" goal never built, `docs/agentic-gateway-architecture.md:264,405-425,479`) support first, as the three concrete asset types; static websites and arbitrary config files are secondary, generalizable cases of the identical storage+registry+API primitive (an "asset" is just bytes + content-type + version, regardless of whether it's a `.tar.gz` CLI release, an MCP `manifest.json`, a `SKILL.md` bundle, an `index.html`, or a `.env.example`) and should be threaded through the same table/API rather than special-cased.

## Suggested scope (tracked as sub-issues)

- [ ] #176 — Object storage + asset registry foundation (Supabase Storage buckets; `stored_assets` metadata table: tenant/project scope, asset_type, version, content hash)
- [ ] #177 — `/v1/assets/*` gateway API gated by a new `StoredPlan` feature flag/quota, reusing the existing virtual-key auth chain
- [ ] #178 — `ferrogate-cli assets push/pull/list` + admin console upload UI
- [ ] #179 — Supply-chain security hardening (scanning/signing/size-type limits/tenant isolation) — required before public exposure

## Acceptance

- [ ] All four linked sub-issues (#176, #177, #178, #179) landed and independently verified.
- [ ] At least one asset of each founder-priority type (CLI binary, MCP manifest, Skill bundle) can be pushed and pulled end-to-end through `/v1/assets/*` using an existing virtual key.
- [ ] Asset access is denied when the tenant's plan does not enable the feature, and denied when the tenant's storage quota is exceeded.
- [ ] Security review (content scanning/signing minimum bar) signed off before any customer-facing/public rollout.
