body:
**Severity: Low** · category: compliance · follow-up from #165

## Summary

#165 added `SECURITY.md` and `docs/security-controls.md` documenting the
security controls FerroGate already has, plus CI-enforced supply-chain
scanning. That closes the documentation-groundwork gap, but FerroGate still
holds no third-party compliance certification (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001,
HIPAA, GDPR-specific attestation). A full SOC 2 Type II audit is a
multi-quarter program (auditor engagement, evidence collection over an
observation window, a written ISMS policy set) with real cost, distinct from
the documentation work in #165.

## Suggested scope

- Evaluate auditor options and rough budget/timeline for a SOC 2 Type II
  Type I → Type II path (many vendors start with a Type I readiness
  assessment before the Type II observation period).
- Identify which `docs/security-controls.md` control families need
  additional evidence/tooling before an audit could start (e.g. formal
  incident-response runbooks, access-review cadence, background-check
  policy for maintainers with production access).
- Decide whether to pursue this in-house or via a compliance-automation
  vendor (Vanta, Drata, Secureframe, etc.), which several competitors
  surveyed in the original gap analysis (Bifrost, Portkey, TrueFoundry, API7)
  appear to use for their published Trust Center pages.

## Acceptance

- A written recommendation (audit path, estimated cost/timeline, vendor
  options) is recorded, informing a go/no-go decision.
- If greenlit, this issue is superseded by a scoped implementation epic with
  concrete milestones.
title: [security][low] Scope and budget a formal SOC 2 Type II audit program

body:
**Severity: High** · category: enterprise / data residency · from a repo-wide capability-gap review of `cluster.node_region`/`cluster.node_zone`

## Summary
`cluster.node_region` and `cluster.node_zone` exist purely as labels today. `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/validate.rs:801-813` validates them only as non-empty strings when set, and `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:936-1052` (`ClusterIdentity`/`ClusterStatus`) carries them through into `/readyz` and admin-status JSON for operator visibility. A repo-wide grep confirms no routing, failover, or model-selection path ever reads these fields: `candidate_model_routes` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:4044`, invoked from `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/chat.rs:1852` and `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/local.rs:2330`) dispatches purely on `RoutingStrategy` (`crates/ferrogate-providers/src/models.rs:13-19`: `Priority`/`LowestCost`/`LowestLatency`/`Balanced`) plus each `ModelRoute`'s static `priority`/`weight`/price fields — none of them region-aware. `TenantContext` and `WorkspaceScope` (`crates/ferrogate-core/src/lib.rs:47-83`) likewise carry organization/project/workspace identifiers but no region/residency requirement.

The result: there is no way today to declare "requests tagged as EU-customer must only route to an EU-hosted provider/model." That's a routing-time compliance guarantee, not a labeling exercise — an operator can advertise `node_region = "eu-west-1"` in every node's config and admin-status will faithfully report it, but a request can still get load-balanced or fall back to a us-east provider with zero enforcement. This blocks any customer selling into GDPR-regulated or data-sovereignty-sensitive markets who needs FerroGate itself to enforce residency, not just document node placement in `/readyz`.

## Why it matters
Region-aware / residency-aware routing is table stakes among gateway competitors:
- **Bifrost** supports weighted routing configurable across cloud regions (e.g. shifting Bedrock traffic between us-east-1/us-west-2).
- **Portkey** ships conditional routing rules and regional data routing (US/EU/India) that keep EU users on EU infrastructure, plus per-workspace data isolation.
- **Kong** offers geo-scoped Teams/Roles and AI Proxy load-balancing across regions.
- **TrueFoundry** advertises an Enterprise multi-region gateway plane with region-aware policy-as-code routing, deploying the gateway nearest to users.
- **API7** documents an active-active multi-region deployment pattern with GSLB-based routing to the nearest healthy region.
- **Cloudflare** cites Enterprise regional data-routing support specifically for data residency.

FerroGate already collects the raw ingredient (`node_region`/`node_zone`) but stops short of the compliance-relevant part: enforcing it at selection time. Without this, FerroGate cannot be pitched into any deal with an EU-residency or data-sovereignty requirement.

## Suggested scope
- Extend `Provider`/`ModelRoute` config (`crates/ferrogate-providers/src/models.rs`) with an optional `region` (or `allowed_regions`) declaration per provider/route.
- Extend `TenantContext` (`crates/ferrogate-core/src/lib.rs:47`) with an optional `required_region` / `region_allowlist` field, resolvable from virtual API key / workspace config, additive via `#[serde(default)]` the same way `workspace_id` was added.
- Add a region-affinity predicate to `candidate_model_routes` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:4044`) that filters or reorders candidate routes to same-region providers when a tenant's `required_region`/`region_allowlist` is set, applied consistently across all four `RoutingStrategy` variants (`Priority`/`LowestCost`/`LowestLatency`/`Balanced`) rather than as a separate strategy.
- Define fail-closed behavior: if a tenant declares a required region and no candidate route satisfies it, reject the request (e.g. a `403`/`model_not_visible`-style rejection, mirroring the existing tenant-visibility rejection in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/chat.rs`) rather than silently falling back to an out-of-region provider.
- Surface the enforced region constraint (and any rejection reason) in admin-status / request-decision logging so operators can audit residency enforcement, not just node placement.
- Add config validation analogous to `validate.rs:801-813` for the new region-allowlist/required-region fields.

## Acceptance
- A tenant/workspace can declare a required region (or region allowlist) that is enforced, not just recorded.
- `candidate_model_routes` excludes (or fail-closed rejects when none remain) out-of-region providers for a tenant with a region requirement, across all routing strategies.
- A request from a region-constrained tenant that has no in-region candidate route is rejected with a clear, logged reason rather than silently routed cross-region.
- Existing deployments without region config see no behavior change (opt-in, additive fields, default-empty).
- Test coverage: config validation for new fields, unit tests on `candidate_model_routes` region filtering per strategy, and an integration test exercising the fail-closed rejection path.
title: [routing][high] node_region/node_zone are reported but never enforced in routing decisions

body:
**Severity: High** · category: enterprise · from provider adapter coverage audit

## Summary

`ferrogate-providers` implements exactly six `ProviderAdapter`s in `crates/ferrogate-providers/src/registry.rs:18-26`: `OpenAiCompatibleAdapter`, `AnthropicAdapter`, `GeminiAdapter`, `GrokAdapter`, `OpenRouterAdapter`, `AzureOpenAiAdapter`. `ProviderAdapterRegistry::adapter_for` (`registry.rs:29-41`) dispatches on a normalized `kind` string and falls through to `AdapterError::UnsupportedProviderKind` for anything else. The registry's own test suite documents this as intentional current behavior — `rejects_unknown_provider_kind_before_runtime_dispatch` (`registry.rs:187-201`) asserts that `adapter_for("bedrock")` returns `UnsupportedProviderKind { kind: "bedrock" }`. There is no equivalent adapter for Google Vertex AI either, and Cohere/Mistral are likewise not first-class `kind`s (they'd only work today if manually shoehorned through `OpenAiCompatibleAdapter`, which doesn't cover Bedrock/Vertex's non-OpenAI-shaped auth or wire formats).

This isn't just a routing table gap: `ProviderConfig` (`crates/ferrogate-providers/src/types.rs:12-19`) only models a single bearer-style `api_key: Option<String>` plus Azure/OpenRouter-specific fields. AWS Bedrock's `InvokeModel`/`Converse` APIs require SigV4 request signing (access key, secret key, session token, region), which has no representation in `ProviderConfig` today. Vertex AI similarly needs a GCP service-account/OAuth2 token flow rather than a static key. Both providers also need new canonical request/response mapping in `crates/ferrogate-providers/src/canonical.rs` since neither speaks the OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic-native wire formats FerroGate currently normalizes against.

Net effect: enterprises with committed AWS/GCP spend, or data-residency requirements that mandate routing through Bedrock or Vertex AI, cannot onboard those endpoints to FerroGate at all today.

## Why it matters

Multi-provider LLM gateways/proxies are expected to cover Bedrock and Vertex AI as table stakes for enterprise adoption:
- LiteLLM: cost tracking and routing across 100+ providers including OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock, Vertex AI, and Cohere.
- Cloudflare AI Gateway: both Bedrock and Vertex AI ship as first-class providers.
- Bifrost: ships AWS Bedrock Guardrails integration, implying Bedrock as a routed model provider.
- Kong: AI Proxy plugin supports Bedrock as a target, with an AI AWS Guardrails plugin validating Bedrock-routed traffic.
- Apache APISIX: markets proxying to 20+ LLM providers, explicitly listing AWS Bedrock.
- Higress: proxies 100+ providers uniformly via `ai-proxy`, including Bedrock-class coverage.

Without this, FerroGate is not a credible drop-in for shops standardized on AWS or GCP committed-spend agreements — a segment competitors already serve.

## Suggested scope

- Add `BedrockAdapter` implementing `ProviderAdapter` (`crates/ferrogate-providers/src/types.rs:175`), targeting the Bedrock `Converse`/`InvokeModel` API, wired into `adapter_for` in `registry.rs` alongside the existing six.
- Add `VertexAiAdapter` implementing `ProviderAdapter`, targeting the Vertex AI `generateContent`/`streamGenerateContent` endpoints, wired into `adapter_for` the same way.
- Extend `ProviderConfig` (`types.rs:12-19`) with the credential shape each new adapter needs — AWS access key/secret/session token + region for Bedrock, GCP service-account/OAuth2 token + project/location for Vertex — without breaking the existing `api_key`-only path for current adapters.
- Add SigV4 request signing for Bedrock (new dependency or in-crate implementation) since none of the existing adapters need it.
- Add canonical request/response mapping for both providers' native formats in `crates/ferrogate-providers/src/canonical.rs`, following the pattern already used for Anthropic/Gemini mapping.
- Cover `prepare_chat_completions`, `normalize_error_response`, `extract_usage`, and `is_retryable_status` for both adapters, matching the trait surface in `types.rs:175` and the existing per-adapter test pattern in `registry.rs`'s `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`.
- Update the `rejects_unknown_provider_kind_before_runtime_dispatch` test (or replace it with a Bedrock/Vertex-resolves-successfully test) once the adapters land, since it currently pins "bedrock" as intentionally unsupported.
- Out of scope for this issue: Cohere and Mistral as first-class `ProviderAdapter` kinds (tracked as a follow-up, lower priority than Bedrock/Vertex given no enterprise committed-spend angle).

## Acceptance

- [ ] `ProviderAdapterRegistry::adapter_for("bedrock")` resolves to a working `BedrockAdapter` instead of `UnsupportedProviderKind`.
- [ ] `ProviderAdapterRegistry::adapter_for("vertex" | "vertex-ai")` resolves to a working `VertexAiAdapter` instead of `UnsupportedProviderKind`.
- [ ] `ProviderConfig` supports SigV4 credentials for Bedrock and service-account/OAuth2 token for Vertex, without regressing existing OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini/Grok/OpenRouter/Azure configs.
- [ ] Chat completion requests can be planned and sent end-to-end through both new adapters against representative Bedrock (`InvokeModel`/`Converse`) and Vertex AI (`generateContent`) fixtures/mocks.
- [ ] Usage extraction, error normalization, and retryable-status classification are implemented and tested for both adapters, matching the coverage level of existing adapters in `registry.rs`.
- [ ] `crates/ferrogate-providers` test suite passes with new adapter-specific tests added, and the now-stale "bedrock is unsupported" assertion is removed or updated.
title: [providers][high] No AWS Bedrock or Google Vertex AI provider adapter

body:
**Severity: Medium** · category: commercialization · from competitive gap analysis (Portkey, TrueFoundry, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Higress)

## Summary

FerroGate's cost attribution is hard-wired to the built-in scope chain — tenant → project → workspace → key — with no way to slice spend by anything a SaaS builder actually cares about at the request level (an end-customer id, a feature flag, an experiment arm, etc.).

Concretely:

- `TenantContext` (`crates/ferrogate-core/src/lib.rs:47`) only carries `organization_id`, `team_id`, `project_id`, `workspace_id`, `user_id`, `api_key_id` — a closed set of fields.
- `BillingEvent` (`crates/ferrogate-billing/src/lib.rs:136-166`) embeds that same `TenantContext` plus routing/usage fields, but has no generic key/value bag.
- The inbound request DTO the gateway actually parses, `ChatCompletionRequest` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/chat.rs:48-52`), only deserializes `model` and `stream` — any `metadata` object a caller sends today is silently dropped before it ever reaches billing.
- `StoredUsageMonthlyRollup` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5765-5778`) aggregates by `scope_type: QuotaScopeKind` (`Tenant | Project | Workspace | Key`, `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5691-5696`) and `scope_id` only — there is no column or dimension for arbitrary tags.
- `GET /admin/v1/usage-reports` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/usage_reports.rs`) and its `UsageReportFilter` / `UsageReportGroupBy` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:1823-1860`, group-by cases at `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:4515-4529`) only support `group_by=scope` and `group_by=period_month`.

Net effect: a platform reselling FerroGate-routed LLM access to its own end customers can attribute cost down to `api_key_id`, but not to whatever identifier that platform actually bills against (a customer/org id in its own system, a product feature, a cost center) unless it provisions one API key per attribution unit — which doesn't scale and defeats workspace/key pooling.

## Why it matters

This is table stakes for gateway products targeting SaaS/platform builders:

- **Portkey** supports free-form `metadata` (e.g. `tenant_id`, `tenant_plan`, `_user`) on every request, surfaced directly in per-tenant/per-user cost analytics.
- **TrueFoundry** propagates an `X-TFY-METADATA` header end-to-end and breaks down cost by arbitrary tags like `customer_id` / `project_id`.
- **Cloudflare AI Gateway** allows up to 5 Custom Metadata key/value pairs per request, filterable in both Spend Limits and analytics.
- **Higress** keeps per-consumer token tables (`consumer_token_table` / `model_token_table`) for consumer-level usage breakdowns outside the tenant hierarchy.

Without this, FerroGate forces resellers into key-per-customer provisioning, which is an operational and quota-management burden compared to competitors that treat metadata tagging as a first-class dimension.

## Suggested scope

- Add an optional `metadata: Option<BTreeMap<String, String>>` field to `ChatCompletionRequest` (and the equivalent Responses-API request struct) in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/chat.rs`, size/key-count bounded (e.g. cap at N keys, M bytes per value) to avoid unbounded storage growth.
- Thread that map through `BillingEventDraft` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:6877-6884`) into `BillingEvent` (`crates/ferrogate-billing/src/lib.rs`) as a new `metadata` field, defaulting to empty for backward compatibility (`#[serde(default)]`).
- Extend the billing ledger and `StoredUsageMonthlyRollup` write path (`upsert_usage_monthly_rollup_delta`, `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:4517`) to also roll up totals keyed by `(period_month, metadata_key, metadata_value)`, without disturbing the existing tenant/project/workspace/key rollups.
- Add `group_by=metadata.<key>` to `UsageReportGroupBy` and `UsageReportFilter::from_query` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:1823-1860`), returned via the existing `GET /admin/v1/usage-reports` endpoint (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/usage_reports.rs`) with the same shape as `AdminUsageReportRow`, adding a `metadata_key` / `metadata_value` column.
- Document the metadata field and size limits in the admin-console / API reference, and surface a metadata filter/breakdown in the admin-console usage view.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Chat completions and Responses API requests accept an optional `metadata` map; unset/omitted metadata is fully backward compatible (existing clients unaffected).
- [ ] `BillingEvent` and the persisted billing ledger record request metadata alongside the existing tenant/project/workspace/key scope.
- [ ] `usage_monthly_rollups` (or an equivalent new table) supports aggregation by at least one arbitrary metadata key without breaking existing tenant/project/workspace/key rollups.
- [ ] `GET /admin/v1/usage-reports?group_by=metadata.<key>` returns per-value cost/token/request breakdowns for that key.
- [ ] Metadata payload size/key count is bounded and rejected/truncated with a clear error rather than growing storage unbounded.
- [ ] Test coverage in `ferrogate-billing` and `ferrogate-cli` (e.g. alongside `usage_reports_e2e.rs`) for metadata propagation end-to-end and for the new group-by option.
title: [billing][medium] No arbitrary metadata tagging for usage/cost attribution beyond tenant/project/workspace/key

body:
**Severity: Medium** · category: commercialization · area: billing

## Summary

`AppState::monthly_budget_exceeded` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:4475`) compares accumulated spend for the current calendar month (from `usage_monthly_rollups`, via `get_usage_monthly_rollup`) against `EffectiveQuota.monthly_budget_usd` and returns `true`/`false` — this is consumed in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs:272` to hard-deny requests with a `429 monthly_budget_exceeded` once `spent >= budget_usd`. There is no intermediate signal: spend is only ever evaluated at the moment of enforcement, and the only observable outcome is "allowed" or "cut off."

`StoredQuotaPolicy` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5727`) has no field expressing a warning threshold, and there is no notification mechanism anywhere in the gateway (`ferrogate-cli`) or `ferrogate-observability` — the only cross-request signaling primitive found is the in-process `tokio::sync::Notify` used by the approval-queue long-poll in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/approval.rs`, which is unrelated (in-memory, single-node, not a tenant-facing notification). Spend increments happen in `increment_usage_monthly_rollups` / `upsert_usage_monthly_rollup_delta` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:4496-4543`) on every settled request, which is the natural place to detect a threshold crossing, but nothing hooks into it today.

Net effect: a tenant's spend can go from comfortably under budget to hard-blocked with zero prior warning, and there is no admin-console surface or outbound channel (email/Slack/webhook) to tell them it's coming.

## Why it matters

Budget-threshold alerting ahead of a hard cap is table stakes among comparable AI gateway/LLMOps products:
- Bifrost ships budget alert thresholds before the hard cap.
- Portkey's Budget Limits feature supports configurable alert thresholds before the cap.
- TrueFoundry sends milestone alerts at 75/90/95/100% of budget via email or Slack.

FerroGate currently only implements the 100% hard-stop (P1-3/P1-4 per the comments in `state.rs`), with no equivalent of the earlier warning tiers these competitors expose. This is a visible gap for any prospect evaluating budget-governance features side by side.

## Suggested scope

- Add `alert_threshold_pct: Option<Vec<u8>>` (or similar, e.g. `[75, 90, 95]`) to `StoredQuotaPolicy` in `ferrogate-storage`, with storage/schema migration and the corresponding Postgres columns/serialization alongside the existing `monthly_budget_usd` column.
- Wire the field through the admin quota-policy CRUD surface (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/quota_policies.rs`) so it's settable/visible via `AdminQuotaPolicy`.
- Add a threshold-crossing check invoked from the existing rollup update path (`upsert_usage_monthly_rollup_delta` / `increment_usage_monthly_rollups` in `ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs`, or a thin wrapper called from `AppState` right after a settled request updates the rollup) that detects when cumulative `cost_usd` for the period crosses a configured percentage of `monthly_budget_usd` that hasn't already been notified for that scope+period+tier.
- Add a notification dispatch hook (new module, e.g. `ferrogate-billing` or `ferrogate-observability`) supporting at minimum a webhook callback, with email/Slack as pluggable follow-on targets; fire it once per threshold tier per scope per billing period (needs idempotency tracking, e.g. a `notified_thresholds` column/table keyed by scope+period, to avoid re-alerting on every request after crossing).
- Surface configured thresholds and firing history in the admin console billing view.

## Acceptance

- `StoredQuotaPolicy` supports one or more configurable alert thresholds (percentages of `monthly_budget_usd`) that can be set/read through the admin API.
- Crossing a configured threshold for a scope+period fires exactly one notification per tier (no duplicate/repeat firing on subsequent requests within the same period).
- At least one concrete outbound channel (webhook) is implemented end-to-end, with a documented extension point for email/Slack.
- A tenant whose spend crosses e.g. 75%/90%/95% of `monthly_budget_usd` receives a notification strictly before the existing `monthly_budget_exceeded` 429 enforcement engages at 100%.
- Test coverage: unit test proving threshold-crossing detection fires once per tier, and that no notification fires when thresholds are unset (backward compatible with existing `StoredQuotaPolicy` rows/tests, e.g. `quota_policy_monthly_budget_exceeded_hard_denies_further_requests` in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs`).
title: [billing][medium] No proactive budget-threshold alerting before a monthly budget is exhausted

body:
## Summary
`ferrogate-billing` computes an abstract "credits" figure (`PriceBook::credits_for_usd`, `crates/ferrogate-billing/src/pricing.rs:134`, driven by `credits_per_usd` / `DEFAULT_CREDITS_PER_USD`) and enforces a USD spend cap via `QuotaPolicy::monthly_budget_usd` (`crates/ferrogate-policy/src/quota.rs:40`, persisted in `crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5738`), but nothing in the repo ever collects money. `ledger::charge()` (`crates/ferrogate-billing/src/ledger.rs:109`) turns a `BillingEvent` into a settled `LedgerEntry` for reporting, and the billing service exposes `GET /v1/billing/ledger` (`crates/ferrogate-billing/src/service.rs`, `service_test.rs:215`) to read it back — that's the entire surface. There is no Stripe (or any other payment provider) SDK dependency anywhere in the workspace, no invoice generation, no dunning/retry-on-decline, no proration, and no table that represents a purchased balance that gets drawn down per request.

This is distinct from the existing metering-export path (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/metering.rs`, `OpenMeteringAdapter` / `MeteringExportProvider`), which only forwards raw usage events to an external system like OpenMeter for *that system* to bill on — it assumes some other platform owns payment collection. The gap here is that FerroGate itself has no way to let an operator resell metered AI access as their own SaaS product: today `monthly_budget_usd` only throttles spend against a number nobody ever paid, and "credits" is a unit conversion (`total_cost_usd * credits_per_usd`), not a wallet balance tied to an actual purchase.

`ferrogate-storage` has `StoredTenant` / `StoredTenantAccount` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5578`, `5587`) and per-tenant quota policy rows, but no `StoredWallet` or `StoredPaymentMethod` concept at all — confirmed absent from the repo.

## Why it matters
Competing AI-gateway/API-management platforms already ship this as a core commercial feature, not an add-on:
- **Cloudflare Unified Billing** — prepaid credits with an auto-top-up threshold, a payment-method-on-file monthly charge, and a surcharge on credit purchases.
- **Kong Konnect Metering & Billing** — prepaid-credit Billing Profiles plus a Stripe integration for self-serve billing, and Custom Invoicing / HubSpot / Salesforce / PayPal / Adyen support for larger accounts.

Without this, FerroGate can meter and rate-limit usage but cannot actually charge for it — an operator standing up FerroGate as a reseller product has to bolt on an entirely separate billing platform, which undercuts the "own your AI gateway as a product" pitch of the admin console work already merged (#157/#158/#159).

## Suggested scope
- `StoredWallet` in `ferrogate-storage`: per-tenant balance (in credits or micro-USD, consistent with `DEFAULT_CREDITS_PER_USD`), auto-recharge threshold/amount, low-balance state, plus Postgres + in-memory repository methods and a schema-version bump to `sql/001_init_postgres.sql` following the existing migration pattern.
- `StoredPaymentMethod` in `ferrogate-storage`: opaque reference to a provider-side payment method (e.g. Stripe `payment_method`/`customer` IDs) — never store raw card data.
- A payment-provider adapter trait in `ferrogate-billing` (mirroring the existing `MeteringProviderAdapter` shape in `ferrogate-cli/src/metering.rs`) with a Stripe implementation: create customer, attach payment method, one-off top-up charge, auto-recharge on threshold breach, invoice generation for postpaid accounts.
- Wire wallet balance into the request-admission path as a new fail-closed check, distinct from and in addition to the existing `monthly_budget_usd` cap: reject/queue requests once the wallet balance is exhausted and auto-recharge either fails or isn't configured.
- New endpoints on the billing service: top-up (create a payment intent / charge), attach/replace payment method, get wallet balance + auto-recharge config, list invoices.
- Ledger integration: each settled `LedgerEntry` debits the wallet; a failed/declined charge surfaces as a dunning state on the tenant rather than silently disabling billing.

## Acceptance
- New `StoredWallet` / `StoredPaymentMethod` types exist in `ferrogate-storage` with Postgres-backed repository methods, covered by both in-memory and Postgres-roundtrip tests.
- A configurable payment-provider adapter (Stripe first) can create a customer, attach a card, and execute a top-up charge end-to-end against Stripe's test mode.
- A request against a tenant with zero wallet balance and auto-recharge disabled is rejected before being routed, distinct from (and testable independently of) the existing `monthly_budget_usd` rejection path.
- Auto-recharge fires a top-up charge when balance crosses the configured threshold, and a declined charge leaves the tenant in a visible dunning state rather than either silently blocking all traffic or silently granting unlimited credit.
- `GET /v1/billing/ledger` entries show wallet debits alongside existing cost/credit fields without breaking existing ledger consumers/tests.
title: [billing][high] No payment-collection or prepaid-credit-wallet integration for self-serve billing

body:
**Severity: High** · category: commercialization · from competitive gap analysis

## Summary

There is no plan/tier/subscription concept anywhere in FerroGate. `StoredTenantAccount` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5587`) carries only `id`, `name`, `slug`, `status`, and timestamps — no `plan_id`, `tier`, or `subscription_*` field. Every tenant created through `POST /v1/admin/register` (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:660`, `handle_admin_register`) gets an identical account shape with identical gateway capability. A grep for `plan_id|tier|subscription_plan` across the workspace returns nothing outside test/comment noise (the only `tier` hits are `agent-worker`'s Docker-vs-Firecracker isolation tier and a stray `x-tier: gold` test header in `ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs`, both unrelated to commercial plans).

Capability differentiation today is only possible by hand-authoring a `StoredQuotaPolicy` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5727`) per scope (`QuotaScopeKind::{Tenant,Project,Workspace,Key}`) via `ferrogate-cli`'s `quota_policies.rs` subcommand, and resolved per-request through `AppState::resolve_effective_quota` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:4563`), which merges at most 4 point-lookups (tenant/project/workspace/key) into an `EffectiveQuota`. That mechanism enforces *limits* (rpm/tpm/model allowlist/monthly budget) but has no notion of a named, sellable product — there's no default bundle a self-serve signup lands on, no way to gate features (e.g. MCP tool governance, self-hosted workers, admin console seats) by plan, and no record of what a tenant is entitled to versus what an operator manually configured for them. `ferrogate-billing` prices *usage* (PriceBook, ledger) but nothing prices *entitlement* — there is no subscription-level product to sell.

## Why it matters

Every adjacent gateway/LLM-infra competitor already productizes tiers as the primary self-serve monetization lever:
- Bifrost: free OSS vs custom-priced Enterprise tier.
- Portkey: Open Source / Developer (free) / Production ($49/mo) / Enterprise, with feature gating per tier.
- LiteLLM: free OSS vs custom-quoted Enterprise, with premium-gated Org/Team-Admin roles.
- Kong Konnect: self-serve Konnect Plus vs custom Enterprise, backed by priceable Features, rate-card Plans, Entitlements, and Subscriptions in Konnect Metering & Billing.
- TrueFoundry: Developer $0 / Pro $499 / Pro Plus $2,999 / Enterprise.
- API7: self-serve Standard cloud tier vs quote-based Premium/Enterprise, plus Developer Portal monetization plans with per-plan pricing and rate-limiting restrictions.

Without a plan/tier primitive, FerroGate has no self-serve upsell path — the admin console (`admin-console`) can register tenants but has no product to sell them beyond identical gateway access, and every commercial differentiation requires manual, per-tenant `StoredQuotaPolicy` authorship rather than a checkout flow.

## Suggested scope

- Add a `StoredPlan` entity to `ferrogate-storage` (id, name/slug, feature flags e.g. `mcp_enabled`, `self_hosted_workers_enabled`, `admin_console_seats`, plus a default quota bundle: rpm/tpm/model-allowlist/monthly-budget defaults).
- Add `plan_id: Option<String>` to `StoredTenantAccount`, defaulting to a `free`/`default` plan on `POST /v1/admin/register`.
- Extend `AppState`'s quota-resolution chain (`resolve_effective_quota`) so plan-level defaults are the base of the merge, with existing `StoredQuotaPolicy` scopes (tenant/project/workspace/key) continuing to override on top — i.e. plan supplies the floor/default, explicit `QuotaScopeKind` policies remain the override mechanism.
- Add plan feature-flag enforcement points at the call sites that gate MCP tool governance (`ferrogate-mcp`) and self-hosted/managed worker dispatch (`agent-worker`), so a plan can disable those capabilities outright rather than only throttling them.
- Add `ferrogate-cli` subcommands (`plans create/list/assign`, mirroring `quota_policies.rs`) and Supabase migration + `validate_postgres_schema` coverage for the new table.
- Surface plan assignment/upgrade in the admin console (list plans, show current tenant plan, change plan).

## Acceptance

- [ ] `StoredPlan` persists in both the in-memory and Postgres/Supabase repositories, with schema-drift guard coverage.
- [ ] `StoredTenantAccount` has a `plan_id`, populated with a default plan on `/v1/admin/register`, and migratable for existing rows.
- [ ] `AppState::resolve_effective_quota` incorporates the tenant's plan defaults as the base of the merge chain, verified by a unit test showing plan defaults apply when no explicit `StoredQuotaPolicy` exists and are overridden when one does.
- [ ] At least one non-quota feature flag (e.g. MCP tool access or self-hosted worker eligibility) is gated by plan and enforced fail-closed when the plan disables it.
- [ ] `ferrogate-cli` can create/list/assign plans end-to-end against both in-memory and Supabase backends.
- [ ] Admin console can display a tenant's current plan and its resolved feature/quota defaults.
title: [billing][high] No productized plan/tier entity — tenants have no sellable subscription level

body:
**Severity: High** · category: security · from MCP transport capability review

## Summary
`ferrogate-mcp`'s network transport is a single hand-rolled client (`HttpMcpClient`) backing both `McpTransport::StreamableHttp` and `McpTransport::Sse` (`crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/lib.rs:435-439` in `connect()`, mirrored again in the config-validation match at `lib.rs:1018-1020`). It does not honor the TLS configuration operators can set, and it has no real HTTPS or SSE transport underneath it:

- `McpServerConfig.tls: McpTlsConfig` (`lib.rs:80`, fields `insecure_skip_verify` / `ca_cert_path` at `lib.rs:103-107`) is deserialized from config but never read anywhere in the connection path — a repo-wide grep for `.tls`/`config.tls` inside the crate returns zero call sites besides the struct definitions. `HttpMcpClient::new` (`lib.rs:590-603`) doesn't even store the field. Setting `ca_cert_path` to a bogus path or `insecure_skip_verify: true/false` has zero observable effect; nothing validates or enforces it.
- `validate_http_endpoint` (`lib.rs:776-784`), used both for server-config validation and inside `HttpMcpClient::new`, accepts `http` **and** `https` schemes — so an `https://` MCP server URL passes validation. But the actual per-request path, `post_http_json` → `parse_http_target` (`lib.rs:786-858`), opens a raw `TcpStream` (no TLS at all) and explicitly bails for anything other than `scheme == "http"` (`lib.rs:832-834`), with the message `"MCP test HTTP client supports http endpoints; configure HTTPS through rmcp transport in production"`. That "rmcp transport in production" path doesn't exist: `rmcp` is only imported for JSON-RPC model types (`CallToolRequestParams`, `CallToolResult`, `ListToolsResult` at `lib.rs:29`), never for its transport. The workspace already enables `rmcp`'s `transport-streamable-http-client-reqwest` feature (`Cargo.toml:67`) and carries `reqwest` with a `rustls` stack (`Cargo.toml:66`), but `ferrogate-mcp`'s own `Cargo.toml` doesn't even depend on `reqwest` — the promised production path was never wired up.
- `McpTransport::Sse` is not a distinct implementation — it maps to the exact same `HttpMcpClient`, which does one `POST` over a `Connection: close` socket and `read_to_end`s a single response body (`post_http_json`, `lib.rs:786-819`). There is no incremental/chunked SSE event parser, so an MCP server that streams `text/event-stream` responses over a held-open connection will not work correctly against this client.

Net effect: an operator who configures `transport: sse` and/or `url: https://...` with `tls.ca_cert_path` set gets no error at config-validation time, then either a confusing runtime bail on first request (https) or a client that silently can't stream (sse) — and the TLS trust settings they set are never enforced regardless of transport.

## Why it matters
MCP is the extension point for `ferrogate-mcp`'s tool-calling / agentic-gateway integration with external tool servers, which are increasingly deployed behind HTTPS and use SSE for long-lived tool-call streams. Competing gateway/governance layers already treat secure, standards-compliant MCP transport as table stakes:
- Kong ships a dedicated MCP traffic gateway with observability/governance over standard HTTPS-based MCP servers.
- TrueFoundry's MCP Gateway supports OAuth 2.0 dynamic discovery and per-server RBAC over secure transport.
- Apache APISIX's `mcp-bridge` exposes MCP servers as governed HTTP/SSE endpoints through the gateway.

FerroGate currently can't terminate TLS trust decisions (`insecure_skip_verify`, `ca_cert_path`) or speak real SSE at all for MCP, which is a functional and trust-boundary gap relative to this bar.

## Suggested scope
- Replace `HttpMcpClient`'s raw `TcpStream` request path with a TLS-capable HTTP client — either wire `rustls` directly (as already done in `ferrogate-storage`'s `PostgresTlsMode` and `ferrogate-cli`'s `metering.rs`/`telemetry.rs`/`acme.rs` rustls clients) or adopt the `rmcp` `transport-streamable-http-client-reqwest` feature/`reqwest` that the workspace already pulls in but `ferrogate-mcp` doesn't depend on.
- Read and enforce `McpTlsConfig`: `insecure_skip_verify` should actually toggle certificate verification, `ca_cert_path` should be loaded into the root trust store used for the connection.
- Make `parse_http_target`/the request path support `https://` end to end, matching what `validate_http_endpoint` already advertises as valid at config time.
- Give `McpTransport::Sse` its own implementation: a persistent-connection, incrementally-parsed `text/event-stream` reader, separate from the single-shot JSON-RPC POST path used for `StreamableHttp`.
- Add early config validation for `ca_cert_path` (file exists / parses as PEM) instead of accepting any value silently.
- Tests: `https://` endpoint connects against a local TLS test server; `insecure_skip_verify: false` without `ca_cert_path` rejects a self-signed cert; `ca_cert_path` pointing at the matching CA connects successfully; SSE transport correctly parses a multi-event chunked stream.

## Acceptance
- MCP HTTP client establishes real TLS connections for `https://` endpoints (no raw unencrypted socket for `https`).
- `McpTlsConfig.insecure_skip_verify` and `.ca_cert_path` are read by the connection path and measurably change certificate-validation behavior, covered by tests.
- `McpTransport::Sse` uses an incremental SSE parser over a persistent connection rather than the single-shot `StreamableHttp` request path.
- Configuring an `https://` MCP endpoint no longer produces the `"MCP test HTTP client supports http endpoints..."` bail error.
- Existing `McpTransport::StreamableHttp` behavior over `http://` is unchanged and existing tests in `crates/ferrogate-mcp/src/lib_test.rs` still pass.
title: [mcp][high] MCP HTTP client ignores McpTlsConfig and has no real HTTPS/SSE support

body:
**Severity: Medium** · category: security · from competitive gap analysis

## Summary

Every request-level limit in FerroGate is keyed off an authenticated identity. `resolve_effective_quota` (`crates/ferrogate-policy/src/quota.rs:60`) merges `rpm_limit`/`tpm_limit`/`monthly_budget_usd` across the tenant/project/workspace/key `QuotaScopeChain`, and the per-key `request_limit_per_minute` override is applied in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs:291` (`min_opt_u64(auth.request_limit_per_minute, quota.rpm_limit)`) via the `ClusterCounterBackend` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:7165`). All of this only starts counting *after* `authenticate()` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs:92`) has already parsed the bearer header and resolved a virtual API key against storage.

There is no earlier gate. A search of the request path (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs`, `state.rs`, `gateway/*.rs`) turns up no `SocketAddr`/`ConnectInfo`/`x-forwarded-for` extraction, no CIDR parsing, and no anonymous/per-source-IP counter anywhere in the crate graph. Concretely:

- Any TCP connection that reaches the listener gets to run key-lookup/auth logic (hashing, storage round-trip) regardless of origin -- there's no IP/CIDR allowlist to reject traffic before that work happens.
- An unauthenticated flood (garbage bearer tokens, credential-stuffing against virtual keys) is not rate-limited at all: `request_limit_per_minute` and `EffectiveQuota.rpm_limit` are only reachable for requests that already carry a *resolvable* key, so failed-auth traffic is unbounded.

This is a real gap, not an intentional tradeoff -- the admin console/gateway CORS work (`AdminConfig::cors_allowed_origin`, `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs:90`) shows the project already has precedent for adding pre-request, config-driven gateway policy, just not for network origin/rate.

## Why it matters

- Portkey ships an Enterprise "Access control & inbound network rules" feature restricting which IPs/geographies may even connect.
- Kong documents IP/network controls as part of a "triple security defense" (mTLS, login auth, WAF) ahead of app-layer auth.
- Cloudflare's "Firewall for AI" plus its anycast edge give DDoS/flood mitigation before traffic ever reaches the gateway process.

FerroGate currently has none of this: every packet that reaches the process pays the full auth-resolution cost before any limit applies.

## Suggested scope

- Add an `ip_allowlist` (CIDR list) config surface, likely on `GatewayConfigProfile`/a new pre-auth section in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs`, checked before `authenticate()` is invoked in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/auth.rs` and before any virtual-key/storage lookup.
- Add a lightweight per-source-IP token-bucket limiter (in-process, reusing the `ClusterCounterBackend` pattern in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs` where practical) applied to all inbound connections/requests ahead of auth, distinct from the existing per-key `request_limit_per_minute`/`EffectiveQuota.rpm_limit`.
- Support both `X-Forwarded-For`/`X-Real-IP` (behind a trusted reverse proxy) and direct peer address, with an explicit config flag for which to trust (avoid trivially spoofable client-IP trust by default).
- Reject/allowlist decision and pre-auth rate-limit rejection should short-circuit before body parsing and be observable via `ferrogate-observability` (structured log/metric distinct from post-auth 401/429s).
- Document the new config keys (README/wiki) and support `/admin/v1/config/reload` for the allowlist without a full restart, consistent with other hot-reloadable config.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Requests from an IP/CIDR not in a configured allowlist are rejected before `authenticate()` runs (no key-resolution/storage round-trip occurs).
- [ ] Unauthenticated/unresolvable-key requests from a single source IP are throttled by a pre-auth token-bucket limiter independent of any virtual key's `request_limit_per_minute`.
- [ ] Config supports at least one CIDR range and a plain IP; invalid CIDR entries fail config validation with a clear error.
- [ ] A documented, explicit config flag controls whether `X-Forwarded-For`/`X-Real-IP` or the raw peer address is used as the client IP, defaulting to the safer (non-spoofable) option.
- [ ] Pre-auth allowlist/rate-limit rejections emit a distinct observability event (log/metric) separate from existing 401/429 auth-quota rejections.
- [ ] Allowlist changes are picked up via `/admin/v1/config/reload` without a process restart.
- [ ] Test coverage: allowlist allow/deny, CIDR matching edge cases, and pre-auth flood throttling under concurrent unauthenticated requests.
title: [security][medium] No pre-auth IP/CIDR allowlist or unauthenticated-request rate limiting

body:
**Severity: High** · category: security · from competitive/enterprise-procurement gap analysis.

## Summary
FerroGate ships real security-relevant controls — `StoredAuditEvent` audit trail (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5864`, appended via `AuditLogRepository`), Argon2 password hashing for admin-console credentials (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:14,1255`), a role/permission-binding RBAC model (`Role`/`RoleBinding` in `crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:111`, distinct from `ferrogate-policy`'s request-time `PolicyEngine`), and ACME/TLS certificate issuance and renewal (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/acme.rs`) — but none of it is packaged into anything a security/procurement reviewer can consume. There is no `SECURITY.md` anywhere in the repo, and a repo-wide search for `SOC2`/`SOC 2`/`HIPAA`/`GDPR`/`ISO27001`/`ISO 27001` returns zero hits outside this issue.

This isn't just a missing document. There's also no vulnerability-disclosure process (no way for a researcher to privately report a finding — no `security.txt`, no listed contact), and no automated dependency/vulnerability scanning in CI: `deny.toml` and `scripts/security-check.sh` wire up `cargo deny` / `cargo audit`, but per `.github/workflows/*.yml` neither is invoked in CI at all — the script only runs them if the tool happens to already be installed locally, and only *requires* them when a developer manually sets `FERROGATE_SECURITY_REQUIRE_TOOLS=1`. So "dependency-scanning posture" is currently "opt-in on a laptop," not an enforced, auditable control.

Enterprise buyers evaluating a self-hosted AI gateway run a standard security-review checklist during procurement (SOC 2 report or bridge letter, sub-processor/data-flow docs, incident-response process, disclosure policy, control mapping). FerroGate has nothing to hand them today beyond source code.

## Why it matters
Every competitor surveyed publishes at least a SOC 2 claim and gates sales on it:
- Bifrost (Maxim/H3 Labs): public Trust Center — SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA, GDPR.
- Portkey: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, GDPR, HIPAA with BAAs.
- LiteLLM: public security/compliance page — SOC 2 Type I certified (Type II in progress), ISO 27001 certified, 0 High/Critical grype image-scan results, CodeQL-backed ISMS, Incident Response Policy available on request.
- Kong: public Trust Center — SOC 2 Type II, PCI DSS 4.0.1, GDPR program, CSA STAR registry, NIST SP 800-218 self-attestation.
- TrueFoundry: SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, HIPAA, with published vulnerability-patch SLAs (Critical in 10 days, High in 30 days).
- API7: public Trust Center — SOC 2 Type II, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, HIPAA, GDPR, reports under NDA.

Without at least a documented disclosure process and a control-mapping page, FerroGate cannot clear the first gate of most enterprise security reviews, regardless of how strong the underlying controls actually are. A full SOC 2 Type II audit is a multi-quarter program with real cost (auditor engagement, evidence collection, a written ISMS); it should not block shipping the groundwork.

## Suggested scope
- Add a top-level `SECURITY.md`: supported-version policy, private vulnerability-reporting contact/process (e.g. a security email or GitHub private vulnerability reporting), and a target response-time commitment.
- Add a `docs/security-controls.md` (or admin-console "Trust" page) mapping shipped capabilities to common control families: audit logging (`StoredAuditEvent` / `AuditLogRepository`), authentication & password storage (Argon2, `ferrogate-auth`), authorization (`Role`/`RoleBinding` RBAC), transport security (ACME/TLS in `ferrogate-cli::acme`), tenant isolation (dedicated Supabase schemas per service, `ferrogate-storage`).
- Wire `cargo deny check licenses bans sources` and `cargo audit` into CI (e.g. `.github/workflows/rust-quality.yml`) as enforced, non-optional jobs, instead of only running when a developer has the tools installed locally and opts in via `FERROGATE_SECURITY_REQUIRE_TOOLS`.
- Document an incident-response process (even a lightweight internal one) referenced from `SECURITY.md`.
- Scope out (separate future issue/epic) the actual SOC 2 Type II audit engagement — evidence collection, auditor selection, ISMS policy set — since that's a multi-quarter program distinct from the documentation groundwork above.

## Acceptance
- `SECURITY.md` exists at repo root with a working private disclosure contact/process and supported-version statement.
- `docs/security-controls.md` (or equivalent) exists, mapping each control family above to the specific shipped FerroGate mechanism and file/crate.
- `cargo deny check licenses bans sources` and `cargo audit` run as required (non-skippable) CI jobs and fail the build on new advisories/license violations.
- README's "Quality And Security" section links to `SECURITY.md` and the control-mapping doc.
- Gap tracked for the full SOC 2 Type II program is filed as a separate follow-up issue, out of scope for this one.
title: [security][high] No compliance certification program or trust documentation (SOC2/HIPAA/GDPR/ISO27001)

body:
**Severity: High** · category: security · from competitive gap analysis

## Summary

FerroGate's guardrail engine is limited to literal keyword/regex matching. `GuardrailRule` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs:639-668`) only supports `keywords: Vec<String>`, `regex: Vec<String>`, and `max_input_bytes`, evaluated by `GatewayState::match_guardrail` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:4632-4694`) as a linear `find_map` over rules with tenant/model/provider scoping — first match wins, effect is either `Deny` or `Redact` via a literal substring/regex replace (`redact_text`, `state.rs:1538`).

There is no entity-aware PII detection (SSN, credit card, IBAN, etc. — only what an operator manually encodes as regex), no prompt-injection/jailbreak classifier, no content-moderation category taxonomy, and critically no extension point to call out to an external detection engine. `ExtensionKind` (`config/types.rs:686-692`) only defines `RequestHook`, `ToolProvider`, `EventSink` — there is no `GuardrailProvider` variant, so guardrails cannot be backed by an HTTP/gRPC callout the way tools already can via `ExtensionKind::ToolProvider` / `McpHttpToolProvider` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/extensions.rs:558-669`).

This is a known, tracked-as-future gap, not an oversight: `docs/agentic-gateway-architecture.md` lists a not-yet-built `ferrogate-guardrails` crate ("Built-in guardrail/mutator hooks (PII, regex, json-schema, webhook)", line 263) as a P2 roadmap item explicitly framed as "Closes the biggest Portkey gap" (line 458). No such crate exists in the workspace today (`ls crates/` has no `ferrogate-guardrails`), confirming this is proposal, not shipped code.

## Why it matters

Every competitor surveyed ships pluggable detection providers beyond hand-rolled regex:

- **Bifrost**: AWS Bedrock Guardrails (50+ PII entities), Azure Content Safety jailbreak/prompt-injection shields, Google Model Armor, GraySwan Cygnal, built-in Gitleaks secret-leak detection
- **Portkey**: native PII redaction plus a guardrail hub (Patronus, Pangea, Azure, AWS Bedrock), Azure Prompt Shields for jailbreak detection, 50+ prebuilt guardrail library
- **LiteLLM**: Presidio-based PII masking, Lakera/Aporia/Vigil/PromptGuard/Gray Swan jailbreak detectors, OpenAI/Bedrock/Azure/Model-Armor content moderation hooks
- **Kong**: AI PII Sanitizer (Presidio+spaCy), AI Prompt Guard + AI Semantic Prompt Guard, Azure/AWS/GCP moderation plugin integrations
- **Cloudflare**: Firewall for AI prompt-injection scoring, DLP PII profiles, Llama-Guard content moderation
- **TrueFoundry**: Bedrock/Azure PII redaction, Azure Prompt Shield/Prisma AIRS/NeMo jailbreak defense, Azure Content Safety moderation
- **Higress/APISIX**: AI Data Masking + ai-security-guard prompt-attack detection, AWS Comprehend/Alibaba content moderation

FerroGate's current offering (literal string/regex match) is table stakes at best and a real security gap for any tenant relying on it to catch PII leakage or jailbreak attempts in production traffic.

## Suggested scope

- Add `ExtensionKind::GuardrailProvider` mirroring the existing `ToolProvider` pattern in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/extensions.rs`, so guardrail evaluation can delegate to an external HTTP callout instead of only in-process regex.
- Extend `GuardrailRule` (or add a parallel `GuardrailProviderRule`) with a `provider` field (e.g. `presidio | bedrock_guardrails | azure_content_safety | model_armor | lakera | custom_http`) and provider-specific config (endpoint, API key ref, categories/entities to check).
- Implement a `custom_http` / webhook provider first (lowest lift, matches the architecture doc's P2 plan) so any external DLP/moderation engine can be wired in without a FerroGate-native classifier.
- Wire provider results into the existing `GuardrailMatch` / `Deny`/`Redact` effect pipeline in `state.rs` so pre-call (`GuardrailStage::Request`) and post-call (`GuardrailStage::Response`) hooks both support provider-backed checks.
- Stand up the `ferrogate-guardrails` crate referenced in `docs/agentic-gateway-architecture.md` as the home for built-in provider adapters, keeping `ferrogate-cli` as the config/wiring layer.
- Document configuration for at least one PII entity-recognition provider (Presidio or Bedrock Guardrails) and one prompt-injection/jailbreak provider (Lakera or Azure Prompt Shields) as reference integrations.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `ExtensionKind::GuardrailProvider` (or equivalent) exists and can be configured alongside `ToolProvider`/`RequestHook`/`EventSink`.
- [ ] At least one HTTP-callout guardrail provider (`custom_http`/webhook) is implemented and covered by tests, invoked from `match_guardrail` or an equivalent async-capable path.
- [ ] A rule can be configured to call an external PII-detection endpoint and receive per-entity match results (not just a matched substring).
- [ ] A rule can be configured to call an external prompt-injection/jailbreak classifier and deny/flag based on its verdict.
- [ ] Existing keyword/regex guardrail behavior continues to work unchanged (backward compatible config).
- [ ] `docs/agentic-gateway-architecture.md` roadmap item for `ferrogate-guardrails` is updated to reflect implementation status.
title: [security][high] Guardrail engine lacks pluggable detection-provider architecture (no PII/jailbreak/moderation hooks)

body:
**Severity: High** · category: security · from capability-gap audit

## Summary

Upstream provider API keys and ACME DNS-01 provider credentials in FerroGate have exactly one storage/resolution path: plain config values or environment variables. There is no pluggable secrets-provider abstraction and no integration with HashiCorp Vault or any cloud KMS/Secrets Manager anywhere in the repo (`grep -ri "vault\|kms"` across `crates/` returns zero matches).

Concretely:

- `Provider.api_key_env` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs:352`) and `ApiKey.key_env` / `ApiKey.key` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs:410-416`) are the only fields for supplying a provider key. `ApiKey.key` is documented inline as "Plain value for local development only. Do not use in production" (line 415-ish), but no production-grade alternative is offered beyond an env var name.
- Resolution happens via straight `env::var(env_name)` calls, e.g. `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs:5027` and `:5036` inside `configured_secret_values()` (used only for log redaction, not even for actually loading the key into the outbound request path) — there is no indirection layer that could later be swapped for a KMS/Vault lookup.
- The ACME DNS-01 Cloudflare integration (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/acme.rs`) takes its `api_token` straight out of `dns_config_value(acme, "api_token")` (`acme.rs:744`), i.e. plain config/env, with no secrets-manager-backed credential source.
- This is distinct from `handle_admin_virtual_key_rotate` (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/virtual_keys.rs:843-933`), which rotates gateway-issued virtual API keys stored in `ferrogate-storage`/`ferrogate-auth` — that endpoint has no bearing on upstream provider credentials or DNS provider tokens, which remain unmanaged.

Net effect: operators must hold provider keys and DNS tokens as raw env vars or config file values, with no rotation-on-sync, no audit trail of secret access, and no centralized revocation path independent of redeploying config. This is a standard blocker in enterprise security reviews for API gateway products.

## Why it matters

Every major competitor in this space already ships pluggable secrets-backend integration:

- **Bifrost** — native sync with HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, with auto-rotation.
- **LiteLLM** — AWS KMS/Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, CyberArk Conjur; auto-creates/deletes secrets tied to virtual-key lifecycle.
- **Kong** — Vault entity supporting HashiCorp Vault (AppRole/K8s auth) and AWS Secrets Manager, including cross-account IAM.
- **TrueFoundry** — AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Parameter Store; stores only the secret path/reference, never the value, in its own config.
- **API7** — Secret Provider objects for Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, and Kubernetes Secrets, referenced via `$secret://` syntax in config.

FerroGate has no equivalent, making it a non-starter for security-review gates that specifically require centralized secret storage for third-party API credentials.

## Suggested scope

- Define a `SecretResolver`/`SecretsProvider` trait (new `ferrogate-secrets` crate, or added to `ferrogate-config`) with a resolve-by-reference API, e.g. `resolve(&SecretRef) -> Result<SecretString>`.
- Ship the current env-var/plain-value behavior as the default `EnvSecretResolver` implementation so existing configs keep working unchanged.
- Add backend implementations behind feature flags: HashiCorp Vault (KV v2, AppRole/K8s auth), AWS Secrets Manager/KMS, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault.
- Extend `Provider`/`ApiKey` config schema (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/config/types.rs`) with a `secret_ref` (or `vault://`, `aws-sm://`, etc. URI-style) field alongside existing `key`/`key_env`, resolved at config-load time.
- Wire the same resolver into the ACME DNS-01 Cloudflare credential path (`crates/ferrogate-cli/src/acme.rs`) so DNS provider tokens can come from the same backends.
- Add scheduled re-sync/hot-reload so rotated upstream secrets propagate to running gateway processes without a full restart, mirroring the existing config hot-reload path already used for provider/model config.
- Emit admin audit events (reusing the pattern in `record_admin_audit_event`, `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/virtual_keys.rs`) on secret resolution/rotation for auditability.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `SecretResolver` trait defined with at least `EnvSecretResolver` (default) and one real backend (Vault or AWS Secrets Manager) implemented and tested.
- [ ] `Provider` and `ApiKey` config structs accept a secret-reference field resolved through the new trait, with existing `key`/`key_env` behavior unchanged and covered by regression tests.
- [ ] ACME Cloudflare DNS-01 `api_token` resolvable via the same `SecretResolver` abstraction.
- [ ] Hot-reload/scheduled re-sync picks up a rotated secret from the backing store without requiring process restart, verified by an integration test.
- [ ] Secret resolution and rotation events are recorded via the admin audit log.
- [ ] Documentation covers configuring each supported backend and migrating from plain `key`/`key_env` config.
title: [security][high] No Vault / cloud Secrets Manager / KMS backend for provider and DNS credentials

body:
**Severity: High** · category: auth / RBAC · affects `ferrogate-auth`, `admin-console`

## Summary
`ferrogate-auth` has a real, generic RBAC engine — `Role`, `Permission { action, resource }`, `PolicyBinding` with wildcard action/resource matching in `RbacAuthService::authorize` (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:104-132`, `:251-296`) — but it is only reachable through a static YAML file loaded at process boot (`ferrogate-auth serve --data <path.yaml>`, documented in `docs/auth-service-contract.md:125-178`). There is no REST endpoint and no admin-console page to create, edit, or delete a `Role` or `PolicyBinding` at runtime. `admin-console/src/components/layout/nav-config.ts` has no "Roles" or "Team" entry anywhere in `NAV_GROUPS` — the closest is "Tenant accounts" under Identity & Access, which manages tenant *records*, not per-user role assignment.

This is compounded by tenant onboarding itself: `handle_admin_register` (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:868`) hardcodes every new membership's role:
```rust
let membership = StoredAdminUserMembership {
    id: next_id("membership"),
    user_id: user_id.clone(),
    tenant_id: tenant_id.clone(),
    role: "owner".into(),
    created_at_unix: now,
};
```
`StoredAdminUserMembership.role` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs`) is a free-text `String`, but it is never set to anything other than `"owner"` anywhere in the codebase (`grep '"owner"'` in `ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs` shows only the three register/login-response call sites). There is also no invite-a-teammate endpoint, so a tenant admin has no way to add a second user to their own tenant, let alone with a restricted role — every registered account is unconditionally an owner of a brand-new tenant it just created.

Net effect: the RBAC engine that exists for gateway-traffic authorization (`model:<logical_model>` checks per `docs/auth-service-contract.md`) is not exposed for the multi-tenant admin console's own access control at all. Multi-user tenants and least-privilege console access are architecturally unsupported today.

## Why it matters
Every adjacent competitor already ships runtime, API-driven RBAC with more than one built-in role and a path to invite teammates:
- Bifrost: 14-resource x 4-operation permission matrix, built-in Admin/Developer/Viewer plus custom roles, all via REST API.
- Portkey: org/workspace RBAC with manager/member roles for full project separation, Enterprise fine-grained roles.
- LiteLLM: `proxy_admin`/`internal_user` roles plus delegated Org Admin/Team Admin roles, with SSO auto-add-to-team.
- Kong Konnect: Teams and Roles scoped to specific resource instances, plus a separate Portal RBAC API for developer-facing roles.
- TrueFoundry: tenant-level (Admin/Member) and resource-level (Viewer/Editor/Admin) RBAC.
- API7: predefined roles (Super Admin, API Provider, Runtime Admin, Viewer) scoped per service/gateway-group plus IAM-style custom policies and dynamic role mapping from IdP attributes.

FerroGate has the underlying primitives (`Role`/`Permission`/`PolicyBinding`) already modeled and matched correctly — it is missing only the runtime surface. Shipping this closes a gap that is otherwise a hard blocker for any team-based (not single-owner) customer deployment.

## Suggested scope
- Postgres/Supabase-backed CRUD endpoints for `Role`, `Permission`, and `PolicyBinding` in `ferrogate-auth`, replacing (or supplementing, for bootstrap/dev) the YAML-only `AuthServiceData` load path.
- A `POST /v1/admin/tenants/{tenant_id}/invites` (or similar) endpoint that creates a `StoredAdminUserMembership` with a caller-supplied, validated role (not hardcoded `"owner"`), plus whatever invite-acceptance flow is needed (email token, pending-invite record, etc.).
- Role-check enforcement in `handle_admin_register`/membership-mutating admin endpoints so only an existing owner/admin can invite or assign roles within their tenant.
- A "Team" or "Roles" resource page in `admin-console` (new entry in `NAV_GROUPS`, likely under "Identity & Access") backed by the new endpoints, covering: list members, invite member, change member role, revoke membership; and list/create/edit/delete custom `Role`s and `PolicyBinding`s.
- Migration/seed for at least two non-owner built-in roles (e.g. `admin`, `member`/`viewer`) so the UI has sensible defaults out of the box.

## Acceptance
- [ ] `Role`/`Permission`/`PolicyBinding` records can be created, listed, updated, and deleted through a REST API without editing or redeploying a YAML file.
- [ ] A tenant owner can invite a second user to their tenant with a role other than `"owner"`, and that role is persisted and enforced by `RbacAuthService::authorize`.
- [ ] `StoredAdminUserMembership.role` is set to a value other than `"owner"` in at least one code path (verified by test).
- [ ] `admin-console` exposes a Team/Roles page reachable from `NAV_GROUPS` that performs the above CRUD/invite operations end-to-end against the new endpoints.
- [ ] Existing single-owner registration flow (`handle_admin_register`) continues to work unchanged for the first user of a new tenant.
title: [auth][high] No runtime API/UI for custom roles or teammate invites — RBAC is YAML-only, every registered user hardcoded to "owner"

body:
**Severity: Medium** · category: security · from competitive gap analysis

## Summary

`ferrogate-auth` has no automated or bulk user-provisioning path. The only way an `AdminUser` row is ever created is the self-service `POST /v1/admin/register` handler (`handle_admin_register`, `crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs`), which always does three things atomically: creates a brand-new tenant account, creates exactly one `StoredAdminUser`, and inserts a `StoredAdminUserMembership` with `role: "owner".into()` hardcoded (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:868`, mirrored again at line 899 for the response view). There is no way to add a second user to an existing tenant, no way to assign any role other than `owner` at creation time, and no way for anything other than an interactive registration form to drive this.

`route_request`'s match arms (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:620`) enumerate the entire admin HTTP surface: `/v1/admin/register`, `/v1/admin/login`, `/v1/admin/refresh`, `/v1/admin/logout`, `/v1/admin/me`. Nothing else exists. A repo-wide `grep -rni scim` across `*.rs`/`*.md`/`*.toml` returns zero hits — there is no SCIM schema, no SCIM route, and no design doc mentioning it.

The storage model already has what's needed to back this: `StoredAdminUser` (identity) and `StoredAdminUserMembership` (`crates/ferrogate-storage/src/lib.rs:5664-5671`, a `user_id`/`tenant_id`/`role` join row) are exactly the two tables a SCIM `/Users` and `/Groups` implementation would read and write. What's missing is the protocol-facing layer: SCIM 2.0 routes, a service-account/bearer-token auth mode for IdP-to-FerroGate calls (as opposed to the existing user-session bearer tokens issued by `issue_session`), and provisioning semantics (create-if-absent, deactivate-on-remove, group-to-role mapping) on top of the existing repositories.

Without this, every enterprise customer with an IdP (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace) must have admins manually register or hand-provision each teammate through the console UI, and there is no way to automatically deprovision an admin user when they leave the IdP's directory — a real access-control gap, not just an onboarding inconvenience.

## Why it matters

Every adjacent AI-gateway product already ships inbound SCIM provisioning as a baseline enterprise feature:

- Bifrost: SCIM 2.0 inbound provisioning for real-time user/team sync.
- Portkey: SCIM-based automated provisioning/deprovisioning via Admin Settings > Authentication Settings > SCIM Provisioning.
- LiteLLM: dedicated "SCIM with LiteLLM" provisioning documentation.
- API7: SCIM auto-sync of users/groups plus IdP-attribute role-mapping rules.

FerroGate's admin console (`6ba9976`, `93e286a`) currently has no answer here, which is a gap for any enterprise buyer doing IdP-driven lifecycle management, and a lingering deprovisioning risk (ex-employees keeping console access) until it's closed.

## Suggested scope

- Add `/scim/v2/Users` (GET list/filter, GET by id, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE/deactivate) and `/scim/v2/Groups` (GET/POST/PUT mapping to tenant membership roles) route handlers in `ferrogate-auth`, alongside the existing arms in `route_request`.
- Introduce a distinct bearer-token auth mode for SCIM calls (a per-tenant SCIM provisioning token, separate from the session tokens `issue_session` mints for interactive logins), scoped only to the SCIM endpoints.
- Map SCIM `POST /Users` to creating a `StoredAdminUser` + `StoredAdminUserMembership` under an *existing* tenant (unlike `handle_admin_register`, must not create a new tenant/project/workspace), with role sourced from SCIM group/attribute mapping instead of being hardcoded to `"owner"`.
- Map SCIM `PATCH/DELETE /Users/{id}` (active: false) to setting `disabled_at_unix` on `StoredAdminUser` and revoking outstanding `StoredAdminUserRefreshToken`s for that user, so IdP-driven deactivation actually terminates live sessions.
- Map SCIM `/Groups` to `StoredAdminUserMembership.role` values, with configurable group-name-to-role mapping per tenant.
- Document the new endpoints and the required IdP-side SCIM base URL/token configuration.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `/scim/v2/Users` and `/scim/v2/Groups` are handled in `route_request` with SCIM 2.0-compliant request/response schemas (`schemas`, `Resources`, `totalResults`, etc.).
- [ ] SCIM requests are authenticated via a dedicated provisioning bearer token, distinct from admin-console session tokens, and rejected with 401 otherwise.
- [ ] SCIM user creation adds a member to an existing tenant (no implicit tenant/project/workspace creation) and supports a non-`owner` role.
- [ ] Deactivating a user via SCIM sets `disabled_at_unix` and invalidates that user's outstanding refresh tokens.
- [ ] Group-to-role mapping is configurable per tenant and covered by an integration test exercising create, update, and deactivate flows.
- [ ] Docs describe how to point an IdP (e.g. Okta/Azure AD) at the new SCIM endpoint.
title: [auth][medium] No SCIM user provisioning endpoint in ferrogate-auth

body:
**Severity: High** · category: security · from competitive gap analysis

## Summary

Admin console authentication in `ferrogate-auth` is email+password only, with no external-IdP path:

- `handle_admin_login` (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:908-996`) validates credentials solely via `verify_password(&payload.password, &user.password_hash)` (Argon2) against `get_admin_user_by_email`.
- `AdminLoginRequest` (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:484-487`) has exactly two fields, `email` and `password` — no `id_token`, `provider`, or `saml_response` field to carry an external assertion.
- `admin-console/src/pages/login.tsx` renders only an email/password `<form>`; there is no "Sign in with SSO" button, IdP picker, or redirect/callback route anywhere in the console's router.
- A repo-wide case-insensitive grep for `oidc`, `saml`, and `sso` returns zero hits outside this issue — there is no JWKS fetch/cache, no Authorization-Code/PKCE handshake, and no SAML assertion consumer service (ACS) endpoint.

Once a user does authenticate (by whatever means), the existing session machinery is IdP-agnostic and reusable: `issue_session` (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:1178-1200`) mints the refresh token and calls `issue_access_token` (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:1202-1220`) to sign the `AdminSessionClaims` JWT from `(user_id, email, tenant_id, role)`. Today `role` is always sourced from a locally stored `AdminUserTenantMembership` row (e.g. `"owner"` on signup, `crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:868`); there is no mechanism to derive or refresh that role from IdP group claims. Note this is a distinct role model from the gateway-side `RbacAuthService` / `PolicyBinding` / `Role` (`crates/ferrogate-auth/src/lib.rs:97-127, 252-321`) used for API-key request authorization — an IdP-group-to-role mapping would need to plug into the admin membership role first, and optionally extend into `PolicyBinding` subjects if SSO-provisioned users should also get gateway-level RBAC bindings.

For a multi-tenant AI gateway sold into enterprises, SSO is typically a hard requirement gating any production rollout, not a nice-to-have — security/IT review commonly blocks procurement on this alone regardless of feature parity elsewhere.

## Why it matters

Every comparable competitor in this space already ships SSO as a baseline or enterprise-tier feature:

- Bifrost: OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE against Okta/Entra/Keycloak/Zitadel/Google Workspace/Auth0, JWKS-validated, plus SAML on its Enterprise tier.
- Portkey: Enterprise SSO via OIDC against the customer's existing IdP, with SAML SSO on Enterprise.
- LiteLLM: Admin UI SSO via Okta/Google OAuth2/Microsoft Entra with automatic role mapping, plus generic OIDC support.
- Kong Konnect: SSO via any OIDC/SAML IdP, including IdP-group-to-team mapping and auto-provisioning.
- TrueFoundry: SAML 2.0 and OIDC across Google, Entra ID, Keycloak, Okta, Auth0, Azure AD.
- API7: SSO via SAML 2.0, OIDC, and LDAP, with per-IdP login options.

Shipping without this puts FerroGate at a checklist disadvantage in any enterprise security review, independent of actual gateway capability.

## Suggested scope

- Add an OIDC relying-party flow to `ferrogate-auth`: Authorization Code + PKCE, discovery-document fetch, and JWKS validation/caching for the ID token, configurable per tenant (client ID/secret, issuer, allowed audiences).
- Extend `AdminLoginRequest`/add a new request type (or a parallel `/admin/v1/auth/sso/*` endpoint pair for `/authorize` redirect + `/callback`) so an OIDC assertion can substitute for the password check in `handle_admin_login`, then fall through to the existing `issue_session`/`issue_access_token` path unchanged.
- Define an IdP-group-claim → tenant-role mapping (config-driven per tenant) that resolves the `role` passed into `issue_session`, and decide whether SSO-provisioned users should also get corresponding `PolicyBinding` rows for gateway-level RBAC.
- Add just-in-time (JIT) admin-user + membership provisioning on first successful SSO login, reusing the existing `upsert_admin_user`/membership repositories rather than requiring pre-created accounts.
- Add a "Sign in with SSO" entry point in `admin-console/src/pages/login.tsx` (button/link triggering the `/authorize` redirect) plus a callback route/page to complete the flow and land in the existing `useAuth`/session context.
- Stretch: SAML 2.0 SP-initiated flow (ACS endpoint, assertion signature validation) as a second path into the same session issuance, for IdPs that don't support OIDC.
- Document supported IdPs and per-tenant SSO configuration (client credentials, issuer, group-to-role mapping) in deploy/config docs.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A tenant admin can configure an OIDC IdP (issuer, client ID/secret, redirect URI) and enable SSO for their tenant.
- [ ] `admin-console/src/pages/login.tsx` offers a "Sign in with SSO" option that redirects to the configured IdP and completes an Authorization Code + PKCE round trip.
- [ ] ID tokens are validated against the IdP's JWKS (signature, issuer, audience, expiry) before any session is issued.
- [ ] A successful SSO login issues the same `AdminSessionResponse` (access + refresh token) as password login, via the existing `issue_session`/`issue_access_token` functions, with no new session-token format.
- [ ] First-time SSO logins are JIT-provisioned as an admin user + tenant membership without manual pre-creation.
- [ ] IdP group claims map to a tenant role (owner/admin/member, per existing membership roles) via configurable mapping, and re-map on each login (not just at JIT-provisioning time).
- [ ] Password login continues to work unchanged for tenants that haven't enabled SSO.
- [ ] Tests cover: valid ID token accepted, expired/invalid-signature ID token rejected, unmapped group falls back to a safe default (or is rejected), and JIT provisioning creates exactly one membership per tenant.

**Epic 1 of 3** for the new admin console (shadcn/ui React SPA). See #158 (frontend) and #159 (deployment).

## Summary
FerroGate currently has zero human-user identity concept anywhere — all auth (gateway Admin API, virtual keys, static API keys) is machine-to-machine bearer-token/scope based (`admin.read`/`admin.write`). The new admin console needs real multi-tenant self-service: an organization signs up (creating a tenant account + its first admin user), then logs in with email/password to manage its own tenant/workspaces/keys, with a superadmin role able to manage the whole system.

## Scope
- New Postgres tables (bump `sql/001_init_postgres.sql` schema version): `admin_users` (email, argon2 password hash, display_name, role, timestamps), `admin_user_tenant_memberships` (user_id, tenant_account_id, per-tenant role), `admin_user_refresh_tokens` (hashed refresh tokens, revocation support). Add corresponding `ferrogate-storage` repository methods (Postgres + in-memory), following the existing repository/schema-migration pattern.
- New dependencies: `argon2` (password hashing) and `jsonwebtoken` (HS256 session tokens), added to whichever crate hosts the auth logic.
- New endpoints on the standalone `ferrogate auth serve` service: `POST /v1/admin/register` (creates tenant + owner user + membership, auto-provisions a durable virtual API key for that tenant, returns a session JWT + the virtual key secret), `POST /v1/admin/login` (verifies password, mints a fresh session JWT + fresh virtual key, revoking the previous one), `POST /v1/admin/refresh`, `POST /v1/admin/logout`, `GET /v1/admin/me`.
- CORS support on both the gateway's Admin API and the auth service's new endpoints (configurable allowed-origin), since the frontend is a separately-deployed service (issue #159).
- The gateway's own `/admin/v1/*` API is NOT modified — the console authenticates to it using the same virtual-API-key mechanism that already exists and is tested, avoiding a second auth scheme on the gateway.

## Acceptance
- Live Docker/Postgres-backed test: register a new organization, log in, refresh a session, confirm a minted virtual key from login can call the gateway's `/admin/v1/status` successfully, confirm login rotates/revokes the previous key.
