The first Rust CI split moved work into reusable workflows, but the test boundary is still too coarse because `rust-workspace-tests` runs the whole workspace as one bucket. FerroGate needs test CI that maps to functional/business modules so failures point to the owning runtime surface.

## Scope

- Replace the coarse workspace test workflow with feature-module test workflows.
- Cover core config/policy/routing, control plane/auth/storage/billing/observability, provider/MCP/agent runtime, gateway CLI/API, and the ferrogate-test harness as separate test gates.
- Keep the required `rust-ci` aggregate check as the branch-protection surface.
- Update `AGENTS.md` so future CI changes keep tests at feature-module granularity.

## Acceptance criteria

- CI orchestration depends on separate feature-module test workflows instead of one monolithic workspace test job.
- Workflow syntax/static checks pass locally.
- Remote GitHub Actions run reaches the stable `rust-ci` aggregate check.
title: Refine Rust CI into feature-module test gates

body:
## Problem

The current Rust CI keeps formatting, linting, schema checks, workspace tests, runtime harness checks, performance smoke tests, and CI image publishing in one workflow file. That makes the CI boundary harder to maintain as FerroGate grows across gateway runtime, control plane, agentic gateway, auth, billing, observability, and deployment packaging.

## Scope

- Split Rust CI execution into module-oriented reusable workflow files.
- Keep a stable `rust-ci` aggregate check because `main` branch protection currently requires that context.
- Move CI image build/publish out of the monolithic CI file while preserving its dependency on the aggregate Rust gate.
- Document the CI structure rule in `AGENTS.md` so future changes do not collapse the checks back into one workflow file.

## Acceptance criteria

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is reduced to orchestration plus the required `rust-ci` aggregate check.
- Module workflow files own quality/schema, workspace unit tests, runtime/performance smoke checks, E2E harness execution, and CI image publishing.
- Local workflow syntax/static checks pass.
- Commit references this issue and the branch is pushed to `main`.
title: Split Rust CI by business module

body:
## Context

Managed agent workers must not gain unrestricted authority just because they run in a sandbox.

The sandbox is an execution boundary, not a trust boundary. All external actions produced by a managed worker must be mediated by the FerroGate AI gateway security model.

Self-hosted workers are different: customers own those hosts and control local tools, network, filesystem, credentials, and processes. For self-hosted workers, FerroGate ingests telemetry and can offer optional governed callback paths, but it does not claim hard enforcement over customer-owned execution environments.

## Scope

For managed workers, these external actions must go through FerroGate:

- ordinary tool calls;
- MCP tool calls;
- CLI and shell command execution;
- skill invocation;
- filesystem access beyond the prepared workspace;
- browser or network automation;
- third-party REST API calls;
- secret and credential access;
- memory reads/writes outside the current session boundary.

For self-hosted workers, these actions should be reported as telemetry when available, but local enforcement is customer-owned unless the customer explicitly routes actions through FerroGate callbacks.

## Required enforcement path for managed workers

Every managed external action must pass through:

- auth bound to tenant, workspace, worker identity, session, run, and service principal;
- tenant/workspace policy checks;
- guardrails for prompts, command strings, tool arguments, request bodies, and responses;
- approval gates for high-risk actions;
- audit events for allowed, denied, approved, failed, and cancelled actions;
- billing attribution for token, runtime, tool, network, and third-party API usage;
- egress control so managed workers do not have direct unmanaged public network access.

## Design requirements

- Managed worker adapters request capabilities; they do not execute external actions directly.
- Managed workers default to no public network egress except the gateway control channel and governed egress path.
- MCP execution in managed workers must use the existing gateway-mediated MCP/tool governance model.
- CLI execution in managed workers must be policy-shaped: allowed commands, denied commands, working directory, env, timeout, stdout/stderr limits, and artifact capture.
- Skills must declare capabilities and permissions before use.
- Third-party REST calls must be represented as governed outbound requests with method, URL/host, path, headers policy, body policy, timeout, and retry limits.
- Secrets are injected only by gateway policy and must not be visible as ambient worker environment unless explicitly granted.
- Self-hosted worker telemetry must be marked as reported evidence, not enforced evidence.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Worker Protocol defines a gateway-mediated capability boundary for managed workers.
- Managed worker sessions cannot execute tool, MCP, CLI, skill, REST, filesystem, browser, memory, network, or secret operations without a gateway authorization decision.
- All managed external actions produce audit evidence linked to tenant, workspace, session, run, worker, adapter, and isolation backend.
- Denied managed actions are visible in run timelines and do not disappear as worker-local failures.
- Self-hosted worker events are accepted as telemetry with explicit trust level and do not imply FerroGate enforcement.
- Policy can distinguish low-risk tools from high-risk CLI/network operations that require approval.

## Verification target

- Unit tests for managed capability authorization decisions.
- Contract tests proving managed adapters route external actions through the gateway boundary.
- Integration smoke for allowed and denied managed MCP/tool/CLI/REST actions.
- Timeline/admin evidence for allow, deny, approval, failure, cancellation, and timeout.
- Self-hosted telemetry tests proving reported events are stored with the correct trust level.

## Depends on

- #81
- #85
- #84
- #82

## Supabase Persistence Constraint

Any new durable control-plane, control-table, worker/session/run, policy, telemetry index, or billing evidence records introduced by this issue must use the Supabase-backed persistence target from #90 and #91. Do not introduce Turso/libSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, or a generic-only Postgres path as the control-table database target.
title: Enforce gateway-mediated capabilities for agent worker tool, MCP, CLI, skill, and REST access

body:
## Context

This is the managed execution slice under the Agent Worker Protocol.

FerroGate should be able to schedule, start, monitor, cancel, recover, and clean up worker runtimes on behalf of a tenant while preserving the same control-plane contract used by self-hosted workers.

## Commercial value

This is the hosted product path: customers do not bring their own VM. FerroGate provides the worker runtime, lifecycle management, isolation selection, observability, and billing evidence.

## Security principle

Managed worker sandboxes must not have unrestricted external authority. All tool calls, MCP tool calls, CLI/shell execution, skill use, REST API calls, filesystem access, browser/network automation, memory access, and secret access must route through the gateway-mediated capability boundary in #86.

## Scope

- Managed worker session creation and teardown.
- Worker template selection by tenant/workspace policy.
- Managed run scheduling and lifecycle transitions.
- Per-tenant and per-workspace concurrency caps.
- Runtime health checks and restart semantics.
- Checkpoint persistence and resume.
- Log, artifact, and event retention policy.
- Usage and billing dimensions for managed worker runs.
- Admin visibility for active sessions, completed sessions, failures, and cleanup status.
- Default-deny worker network egress except the gateway control channel and governed egress path.

## Process boundary

Managed runtime provisioning must be executed by an independent module process named `agent-worker`, not by embedding Firecracker or microVM lifecycle control inside the AI gateway process.

The API/control plane handles authentication, tenant/workspace policy, quota and concurrency checks, worker template selection, isolation selection, capability envelope creation, audit, scheduling, and durable lifecycle evidence. After that decision, `agent-worker` owns the host-level lifecycle actions for the selected isolation backend.

`agent-worker` is responsible for:

- prepare;
- start;
- exec-or-attach;
- stop;
- snapshot-or-checkpoint;
- collect logs;
- collect artifacts;
- cleanup.

The gateway communicates with `agent-worker` through an explicit management API/control protocol and must not directly own Firecracker jailer setup, kernel/rootfs preparation, tap/network namespace wiring, snapshot management, handler launch, adapter binary probing, agent harness startup, or cleanup implementation details.

### Gateway-to-agent-worker management protocol

The management API between the gateway and `agent-worker` is a stable internal control-plane protocol. It must be explicit enough that the gateway can safely route lifecycle decisions to any compatible worker process without depending on worker internals.

Protocol requirements:

- Version every management envelope with a protocol version and reject unsupported versions fail-closed.
- Standardize action names for `provision`, `start`, `exec`, `cancel`, `snapshot`, `collect_artifacts`, and `cleanup` before exposing concrete worker transports.
- Carry `request_id`, `idempotency_key`, `tenant_id`, `workspace_id`, `worker_id`, optional `session_id`, optional `run_id`, issue time, deadline, key id, nonce, security algorithm, and encryption state on every management request.
- Sign a canonical request representation so retries, audits, and independent implementations verify the same bytes.
- Reject missing signatures, wrong secrets, unsupported algorithms, stale timestamps, expired deadlines, and replayable nonces.
- Require encrypted transport or an mTLS-bound management channel. Shared-secret signatures are authentication and integrity evidence; they are not a substitute for encrypted payload transport.
- Use constant-time signature comparison for MAC verification.
- Keep key rotation explicit through `key_id`; do not bake a single global secret into worker lifecycle code.
- Standardize failure responses for policy denied, quota exceeded, incompatible backend, handler unavailable, worker busy, provision failed, run failed, timeout, cancelled, cleanup failed, invalid signature, stale request, and unsupported protocol.
- Preserve idempotent behavior for duplicate lifecycle requests with the same idempotency key.
- Emit structured lifecycle evidence for every accepted or rejected management request.

The initial implementation may use a local in-memory/fake control client for tests, but the contract must not assume in-process execution. A later HTTP/gRPC/Unix-socket transport must implement the same envelope semantics instead of inventing a second protocol.

### Agent-worker internal handler boundary

The microVM-backed `agent-worker` is a standalone process. The gateway initiates managed execution by calling the `agent-worker` management API, for example create/provision session, submit run, cancel, stream status, collect artifacts, and cleanup. After the management API request is accepted, `agent-worker` owns the internal handler chain:

- choose the framework handler inside the worker process;
- probe and validate local adapter binaries or SDK shims such as Codex CLI, Claude Code, Hermes, or native harness;
- prepare the Firecracker microVM runtime bundle;
- start the microVM and attach the selected handler/agent harness inside that isolation boundary;
- translate handler events back into normalized worker protocol events;
- request gateway-mediated capabilities for tools, MCP, CLI, REST, filesystem, network, secrets, and memory instead of executing those actions directly;
- report lifecycle, logs, artifacts, checkpoints, billing dimensions, and cleanup evidence back to the gateway/control plane.

The gateway must not run the framework handler, probe host PATH for adapter binaries, spawn Codex/Claude/Hermes, or directly manage handler lifecycle. Gateway code may validate policy, call the `agent-worker` management API, persist reported evidence, and expose Admin/API visibility for what `agent-worker` reports.

## Lifecycle states

The managed worker lifecycle should expose at least:

- `queued`
- `provisioning`
- `starting`
- `running`
- `draining`
- `completed`
- `cancelled`
- `failed`
- `expired`
- `cleaned_up`

## Scheduling requirements

- Enforce tenant and workspace concurrency before provisioning.
- Select a worker template and isolation backend from policy.
- Attach a run/session to one tenant, one workspace, and one worker identity.
- Fail closed when no compatible worker template or isolation backend exists.
- Preserve enough evidence to explain why a worker was selected.
- Attach an explicit capability envelope to the worker session before it starts.

## Data model requirements

Add or prepare durable records for:

- worker template;
- managed worker instance;
- agent-worker instance/process identity;
- session lifecycle;
- run lifecycle;
- isolation backend selection;
- microVM or sandbox instance identity when applicable;
- resource limits;
- capability envelope;
- billing dimensions;
- cleanup evidence.

## Acceptance criteria

- A tenant can request a managed worker session through the control plane.
- The runtime can start, stop, cancel, and clean up without exposing framework details to clients.
- Firecracker or equivalent microVM lifecycle control runs through `agent-worker`, not inside the AI gateway process.
- Quotas and concurrency caps are enforced before worker provisioning.
- Lifecycle transitions produce durable evidence and admin visibility.
- The gateway-to-agent-worker management protocol is versioned, signed, replay-resistant, idempotent, deadline-bound, and transport-encryption ready.
- The implementation can later swap isolation layers without changing the control-plane contract.
- Managed workers cannot perform unmanaged tool, MCP, CLI, skill, REST, filesystem, browser, memory, network, or secret operations.
- Failures are explicit and auditable: provision failed, runtime failed, adapter failed, policy denied, quota exceeded, timeout, and cleanup failed.

## Verification target

- Unit coverage for scheduler policy and quota decisions.
- Integration smoke for session create, run submit, cancel, complete, and cleanup.
- Contract smoke proving the gateway schedules work through `agent-worker` instead of directly controlling the microVM backend.
- Contract smoke proving management envelopes reject unsupported protocol versions, invalid signatures, wrong secrets, stale requests, expired deadlines, and duplicate replay where nonce/idempotency policy forbids it.
- Integration smoke proving unmanaged egress/action attempts are denied.
- Admin API/OpenAPI coverage for managed worker session visibility.
- Evidence that cleanup runs even after worker failure.

## Depends on

- #81
- #83
- #86

## Supabase Persistence Constraint

Any new durable control-plane, control-table, worker/session/run, policy, telemetry index, or billing evidence records introduced by this issue must use the Supabase-backed persistence target from #90 and #91. Do not introduce Turso/libSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, or a generic-only Postgres path as the control-table database target.
## Protocol hardening addendum

The gateway-to-`agent-worker` boundary is a stable internal control-plane API, not an ad hoc command channel.

### Stability requirements

- Use one versioned management envelope across Unix socket, future HTTP/gRPC, and any remote transport.
- Preserve canonical signing bytes across implementations; transports must not invent separate request shapes.
- Every request must carry `request_id`, `idempotency_key`, `tenant_id`, `workspace_id`, `worker_id`, optional `session_id`, optional `run_id`, `issued_at`, `deadline`, `key_id`, `nonce`, `action`, and `protocol_version`.
- Duplicate idempotency keys must return stable idempotent results where the action is retryable; nonce replay must fail closed where replay is forbidden.
- Use bounded request size, bounded read/write timeouts, explicit deadline handling, and structured response codes for all failure paths.
- A slow or malformed client must not block the server from accepting later management requests.

### Security requirements

- Shared-secret MAC is authentication and integrity evidence only; it is not payload confidentiality.
- Same-host Unix socket transport may use `local_unix_socket` as the transport security marker, with filesystem permissions and process identity checks as the local trust boundary.
- Any cross-host or network transport must use real mTLS or real symmetric AEAD payload encryption. A boolean `encrypted=true` marker is not sufficient by itself.
- If symmetric AEAD is implemented, define algorithm, key lookup/rotation, nonce construction, associated data, max message size, decrypt failure mapping, and replay-window semantics before accepting production traffic.
- Key rotation must be `key_id` based; no single hardcoded global secret in lifecycle code.
- Signature and MAC checks must use constant-time comparison.
- Secrets, adapter paths, provider tokens, and capability credentials must never be returned in management responses or logs.

### Standard API requirements

- Standard actions remain explicit: `probe_handlers`, `provision`, `start`, `exec`, `cancel`, `snapshot`, `collect_artifacts`, and `cleanup`.
- Standard response codes include `unsupported_protocol`, `unsupported_action`, `invalid_signature`, `transport_security_required`, `stale_request`, `expired_deadline`, `nonce_replay`, `idempotency_conflict`, `policy_denied`, `quota_exceeded`, `incompatible_backend`, `handler_unavailable`, `worker_busy`, `provision_failed`, `run_failed`, `timeout`, `cancelled`, and `cleanup_failed`.
- Gateway code may schedule, authorize, persist, and call the management API. `agent-worker` code owns handler probing, Firecracker/microVM preparation, lifecycle execution, logs/artifacts collection, and cleanup.
- Framework handlers such as Codex CLI, Claude Code, Hermes, or native harnesses are selected and launched inside `agent-worker`/microVM scope, never by the gateway.
- All tool, MCP, CLI, REST, filesystem, network, secret, browser, memory, and skill actions from the running agent must still go through the gateway-mediated capability path from #86.
title: Implement FerroGate-managed worker sessions and lifecycle

body:
## Context

The Worker Protocol must not be limited to one SDK or one vendor.

FerroGate needs a pluggable framework adapter layer that can run multiple worker frameworks behind the same control-plane contract.

Initial framework targets:

- Claude Code / Claude Agent SDK for code-oriented workers;
- Codex SDK for OpenAI-native coding workers;
- Hermes for general-purpose multi-step workers and memory-heavy flows;
- native minimal harness for fallback, smoke tests, and deterministic CI coverage.

## Commercial value

This lets FerroGate support customer-preferred agent stacks without redesigning tenant policy, billing, audit, lifecycle, or isolation contracts.

## Security principle

Adapters translate framework behavior into FerroGate protocol events.

For managed workers, adapters must convert external actions into gateway capability requests. Tool calls, MCP calls, CLI/shell commands, skills, REST calls, memory, filesystem, browser/network automation, and secret access must use #86.

For self-hosted workers, adapters report telemetry produced by the customer-controlled runtime. They may optionally call FerroGate governed callbacks, but FerroGate does not claim hard enforcement over customer-owned local access.

## Runtime ownership boundary

For FerroGate-managed workers, framework adapters and their concrete handlers run inside the standalone `agent-worker` process, not inside the AI gateway process. The gateway calls the `agent-worker` management API from #85 to request session/run lifecycle actions. `agent-worker` then selects and runs the internal handler for Codex CLI, Claude Code, Hermes, or native harness inside the selected isolation backend, normally a Firecracker microVM.

Adapter binary probing, SDK/process launch, handler startup, harness supervision, event streaming, artifact collection, checkpoint handling, and handler cleanup belong to `agent-worker`. Gateway handlers must not probe the host PATH for adapter binaries, spawn agent harnesses, or directly run framework-specific code. Gateway code may store and expose adapter metadata/evidence reported by `agent-worker`, and it may enforce capability decisions when `agent-worker` asks for gateway-mediated actions.

The adapter layer must not define a separate management protocol. It reports readiness, version, capabilities, lifecycle events, artifacts, and normalized framework events through the same signed, versioned, deadline-bound, idempotent gateway-to-agent-worker management contract defined in #85.

## Scope

- Define the framework adapter interface behind the worker protocol.
- Add adapter metadata and capability negotiation.
- Normalize framework-specific events into one worker event schema.
- Map managed framework tool calls back into FerroGate-governed tool dispatch.
- Map self-hosted framework actions into reported telemetry events with explicit trust level.
- Map framework checkpoint/session concepts into FerroGate checkpoint records.
- Support framework-specific launch and handshake logic without exposing it in the public API.
- Support version pinning and runtime metadata for each adapter.
- Leave room for additional frameworks without API redesign.

## Adapter interface requirements

Every adapter should expose:

- `name`
- `version`
- `capabilities`
- `start_session`
- `submit_run`
- `authorize_capability` for managed execution
- `report_event` for self-hosted telemetry
- `cancel_run`
- `resume_run`
- `stream_events`
- `collect_artifacts`
- `close_session`

## Capability vocabulary

Start with these normalized capabilities:

- `tools`
- `mcp`
- `memory.read`
- `memory.write`
- `checkpoint`
- `artifacts`
- `subagents`
- `filesystem`
- `shell`
- `browser`
- `rest.egress`
- `secrets.read`
- `streaming`

## Event normalization

All adapters must emit one normalized event stream with framework-specific data kept under an opaque metadata field.

Minimum event types:

- `session.started`
- `run.started`
- `capability.requested`
- `capability.allowed`
- `capability.denied`
- `model.requested`
- `tool.requested`
- `tool.approved`
- `tool.denied`
- `tool.completed`
- `mcp.tool.requested`
- `cli.requested`
- `rest.requested`
- `memory.read`
- `memory.write`
- `checkpoint.created`
- `artifact.created`
- `run.completed`
- `run.failed`
- `run.cancelled`
- `session.closed`

## Acceptance criteria

- A worker session can target any supported adapter without changing the client contract.
- The control plane receives the same lifecycle and event schema from Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and native harness adapters.
- Framework-specific details stay out of the public worker API.
- Adapters can be added, removed, disabled, or version-pinned independently.
- The design remains compatible with both self-hosted and FerroGate-managed worker modes.
- Adapter capabilities can be used by policy and scheduler decisions for managed execution.
- Managed adapter tests prove external actions are converted into gateway authorization requests instead of being executed directly.
- Self-hosted adapter tests prove reported events are stored as telemetry rather than enforced gateway decisions.

## Verification target

- Unit coverage for adapter capability negotiation and event normalization.
- Contract tests using the native harness adapter.
- At least one smoke path for each first-class adapter when the dependency is available.
- Golden event fixtures proving all adapters map into the same event schema.
- Deny-path fixtures for unmanaged managed-worker tool/MCP/CLI/REST/secret access.
- Self-hosted telemetry fixtures for reported tool/MCP/CLI/REST/skill events.

## Depends on

- #81
- #83
- #85
- #86

## Supabase Persistence Constraint

Any new durable control-plane, control-table, worker/session/run, policy, telemetry index, or billing evidence records introduced by this issue must use the Supabase-backed persistence target from #90 and #91. Do not introduce Turso/libSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, or a generic-only Postgres path as the control-table database target.
title: Add pluggable worker framework adapters for Claude Code, Codex, and Hermes

body:
## Context

This is the self-hosted execution slice under the Agent Worker Protocol.

The customer owns the VM/host and controls the agent process, local tools, filesystem, network, credentials, and framework runtime. FerroGate does not claim hard enforcement over that environment.

The goal is to let a customer-owned worker connect to FerroGate so the platform can receive lifecycle, usage, artifact, and observability data, and optionally dispatch runs when the customer opts into remote orchestration.

## Commercial value

This enables enterprise customers to keep agent execution inside their own infrastructure while still using FerroGate for registration, identity, visibility, audit timelines, usage reporting, and optional governed callbacks.

## Scope

- Worker registration flow for tenant-owned hosts.
- Worker identity issuance and rotation.
- Remote transport for heartbeat, status, lifecycle events, logs, artifacts, and usage telemetry.
- Optional session/run dispatch if the customer enables remote orchestration.
- Event streaming for logs, tool calls, MCP calls, CLI usage, skills, checkpoints, artifacts, and lifecycle state.
- Tenant/workspace attribution for all reported telemetry.
- Admin visibility for connected workers, stale workers, runs, artifacts, and event timelines.
- Clear trust marking that self-hosted events are customer-provided telemetry, not proof of FerroGate enforcement.

## Out of scope

- Hard-blocking local CLI, MCP, REST, filesystem, network, or secret access on the customer's host.
- Claiming sandbox isolation for customer-owned execution environments.
- Forcing customer tools through FerroGate unless the customer explicitly configures governed callbacks or managed execution.

## Protocol requirements

The self-hosted worker should support:

- `register_worker`
- `probe_worker`
- `heartbeat`
- `stream_events`
- `upload_artifact`
- `fetch_checkpoint`
- `start_session` when remote orchestration is enabled
- `submit_run` when remote orchestration is enabled
- `cancel_run` when remote orchestration is enabled
- `resume_run` when remote orchestration is enabled
- `close_session` when remote orchestration is enabled

## Security requirements

- Use mTLS or an equivalent mutually authenticated transport.
- Worker tokens must be scoped to tenant/workspace and rotatable.
- A worker cannot report telemetry under a tenant/workspace outside its identity envelope.
- Secrets must not be logged in worker events or artifacts.
- Telemetry ingestion must validate size limits, schema, timestamps, run/session IDs, and tenant/workspace attribution.
- Self-hosted workers should be visually and API-distinct from managed workers so operators understand the enforcement boundary.

## Data model requirements

Add or prepare durable records for:

- self-hosted worker registration;
- worker capability envelope;
- worker heartbeat/status;
- telemetry trust level;
- session lifecycle when reported;
- run lifecycle when reported;
- event stream cursor;
- artifact metadata;
- checkpoint metadata.

## Acceptance criteria

- FerroGate can register a self-hosted worker and list it in the control plane.
- The worker can stream normalized lifecycle and observability events back to FerroGate.
- Telemetry is attributed to tenant, workspace, worker, session, and run.
- Run lifecycle state is visible through an admin path when the worker reports it.
- The protocol remains framework-neutral and can report Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, or native worker events.
- The UI/API distinguishes self-hosted telemetry from managed-worker enforced actions.
- Failure modes are explicit: offline worker, expired identity, invalid tenant scope, invalid telemetry schema, stale heartbeat, and rejected artifact upload.

## Verification target

- Unit coverage for worker identity validation and tenant/workspace telemetry attribution.
- Integration smoke for registration, heartbeat, event ingestion, artifact upload, and stale-worker detection.
- Admin API/OpenAPI coverage for self-hosted worker surfaces.
- Negative tests for cross-tenant telemetry spoofing and oversized artifacts/events.

## Depends on

- #81

## Supabase Persistence Constraint

Any new durable control-plane, control-table, worker/session/run, policy, telemetry index, or billing evidence records introduced by this issue must use the Supabase-backed persistence target from #90 and #91. Do not introduce Turso/libSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, or a generic-only Postgres path as the control-table database target.
title: Implement self-hosted worker registration and remote transport

body:
## Context

Commercial multi-tenant worker execution needs a replaceable isolation layer.

Docker alone is not the end state. The platform must be able to select stronger or weaker isolation depending on tenant policy, workload risk, and deployment environment.

## Recommended backend order

Default commercial preference:

1. Firecracker or equivalent microVM for high-risk managed multi-tenant runs.
2. Kata Containers when Kubernetes/container-native operations matter more than direct microVM control.
3. gVisor for lower-friction container sandboxing and transitional deployments.
4. Rootless Docker for low-risk/internal workloads.

Do not use in-process WASM as a managed worker boundary. The gateway should fail closed until the external `agent-worker` Firecracker microVM transport exists; external process adapters are local test/harness compatibility only.

## Commercial value

This lets FerroGate sell one worker product while supporting different deployment risk profiles:

- low-cost developer tier;
- self-hosted enterprise tier;
- managed sandboxed tier;
- high-isolation regulated tier.

## Security principle

Isolation prevents process and tenant breakout. It does not grant authorization. Even inside the strongest isolation backend, external actions must still route through #86.

Managed isolation backends should default to no direct public network access. Third-party REST, MCP, CLI network access, browser automation, and secret retrieval should use the gateway-mediated capability path.

## Runtime ownership boundary

The isolation backend interface belongs behind an independent module process named `agent-worker` for managed execution. The AI gateway/control plane selects policy, schedules work, creates the capability envelope, and records evidence; it must not directly control Firecracker or microVM lifecycle details in the gateway process.

For Firecracker or equivalent microVM backends, `agent-worker` owns host-level lifecycle operations:

- prepare kernel/rootfs/runtime bundle;
- configure jailer, tap, network namespace, filesystem, and resource limits;
- start the microVM;
- exec or attach the agent workload;
- stop, snapshot or checkpoint;
- collect logs and artifacts;
- cleanup host resources.

The gateway talks to `agent-worker` through an explicit control protocol. This keeps Firecracker-specific implementation details out of the AI gateway hot path and preserves the ability to swap isolation backends without changing client-facing APIs.

## Scope

- Define isolation backend interface.
- Record isolation backend selection per session/run.
- Support resource limits, network policy, filesystem policy, secret injection, and cleanup hooks.
- Select isolation target by tenant/workspace policy and worker template capability.
- Keep isolation details out of the framework adapter interface and the AI gateway hot path.
- Allow managed worker sessions to swap isolation backend without changing client APIs.
- Provide governed egress controls for managed workers.

## Isolation interface requirements

Every isolation backend should expose:

- `backend_name`
- `backend_version`
- `capabilities`
- `prepare`
- `start`
- `exec_or_attach`
- `stop`
- `snapshot_or_checkpoint`
- `collect_logs`
- `collect_artifacts`
- `cleanup`

## Policy dimensions

Isolation selection should consider:

- tenant tier;
- workspace policy;
- worker template;
- requested framework adapter;
- required tools and capabilities;
- network egress policy;
- filesystem policy;
- secret access policy;
- max runtime duration;
- CPU, memory, disk, and process limits.

## Evidence requirements

Each run/session should record:

- selected isolation backend;
- backend version;
- `agent-worker` instance/process identity;
- microVM or sandbox instance identity when applicable;
- resource limits;
- network policy;
- filesystem policy;
- governed egress policy;
- cleanup outcome;
- failure reason if provisioning or cleanup fails.

## Acceptance criteria

- The managed worker backend can select an isolation target by policy.
- The control plane records the isolation backend and policy envelope used for each run.
- Firecracker or equivalent microVM lifecycle control is delegated to `agent-worker`, not embedded in the AI gateway process.
- Backend changes do not require worker protocol changes.
- Stronger isolation backends can be introduced without changing client-facing APIs.
- Rootless Docker/gVisor/Kata/Firecracker can be represented by the same interface even if only one backend is implemented in the first slice.

- #86

## Context

FerroGate needs a commercial agent execution boundary that supports both customer-hosted workers and FerroGate-managed workers without binding the product to one framework or one isolation primitive.

The control plane must stay unified while the execution plane, isolation layer, and worker framework remain pluggable.

## Design document

See `docs/agent-worker-protocol.md`.

## Product requirements

- One control plane for tenant/workspace identity, worker registration, policy, quota, billing, audit, trace, artifact, and checkpoint evidence.
- Two execution modes:
  - customer-hosted remote workers on tenant-owned VMs/hosts;
  - FerroGate-managed workers provisioned and scheduled by the platform.
- Replaceable isolation backends for managed workers.
- Framework-neutral worker protocol so Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and future frameworks can be added without changing client APIs.
- Tenant isolation, lifecycle visibility, and commercial billing dimensions from the first implementation slice.
- Gateway-mediated capability boundary for tool calls, MCP calls, CLI, skills, REST calls, secrets, memory, filesystem, and browser/network automation.

## Managed worker process boundary

FerroGate-managed worker provisioning must be split across the control plane and an independent host-side module process named `agent-worker`.

The API/control plane owns authentication, tenant/workspace policy, quota and concurrency checks, worker template selection, isolation backend selection, capability envelope creation, scheduling decisions, billing/audit attribution, and durable lifecycle evidence.

After the control-plane decision is recorded, `agent-worker` owns host-level lifecycle actions for the selected isolation backend. For Firecracker or equivalent microVM backends, `agent-worker` must own kernel/rootfs/runtime bundle preparation, jailer setup, tap/network namespace wiring, resource limits, microVM start/stop, exec-or-attach, snapshot/checkpoint, log/artifact collection, and cleanup.

The AI gateway process must not directly embed Firecracker jailer setup or microVM lifecycle control. It communicates with `agent-worker` through an explicit control protocol so the isolation backend can be swapped without changing the public worker API or coupling microVM implementation details into the gateway hot path.

## Worker protocol objects

- `tenant`
- `workspace`
- `worker`
- `worker_template`
- `agent_worker_instance`
- `session`
- `run`
- `event`
- `artifact`
- `checkpoint`
- `tool_call`
- `policy_decision`
- `capability_request`
- `isolation_backend`

## Required protocol operations

- `register_worker`
- `probe_worker`
- `start_session`
- `submit_run`
- `cancel_run`
- `resume_run`
- `heartbeat`
- `stream_events`
- `upload_artifact`
- `fetch_checkpoint`
- `authorize_capability`
- `close_session`
- `provision_managed_worker`
- `stop_managed_worker`
- `cleanup_managed_worker`

## Progressive implementation slices

1. #83 Self-hosted worker registration and remote transport.
2. #85 FerroGate-managed worker sessions and lifecycle.
3. #86 Gateway-mediated capability boundary for tool/MCP/CLI/skill/REST access.
4. #84 Pluggable worker framework adapters for Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and future frameworks.
5. #82 Replaceable isolation backends for managed worker execution.

## Acceptance criteria

- The protocol document defines the core objects, operations, lifecycle, and non-goals.
- The design distinguishes self-hosted, managed, and hybrid worker modes.
- The design explicitly covers quotas, concurrency, version pinning, isolation evidence, artifacts, checkpoints, and billing dimensions.
- The design treats the sandbox as an execution boundary, not as the authorization boundary.
- Managed Firecracker or equivalent microVM lifecycle control is delegated to `agent-worker`, not embedded in the AI gateway process.
- Follow-up issues are ordered so each slice can land independently and be verified.
- The public control-plane contract does not expose framework-specific semantics.
- The public control-plane contract does not expose Firecracker-specific lifecycle implementation details.

## Related

- #48 Agent protocol ingress governance
- #59 Opt-in WASM sandboxed runtime
- #79 Structured OpenTelemetry agent execution spans
- #82 Replaceable isolation backends
- #85 FerroGate-managed worker sessions and lifecycle
- #86 Gateway-mediated capability boundary
title: Define Agent Worker Protocol for commercial self-hosted and managed workers

## Summary

FerroGate currently has useful agent execution evidence through Admin API timelines, durable `agent_run` / `agent_run_event` records, audit events, request logs, billing events, and request/trace id propagation. That is enough for operator inspection inside FerroGate, but it is not the same as full agent execution tracing in an external tracing system.

Add a first-class agent trace export path that turns each agent run into a structured OpenTelemetry trace/span tree, so operators can inspect agent runs, turns, WASM host ABI calls, governed tool dispatch, approvals, provider calls, billing writes, and failures in systems such as Tempo, Jaeger, Honeycomb, ClickHouse-derived traces, or an OTLP collector.

## Current state

Implemented today:

- `POST /v1/agent-runs` creates explicit opt-in agent runs.
- `/admin/v1/agent-runs` and `/admin/v1/agent-runs/{run_id}` expose retained/durable run evidence.
- `agent_run_id` and `trace_id` are stored on request logs, billing events, audit events, durable agent run records, and durable agent run events.
- The observability crate can build OTLP metrics/logs/traces requests, and request logs are exported as coarse `ferrogate.gateway.request` spans.
- WASM host ABI events such as log/state/tool dispatch are recorded as agent-linked audit events.

Missing for full agent tracing:

- no explicit `agent.run` root span with child spans for turns, provider steps, WASM execution, host ABI calls, tool dispatch, approval wait, billing, and final status;
- no W3C `traceparent` / `tracestate` ingress and propagation contract for agent runs;
- no stable span-id hierarchy tied to `agent_run_id`, turn, tool call id, and request id;
- no direct OTLP span export for `StoredAgentRunEvent` / audit-derived agent execution events;
- no tests proving an agent run appears as a coherent external trace rather than only as Admin API timeline JSON.

## Proposed scope

- Define an agent execution span model in `ferrogate-observability` with stable names such as:
  - `ferrogate.agent.run`
  - `ferrogate.agent.turn`
  - `ferrogate.agent.provider.step`
  - `ferrogate.agent.wasm.execute`
  - `ferrogate.agent.wasm.host_abi`
  - `ferrogate.agent.tool.dispatch`
  - `ferrogate.tool.approval.wait`
  - `ferrogate.billing.write`
- Build OTLP span records from durable agent run events and related audit/request/billing records.
- Preserve redaction: no raw prompt body or raw tool payload unless the existing recording policy explicitly allows it.
- Accept and propagate W3C `traceparent` when present; otherwise keep generating an internal trace id.
- Ensure downstream provider/tool calls receive the correct trace context where the protocol supports it.
- Keep the Admin API timeline as the local evidence surface; OTLP export should be an additional external observability path, not a replacement.

## Acceptance criteria

- An agent run exports a root `ferrogate.agent.run` span with `agent_run_id`, tenant/API key context, provider, status, and duration.
- Agent turns, WASM execution, WASM host ABI operations, governed tool dispatch, approval waits, and failures appear as child spans or span events with stable parent-child relationships.
- Existing request-log spans and billing/audit-derived records correlate to the same trace id.
- `traceparent` ingress is accepted and propagated without breaking existing `x-ferrogate-trace-id` behavior.
- OTLP export tests cover default agent run, WASM provider run, and WASM host ABI tool dispatch.
- `ferrogate-test` or focused integration tests prove the exported trace can be reconstructed from a real agent run.
- README/Product Overview can accurately state full agent execution tracing once this lands.

## Out of scope

- Replacing the Admin API timeline.
- Exporting raw prompts/tool payloads by default.
- Building a hosted tracing UI inside FerroGate.

Related: #59, #49, #55, #70, #78

## Supabase Persistence Constraint

Any new durable control-plane, control-table, worker/session/run, policy, telemetry index, or billing evidence records introduced by this issue must use the Supabase-backed persistence target from #90 and #91. Do not introduce Turso/libSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, or a generic-only Postgres path as the control-table database target.
title: Export agent execution timelines as structured OpenTelemetry spans

## Summary

Track removal of temporary cargo-audit ignores for rustls-webpki advisories currently pulled through the remote libSQL/Turso storage stack.

## Root Cause

FerroGate depends on `libsql = 0.10.0-pre.4` with the `remote` and `tls` features enabled so the storage module can connect to Turso Cloud/libSQL over the native libSQL client path. That crate currently pulls:

- `libsql 0.10.0-pre.4 -> hyper-rustls 0.25 -> rustls 0.22.4 -> rustls-webpki 0.102.8`

`cargo audit` reports:

- RUSTSEC-2026-0049
- RUSTSEC-2026-0098
- RUSTSEC-2026-0099
- RUSTSEC-2026-0104

Crates.io currently reports `0.10.0-pre.4` as the latest libsql crate version, so there is no direct version bump available at release time.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Upgrade libsql or replace the remote TLS connector path once a libsql release uses rustls-webpki >= 0.103.13 or another non-vulnerable TLS stack.
- Remove the four rustls-webpki advisory ignores from `.cargo/audit.toml`.
- `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=1.88.0 scripts/security-check.sh` passes without those temporary ignores.
- Add a short release note when the ignore is removed.

Related: #75
title: Track libsql TLS dependency upgrade for rustls-webpki advisories

## Summary

FerroGate already has the lower-level extension surfaces for agent-native operation: plugins, tools, MCP servers, workflow policy, and agent runtime dispatch. The missing product layer is a first-class skill package model that agents such as Pi Agent, Codex-style agents, and Claude Code-style agents can discover and use without bypassing gateway governance.

A skill should be a higher-level capability package, not a separate ungoverned execution path. It should expand into existing governed resources: plugin registrations, tools, MCP servers, prompt/workflow policy, and permission declarations.

## Proposed scope

- Add a typed `skills` or `skill_packages` control-plane resource with id, name, version, description, compatibility, enabled state, permissions, and declared capabilities.
- Allow a skill package to reference or embed:
  - plugin registrations,
  - tool definitions or tool-provider plugins,
  - MCP server/tool bindings,
  - prompt templates,
  - agent workflow policies,
  - runtime compatibility metadata for Pi Agent and other agent runtimes.
- Expose skill discovery through Admin API and an agent-facing discovery endpoint.
- Ensure skill activation/deactivation updates the underlying governed plugin/tool/MCP/workflow surfaces atomically through reload validation.
- Preserve gateway governance: auth, human approval gates, policy evaluation, audit, usage/metering, workflow budgets, and MCP/tool allowlists still apply to skill-provided capabilities.
- Provide OpenAPI and ferrogate-test coverage for create/list/detail/disable and agent discovery.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Operators can register a skill package with typed validation.
- [ ] Agent-facing discovery lists only skills/capabilities visible to the authenticated tenant/API key.
- [ ] Skill-provided tools and MCP capabilities are executed only through existing FerroGate tool/MCP governance.
- [ ] Disabling a skill removes or disables its exposed capabilities without leaving stale tool entries.
- [ ] Audit evidence links executions back to the skill package id/version when present.
- [ ] `ferrogate-test` covers skill registration, discovery, tool/MCP execution through the skill, disable behavior, and no secret leakage.

## Design note

Pi Agent integration should consume this skill layer as a capability catalog. Pi Agent should not connect directly to arbitrary tools or MCP servers outside FerroGate, because that would bypass gateway approval, policy, audit, and budget controls.

FerroGate already has MCP server configuration and local extension/tool execution paths, but third-party app integration needs a durable plugin model with clear lifecycle, registration, permissions, versioning, and operator visibility. Without this boundary, every integration risks becoming custom gateway code or fragile config-only wiring.

## Summary

Add an analytics delivery boundary for traces, request logs, usage metrics, billing/metering analytics, dashboard aggregates, and future observability evidence.

This issue is deliberately separate from the durable control-plane storage work in #66/#67. Control-plane state is optimized for point lookup and transactional CRUD. Analytics state is optimized for high-ingest writes, time-window scans, aggregation, and dashboard/reporting queries.

## Storage Decision Matrix

| Scenario | Better fit |
| --- | --- |
| API key / policy / config point lookup | SQLite / Turso / PostgreSQL |
| Control-plane CRUD | SQLite / Turso / PostgreSQL |
| Recent request list, small-scale local testing | SQLite can be acceptable |
| Massive request logs | ClickHouse |
| Traces / spans queries | ClickHouse |
| Usage metrics aggregation | ClickHouse |
| Billing / metering analytics | ClickHouse |
| Dashboard chart statistics | ClickHouse |

The important rule is simple: do not put high-write observability and warehouse-style analytics behind the same abstraction used for API key, policy, and config CRUD.

## Architecture

FerroGate should support two analytics delivery modes.

### 1. Pipeline provider mode

Vector is the default analytics pipeline provider:

- `FerroGate -> Vector -> ClickHouse`
- `FerroGate -> Vector -> other data warehouses / sinks`

Vector handles collection, buffering, transformation, retry, fan-out, sink diversity, and operational pipeline configuration. Vector is not the database; it is the delivery pipeline.

### 2. Direct warehouse mode

ClickHouse is the first direct warehouse provider:

- `FerroGate -> ClickHouse`
- future: `FerroGate -> other data warehouse providers`

Direct mode is useful when operators want fewer moving parts, a dedicated high-throughput adapter, or a simpler self-hosted topology.

## Scope

- Add typed `analytics.*` config separate from `storage.*` control-plane config.
- Define provider-neutral analytics event contracts for:
  - request log events
  - trace/span evidence
  - usage metrics and usage aggregates
  - billing/metering events
  - provider/model latency, error, and routing-decision evidence
  - dashboard/reporting aggregate inputs
- Add Vector as the default pipeline provider.
- Add ClickHouse as the first warehouse/query provider.
- Keep analytics delivery asynchronous and non-blocking for the gateway hot path unless the operator explicitly configures strict delivery.
- Add buffering, batching, backpressure, retry, and failure visibility policies.
- Add ClickHouse schema/bootstrap SQL under a provider-specific SQL directory.
- Add Admin API/runtime evidence showing analytics mode, provider health, last delivery error, and ingestion/query status without exposing secrets.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Config supports pipeline mode with `analytics.provider = "vector"`.
- Config supports direct warehouse mode with `analytics.provider = "clickhouse"`.
- Vector mode emits structured request/trace/usage events to a local Vector container and routes them into ClickHouse in an E2E test.
- Direct ClickHouse mode writes the same canonical analytics events without Vector.
- ClickHouse schema initialization is versioned and committed under `sql/` or a provider-specific SQL directory.
- `ferrogate-test` includes opt-in Docker-backed scenarios for:
  - Vector pipeline delivery into ClickHouse
  - direct ClickHouse delivery
- Admin/runtime status reports analytics mode and provider health.
- Memory/Turso/PostgreSQL control-plane storage behavior is not regressed.

## Out of Scope

- Replacing Turso/libSQL as the default commercial control-plane durable storage provider.
- Treating Vector as a database.
- Treating ClickHouse as the control-plane CRUD database for API keys, policies, config, prompt metadata, or MCP/tool approval state.
- Building a hosted analytics UI in this issue.

Related: #66 #67 #12
title: Add analytics delivery providers for Vector pipelines and ClickHouse warehouses

## Summary

Turn durable control-plane storage into a first-class system boundary instead of a SQLite-only implementation detail.

This issue defines the shared repository/provider contract used by the gateway control plane to persist low-frequency, transactional runtime state: API keys, tenants/projects, policies, gateway/control-plane config resources, prompt template metadata, MCP/tool approval state, and future agent/control-plane state.

High-write observability and analytics data is explicitly out of this storage boundary and belongs to #70.

## Motivation

FerroGate is moving from a config-driven gateway toward an operator control plane. In-memory state and file-only config are not enough for commercial deployments because admin changes, policy state, approval decisions, and operator-managed resources must survive restarts and be inspectable later.

The storage boundary must be optimized for point lookup and control-plane CRUD, not warehouse analytics.

## Storage Decision Matrix

| Scenario | Better fit |
| --- | --- |
| API key / policy / config point lookup | SQLite / Turso / PostgreSQL |
| Control-plane CRUD | SQLite / Turso / PostgreSQL |
| Recent request list, small-scale local testing | SQLite can be acceptable |
| Massive request logs | ClickHouse via #70 |
| Traces / spans queries | ClickHouse via #70 |
| Usage metrics aggregation | ClickHouse via #70 |
| Billing / metering analytics | ClickHouse via #70 |
| Dashboard chart statistics | ClickHouse via #70 |

## Scope

- Add typed storage configuration with `memory` as the local/dev default and durable providers selected explicitly.
- Define provider-neutral repository traits and transaction/migration boundaries in `ferrogate-storage` for control-plane resources.
- Wire admin/control-plane services through repository interfaces instead of process-local maps where persistent state is required.
- Preserve current in-memory behavior for tests and lightweight local development.
- Provide startup validation and admin evidence showing which storage backend is active.
- Document what state is durable control-plane state and what remains ephemeral or analytics-oriented.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Gateway startup reports the active storage backend through config validation and an admin/runtime evidence endpoint.
- At least one persisted control-plane state path proves the repository contract end-to-end across restart.
- In-memory mode remains available and remains the default for local tests unless durable storage is configured.
- Existing admin, policy, API key, prompt/control-plane metadata, and MCP/tool governance code uses the storage boundary where persistence is required.
- `ferrogate-test` has a restart scenario proving durable control-plane state survives process restart.
- Runtime traces, request logs, usage metrics, billing/metering analytics, and dashboard aggregates are not added to this storage abstraction except for tiny local/test-only compatibility paths.

## Out of Scope

- Implementing every database provider in this issue.
- Hosted control plane UI.
- Distributed consensus or multi-writer HA semantics.
- High-ingest observability storage, trace/span analytics, usage metric aggregation, and billing/metering warehouse queries. Those belong to #70.

SQLite remains useful for single-node local deployments, but Turso/libSQL gives operators a managed serverless database path with familiar SQLite semantics and cloud durability.

## Motivation

The first production storage slice needs a low-friction hosted database story for point lookup and control-plane CRUD. Turso/libSQL is a strong default for FerroGate because it keeps the embedded SQLite development path close to the cloud runtime model while avoiding operators having to run PostgreSQL/MySQL before they can persist gateway control-plane state.

Turso/libSQL is not the primary analytics warehouse for high-write traces, usage metrics, or dashboard aggregates. Those belong to #70.

## Storage Decision Matrix

| Scenario | Better fit |
| --- | --- |
| API key / policy / config point lookup | SQLite / Turso / PostgreSQL |
| Control-plane CRUD | SQLite / Turso / PostgreSQL |
| Recent request list, small-scale local testing | SQLite can be acceptable |
| Massive request logs | ClickHouse via #70 |
| Traces / spans queries | ClickHouse via #70 |
| Usage metrics aggregation | ClickHouse via #70 |
| Billing / metering analytics | ClickHouse via #70 |
| Dashboard chart statistics | ClickHouse via #70 |

## Scope

- Add `turso`/`libsql` storage configuration for database URL, auth token, namespace/tenant metadata, migration mode, and connection/runtime limits.
- Implement schema bootstrap/migrations for the durable control-plane state covered by the storage contract.
- Persist admin-created API keys, policies, gateway/control-plane config resources, prompt template metadata, and MCP/tool approval state where those repository contracts exist.
- Add retry/timeout/error mapping appropriate for gateway startup and admin/control-plane paths.
- Add redaction rules so Turso URLs/tokens never leak into logs, admin API responses, exports, or runtime evidence.
- Document local libSQL/Turso Cloud setup and backup/export guidance.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A configured Turso/libSQL database preserves admin-created control-plane state across gateway restart.
- `ferrogate-test` includes an opt-in Turso/libSQL scenario that creates control-plane state, restarts the gateway, and verifies the state still exists.
- Startup fails closed with a clear error when Turso credentials are invalid and durable storage is required.
- Secret values are redacted in logs, admin API responses, exports, and runtime evidence.
- In-memory and local SQLite modes remain unaffected.
- Request logs, traces, usage metrics, billing/metering analytics, and dashboard aggregates are not implemented here as primary Turso/libSQL persistence paths; they are tracked by #70.

## Out of Scope

- PostgreSQL/MySQL implementation.
- Cross-region active-active write conflict resolution.
- Hosted SaaS control plane features.
- High-ingest analytics storage for traces, request logs, usage metrics, billing/metering analytics, or dashboard aggregates.

Related: #12 #67 #70
title: Add Turso/libSQL durable storage provider as the default cloud backend

## Summary

Split from #51 and the review comment by @rpelevin: human-in-the-loop approvals must be bound to the exact tool action that will later dispatch, not merely to a tool id, server id, or risk class.

Without an immutable action fingerprint, a pending approval can become stale or unsafe if arguments, caller identity, policy version, or target server binding changes before the approve call arrives. That is a production security boundary, not UI polish.

## Problem

#51 covers approval gates generally. This issue tracks the narrower invariant that an approval request authorizes one specific canonical tool action only.

An approval record should expose two views:

- Operator-visible summary: tenant, API key, tool, server, risk reason, expiry, status, and redacted argument summary.
- Execution-binding fields: request id, canonical argument digest or immutable argument snapshot, policy id/version, caller identity, target server identity, approval status, reviewer authority, and terminal outcome.

The gateway must reject stale approvals when any execution-binding field no longer matches the pending action.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Approval records include an immutable action fingerprint derived from canonical tool name, server identity, canonicalized arguments, caller/API key identity, tenant context, policy id/version, and request id or equivalent nonce.
- The approve path verifies the fingerprint before dispatch and fails closed if arguments, caller, policy, tool, or server binding changed.
- Expired approvals are terminal and cannot be resumed by a delayed approve call; a new attempt must create a new approval id/fingerprint.
- Denied approvals are terminal; retrying with the same approval id does not execute the tool.
- Admin approve/deny calls record reviewer identity and authority without exposing raw sensitive arguments unless body logging policy permits it.
- Audit events can prove approval_requested, approval_granted, approval_denied, approval_expired, and terminal tool outcome for the same fingerprint.
- Tests cover changed arguments, approve after expiry, unauthorized approver, deny then retry with the same approval id, server/tool binding mismatch, and approval decision without matching terminal tool outcome.

## Out of Scope

- Building a web approval UI.
- Durable approval storage beyond repository contracts needed for #12.
- General workflow graph interrupts tracked by #50.

Related: #51, #12, #50

Source: https://github.com/lianluo-esign/ferrogate/issues/51#issuecomment-4702339804
title: Bind tool approvals to immutable action fingerprints

## Summary

FerroGate needs provider coverage that spans mainstream commercial models and mainstream open-source models. The surface should stay explicit about what is first-class, what is OpenAI-compatible, and what still needs validation.

The goal is to make the matrix visible in one place so the provider surface stays honest as the product grows.

**Hard requirement:** 从主流商业模型到主流开源模型都需要支持。The gateway must support the full practical range operators expect, either as first-class adapters or as documented OpenAI-compatible upstreams with known constraints.

## Current shipped provider surface

### First-class provider kinds

- openai / openai-compatible
- azure / azure-openai
- anthropic
- gemini
- grok / xai
- openrouter

### Shared compatibility path

These can use the OpenAI-compatible adapter path when they present a compatible `/v1/chat/completions` or `/v1/responses` surface:

- direct OpenAI-compatible upstreams
- third-party OpenAI-compatible gateway/proxy layers, subject to validation
- mainstream open-source model gateways / servers when they expose compatible request and response shapes

Examples to validate explicitly:

- newapi
- sub2api
- CLIProxyAPI
- DeepSeek
- vLLM-backed model endpoints
- llama.cpp-backed model endpoints
- TGI / TGI-compatible model endpoints
- Ollama-compatible endpoints

### Needs explicit decision

- Any upstream that requires distinct auth, routing, model naming, or tool-call semantics should either get a first-class adapter or be documented with known constraints.

## Proposed scope

- Add direct support where a commercial or open-source model provider needs distinct endpoint/auth/model handling beyond the existing OpenAI-compatible adapter.
- Audit whether newapi, sub2api, CLIProxyAPI, DeepSeek, and mainstream open-source gateways/servers can be supported as pure OpenAI-compatible endpoints or need explicit compatibility adapters.
- Document which provider/proxy surfaces are supported as first-class kinds and which are supported only through the OpenAI-compatible path.
- Add catalog / model routing coverage so operator config and admin surfaces can show the correct upstream capability metadata.
- Add focused regression tests for provider kind resolution, request preparation, error normalization, and tool-call passthrough where the upstream supports it.

## Compatibility matrix

| Surface | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| openai / openai-compatible | supported | shared adapter path |
| azure / azure-openai | supported | dedicated adapter |
| anthropic | supported | dedicated adapter |
| gemini | supported | dedicated adapter |
| grok / xai | supported | dedicated adapter |
| openrouter | supported | dedicated adapter |
| direct OpenAI-compatible gateways | partial | supported if they preserve OpenAI-compatible request/response shapes |
| newapi | partial / needs validation | may fit the shared adapter path, but needs explicit operator verification |
| sub2api | partial / needs validation | may fit the shared adapter path, but needs explicit operator verification |
| CLIProxyAPI | partial / needs validation | may fit the shared adapter path, but needs explicit operator verification |
| DeepSeek | open | needs a decision on first-class adapter vs compatible upstream documentation |
| vLLM / llama.cpp / TGI / Ollama-compatible open-source endpoints | partial / needs validation | supported when they behave like OpenAI-compatible upstreams; otherwise needs a first-class adapter or documented constraints |

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The provider registry clearly distinguishes first-class provider kinds from generic OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
- [ ] Mainstream commercial providers are supported through either first-class adapters or explicit OpenAI-compatible documentation with known constraints.
- [ ] Mainstream open-source model endpoints are supported through either first-class adapters or explicit OpenAI-compatible documentation with known constraints.
- [ ] Third-party OpenAI-compatible gateway/proxy surfaces are classified as supported, partially supported, or unsupported with a stable operator-facing explanation.
- [ ] Provider/model selection and fallback continue to work across the supported surface.
- [ ] Tests cover the supported provider matrix and reject unsupported kinds with stable errors.

## Out of scope

- Per-vendor marketing compatibility claims.
- Automatic discovery of every upstream proxy implementation on the internet.
- Changing the default gateway hot path semantics for existing supported providers.

## Related work

- Related: #11, #44, #54
- This issue tracks the missing provider coverage and compatibility matrix gaps that are not already explicit in the shipped registry.
title: Add provider coverage for DeepSeek and OpenAI-compatible gateway proxies

## Summary

FerroGate should ship a default agent harness, but the harness must not run inside the gateway hot path. The gateway remains the scheduling and governance front door; a dedicated runtime owns the reason→act→observe loop, and untrusted execution happens inside a WASM sandbox.

This issue defines the execution-side slice of the agent platform:
- a built-in default agent harness for common use cases
- a provider contract for third-party agent implementations
- a WASM sandbox boundary for isolated execution
- run/session/checkpoint evidence for long-lived agent work

## Proposed scope

- Define a dedicated agent runtime boundary instead of embedding the loop in the gateway request path.
- Ship a default FerroGate agent harness with a simple bounded loop and first-party tool integration.
- Add a provider interface so third-party agent providers can plug in without gaining gateway-process privileges.
- Add a Wasmtime/WASI-backed sandbox executor for agent code and plugin-like execution.
- Expose a minimal host ABI for logging, bounded state, and gateway-mediated tool dispatch.
- Support bounded agent loops with max turns, timeout, cancel, and budget enforcement.
- Keep tool execution under existing gateway governance paths.
- Stream run and tool events to logs/admin surfaces with stable run IDs.

## Design direction

- Default agent implementation: use a small FerroGate-owned harness, not a generic third-party framework as the core.
- Third-party providers: integrate through a provider contract, not by loading arbitrary in-process code.
- Isolation: WASM sandbox is the hard boundary for untrusted execution.
- Evidence: run/session/checkpoint records belong on the control-plane side so long-running work remains observable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A request can opt into an agent run without changing default chat/completions behavior.
- [ ] The default agent harness executes outside the gateway hot path.
- [ ] Agent code executes inside a deny-by-default WASM sandbox with bounded capabilities.
- [ ] The runtime can stop at max turns, timeout, or cancellation.
- [ ] Tool calls still pass through existing gateway auth/policy/billing/audit paths.
- [ ] Run and tool events are observable with stable IDs.
- [ ] Third-party agent providers can be integrated without giving them direct gateway-process execution privileges.
- [ ] Default non-agent requests remain unchanged.

## Out of scope

- Arbitrary plugin ecosystems.
- Replacing built-in/MCP tool governance.
- Full workflow graph execution.
- Durable checkpoint storage beyond the initial run timeline.

## Related work

- Related: #49, #50, #51, #17
- This issue is the execution-runtime slice that those control-plane and governance issues can build on.
title: Add opt-in WASM sandboxed agent runtime

## Summary

Split the runtime state, storage repository, and configuration normalization boundaries before implementing more durable backend work.

## First-principles problem

The gateway needs durable control-plane evolution, but the shortest correct path is not to bolt a database onto the current `AppState`. The root problem is that runtime state currently mixes config snapshots, provider registries, routing indexes, in-memory repositories, cluster counters, observability sinks, MCP state, cache, drain state, and ACME state in one large structure.

Issue #12 covers durable storage implementation. This issue is the prerequisite boundary repair that keeps #12 from becoming a database-shaped patch over a mixed responsibility object.

## Current risk

- `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/state.rs` directly owns in-memory repositories even though `ferrogate-storage` exposes repository traits.
- `ferrogate-config` and `ferrogate-cli/src/config` both define configuration-shaped models, making schema drift likely.
- Future admin CRUD, durable storage, and cluster control-plane work will keep adding fields and methods to one central file unless the ownership boundaries are clarified.

## Proposed slice

- Introduce a small runtime repository bundle interface used by `AppState`; keep the current in-memory implementation as the default.
- Move storage retention/application logic behind that bundle instead of directly manipulating repository concrete types in `AppState`.
- Clarify the config ownership boundary: either make `ferrogate-config` the normalized config source or explicitly mark its `GatewayConfig` as a parser/intermediate model and map it into the runtime config in one place.
- Split `AppState` responsibilities by real runtime constraint, not by generic layers: runtime catalog, control-plane repositories, observability sinks, cluster runtime, and AI decision services.

## Acceptance criteria

- `AppState` no longer directly hardcodes concrete in-memory repository types for request logs, audit events, and usage aggregates.
- In-memory storage remains the default behavior.
- The config parser/runtime config boundary is documented in code and has a single mapping path.
- The change is compatible with #12 and does not implement SQLite prematurely.
- Existing admin list/read behavior for request logs, audit events, metering/billing events, and usage aggregates is preserved.

## Verification

- Add or update focused repository/state tests covering in-memory default behavior and retention.
- Run allowed local checks: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo metadata --locked --format-version=1`, `git diff --check`.
- Let GitHub Actions run compile/test authority per repo contract.

Related: #12
title: Split runtime state storage and config boundaries before durable backends

## Summary

Refactor the AI gateway request path into explicit decision stages so routing, policy, provider attempts, cache behavior, tool injection, usage settlement, and observable evidence are represented as typed pipeline data instead of being buried in one long handler.

## First-principles problem

An AI gateway must explain why a request was accepted, which provider/model was attempted, which policy or budget decision applied, what failed, what fallback happened, and how usage was settled. That is the product requirement. The implementation shape should follow that requirement, not a growing handler template.

Today `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/chat.rs` handles auth, gateway profile resolution, drain checks, request parsing, authorization, policy, routing, cache, tool injection, provider dispatch, fallback, logging, and billing settlement in one large path. That makes correctness hard to audit and makes future provider/policy changes likely to add more local patches.

## Proposed slice

- Define a typed AI request pipeline with explicit stage outputs, for example:
  - ingress/body parse
  - authenticated tenant/API key context
  - gateway profile/config decision
  - model and provider route plan
  - policy and budget decision
  - provider attempt/fallback result
  - usage and request-log settlement
- Keep endpoint-specific differences (`/v1/chat/completions` vs `/v1/responses`) visible but avoid duplicating the shared decision path.
- Preserve existing external behavior while moving evidence-producing decisions into named structs/functions.
- Make failure responses and request-log records originate from the same decision/error representation where practical.

## Acceptance criteria

- The main AI handler no longer owns all decision stages inline.
- Each provider attempt records enough typed data to explain provider, provider model, status/error, fallback reason, and settlement path.
- Existing auth, policy, cache, fallback, streaming, and non-streaming behavior is preserved.
- Regression coverage exists for at least one success path, one policy/auth failure path, one provider failure/fallback path, and one streaming path.
- Operator-visible logs/admin evidence remain stable or improve.

## Verification

- Add or update focused regression tests for the changed AI request path.
- Run allowed local checks: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo metadata --locked --format-version=1`, `git diff --check`.
- Let GitHub Actions run compile/test authority per repo contract.
title: Extract an explicit AI request decision pipeline

body:
## Summary

Replace the current provider dispatch path's hand-written HTTP/TLS implementation with an explicit provider transport boundary backed by a mature HTTP client or Pingora-supported client surface.

## First-principles problem

FerroGate is an AI gateway. The core requirement is not merely to send a POST to an upstream provider; it is to preserve provider protocol correctness, streaming behavior, timeout/cancellation semantics, TLS correctness, and debuggable upstream failure evidence.

The current implementation in `crates/ferrogate-cli/src/gateway/dispatch.rs` manually parses provider URIs, opens TCP/TLS sockets, writes HTTP/1.1 request bytes, and reads response headers/bodies. That makes FerroGate own protocol behavior that should not be bespoke gateway code.

## Current risk

- Streaming providers commonly rely on chunked/SSE behavior that hand-rolled response reading can mishandle.
- HTTP/2, trailers, proxy behavior, connection reuse, and subtle header semantics are not represented.
- Future fixes are likely to become protocol patches instead of addressing the root cause.
- The dispatch code is hard to extend with transport-level observability and retry classification.

## Proposed slice

- Introduce a `ProviderTransport` boundary for non-streaming and streaming provider requests.
- Move the current implementation behind that boundary only as a temporary compatibility implementation if needed.
- Prefer a mature HTTP client or Pingora-supported client path for actual dispatch.
- Preserve adapter-local provider request construction; do not leak provider-specific quirks into gateway core.
- Add focused regression coverage for HTTP error bodies, streaming first-byte/first-chunk forwarding, response size limits, timeout behavior, and TLS endpoint handling.

## Acceptance criteria

- Provider dispatch code no longer hand-writes raw HTTP request lines as the primary transport path.
- Non-streaming `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/responses` provider forwarding still returns provider status, content type, body, and stable gateway errors.
- Streaming dispatch forwards provider streaming data without buffering until completion.
- Timeout and oversized-response behavior remain explicit and tested.
- The selected transport dependency or Pingora client path is justified in the implementation notes/commit message.

## Verification

- Add or update focused transport tests.
- Run allowed local checks: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo metadata --locked --format-version=1`, `git diff --check`.
- Let GitHub Actions run compile/test authority per repo contract.
title: Replace hand-rolled provider HTTP transport with a real transport boundary
